Sports.title: McIlroy: LIV Golf was half a good idea
Sports.content:
Rory McIlroy believes LIV Golf was "half a good idea, executed poorly" and the breakaway is no longer a threat to the traditional game as it tries to relaunch after filing for bankruptcy.

Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) ploughed in £3.7bn over four years, luring the likes of Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau away from the PGA Tour, before withdrawing its support this year.

That led to Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings in the United States with a view to relaunching as LIV 2.0, having received a potential $300m (£227m) backing from BC Partners Capital providing a specified number of players re-sign for the new venture.

Rahm has already announced he will not be continuing and news this week that any player signing up for LIV will be barred from DP World Tour membership and Ryder Cup eligibility has delivered a crippling blow.

"LIV had probably like, half of a good idea that was executed pretty poorly," McIlroy told the Bloomberg New Economy forum in New Delhi, where he is playing this week in the DP World India Championship.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Inci Mehmet explains why Jon Rahm is to quit LIV Golf after deeming the terms offered for the proposed relaunch of the breakaway series 'unacceptable'

"They had a lot of capital but I think a lot of that capital was wasted in some ways and I think they could have used that money a lot more strategically and could have partnered with some of the governing bodies of the game and certainly could have done better things with it instead of just enriching tour pros who were already making a lot of money.

"BC Partners have come in and seen an opportunity (but) it looks like every day that goes by there's another player that was on LIV who is not going to join LIV 2.0 so I think it is going to be very difficult to get out of this Chapter 11 bankruptcy and go forward.

"But if they do it is certainly not going to be a threat to the traditional order of the game as it once was."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Geraint Hughes explains what is next for LIV Golf and what will happen to their players after they filed for bankruptcy

A more pertinent issue now seems to be what happens to those players quitting LIV.

The PGA Tour invokes a one-year suspension, denying them access until August next year, and while the DP World Tour has stiffened its rules its membership remains divided.

"I'm sure some members who stayed loyal would feel hard done by if these guys can just walk straight back in but, on the other side, having these players back on the tour is good for business and it can drive revenues up and everyone can benefit from that," added McIlroy.

"I would vote for them to come back. A rising tide lifts all boats and I think having some of these players back is beneficial for the business of the tours."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player The Sky Sports Golf Podcast team predict their USA and Europe Ryder Cup teams for 2027

It is not a view shared by six-time DP World Tour winner Joost Luiten.

"Four years ago they didn't give a s*** about the DP World Tour," he told Today's Golfer.

"They made a decision to go after the money and now all of a sudden, the money is gone and they want to come back and act like nothing happened. I don't think that's right.

"If they think they are that good then show it at Q-School (qualifying school) and beat the guys. That's how every other guy that wants to play on this tour has to go."

Sports.title: 'State of the Game' report finds most English clubs living on financial brink
Sports.content:
The Independent Football Regulator (IFR) has produced a 'State of the Game' report, which has taken a forensic look at English football over the past 18 months, concluding that the game's finances are dangerously exposed, with the majority of clubs living on the edge of financial disaster.

The IFR added that interest and investment from around the world continues to grow within English football, but the underlying foundations of the pyramid are under intense strain and require urgent reform.

Despite over £9bn generated in revenue, 94 per cent of clubs are loss-making, with long-term security being put at risk through excessive short-term spending to keep up with rivals. This, the IFR says, has led to a "dangerous cocktail of rising debt and an over-reliance on owner funding, leaving clubs and their fans at risk".

The report acknowledges that the success of the Premier League has driven economic success, making English football the "richest, best and most deeply competitive in the world".

However, it points to "financial cliff-edges between and within leagues", with the average Premier League club making more than eight times the revenues of an average Championship club, and the system of parachute payments paid by the Premier League to Championship clubs relegated contributing to significant overspend by clubs in the Championship.

Indeed, the report highlights player wage inflation leading clubs to take big risks chasing a place in the Premier League.

The State of the Game report found that lower down the pyramid the pressure from operating costs was also on the rise, with 17 EFL and National League clubs incurring costs exceeding revenues. These clubs would be loss-making even if they did not pay their players.

It uncovered too that more than 60 per cent of EFL and National League clubs are technically insolvent, with their liabilities exceeding the book value of their assets.

And it found that more than a quarter of clubs would be unable to survive for more than one month if owner funding was withdrawn, with the majority lacking a basic contingency plan to mitigate their risk.

'We're trying to take an interventionist approach'

Chair of the IFR David Kogan told Sky: "I think what we see in English football is two completely different positions.

"The first is £9bn comes in every year, yet we have 94 per cent of the clubs of the 160 we regulate are trading unprofitably.

"We have 32 clubs that have got less than 30 days' cash cover in their accounts. So if the owner walks away or drops dead, they're insolvent and go bust.

"So what we see in football is rising debt. It's a problem of cash cover and liquidity within clubs, and it's a lack of management, and what financial management? And now we're in a position to help those clubs achieve a more stable future."

Kogan added: "What we're implying is today there's enough money going through into the Premier League and the EFL and into their individual clubs for the sun to shine. This is exactly the moment when we need to address structural issues because once that sun stops shining, those clubs will be in real trouble.

"So what we are trying to do is get ahead of the problem and take an interventionist approach with individual clubs that need it to help them get to the point of being stable and secure because too many clubs get close to the edge and depend on one thing and one thing only, which is a new owner coming down the track.

"That supply of owners may dry up, and supply of media money may dry out so we have to now get ahead of the game and give them levels of security and stability that allow them to go into the future."

The IFR's six-point plan...

The IFR report offered solutions, issuing a six-point plan to address some of the issues it has identified.

The plan includes measures for clubs to improve how they manage financial risk, including holding more cash and putting robust contingency plans in place in case owner funding is withdrawn; it also outlines how revenue distribution should be reformed to ease cliff-edges throughout the pyramid, urges action on rising losses and calls on clubs to show how they take fans' views into account, and the steps they are taking to improve diversity and governance in the boardroom.

It also highlighted yet again that the current distribution arrangements in English football create risk and should be reformed.

For several years the Premier League and EFL have been discussing and negotiating a new financial distribution model, but no agreement has yet been finalised. The IFR has consistently said, and has said once again in this report, that it is preferable that the Premier League and EFL come to an agreement themselves, but again mentioned that the IFR could apply a "back-stop" power to intervene if the Premier League and EFL do not come to an agreement.

The IFR said its goals on reform of the current distribution model were to:

Maintain the Premier League as the leading football league in the world and the Championship as the leading second-tier competition.

Maintain vital funding for the wider game.

Mitigate the financial impact of relegation from the Premier League.

Reduce the distortive impact that parachute payments have on financial incentives within the Championship.

Protect clubs by giving clubs the opportunity to rebuild their balance sheets and reduce risk.

Consider short-term support to clubs that face severe financial distress.

Kogan said: "There are three moves that are taking place that we think will help on this.

"First is that the Premier League and the EFL are currently discussing a new distribution deal with the game, which will radically change the amount of money going from the Premier League down to the lower leagues. And that will have associated with it controls on how that money is spent, which actually will go to the stability of those lower leagues, but we're going to see more money flowing down, assuming the deal is done, and we're going to see cost controls involved in that.

"The second is that from November onwards we're going to be licensing clubs, and by licensing those clubs we're going to intervene directly in individual clubs where we think they've got exposures that we can help them resolve and that includes things like having a business plan that involves having cash cover more than 30 days; it involves having genuine provision for the debts that they've raised.

"And the third thing we're doing is working with leagues to actually look at cost controls over a longer-term basis to actually build in financial stability as we go forward."

Sports.title: Zverev celebrates becoming year-end No 1 with Bublik win in Shanghai
Sports.content:
Alexander Zverev celebrated becoming the year-end No 1 with a 7-6 (8-6) 4-6 7-6 (7-1) victory over Alexander Bublik to reach the quarter-finals at the Shanghai Masters.

Zverev, who won the French Open and US Open this year, never looked 100 per cent comfortable, and admitted his "ankle was acting up" following his win.

The top seed will take on ninth seed Alex de Minaur next after the Australian produced one of his best performances of the year to beat Karen Khachanov in straight sets 6-3 6-4 to advance.

With current world No 1 Jannik Sinner out for the rest of 2026 due to a knee injury and Carlos Alcaraz unable to overtake Zverev this year, the German was competing for the first time since he clinched the year-end No 1 honours for the first time on Monday.

"It is very, very special. To finish the world No 1 is a different kind of feeling," said Zverev. "It's a different kind of responsibility on your shoulders. I'm looking forward to that because I'm close to being 30 years old. It's a special feeling to achieve that."

Former British No 1 Tim Henman was full of praise for Zverev at the Laver Cup in London last month.

"You've got to earn the ranking points, and the way he's played this year has been absolutely phenomenal," he told the ATP Tour.

"He was a service game away from being in all four Slam finals. To have been working so hard and then not being able to win a Slam, and winning two this year and reaching the Wimbledon final, it's phenomenal.

"Twelve months ago, he had a tough time. He wasn't playing well, and he didn't play well in the Laver Cup. The transformation 12 months on is phenomenal."

Henman added: "When you see the way he's been stepping up in the big matches, he hasn't always played his best, but he's found a way to win. Then you give yourself a chance to play better. The way he's played in the Slams speaks for itself."

Iga Swiatek has played at every edition of the WTA Finals since ‌2021, but with the Pole running out of time to claim a place at this year's season-ending tournament ‌she knows the importance of going deep at her few remaining events.

The six-time major ​champion has won only one tournament this year at the Canadian Open in August and failed to advance beyond ​the quarter-final stage at all four Grand Slams.

The 25-year-old, ‌who won the WTA Finals in 2023, is 10th in the qualifying table for the November ​8-15 tournament at Indian Wells with only four of the eight spots still up for grabs.

"Obviously I'm aware of the situation and it would be great to get into the Finals, ‌for sure it's our goal," Swiatek said.

"It's the first time I've faced a situation like that, to ‌get into the finals.

"It's a challenge, but I feel like it's a positive one and I'm really motivated. There are still a few tournaments ahead."

Sports.title: 'What do you want us to do?' - Maresca defends Anfield celebrations
Sports.content:
Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca has defended the post-match celebrations of his squad following their 3-0 win at Liverpool on Sunday.

The trip to Merseyside was City's first game after an independent commission found them guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of Premier League financial rules.

The club have since appealed the verdict and continue to deny any wrongdoing.

City players were pictured celebrating with the travelling away fans following full-time at Anfield - after goals from Erling Haaland, Jeremy Doku and Rayan Cherki secured the victory - which sparked criticism across social media.

When asked about the celebrations and the comments that followed ahead of facing Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League on Wednesday, Maresca said: "Criticised for what? We won 0-3 at Anfield. What do you want us to do?

"I am here today; the players are here today to win tomorrow. We work every day to win games.

"It is the only thing that we can think and focus on. The rest is just things from outside which we need to deal [with]. We were so, so happy from inside the pitch and the dressing room."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Man City take to the pitch for the first time since being found guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of Premier League financial rules by an independent commission. City have lodged their appeal against the verdict and deny wrongdoing

'I don't stress about things I can't control,' says Maresca

The City boss then reiterated that he remains calm regarding the situation with the process ongoing.

City submitted their appeal on Thursday October 1 and the Premier League has new rules this season which state an appeal has to be heard within 12 weeks of it being lodged. The appeal can last a maximum of five days - held over a block of days, so Monday to Friday.

However, City may try to delay the appeal process by arguing that the new rules should not apply in this case as City were charged in 2023 - three years before the new rules were introduced.

But, as it stands, the five-day appeal, to be heard by a new three-person panel, has to be finished by mid-December.

"I said many times, I am completely calm and relaxed. I promise you that I stress a lot about game plan and how we train," Maresca added.

"I don't stress about things I don't control. The message with players will be the same.

"As I said, we know how serious the situation is. It is not something we can do something [about]. Where we can do something is inside the pitch.

"The noise around the team is a big noise but we need to try to deal with that and try and make our noise, to win games."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player FREE TO WATCH: Highlights from Liverpool's match against Manchester City in the Premier League

Dias: I stand by Maresca's words

City captain Ruben Dias, who played the full 90 minutes in the victory, echoed the statement from his manager, as he added: "I very much stand by the manager's words. It's a win at Anfield.

"In whatever circumstance, be it early in the season or late in the season, we will enjoy it just as much and celebrate however we feel in the moment. It's a show of how much it means to us.

"If there's more or less noise, for whatever reason, it's all the same. Same as before because people don't love us winning and we love to win.

"It's a normal scenario where whenever you win, there are people that are not happy with it because they have the same ambition to win.

"It all mixes together a little bit but mainly we know it's not easy to get three points at Anfield. That is definitely the main reason. We're here for the points and to win competitions; that's the main thing on our minds."

Dias also revealed the City players held a meeting after news of the guilty verdict broke on September 29.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ruben Dias has revealed how the Manchester City players responded after they found out the club were given a guilty verdict regarding serious financial breaches; City have appealed and deny all wrongdoing

"When it broke, we felt we should have a conversation as soon as we got back," he said, regarding their return from the international break.

"We did, for everyone to be on the same page and be clear about our peace of mind. We moved on from there.

"It happened in a moment when we were not together but quickly we reached out to each other, found calm and progressed forward."

'City players sent message with celebrations'

Sky Sports News' Ben Ransom at Maresca's press conference:

"We all saw those scenes at Anfield. The City fans wanted to show their support throughout the game to the club and the players, and the players reciprocated when they scored each of the three goals in front of them, and again at the end of the game when the result was confirmed.

"That was all set against the backdrop of the intense goading from the Liverpool fans who wanted to have their say about how they felt about the findings of that independent commission.

"For the players, I think it was as much about sending a message back to the fans at the end that they valued their support, but also a little bit of them wanting to send a message to the wider football world, to other clubs in the Premier League as well.

"They are defiant in the face of that verdict, certainly while the appeal is ongoing."

Sports.title: Barrios strikes after 53 seconds as Atlético pile misery on 10-man Manchester United
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick had seen it in his players, he said, but no one else can. Not so far this season, where they have suffered their worst start in 40 years, and not here in Madrid where Manchester United’s manager insisted that they would embrace the challenge. The reaction was coming, he said; he was sure of it. Instead, they were a goal down after just 53 seconds and another defeat did. That early opener from Pablo Barrios and a second from Ademola Lookman late on meant a 2-0 defeat.

So much for a reaction, a rebellion: instead, there was a kind of resignation, a sense that this is just their reality: a game that began badly, barely got better, and finished even worse. Even the late red card for Leny Yoro at 1-0 which can be offered up in mitigation may not be really; this isn’t what United are supposed to be.

“Sometimes when it’s not quite going for you, you see who’s really there,” United’s manager had said, a message that perhaps hinted at something deeper, but for the opening goal no one was really there. They weren’t there on the left, where Lee Kang-in’s pass sent Álex Baena into a wide-open space; they weren’t there to close him down as he cut into the area; and they weren’t there on the right either, where Barrios was running through and no one was running back. Baena laid it back across and Barrios shot first time; Ayden Heaven, scrambling, did get there but not decisively and the ball came off him and into the net.

Barrios ran off holding up six fingers, the number of the club captain, Koke, whose mother had passed away in the hours before kick-off. From the bench Koke’s shirt was raised. All around the Metropolitano, supporters roared. Atlético weren’t going to stop either, Baena’s effort soon hitting Lisandro Martínez, although United did find a foothold and may feel that they should have found a way back into this.

View image in fullscreen Pablo Barrios gives Atlético Madrid the lead inside the opening minute. Photograph: Susana Vera/Reuters

Bryan Mbeumo had two clear chances: the first, after lovely footwork on the right, went wide; the second, after a neat exchange with Youri Tielemans after Carlos Baleba had robbed Cristian Romero, was blocked by Jan Oblak by the post on the other side. From the corner, Baleba headed straight at the keeper.

That was short-lived though, Atlético soon reasserting themselves. If they didn’t always find a way through, the final pass often astray, they moved the ball with a pace and conviction United couldn’t match. Barrios and Baena couldn’t be controlled and the spaces that opened were vast. The pressure that United applied tended to arrive late or not at all. On the touchline, too, the contrast was stark. Both managers wore black but while Diego Simeone prowled, Carrick stood motionless in the corner, chin in his hand. Simeone was booked for waving an imaginary card. Maybe United’s manager could try that. Something, anyway.

By half-time, Atlético had enjoyed 66% of possession; they could also have had a bigger lead. Álex Grimaldo rattled a superb free-kick off the bar and just before the break Johnny Cardoso’s sweeping shot flew into the net only for the video assistant referee to reveal a Marcos Llorente handball in the buildup.

View image in fullscreen Leny Yoro trudges off after being shown a red card. Photograph: Adam Davy/PA

A neatly floated ball from Barrios led to a Julián Alvarez volley against the post early in the second half. Again, the space, time and the ease with which the move played out was just too big. At the other end, Bruno Fernandes then had a wonderful opportunity to level it. Tielemans did superbly to find him, the ball sitting up on the edge of the area and Oblak coming some way from his line to meet him – the kind of opportunity, in short, that is supposed to only end one way but that this time ended another. United’s captain lifted it past the keeper and a fraction wide of the post. Soon, Atlético were back again, Baena bending wide.

On 65 minutes, three came and three went, Marcus Rashford, Tielemans and Baleba making way for Mason Mount, Amad Diallo and Joshua Zirkzee. In truth, the change had already begun: nothing radical, but a shift. Atlético appeared to have settled, which perhaps suited United, the threat no longer so present. The ball was moved more swiftly now; it was also theirs for the first time. And the lead was still only one. Fernandes was increasingly involved and, after a short corner, swung a shot against the bar.

Which was when it finally, definitively fell apart. Suddenly, there was Jonathan David running through the middle on to a Morten Hjulmand ball. Yoro went running with him and the pair fell. Although Glenn Nyberg didn’t give a foul upon first view, allowing the move to play out with David scrambling the ball to Ademola Lookman to shoot, he was called to the screen to see the challenge again. When he returned, he had a red in his hand. The decision felt harsh; it was also the end, the same two men finishing this. A minute later, Atlético were running through them again. Grimaldo slotted a pass into David, well inside the area, and although his shot was saved by Senne Lammens there was Lookman to score. Heaven and Bruno were removed; this was done, nothing left to fight for, another night ending in defeat.

Sports.title: Timber’s touch of class and supersub Saka secure Arsenal win against Lille
Sports.content:
Twelve wins in a row and counting. On a night when Arsenal remembered Ken Friar – the club’s life president who was instrumental in their move from Highbury to the Emirates in 2006, it was fitting that Mikel ­Arteta’s side should rack up yet another Champions League milestone at their home that has become a fortress.

Such has Arsenal’s dominance been here in recent seasons that when Bukayo Saka slotted home their third against a dogged Lille side, it was the 36th goal they have scored at the Emirates in the league or group stage since returning to Europe’s top table under Arteta three years ago.

Arsenal have also now racked up 14 successive league-stage victories in this competition, even if Arteta’s side were made to work for this one and had to wait until the 64th minute to find the breakthrough. That came from the unlikely source of Jurriën Timber after Arsenal’s second-string attack – and Viktor Gyökeres in particular – had looked laboured at times.

But while Arteta may be concerned that it needed the introduction of Saka from the bench along with Martin Ødegaard and Kai Havertz to put this game to bed as Eberechi Eze added a second, they never looked in any danger of losing their proud record as Olivier Giroud received a standing ovation on his return to north London.

Arsenal paid tribute to Friar, who worked his way up from the box office to club secretary before becoming managing director in the 1980s, when his death at the age of 92 was confirmed earlier in the day and the players wore black armbands as a mark of respect. He would have been especially proud of their formidable record here under Arteta in this competition that stretches back to the 2023-24 season when they returned after an absence of six years. It’s little wonder that Arteta was so reluctant for redevelopment plans to go ahead given the disruption any temporary move away to Wembley or elsewhere would have caused.

Despite the absence of Piero Hincapié and Martín Zubimendi after they were both injured during the warm-down after the victory over Leeds on Saturday, the Arsenal manager was still able to make five changes.

Lille’s manager, Davide Ancelotti, who worked under his father, Carlo, at Everton and Real Madrid among others before being appointed during the summer in only his second senior role, resisted the temptation to start with 40-year-old Giroud against his former club. Aside from former Tottenham midfielder Nabil Bentaleb anchoring the midfield, the French side who have made a promising start to the new campaign largely went with youth over experience.

They managed to keep the hosts quiet for the opening 20 minutes without really threatening David Raya.

View image in fullscreen Bukayo Saka slots home Arsenal’s third goal from close range. Photograph: Matthew Childs/Action Images/Reuters

Restored to his favoured right flank after excelling on the left against Leeds, Noni Madueke was once again Arsenal’s most dangerous outlet and the England forward combined with Timber to set up Bruno Guimarães and then Mikel Merino for decent chances that were spurned.

Ayase Ueda had the ball in Raya’s net after Bentaleb’s shot deflected off Timber and hit Hakon Haraldsson on the way through, with the video assistant referee confirming the Japan striker was marginally offside. But Arsenal lacked creativity with captain Ødegaard only watching from the bench and Gyökeres showing plenty of hustle and bustle yet making little real impact.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Normally such a reliable finisher, Merino snatched at a chance from 10 yards out that he normally would have buried after Lille failed to clear a cross.

It summed Arsenal’s first half up when Gyökeres could not get out of the way after Eze forced Berke Özer into his first proper save and was promptly flagged offside. Özer then had to scramble the ball away from the feet of the Sweden striker after spilling a shot from Guimarães on the stroke of half-time.

Arsenal resumed their domination of the ball after the break and continued to find Lille’s defence a tough nut to crack. The German referee waved away appeals when Guimarães went down in the area under pressure from Alexsandro but the Arsenal midfielder seemed to be looking for the contact.

A wayward effort that almost made it into the upper tier from Madueke was the signal for Arteta to summon Ødegaard Saka and Kai Havertz to get ready from the substitutes’ bench. Before they had time to be introduced, Arsenal finally found the breakthrough when Madueke set up Timber to apply a deft finish with his right foot after a brilliant first touch. Saka made an immediate impact by setting up Eze to dispatch the second with his left foot less than three minutes later before adding a third after combining with Havertz and Ødegaard. Lille must have wondered what had hit them.

As well as the chance to pay their respects to Giroud, the Arsenal fans were treated to a late cameo from the dazzling teenager Max Dowman to round off another very satisfying evening that has become the norm in these parts.

Sports.title: James and Russo lead rout of Greece as ruthless England set up Ukraine playoff
Sports.content:
A mercurial Lauren James scored two and provided an assist in a thrilling four-goal first 45 minutes against Greece, as England put themselves two games away from securing their place at the World Cup.

James’s double was matched by Alessia Russo, who scored either side of the break, and her Arsenal teammate Georgia Stanway was also on the scoresheet, with the Lionesses setting up a playoff final against Ukraine in November and December. It was a clinical and slick statement from England, albeit against a team they should bypass with ease.

Any Greek hopes of arriving in Leicester and launching a Trojan horse-style smash and grab, after a hugely impressive performance in their 3-1 defeat by an unconvincing Lionesses team in Crete, were quickly dashed.

Sarina Wiegman had said on the eve of the game that she wanted to see improvement in the final third. “It’s staying onside, having the final pass, the right pass at the right moment, the run at the right time and deciding what option you choose,” she said.

In the King Power Stadium, which had a club vibe to it before kick-off as dance remix after dance remix blared out, the Lionesses responded to their manager’s call, Russo producing the first goal from the first shot and first attack in the third minute.

View image in fullscreen Alessia Russo gets England up and running with a third-minute goal. Photograph: Andrew Boyers/Action Images/Reuters

James was the architect, the Chelsea player driving forward and picking out the No 9 who shrugged herself clear of Eleni Markou’s challenge before firing a low shot into the net.

It was Russo’s fourth goal in four games for club and country, with the Arsenal forward having gone five Women’s Super League matches without a goal prior to this run, and it was a sign of things to come from a team keen to shake off criticism of their lack of ruthlessness.

James was in majestic form, her injury worries behind her this season, and England fans were treated to a glimpse of what they missed at the Euros in Switzerland in 2025 where a less than half-fit James struggled and looked frustrated as her body failed to meet her demands on it.

She delivered England’s second and fourth in Leicester, her two first-half goals sandwiching Georgia Stanway’s header into the far corner from Lauren Hemp’s chipped cross. For her first, the 25-year-old cushioned Maya Le Tissier’s pass before sending a rising drive goalwards with her left foot and her second was far simpler, the unmarked forward turning in Hemp’s ball from close range.

View image in fullscreen Georgia Stanway heads in England’s third goal as they swiftly put the result beyond doubt. Photograph: Andrew Boyers/Action Images/Reuters

It was an emphatic first 45 minutes from England, who converted four of their six shots on target and allowed Greece only 16% possession. The only disappointment was the debutant Lexi Potter’s goal being ruled out for a fairly innocuous challenge by Stanway on Markou that the referee, Rasa Grigone, deemed a foul.

Job well and truly done, James was withdrawn at half-time in favour of Beth Mead, Wiegman’s jewel safely nestled back in a velvet pouch after shining so brightly.

England picked up where they left off after the break. Stanway was denied by a VAR check on the narrowest of offside calls after she beautifully brought the ball down with her outstretched foot in mid-air before firing a half-volley into the net.

Quick Guide Roundup: Scotland and Wales advance to playoff finals Show Melissa Andreatta claims her Scotland side “stuck to our principles” in the 3-2 win over Czechia which booked a place in round two of the Women’s World Cup play-off against Sweden. Leading 2-0 from the first leg of the round one play-off but losing Caroline Weir to an injury in the warm-up at St Mirren’s Marbill Coaches Stadium, Scotland found themselves a goal down in the third minute when the Czechis full-back Denisa Vesela sent a shot from 30 yards soaring over a helpless Sandy MacIver. That lead lasted only two minutes before Lauren Davidson clipped in an equaliser from 12 yards but the visitors steeled themselves again and in the 32nd minute Klara Cahynova headed in a corner from Michaela Khyrova. However, Kathleen McGovern levelled early in the second half following a botched clearance by the Czechia defender Lucie Bendova and in the 72nd minute, when Barbora Votikova, the visiting goalkeeper, spilled a cross from the substitute Erin Cuthbert, Christy Grimshaw was on hand to lift the ball over the line and the home side ran out deserved winners. The Scots will take on Sweden, who beat Lithuania 10-0 on the night and 15-0 on aggregate, in a two-legged tie with the matches taking place between 26 November and 5 December, with Scotland at home first. Andreatta told BBC Scotland: “What it showed is what Scotland’s all about. “We stuck to our principles, ground out a result and that puts us in a good place for what’s ahead. I think these two games being so tough and testing us in all different ways, gives us the confidence to go again against Sweden." Wales took a step towards qualifying for the Women’s World Cup for the first time after a 3-0 win over Albania at Parc y Scarlets. Rhian Wilkinson’s side, who won the reverse fixture 1-0 in Shkoder last week following Ezmiralda Franja’s own goal, also set a new national record after extending their unbeaten run to 10 matches. Any nerves on the night were eased when Mayzee Davies headed home in the 34th minute, while Elise Hughes and Hannah Cain struck after half-time to seal a comprehensive 4-0 aggregate triumph. Wales will next take on Norway in their playoff final in December for the right to head to Brazil next year. Norway sit 13th in the world rankings, 18 spots higher than Wales. Kess Elmore marked her first Northern Ireland start with a goal but could not prevent them from falling to a 3-1 loss to Portugal, completing a 7-1 aggregate defeat in their playoff. The Republic of Ireland put Kazakhstan to the sword again, claiming a 12-0 aggregate win to move closer to qualifying. An 8-0 victory in last week’s first leg in Astana meant the Republic were all but home and hosed. Jessie Stapleton bagged the Republic’s final goal in the Kazakh capital and the Leicester defender opened the scoring just before half-time, while Katie McCabe struck just after the interval. The substitute Lucy Quinn and Denise O’Sullivan were also on target as the Republic cruised into the play-off final, where they will take on Poland across two legs in December. Press Association Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Wiegman leapt on the opportunity presented by the 7-1 aggregate scoreline to rotate further at the hour mark, with Niamh Charles, Jess Park and Freya Godfrey given a chance to demonstrate why they should be on the plane to Brazil should England overcome Ukraine.

Whether the changes took the sting out of the game or England just eased back on the intensity given the margin did not really matter, because the home team remained in complete control of the ball. Their more than 50-place superiority in the Fifa world rankings was far more evident in Leicester than it had been in Heraklion.

Russo was the beneficiary of England’s patience as the clock ticked down, collecting Keira Walsh’s angled pass before she raced clear, stepped around the goalkeeper, Styliani Katergiannaki, and rolled the ball into the empty net.

Chants of “we want six” rang round the buoyant ground as added time approached but that another did not arrive could not dampen the mood of the crowd and the show they had been treated to.

Ultimately, despite the performance put on, there is very little to be learned from a game against a team so far below England’s level. Any slip-up would only ever have been of England’s own making, as the poor defending for Greece’s goal in Crete demonstrated. However, perhaps that sluggishness could be attributed to a rustiness after a four-month break from international football.

Ukraine are up next, the homeless team preparing to face the European champions after a 4-1 aggregate defeat of Slovakia.

England met Ukraine in their World Cup qualifying group and, with a 9-1 aggregate win secured earlier in the year, it would take the most almighty of collapses for England to fail to book their place in Brazil now.

Sports.title: Football regulator chair insists he will resign if politically pressured over Manchester City
Sports.content:
The chair of the Independent ­Football Regulator (IFR), David Kogan, has said he will resign if he faces any political pressure on how to respond to Manchester City being found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules over a nine-year period, insisting “my independence is absolute”.

Kogan could remove City’s Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) should the damning verdict of an independent commission be upheld at the end of an ongoing appeal process. ­Concern had been raised, however, that the proximity of City’s ­ownership to Abu Dhabi’s rulers could trigger a political intervention by the UK ­government and an immediate test of the new regulator’s powers.

Those concerns have been rebuffed by Kogan. “Our independence is absolute and my independence personally is absolute,” he said. “I [have] made it very clear … any form of political interference on the way we operate is going to result in my resigning from this role, and I stand by that completely. And, just to be crystal clear, we’ve come under absolutely no political pressure whatsoever on this or any other topic.”

Kogan was speaking on Tuesday at the launch of the long-awaited State of the Game report, a document that lays out the financial challenges facing the English football pyramid. The City case has cast a huge shadow as the regulator prepares to introduce a new licensing regime for clubs later this season. “We have powers within the legislation that allow us to review not only owners and directors and senior executives, but also whether those owners are fit and proper ­people to run clubs going forward,” said Kogan, describing the process by which the regulator might intervene.

“That process is reliant on us ­having very detailed knowledge and information, which requires a ­certain amount of investigation. Then we would take judgments based on the legal advice that we then receive.”

Should a club owner ultimately be found to have failed a “fitness” test related to “integrity, honesty and financial soundness”, the regulator could force the club to be sold. “We deal with issues of this type much more frequently than you might realise because we are constantly looking at clubs,” Kogan said, stating if any decision by the regulator became the subject of legal action then clubs would be asked to foot the bill through a funding levy.

View image in fullscreen David Kogan reiterated that the regulator had powers to determine whether owners such as Manchester City’s were ‘fit and proper’. Photograph: Ben Whitley/PA

The acceleration of revenues among the Premier League’s biggest clubs is one of the key findings in the State of the Game report. The highest earning top-flight club currently earns 605 times the revenue of the lowest earning National League club. At the same time, spending has increased at all levels of the game, with 94% of the 116 clubs under the regulator’s regime posting a financial loss in 2025-26. In one particularly eye-catching statistic, the report found 11 Football League clubs recorded costs that exceeded their income even once player wages had been stripped out.

Kogan argued that a number of external factors that fall outside the regulator’s purview are affecting the game, including the expansion of the club calendar, the regulation of ­players’ agents and the recent rise in interest rates. However, he argued that one key measure – the agreement of a redistribution deal between the Premier League and EFL – could unlock change immediately.

While Kogan accepts the Premier League’s argument regarding the need for parachute payments due to “colossal” drops in revenue caused by relegation, he believes they have had a “distortive effect that’s grown over the years”. Kogan said that if a deal was done that reduced parachute payments but increased the amount going to all clubs then “that will go some way towards looking at the ­distorted effect”. Once that money was distributed, he said, “you’re going to see a softening effect going through down the 116 clubs”.

View image in fullscreen Manchester City’s owner, Sheikh Mansour, and chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, are under scrutiny. Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

The Premier League welcomed the publication of the report, arguing: “It recognises what English football has built – the world’s most popular league, the leading second tier, and a pyramid of unmatched depth.”

The league argued that a recent offer of financial redistribution to the EFL – understood to amount to £320m per season – “meets the ­objectives the IFR has set out in its report” and said it “remains ­committed to concluding a long-term partnership with the EFL that is fair, generous and ­balances the interests of all clubs”.

The EFL said the report’s findings “reinforce the EFL’s longstanding position that English football generates sufficient revenue to sustain both a successful Premier League and a thriving pyramid” and it remained “committed to working constructively with the Premier League and the regulator to secure a financial settlement in the interests of the whole game”.

Meanwhile, the secretary of state for digital, culture, media and sport, Lisa Nandy, said the stark figures covered in the report had “blown the doors off the game”. She urged football authorities to “consider these findings for the good of the game, for the fans, and for the communities of which they are so often the bedrock”.

Sports.title: Iraola has ‘100% trust’ in Wirtz and Barcola but tells others to step up
Sports.content:
Andoni Iraola has said he trusts Liverpool’s big-money signings Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola “100%” but needs players to step up in the absence of his three leading goalscorers.

Liverpool will again be without Alexander Isak, Cody Gakpo and Dominik Szoboszlai when visiting the Austrian side Lask in the Champions League on Wednesday. Iraola said he did not know when any of the trio, all of whom are carrying minor injuries sustained on international duty, would be available.

Their absence heightened the responsibility on Wirtz and Barcola against Manchester City on Sunday but both struggled as Liverpool suffered their first defeat under Iraola. Barcola is yet to produce a goal or an assist in six appearances since his £123m arrival from Paris Saint-Germain, or even win possession in the final third, while Wirtz has one assist this season and continues to underwhelm in a Liverpool shirt.

“Cody, Alex and Dom are our top scorers this season and now we don’t have them. We need other players to give us those numbers,” said Iraola. “We trust the players we have now to play in those positions. With Bradley and Flo, they have had good games and bad games this season like everyone else. We know their level and we know they will give us good performances.

“The other day, if [Lewis] Koumas scores the goal that he connects with really well, then it is one assist for Bradley Barcola. His performance would be exactly the same but we will all say: ‘Oh, he played really well with an assist.’ Sometimes we focus only on the numbers. With Bradley, the other day he had good situations and we did not finish them. Bradley and Flo are players that I trust 100%.”

View image in fullscreen Bradley Barcola (left) has not won possession in the final third this season. Photograph: Jon Super/AP

The Liverpool head coach confirmed he was likely to make changes in Linz, with several players knocks against City.

Iraola insisted he was happy with the team’s spirit, attitude and work rate in Sunday’s defeat, “including from the offensive players”, but not with the collective response to Ryan Gravenberch’s harsh dismissal. “A lot of what happened after we went down to 10 men was because we conceded straight away,” Iraola said. “We were making adjustments and then you go 1-0 down and it’s different, because then you have to go [for it] and you get caught in-between.

“The goal we conceded straight away hurt us. If we had made the adjustments earlier and been more compact at 0-0, it becomes a lot easier. But once you concede it’s not enough to just be compact. You need to go a little bit more and then spaces open.”

Virgil van Dijk is in line to captain Liverpool for a 200th time in all competitions on Wednesdaytonight.

Sports.title: Maresca says he would describe Manchester City as ‘cheats’ if he were a United fan
Sports.content:
Enzo Maresca has admitted he would describe Manchester City as “cheats” if he were a Manchester United or Arsenal fan. The manager’s ­comments came as he suggested it had been harder for City’s supporters to deal with the scandal surrounding the club than it had been for him or the players.

Maresca guided City to an ­impressive 3-0 win at Liverpool on Sunday in their first game since the club were found guilty of more than 100 charges related to breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules. He was asked whether the performance was down to the team being brought closer together by the guilty verdict.

“It probably has been more tough for our fans than for the players or for me as it’s more complicated,” he said, “because if I am an Arsenal fan or a United fan and you are a City fan, I can tell you: ‘Hey, my friend, you cheat’ – or this kind of thing. But we were happy at the end of the game and inside the changing room. We were very happy celebrating the three points because we know how difficult it is at Anfield.”

City, who have appealed against the independent commission’s ­ruling and continue to protest their innocence, have drawn criticism for the exuberant manner of Sunday’s celebration. Maresca defended the revelry but is conscious of the need to focus on Wednesday’s visit of Paris Saint-Germain in their second Champions League game of the season, following their 2-0 victory at Porto.

“We won 0-3 at Anfield,” Maresca said. “Even if it was 0-1 it would be exactly the same. We are here today to win tomorrow’s game and we work every day to win games. It’s the only thing that we can think; we can be focused. The rest is just things from outside that we need to deal with but we were so happy inside the pitch and you cannot imagine inside the changing room.

View image in fullscreen Enzo Maresca (right) talks with Enzo Fernández during a training session on the eve of the clash against PSG. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

“I promise you that I stress a lot about the gameplan and how we can train every day but I don’t stress about things I don’t [control]. The message to the players will be the same. We know how serious the situation is but at the same time it’s not something that we can do [anything about].”

Rúben Dias, City’s captain, echoed his manager. “When you build yourself as a player, you build yourself against any noise,” the defender said. “Personally, and I feel like I speak for the whole group, we’re very calm. We trust the club, and we’re very focused on enjoying football. People don’t love us winning and we love to win.”

Pep Guardiola is expected to be at the Etihad Stadium on Wednesday in a show of support for City’s owners. “In case he’s coming, it’s a nice feeling,” Maresca said of his predecessor. “Especially for him, because this has been his house for 10 years. It’s exciting for everyone.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Luis Enrique, PSG’s head coach, said City should keep all the ­trophies won from 2009-18, the timeframe of the guilty charges. “The first time that you hear [about the verdict], is it is a surprise,” he said. “But we need to respect the process and wait for the final decision. The authorities are responsible for making these decisions. But speaking only about football, they deserved those trophies. I love their football. Beyond that, we have to wait for the judges’ decision.”

Luis Enrique played with ­Guardiola at Barcelona. The 56-year-old was asked what he would say to his ­former teammate. “Nothing ­serious,” he said. “The trophies you win on the pitch remain on the pitch. They deserved to win that and I hope they can avoid the sanction. But we have to wait. The things I will say to Pep I will do in private.”

City claimed three Premier League titles, one FA Cup, and three League Cups in the nine-year span.

Sports.title: Patrice Motsepe’s Caf presidency under pressure after Afcon U-turn as Eto’o waits in wings
Sports.content:
Patrice Motsepe’s leadership of the Confederation of African Football (Caf) is under growing pressure, with officials from across the continent warning they have lost trust in the president and rivals including Samuel Eto’o positioning themselves potentially to replace him.

A return to a biennial Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) cycle is expected to be confirmed at Caf’s executive committee meeting in Abidjan next month after Motsepe surprisingly announced the U-turn last week – 10 months after the decision was taken to hold it every four years. That move is said to have wide support within Africa, but several sources have said there has been a weakening of trust in Caf’s leadership, with some questioning Motsepe’s management.

Most national association presidents are said to have been unaware Motsepe intended to announce the proposed change to Afcon’s frequency until the issue was raised at a strategic conference in Cape Verde last week. Motsepe confirmed he was not intending to stand for re-election for a third time when his term expires in 2029 and pledged Africa’s “unconditional support” for Gianni Infantino’s re-election as the Fifa president in March on the “unanimous” behalf of all 54 of Caf’s member associations.

It is understood Infantino remains extremely popular in Africa even though there are 10 to 15 member associations who would consider voting against him, as revealed in August. Motsepe’s potential rivals for the Caf presidency are believed to be attempting to gain Infantino’s approval should the South African billionaire be persuaded to step down early.

View image in fullscreen Former Barcelona forward Samuel Eto’o is the president of Cameroon’s federation and a member of Caf’s executive committee. Photograph: Steve Luciano/AP

They include Eto’o, the former Barcelona and Inter striker, who is the president of Cameroon’s federation and a member of Caf’s executive committee, Ahmed Yahya of Mauritania, Côte d’Ivoire’s Yacine Idriss Diallo, and Souleiman Waberi, a Fifa council member from Djibouti who has been charged with embezzlement and money laundering. He has denied the allegations. Other candidates may emerge from southern Africa.

Sources indicate that Infantino could hold the key to whether Motsepe continues. The other option would be to challenge Motsepe through Caf’s statutory mechanisms, which say an extraordinary general assembly can be convened after a written request from at least two-thirds of the members of the executive committee.

Infantino is thought to have fallen out with Motsepe after Motsepe allowed the Somali referee Omar Artan, who was denied entry to the United States for the 2026 World Cup, to take charge of Uefa’s Super Cup final in August amid growing tensions with European football’s governing body. However, sources have indicated their relationship has improved in recent weeks as Infantino has sought to solidify his support in Africa.

Motsepe promised annual distributions of about $700,000 (£528,000) from Caf to each association at the conference in Cape Verde – an increase of $500,000 – and is understood to have increased payments to executive committee members for attending meetings from $150 to $350, and to have introduced for them an annual bonus payment of about $8,000.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

That is despite growing concerns over Caf’s finances, with a broadcast deal signed with IMG due to expire after the 2027 Afcon. As reported by the Guardian in February, there are major doubts about whether that tournament will go ahead owing to questions over the readiness of Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda to host in June and July. Some sources are predicting that tournament could be pushed back to Christmas and the new year, which would cause major disruption to the European club season.

Caf is believed to have broadcast offers for future tournaments from IMG and an unnamed firm, although it is not known how the package will be structured and whether the proposed return to a two-year cycle could affect its commercial value. A Caf spokesperson said the process remained ongoing and that no rights had been awarded.

Sports.title: Football Daily | Coventry come to life at last – are their slapstick days behind them?
Sports.content:
FRANK CHAT

After years of circling the drain, Coventry City didn’t so much drop out of the Premier League 25 years ago as face-plant through its floorboards in slapstick style. In the intervening period, they endured their first experience of the fourth tier and were forced to live as tenants in their own city, before suffering the indignity of having to go cap-in-hand to neighbouring villages, looking for sofas on which to crash. Even the more recent good times were frustrating for the Sky Blues, as they lost a Championship playoff decider on penalties and were cruelly denied a place in the 2024 FA Cup final within the space of 11 months. It was all a far cry from that joyous afternoon in 1987 when Brian “Killer” Kilcline limped up the Wembley steps to hoist the FA Cup aloft.

Given all they have had to put up with, most Coventry fans would probably have relished the prospect of seeing their team get beaten repeatedly upon their return to the Premier League, if only because it meant their arduous return to English football’s top table was finally complete. And for a while that is exactly what looked likely to happen, as they lost their opening four league games, shipping 10 goals without reply. More astute observers will have noticed that three of those matches were against Arsenal, Manchester City and Brighton, sides that currently occupy the top three places. But while they may have lost them all, Coventry were at least creating the kind of chances that they have since begun to convert with aplomb.

Following Monday night’s shellacking of a comically shambolic and charitable Newcastle side, Coventry have now put together back-to-back wins and won their first top-flight game at home since a semi-thatched John Hartson scored the only goal of their victory over Sunderland at Highfield Road in April 2001. “We have to keep very much our feet on the ground because it’s so hard in this league,” honked Frank Lampard, having seen his young and inexperienced side bag four goals against the hapless Magpies. “If we think we’ve cracked it, if we think everything is fine … well, it’s not.” Of course, Lampard is right not to lose the run of himself and Coventry have plenty of road left to run. But following a night when Jack Rudoni announced himself as the top-flight midfielder many Coventry fans suspected he might be, things are definitely looking up.

The Premier League season is still in its infancy but already shrouded in more uncertainty than any that has been played before, not least because the team currently occupying first place look far more certain to go down than any of the 19 sides propping them up. Given the signs of life being shown by the three promoted sides, the battle against relegation already looks like shaping up to be an eight- or nine-way fight, a skirmish that is likely to be eminently more entertaining and far less weird than the current phoney war being played out at the top. Of course, if historical precedent is anything to go by, there’s also every chance this is just a temporary blip and Coventry could be playing League Two football – possibly against Manchester City – again in three years’ time.
