World.content:
NewsFeed Funeral for Egyptian flight attendant killed in Houthi attack on Riyadh

Mourners in Beheira, Egypt bid farewell to 28-year-old Azza Ramzy, a Flynas flight attendant killed in a Houthi attack on the Riyadh airport. She was among 13 people killed in the October 10 attack, which was the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.

World.title: Scientists urge tighter AI controls to prevent global cyber risks
World.content:
The call comes as polls cast doubt on political leaders’ ability to manage AI risks amid US midterm elections.

A group of more than 300 scientists from around the world is calling for urgent changes to how artificial intelligence is developed and deployed amid growing concerns about its unpredictable behaviour.

The letter, released on Tuesday and signed by researchers representing universities and research institutes in 32 countries, warned that failures to follow basic cybersecurity practices could lead to damage to critical infrastructure.

Many recent incidents in which AI models escaped secure environments could have been prevented with stronger security systems, the scientists said.

They recommended that organisations developing and testing advanced AI systems capable of carrying out cyberattacks do so in more tightly controlled environments, including “air-gapped” systems that are not connected to the internet.

Growing concerns

The letter comes amid growing concerns about AI’s capabilities and its potential impact on everyday users. On Monday, Anthropic warned that its AI models could soon be capable of creating self-spreading malware that could affect everyday internet-connected devices, including smart TVs, security cameras and smart appliances such as ovens.

The report found that AI systems could identify unfamiliar devices without human intervention. The company, led by Dario Amodei, warned that smaller AI models could be capable of carrying out autonomous attacks by the end of the year.

The malware could also be difficult to contain because it might take days to infect a device and could spread across multiple machines rather than remain concentrated in a single, controlled location.

Taking control of internet-connected devices can have immediate consequences. In France, for example, hackers compromised cooling systems across hundreds of supermarkets, raising temperatures and causing more than $220,000 in damage.



Meanwhile, Axios news organisation reported on Friday that Anthropic, OpenAI and other major AI company executives are privately preparing for the possibility of a catastrophic AI-related incident that could disrupt access to major financial services, the internet and potentially critical infrastructure such as water and power systems. Several industry insiders believe a major incident could occur within the next six months to a year, it said.

The scientists also called for more safeguards, including the creation of an international organisation to establish a set of best practices for AI alignment and containment along with timely reporting of incidents.

One of the signatories, David Lie, a professor at the University of Toronto’s Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, said his concerns began after OpenAI’s AI agents bypassed controls and hacked into servers at the tech company Hugging Face.

“One is that OpenAI, in setting up its test environment, didn’t appreciate how capable its agents were,” Lie said.

“These were the AI agents that they were designing. Second is that the AI agents independently found each other and chose to collaborate on this attack, and third is that they also intentionally tried to deceive and mislead their human creators.”

Political pressures

The letter underscores growing public concern about AI, including in the lead-up to the US congressional midterm elections. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found that 57 percent of voters said President Donald Trump’s administration was not taking AI risks seriously enough, while 54 percent said the same of Congress.

An AP-NORC poll echoed those findings, with about 80 percent of respondents saying the government should keep AI under human control. Respondents also expressed little confidence in either party’s ability to manage the technology: 39 percent said neither Republicans nor Democrats could be trusted to do a good job of reining it in, while 23 percent expressed greater confidence in Democrats and 21 percent in Republicans.

World.title: Iconic Iguazu Falls walkway dismantled amid record water levels
World.content:
NewsFeed Iconic Iguazu Falls walkway dismantled amid record water levels

The Devil’s Throat walkway at Brazil’s Iguazu Falls is dismantled to prevent surging waters, which reached nearly eight times the historical average, from sweeping it away. Heavy rainfall linked to El Nino forced Brazilian authorities to temporarily close the walkway on Sunday.

World.title: DR Congo Ebola cases pass 9,000 as efforts to curb transmission falter
World.content:
Confirmed Ebola cases have surpassed 9,000 in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) outbreak, according to Health Ministry data, as efforts to stifle transmission falter.

The ministry reported 9,066 confirmed cases and 4,381 deaths on Tuesday – a death toll of nearly half the known cases.

The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, has become the largest and deadliest in the DRC’s history. Globally, the toll is only second to the 2014 to 2016 West African epidemic, which saw 28,600 confirmed cases and more than 11,000 deaths across Guinea, ⁠⁠Liberia and Sierra Leone, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

The Bundibugyo strain currently has no approved vaccines or treatments and has raised concerns over cross-border transmission.

Last week, Kenya reported its first imported case in which a Kenyan national who lived in the DRC travelled through Uganda before reaching Nairobi, where he died.

Uganda also reported 20 cases and two deaths earlier in the year, but the country was declared Ebola-free in August.

The current outbreak in the DRC was announced in mid-May, but some experts suspect it began as early as February. The virus, which is transmitted through contact with bodily fluids, has spread to seven provinces in the north and east.

Efforts to contain the virus face obstacles as health workers and other responders in the DRC face mistrust in local communities, with many believing the disease is a ruse for officials to siphon off money. The outbreak is also occurring amid an ongoing conflict between the M23 rebel group and government forces, making transport of healthcare resources to remote regions difficult.



A local politician in eastern DRC was beaten to death in September after he defended the government’s Ebola response on the radio, according to his political party.

A clinical trial to evaluate vaccine efficacy against the Bundibugyo strain is being prepared for the DRC in the coming weeks, WHO Health Emergencies Programme Executive Director Dr Chikwe Ihekweazu said on Tuesday.

World.title: Pope diagnosed with lung cancer but had successful surgery, Vatican says
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer but had successful surgery to remove a lower lobe of his right lung, the Vatican has said in a medical bulletin.

The 71-year-old underwent a 90 minute surgery on Tuesday at Rome's Gemelli Hospital and was subsequently diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma.

"After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room on the 10th floor," the Vatican said in a statement.

The lump was first detected during what the Vatican has described as "routine checks".

Earlier, large crowds gathered outside the hospital to greet the Pope, with some waiting for several hours.

They cheered greetings and well wishes as he passed, while he waved and smiled back through the lowered back window of his car.

He was then met by staff on the hospital steps. "I'm sorry," one of them commiserated, to which the Pope gave a smile and a shrug. "We're here for you," he was assured.

In its statement, the Vatican said the whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical".

A Vatican source told Agence France-Presse news agency further tests were being carried out to see if there was any sign the cancer had spread.

It was Leo XIV himself who on Sunday announced news of his operation to the world, speaking from the balcony in St Peter's Square after delivering the traditional Angelus blessing.

He said the nodule, or growth, on his lung was "contained" and had been found "at a very early stage", but that doctors had advised him to have it removed.

Gemelli's thoracic surgery team operated on the Pope, whose schedule has already been cleared until 20 October to give him time to recover.

Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was pulmonary adenocarcinoma, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said.

The Vatican has stressed that the pontiff, who is generally thought to be fit, had no symptoms of infection or illness.

World.title: MI5 chief warns of threats to UK from Russia, Iran and AI
World.content:
MI5 is devoting more resource to countering state threats than during the Cold War, the head of the intelligence service has said.

Sir Ken McCallum said threats from foreign adversaries had quadrupled in the last decade, with Russia "aggressor number one" as well as increased Iran-linked aggression against Jewish sites and military bases.

At an annual speech in London, MI5's chief said Russia was waging hybrid warfare at a time when AI was "supercharging the cyber-security contest between attackers and defenders".

He also warned of rising threats from "extreme right-wing terrorism" and said MI5 had "caught terrorists seeking to exploit AI," including by integrating the technology with drones.

He said the biggest threat from the misuse of AI was extremist groups using the technology to harness new and existing bioweapons.

However, he noted that work countering terrorism and state threats was now "pretty much of equal scale" which he described as a "huge shift" in recent years.

Sir Ken said Russia had stopped short of "conventional conflict" against Nato and is instead trying to unsettle European countries while its progress in its full-scale invasion of Ukraine is "minimal and horrifically costly".

Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyber-attacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary.

These are quite often employed using proxies, but Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary.

Sir Ken said MI5 successes in identifying and expelling Russian spies from the UK had left the Kremlin dependent on paying proxies for attempted attacks.

"With its traditional covert footprint eviscerated by almost 1,000 expulsions since the invasion, the Kremlin's global toolkit is weak, he said.

"So we see them scrambling to pay criminals to do their bidding."

He added: "These are not the actions of a great power with the strategic upper hand."

His comments come as a growing number of leaders across Europe have warned Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine.

Asked after the speech about Prime Minister Andy Burnham's recent comments that Russia interfered with the Brexit referendum, Sir Ken said it was "not new news" that there had been attempts from Moscow but distinguished between "interference attempted" and "outcome achieved".

He said it was a matter of public record that there were pieces in Russian media and "so-called internet trolls and bot farms" seeking to influence the Brexit debate, but also stressed that the result of the 2016 referendum was "not in dispute".

He added that he was "worried" about the the ongoing debate on Russian interference.

"I am a little bit anxious that we don't play into our adversaries' hands by making these trolls look 10ft tall," he told reporters.

World.title: Missiles intercepted near Riyadh after Saudi coalition hits Yemen fuel depot
World.content:
Missiles and drones have been intercepted over Riyadh after the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen struck a fuel depot near the Houthi-controlled capital, Sanaa, its spokesperson says.

Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki said several projectiles targeting the Saudi capital and other cities were intercepted after the coalition carried out a strike on the Yemen Petroleum Company's al-Sabaha facility on Tuesday night.

The Houthis warned they would target the airport and Aramco refinery in Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, and Aramco's headquarters in the eastern city of Dammam.

Al-Maliki later said missiles targeting cities including Dammam had been intercepted, while shrapnel had fallen in a residential area in Dhahran.

It came as the Saudi cabinet, chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, said the Iran-backed group would "bear the consequences" of its recent deadly attacks on the kingdom.

Thirteen people were killed when a missile hit King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday, while another person was killed in a similar attack there the following day.

On Tuesday, the coalition said its forces had destroyed three drones north of Riyadh.

The Houthis have said they are targeting airports, oil and gas facilities, and military bases in Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones in response to deadly Saudi strikes on territory that they control in western Yemen, including Sanaa.

The Saudi-led coalition has been providing air support for Yemeni pro-government forces mounting an offensive on Yemen's Red Sea coast and several other front lines.

World.title: Ex-gang boss sentenced to 40 years for orchestrating Tupac Shakur's murder
World.content:
Former gang boss Duane "Keffe D" Davis has been sentenced to at least 40 years in prison for orchestrating the murder of Tupac Shakur.

A jury found Davis, 63, guilty in September of one count of murder with a deadly weapon for the rap superstar's death in a drive-by shooting in Las Vegas on 7 September 1996. He has said he will appeal the verdict.

Prosecutors argued that although Davis did not fire the gun himself, he was the ringleader of the group that committed the murder. He admitted in his memoir that he had provided the gun used in the crime.

Davis' conviction was the first in a cold case that has intrigued hip-hop fans for nearly 30 years.

Prosecutor Marc DiGiacomo argued during Tuesday's sentencing hearing that Davis spent years "publicly grandstanding" and bragging about his role on Shakur's death, which he said, "had wide-ranging effects upon the world".

World.title: Cornell bans all fraternity parties over gang sex assault allegations
World.content:
"It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe. We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action," he added.

Fraternities have existed at university campuses across the US for decades and function as all-male social clubs where the students live, study and socialise. Over the years, the groups have become notorious for binge-drinking, partying and dangerous hazing rituals.

In a statement, a lawyer representing Doe said she filed a civil lawsuit "to achieve her aim of improving Cornell and its response to abuse claims".

"While the steps announced today are helpful to achieve this goal, they are too late to protect Ms. Doe," said lawyer Thomas Giuffra.

Cornell's president said anyone who violated the new fraternity party policy at the New York university would be suspended.

The school also said it planned to improve support for survivors of sexual assault, including more staff to help people report sexual misconduct and navigate other support systems as well.

Through Title IX, the federal law that governs how universities handle sexual assault claims, schools are required to provide measures of support to help survivors stay in school after assaults. Doe's lawyer has said she dropped out after the alleged assault.

The president said the school will allow New York State Police's trauma-informed officers to investigate allegations of sexual assault on its campus.

These officers will interview survivors who want to pursue criminal charges and prepare "comprehensive investigative summaries for the appropriate law enforcement agency", Kotlikoff said.

Cornell has faced criticism over the information shared with the local district attorney's office about Jane Doe's allegations.

Out of hundreds of documents that US media outlets have obtained from Cornell's investigation into the assault, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said that in 2024, his office received only a six-page statement signed by the victim as well as Snapchat messages in which the men at the fraternity party advertised a free sexual encounter with Doe.

State officials have also criticised Van Houten's decision not to bring charges or interview victims and witnesses himself. New York Governor Kathy Hochul has appointed the state's attorney general, Letitia James, to investigate the case.

Kotlikoff said Cornell would be bringing in national sexual violence prevention experts to examine "the factors leading to campus sexual violence and strategies to promote responsible sexual citizenship".

He said the steps were the first toward "systematic change" on campus.

World.title: Trump ousts Kimberly Guilfoyle as US ambassador to Greece after corruption allegations
World.content:
President Donald Trump's administration has asked Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign from her position as US ambassador to Greece, White House press secretary Katie Zacharia has announced.

Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host, had been facing mounting scrutiny after reports she allegedly asked a Trump donor to pay her hefty credit card bill in exchange for access to his administration and behaving inappropriately while in Athens.

Trump said she had done a good job, but she will "not be there" in Greece any longer. "I didn't like what I read," he said.

Guilfoyle vowed to defend herself against the "false" claims and said the ambassadorship had been the "honour of a lifetime".

Zacharia announced during her first - and unusually short - media briefing that Guilfoyle "had been asked to resign" without providing more details.

"She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well," she said.

Guilfoyle, the 57-year-old ex-wife of California Governor Gavin Newsom, was first nominated as envoy to Athens in December 2024, a month before Trump returned to the White House as president.

In a lengthy post on X, Guilfoyle thanked President Trump, said she would always be a loyal supporter and denied any wrongdoing.

"I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity," she wrote, adding that she will "not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service".

Her position had become increasingly tenuous as allegations of improper behaviour mounted over the past week.

A series of text messages seen by the BBC - and first reported by The Wall Street Journal - appear to show Guilfoyle asking for the money from Eric Deters, a long-time Trump ally.

"It won't show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express," she wrote in one Signal message.

In another message - dated just days before her US Senate confirmation hearing last July - Guilfoyle wrote: "Honey please I need you to get this done for me today."

World.title: Horrified witnesses recount fatal rollercoaster incident at Six Flags
World.content:
Warning: This article contains some graphic details

One person has died and others were injured after an incident on a rollercoaster at an amusement park in the US state of Georgia.

The Cobb County Police Department is investigating Monday's death at Six Flags Over Georgia, about 15 miles (24km) from Atlanta.

The ride involved has not been specified but aerial footage from news helicopters showed the Goliath rollercoaster stopped midway, with riders being helped off by workers.

Horrified witnesses have told local media they saw a man ejected from the ride and police say preliminary information indicates this was the case.

Six Flags said it was temporarily closing nine rides across the US and Canada as a precaution.

It said it was "deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today. Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest's family, friends, and loved ones".

The Cobb County Police Department said the incident happened just before 16:00 local time (20:00 GMT) on Monday.

It said officers working at the park found the man, identified as Atlanta resident Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, 42, beneath the ride. He was unresponsive and not breathing.

"Preliminary information gathered through witness and employee interview indicates Kariem was ejected from the ride and struck other patrons before falling beneath the attraction," police said in a statement.

The Office of Commissioner of Insurance and Safety Fire, which enforces amusement park safety rules and standards in Georgia, said it was also reviewing the incident "to ensure full compliance with all applicable policies and procedures".

Local CNN affiliate WXIA quoted a witness saying Kariem had come loose from his seat and had then struck the rollercoaster and some of his fellow riders before falling onto the roof of a nearby haunted house attraction.

The incident was captured in souvenir photos that were automatically taken of the rollercoaster while it was in motion, the witness added.

A husband and wife, who were on the ride, also told WXIA that Kariem fell from the ride and was struck by it. They said workers at the park had checked their safety harnesses before the ride set off.

"We were having a great time and to just screaming 'Oh my God, what is happening?'," the woman said.

World.title: Russia's offensive ability is broken, Kyiv's former top general tells BBC
World.content:
Ukraine has stabilised the front line and "broken Russia's ability to advance" by killing so many of its men, Ukraine's former commander-in-chief has said in an interview with the BBC.

Gen Oleksandr Syrskyi made the comments in an exclusive interview, his first since he was dramatically forced from his post in the summer.

He addressed his sacking, disagreeing with his critics who declared him too "old school" to command Ukraine's new, technologically advanced forces.

He also pushed back against allegations made by soldiers who previously served under him, who told the BBC they were ordered to remain at their positions even when they were almost surrounded by Russians, leading to high losses.

Syrskyi said that Moscow's overall losses in the war were six times higher than Ukraine's. "If you count only dead, then it's up to 11 times," he added.

Neither Russia nor Ukraine officially release the numbers of their dead. Ukraine's military says it inflicted record losses this year on Russian soldiers in September, although that cannot be verified.

UK intelligence chiefs estimate Russia has lost around half a million men killed in Ukraine since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022. The US-based Center for Strategic and International Studies meanwhile believes, external Ukraine has lost up to 150,000 troops killed by June 2026.

He says this difference in death toll â as well as technological advances, and a strategy of attacking weak points in Russia's lines while containing their advances in other parts â accounts for the current stalemate at the front.

In the first six months of 2026, Russia managed overall to seize 61 sq km, the general said. "It's an indication that the front line has been stabilised."

The Institute for Study of War (ISW) has also confirmed this trend. One of its recent reports, external says that in September 2026, Moscow lost more territory than it took.

World.title: Tinubu can’t handle insecurity: Why does he want another term?, By Ugoji Egbujo
World.content:
A nation that conscripts its graduates cannot lose them on a federal highway, allow exchange of ransom, and call the aftermath a rescue.

A few days ago, thirty prospective corps members left Oyo for the East. Twenty were taken near Owerri, on the Owerri–Onitsha road at Umunoha. Ten escaped. The local people who witnessed the abduction could not stand the apathy of the security agencies, so they blocked the road to force a chase. The situation borders on hopeless.

When the police woke from their slumber, they announced that their drones had located the hostages and their abductors. The impression sold to the public was that they had them surrounded. Perhaps the corps members would be luckier than the Chibok girls, who were taken away without the government knowing which way the terrorists went with them. The Owerri police said they could not immediately exrract the hostages because the area was mined. The story did not instill any hope. The nation listened with resignation.

Youth corps members are supposed to be the babies of the federal government. The government cannot conscript youths into a compulsory national service in far-flung places and fail to protecr them. The mass abduction of citizens, let alone corps members, should provoke any responsible government. But perhaps not a government that cares more about optics than substance, about politics and retaining power than purposeful leadership. The real tragedy is that the government has lost sense of shame .

A few days after the kidnap, the government announced triumphantly that it had rescued the corps members, crediting the rescue to the joint security team and emphasising that no ransom was paid. While the government was basking in glory, pictures emerged of the abducted, frazzled corps members moving furtively on a village street, all alone. Could they have been rescued and allowed to walk bush paths?

The parents then went on television. They had scraped, borrowed, and paid. The demand opened at ₦50 million a head and was bargained down to about ₦5 million or ₦6 million, some of it in dollars. The government that said it was watching captives and captors by drone had not noticed the families negotiating, gathering the money, and flying to Owerri to deliver it. It had not seen the captives leave. The Imo commissioner of police says he is not aware of any ransom. Claiming a rescue while the people who paid are on television is worse than silence. It is complicity.

Orire followed the same script. Only with a worse ending. Forty-four pupils and teachers were taken from Oriire in Oyo on 15 May and held for fifty-six days. The presidency said security forces rescued them, arrested eight, killed some, and paid no ransom. A surviving teacher, Zaccheaus Olatunde, told a different story. Two teachers were killed . Sone negotiatipn happened. No fighting took place. The survivors were shown the way home. No public accounting has yet matched the official version to a captured camp. Yet another ‘miraculous’ release passed off as military rescue .

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The terrorists who carried out the Oriire abduction are not ghosts. The Oyo government insinuated as much. In the case of Owerri, two species of bandits operate in the neighbourhood where the kidnapping happened. Unknown gunmen have a camp and control the left side heading into Owerri, while rogue Fulani herdsmen operate in the forest on the right side. The security agencies are aware of the presence and identity of these groups. The Governor of Zamafara said the same thing. That was why the local people at Uumnoha went irate when the corps members were abducted and the agencies hesitated to give an immediate chase. What exactly is Tinubu’s strategy against the rampaging insecurity?

What, then, is the strategy? Mass kidnapping is now followed by a release, and the release is claimed as a rescue. The exchanges are mediated by ransoms. Kidnappers keep the money and the camp. Security agencies have not learned hostage work, and the public is asked to applaud a story the payers have already contradicted. A trade conducted on those terms can only fatten the crime. Ransom is not rescue. The scourge is festering.

Recently it was reported that NNPC booked ₦11.2 trillion as receivables from the federation for advances and the cost of protecting oil and gas assets. We pay local mercenaries and shadowy folks ungodly sums to do the basic work of the police and the military, which are massively underequipped and miserably understaffed. Why have we made being an outlaw so rewarding? Why is the nation-state so weak? We cant live by random ransoms.

Tinubu’s first tenure has been marred by insecurity. But Tinubu wants a second term even though he has no clue how to tackle it. Nothing in the first term shows a strategy. Mass abduction, a week of tales, a release, a denial of ransom, no convictions: that is the operating model.

Tinubu met this model. He has not broken it. The South-East unknown gunmen and north-west bands are known to local security agencies. But they are not cleared. The police are too thin for the territory. The army is spread across internal duties it was not built for. The pipelines are hired out to mercanaries who are paid hundreds of billions and who it appears are helping the reelection effort. What new idea has Tinubu got?

Tinubu wants a second term anyway. Nothing in the first has shown a plan that would make the second different. Kidnappers cannot keep walking away with the ransoms while the government blows its trumpets. What, exactly, would he come back to do?

Ugoji Egbujo writes from Lagos.

World.title: The weaponisation of yesterday, By Umar Yakubu
World.content:
If Nigeria is to break this destructive cycle, we must transition from what Nietzsche termed “reactive” history to a critical history — a deliberate practice that scrutinises past structural failures, disarms historical grievances, and prioritises civic nation-building over score-settling… Until we stop using yesterday as a weapon to fight today’s political battles, we will remain trapped in Hegel’s grim reality: a nation that speaks of its history incessantly, yet learns absolutely nothing from it.

An excess of history makes life wither and degenerate – Nietzsche

During the recent presentation of the book, Emirs of Zazzau: A Biographical Study (1808–2025), in Zaria, Professor Usman Bugaje made a compelling case for the imperative of historical knowledge. He reminded the audience of the indispensable need to study history if we are to understand our present and navigate our future.

His call echoes a familiar refrain heard across our public space: we must study history so that we do not repeat it. Yet, as the contemporary state of our country so vividly demonstrates, this moral maxim is flawed in its popular execution. Do we truly learn from history in Nigeria? Or do we absorb the past merely to stock an arsenal of grievances, inciting new hatreds under the guise of remembrance?

When examined through the lens of political philosophy, Nigeria’s fraught relationship with its past reveals a tragic paradox: historical knowledge, rather than serving as a lamp for national building and institutional enlightenment, has too often been transformed into a flame for social division.

The Fallacy of the Lesson

In his Lectures on the Philosophy of History, the German philosopher Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel made a stark observation that remains unnerving in its precision: “What experience and history teach is this — that nations and governments have never learned anything from history, or acted upon principles deduced from it.”

Hegel’s insight was born, not out of structural critique of human governance. States rarely act out of wisdom derived from old textbooks. In Nigeria, this Hegelian paradox is visible in the cyclical nature of our political and economic crises. The structural failures that precipitated the tragic collapse of the First Republic — unbridled regionalism, electoral fraud, state-sanctioned corruption, and the politicisation of everything serious, such as the security and economy — are continuously replicated by successive generations of political elites. Each generation claims to understand the national tragedies of the past, yet each reproduces the exact institutional dynamics that triggered those ruptures.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

We quote history in anniversaries and public lectures, but our approach to governance largely remains unchanged. Some will argue that it is worse. We do not learn from history because we treat historical knowledge as an ornamental academic exercise, rather than an imperative for structural reform.

When history is weaponised…memory becomes a catalyst for retribution instead of being a teacher of reflection, caution and progress. Every new generation is taught whom to mistrust based on acts committed long before they were born.

The Arsenal of Memory

If we do not extract constructive lessons from the past, what then do we do with it? We seem to have turned it into a weapon.

In his essay On the Use and Abuse of History for Life, Friedrich Nietzsche distinguished between historical memory that serves human flourishing and history that poisons the present. Nietzsche warned against an obsession with the past that creates a “reservoir for grievances” — a state wherein a society becomes so intoxicated by old injuries that it loses the capacity to build a viable future.

This, for me, is the central dilemma of modern Nigeria. I have often told a few friends that I sympathise with people who possess retentive memories, because most of them use that gift to remember grievances, rather than the good. The engagement with our past has largely devolved into a competitive accounting of historical injury. The 1966 military coups and the devastating Civil War are rarely examined through an objective, institutional framework meant to foster structural reconciliation. Instead, they are routinely weaponised in daily political discourse to justify ethno-regional marginalisation or to cultivate sub-national resentment.

Across the geopolitical zones, historical narratives of pre-colonial dominance, colonial favour, and post-independence betrayals are invoked not to build empathy, but to validate contemporary prejudice, resource hoarding, and political exclusion. And who benefits from all this chaos? The people or the elite?

As my friend Husein Adeto Bello succinctly observed, the underlying issue lies in why people engage with the past in the first place: many study history merely to acquaint themselves with historic grievances and inherit legacy talking points, without ever pausing to ask what they can do to ensure their generation — and the next — does not perpetuate those same grievances.

When history is weaponised in this manner, memory becomes a catalyst for retribution instead of being a teacher of reflection, caution and progress. Every new generation is taught whom to mistrust based on acts committed long before they were born.

Whose History Are We Learning?

This brings us to a fundamental question in the philosophy of history: Whose history is actually being told?

History is never a neutral recording of facts; it is an interpretive narrative shaped by power and context. In a multi-ethnic federation formed through arbitrary colonial amalgamation, there is no singular, universally accepted “Nigerian narrative.” There exists, instead, a contested marketplace of competing ethnic, regional, and religious memories.

When history is learnt through the narrow lens of tribal insularity, it fails to construct a shared civic identity. Instead, it codifies “us versus them” dynamics, ensuring that the act of remembering directly incites more hatred. And we can’t grow with such history.

The historical decision to remove history from the basic school curriculum for years left a critical void. A generation grew up learning their past not from rigorous, critical academic inquiry, but from informal, highly partisan narratives. These informal histories function primarily as national myths of triumph and victimisation:

One group learns a history in which they are the perpetual victims of systemic betrayal.

Another learns a history framing them as the rightful, historical custodians of power.

Yet another learns a history that regional erasure has rendered almost invisible.

When history is learnt through the narrow lens of tribal insularity, it fails to construct a shared civic identity. Instead, it codifies “us versus them” dynamics, ensuring that the act of remembering directly incites more hatred. And we can’t grow with such history.

Reclaiming Yesterday for Tomorrow

The continuous cycle of political instability, inter-communal conflict, and ethnic polarisation in Nigeria validates the fear that knowing the past can easily degenerate into nursing old wounds.

If Nigeria is to break this destructive cycle, we must transition from what Nietzsche termed “reactive” history to a critical history — a deliberate practice that scrutinises past structural failures, disarms historical grievances, and prioritises civic nation-building over score-settling.

Until we stop using yesterday as a weapon to fight today’s political battles, we will remain trapped in Hegel’s grim reality: a nation that speaks of its history incessantly, yet learns absolutely nothing from it.

Umar Yakubu is the executive director of the Center for Fiscal Transparency and Public Integrity.

World.title: Akpabio insists on jail term for attempted suicide as Senate passes decriminalisation bill for second reading
World.content:
A bill seeking to decriminalise attempted suicide in Nigeria has passed second reading in the Senate, despite Senate President Godswill Akpabio insisting that people who survive suicide attempts should remain liable to imprisonment.

Mr Akpabio announced the passage of the bill

during Tuesday’s plenary after a majority of senators supported it through a voice vote.

The bill was subsequently referred to the Senate Committees on Health (Secondary and Tertiary) and Judiciary, Human Rights and Legal Matters for further legislative action.

The bill, sponsored the senator representing Cross River South Senatorial District, Asuquo Ekpenyong, seeks to decriminalise attempted suicide and establish a legal framework for suicide prevention, treatment and support for survivors of suicide attempts.

It also seeks to address the conflict between existing criminal laws that punish attempted suicide and the National Mental Health Act, which recognises the need for medical intervention in mental health emergencies.

Leading the debate on the bill, Mr Ekpenyong argued that while the National Mental Health Act recognises attempted suicide as a psychiatric emergency requiring treatment, Section 327 of the Criminal Code and Section 231 of the Penal Code criminalise the act.

He said the provisions were contradictory and required legislative intervention.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The senator manitained that the bill seeks to replace punitive measures with appropriate medical assessment, treatment and continuing support for survivors of suicide attempts.

He warned that criminalising attempted suicide could discourage people from seeking help, encourage families to conceal such incidents and prevent health workers from reporting cases promptly.

He added that treating suicide attempts as criminal offences could deepen the stigma surrounding mental health conditions and undermine efforts to obtain reliable data for national suicide prevention programmes.

Debate

Most senators who participated in the debate supported the bill.

Dayo Faduyile, the senator for Ondo South and a medical doctor, said attempted suicide should be treated as a medical emergency rather than a criminal offence.

He argued that depression and other mental health conditions could impair a person’s judgement, making treatment and recovery more appropriate responses than punishment.

Mr Faduyile also noted that some people who survived suicide attempts had subsequently died by suicide while in detention.

He warned that imprisonment or police custody could not adequately address the underlying medical conditions that might lead to suicide attempts.

“The best way to treat anybody who did not succumb to a suicide attempt is actually not to criminalise it. They need help,” he said.

Bauchi Central Senator, Abdul Ningi, also argued that the circumstances surrounding suicide attempts were often linked to mental health challenges and should be addressed through medical intervention rather than punitive measures.

However, Senate Leader Opeyemi Bamidele cautioned that some provisions of the Administration of Criminal Justice Act did not automatically apply across all states, depending on the legal frameworks adopted by their respective Houses of Assembly.

Mr Bamidele said the Senate needed to establish the extent to which the proposed amendment would apply nationally before proceeding with the legislation.

Akpabio insists on punitive measures

Responding to the debate, Mr Akpabio argued that attempted suicide should remain punishable by imprisonment, warning that removing the penalties could encourage the act.

“If you attempt suicide, make sure you die. Anyone who attempts and fails will go to jail,” he said.

The senate president also called for adequate input from state Houses of Assembly, urging state lawmakers to express their views on the bill during the public hearing to avoid potential legal conflicts.

What the law says

Under Nigeria’s existing criminal laws, attempted suicide remains a punishable offence, although the 1999 Constitution does not expressly criminalise the act.

Section 327 of the Criminal Code Act provides for up to one year’s imprisonment for anyone who attempts to take their own life, while Section 231 of the Penal Code prescribes up to one year’s imprisonment, a fine or both. The applicable provisions and penalties may vary across jurisdictions.

The existing legal framework has, however, raised concerns about its compatibility with the National Mental Health Act, 2021, which recognises attempted suicide as a psychiatric emergency requiring immediate intervention. The law defines psychiatric emergencies to include attempted suicide and provides a framework for mental healthcare and support.

World.title: Senate asks FG to release ecological funds to tackle erosion, landslides in Cross River
World.content:
The Senate has asked the federal government to release funds from the Ecological Fund to Cross River State to address erosion and landslides that have claimed several lives and displaced residents.

The upper chamber made the call on Tuesday after adopting a motion sponsored by the senator representing Cross River South Senatorial District, Asuquo Ekpenyong, on the need to address the state’s worsening ecological crisis.

Moving the motion, Mr Ekpenyong said erosion and landslides threaten lives and property in several communities, particularly in Calabar metropolis, including Atakpa, Edim Otop, Ikot Effangha Mkpa, Nyaghasang, Ikot Anwatim, Nasarawa/Bacoco, Akai Effa, Bayside, Summit Hills and Anansa.

The senator referenced an incident in July in which a landslide at Ikot Anwatim killed five people, including four siblings from the same family. The incident also destroyed two houses and left two other residents injured.

He also reported another landslide in Edim Otop that killed an eight-year-old girl, warning that more lives could be lost if the underlying causes were not urgently addressed.

Mr Ekpenyong identified poorly designed drainage systems, indiscriminate waste disposal, unregulated sand mining, vegetation removal and vandalism of drainage infrastructure as factors worsening erosion in the state.

He urged the Senate to prevail on the federal government to approve, allocate and release adequate funding from the Ecological Fund for emergency stabilisation and comprehensive erosion-control measures, prioritising communities where lives have been lost and residents remain at immediate risk.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The senator also called on the Federal Ministry of Environment, in collaboration with the Cross River State Government and relevant agencies, to immediately assess high-risk locations and commence appropriate emergency protection works.

He further urged the Federal Ministries of Environment and Works to prioritise funding for erosion-control projects in the state and ensure that major interventions are supported by proper geotechnical and hydrological assessments, sound engineering designs, effective supervision and environmental safeguards.

The motion and its prayers received the support of the majority of senators during a voice vote.

Following its adoption, Senate President Godswill Akpabio directed the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) to work with the Cross River State Emergency Management Agency and affected local government councils to provide temporary shelter, food, medical care and psychosocial support to bereaved and displaced families.

Mr Akpabio also directed NEMA to facilitate the safe evacuation and temporary relocation of residents facing imminent danger, while establishing effective early-warning systems and monitoring unstable locations.

He further mandated the Senate Committee on Environment to inspect affected communities, assess existing interventions and engage relevant agencies on funding and implementation.

The committee is expected to report back to the Senate with recommendations for further legislative action.

Ecological Fund

The Ecological Fund was established in 1981 to enable the government to address serious environmental problems across the country, including erosion, flooding, desertification and other ecological emergencies. It is administered through a funding arrangement that provides shares for the federal, state and local governments to address ecological challenges within their respective jurisdictions.

READ ALSO: Senate postpones security summit in honour of plane crash victims

Under the existing sharing formula, 1 per cent of the fund goes to the federal government, while states receive 0.72 per cent and local governments 0.60 per cent. The federal government’s share is further distributed among the Ecological Project Office and other designated agencies, including the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA).

The Ecological Project Office, domiciled in the Office of the Secretary to the Government of the Federation, coordinates ecological intervention projects across the country.

However, the fund faces competing demands from communities affected by environmental degradation. In May 2024, the Ecological Project Office called for increased funding, saying available resources were insufficient to meet the growing requests for intervention projects across the country.

Nigeria continues to face significant ecological challenges, including gully erosion, flooding, landslides and desertification. The World Bank has identified poor land and water management, inadequate planning, environmental degradation and climate variability as factors contributing to these problems. Such hazards threaten lives and livelihoods, destroy homes and infrastructure, and place additional pressure on public resources.

World.title: Nigeria condemns death of citizen in South African police custody
World.content:
The Nigerian Consulate General in Johannesburg has called for a thorough investigation into the death of a Nigerian, Chimezie Odueze, allegedly tortured by officers of the South African Police Service (SAPS) in Cape Town.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, the Consul General, Ninikanwa Okey-Uche, said Mr Odueze died on 9 October in the Parklands area of Cape Town.

The consulate said reports that Mr Odueze was tortured by police officers before his death had caused shock and pain to his family, the Nigerian community and Nigeria’s two diplomatic missions in South Africa.

According to the statement, Mr Odueze was arrested at a shopping centre on suspicion of drug possession and taken to his home for a search. The consulate said no drugs were found at the residence, but the Nigerian national was allegedly tortured to death.

The consulate described the incident as one too many, saying the recurring reports of extrajudicial killings of Nigerians in South Africa raised serious concerns about the safety of Nigerians and other foreign nationals in the country.

It also warned against the stereotyping of Nigerians, saying some elements were disregarding South African legal processes and wrongfully generalising Nigerians in the country.

The consulate called on South African authorities to conduct a thorough investigation and ensure that those responsible were brought to justice.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“No matter what the allegations may be, there are processes and steps to justice,” Ms Okey-Uche said in the statement, insisting that suspects must be given a fair hearing in court and that no one should take the law into their own hands.

The consulate also urged Nigerians in South Africa to remain calm, law-abiding and security-conscious amid ongoing xenophobic and Afrophobic attacks and threats against foreigners.

READ ALSO: Nigeria elected to UN Human Rights Council

It extended its condolences to Mr Odueze’s family and assured Nigerians that it would continue to press for their welfare and fair treatment in South Africa.

PREMIUM TIMES reports that about 1,640 Nigerians have been evacuated from South Africa since the recent wave of xenophobia began in April. A batch of 33 Nigerians was repatriated in August and another 105 in September.

At least five Nigerians have been killed since the latest round of violence began.

PREMIUM TIMES reported the most recent incident in July. The victim, Chika Simon, died during an encounter with the South African Police Service (SAPS)

The Nigerian consulate said he died under questionable circumstances.

This paper also reported previous deaths. These are: Amaramiro Emmanuel, Ekpenyong Andrew, Emeka Iroegbu and Musa Joe.

The Nigerian government has demanded a thorough investigation into the death of Nigerians killed in South Africa. The investigations into these cases are still pending, and no arrests have been made.

World.title: Lagos publishes nationwide directory to help GBV survivors access support
World.content:
The Lagos State government has published a directory of gender-based violence (GBV) coordinators across Nigeria’s 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory to help survivors report abuse and access support services.

The directory, released through the Domestic and Sexual Violence Agency (DSVA), contains office addresses, telephone numbers and email addresses for state-level GBV response contacts.

Onadipe Opebere, head of the agency’s public affairs unit, announced the release in a statement on Monday.

The publication follows a two-day National Convening of GBV State Coordinators hosted by Lagos State to strengthen collaboration among those working on GBV prevention and response.

The initiative received support from the Rule of Law and Anti-Corruption (RoLAC II) Programme, funded by the European Union and implemented by the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance (International IDEA).

“The directory provides key contact details of GBV State Coordinators, serving as a practical resource to support reporting, referrals, and access to appropriate response services for survivors of Sexual and Gender-Based Violence,” the statement reads.

“It is designed to strengthen coordination and referral pathways among stakeholders working in GBV prevention and response, while making it easier for citizens to identify and connect with the appropriate state-level contacts.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The agency urged individuals, government institutions, civil society organisations and community groups to use the directory and share it within their networks.

Ms Opebere said the agency remained committed to strengthening partnerships and coordinated responses to GBV, while helping survivors across Nigeria access timely and appropriate support.

The DSVA is a Lagos State government agency responsible for responding to domestic and sexual violence and providing support services to survivors.

Why GBV is persistent in Nigeria

Deep-rooted cultural norms, gender inequalities and economic dependence have been identified as factors that contribute to the persistence of GBV in Nigeria.

Societal expectations that men should exercise authority while women remain submissive can reinforce unequal power relations and normalise abusive behaviour.

Economic dependence can also make it difficult for some survivors to leave abusive relationships or seek help, particularly when they lack the financial resources to support themselves and their children.

Although Nigeria has enacted laws to address GBV, including the Violence Against Persons (Prohibition) Act, 2015, enforcement remains uneven across the country. The law criminalises several forms of violence and abuse, but gaps in implementation and access to justice continue to pose challenges to efforts to protect survivors.

World.title: The secrets hiding in our environment, By ‘Tope Fasua
World.content:
In several of my books I have agonised over our environment and the need for us to take a keen view and obsess about how we present ourselves. I recall writing a few articles with titles such as “It’s The Environment, Stupid!” (in the style of the famous Clintonian campaign slogan around the Economy in 1998), and “We Cannot Emphasise the Environment Enough”, among others. I pushed the matter in the public space to the extent that Nigeria – and most of Africa – really have little business for now, with the big Climate Change discussions which is the new obsession among developed countries who love to set agenda for everyone. I believe that being corralled into the Climate Change agenda may distract us from what really matters for us, and what is immediately achievable, which is the subject of how we can really take care of our own environment and pick up after ourselves. You cannot enroll for a PhD when you should be learning the ropes in primary school.

My many urban sojourns within Nigeria in recent times has compelled me to write on the environment, again. There seems to be an explosion of urban waste in places like Lagos, Abuja, Port Harcourt, Kano, and perhaps every state capital and large cities across Nigeria, with varying degrees of success in terms of their management. Refuse dumps have been occurring in different places where they hadn’t been in the past. At some point, it looked like deliberate sabotage – and that could be valid because all over the world one of the easiest ways to bring down governments is for whatever mafia that controls waste management to strike. We’ve seen this in the US (New York, New Jersey, California etc), in Italy (Napoli) and in the UK (Birmingham, London) etc.

Driving up the bridge from Bank Anthony way towards the local airport, there is a new refuse dump right at the beginning of the ramp. I recall when people from Old Ojo Road would rush across the express road to dump refuse on the rail track that was being constructed but hadn’t been commissioned. I recall the refuse dumps that assail the eyes when you take the train ride from Yaba to Abeokuta or Ibadan. Even in Gbagada, the green areas have been assaulted. This gives one great concern. In Abuja, many incidences of fly-tipping are recorded; people dumping their trash anywhere, perhaps at night. Large roundabouts are a popular spot. Also, the streams and waterways that snake through Abuja are favorite dumping spots. Even some prime lands which owners have abandoned over time are good spots for the dumping of waste. It’s just overwhelming!

Now, the reason they call some countries ‘shit-hole’ countries is because of their management of urban waste. No matter how adept a nation gets in building fantastic structures and infrastructure, the inability to get on top of waste management is a dead giveaway. Waste management and environmental sanity are therefore arduous tasks, especially because they require unending attention and action. But the approach whereby the government is the victim, running everywhere to pick up after people, and being vulnerable to sabotage, to political vendetta and such, can no longer be the solution. The new approach must actively involve everybody. The incentives must change and be enhanced. Can streets take responsibility for their own outlook? Can communities get rewarded for doing the right thing? Can everyone become a watchdog against improper behaviours? Can the structure we currently have for waste management be expanded urgently, with more equipment, more staff, more technology, and better logistics? Can waste management, and the obsession with a clean environment all over Nigeria be declared as an emergency?

Because what we see as chaos presently, with which political opposition can take digs against incumbent governments, is actually telling us something. It masks great secrets for where we must now head as a people.

The first secret is that an explosion of urban waste actually means urban growth, and probably better standards of living for the people. This World Bank article confirms this theory, meaning that the poverty narrative around Nigeria may not be the reality. The larger part of our urban waste consists of plastics, cartons, food waste, clothing, and such like. The ubiquity of waste management issues should therefore not be seen simply as a disadvantage but as a sign that standards of living are increasing, therefore justifying the larger investments we must now make.

In some of my earlier books, I espoused how Nigeria could launch a large program which encompasses several ministries and which may be titled “Cleanest, Safest, and Most-Organised Nation in Africa Project”. I’ve been thinking about this for over a decade now and it keeps coming back. It is a project that allows us to work on the brains, minds and hearts of our people, to help us gain ownership of our country, one and all, to attract global respect, new investment and tourism, and help take the sail away from the incessant security challenge that we have. I cited the Broken-Windows Theory as an underpinning theoretical framework around such a project, because we need to understand that the bad habits that have now become a culture instead and so must be tackled at a high and comprehensive level.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The environment holds the secret to our greatness as a people. Whereas many Nigerians actively work towards the undoing of the country, but the efforts and striving of the true patriots who want her to make real progress will be enhanced if our environment is spick and span – or tending close to that. Nigeria needs investments. But before investments, we need our respect back from the world. This respect will not be obtained by force of arms but gently and quietly through how we reposition ourselves – especially our environment.

This is why I respect the work being done by people like Tokunbo Wahab in Lagos State. He gets it. Without those valiant efforts, that state – the most urbane in Nigeria and one which qualifies as a middle-income economy – would easily drown in filth and waste. The work hasn’t been fully grappled though. There is still so much to do. Tokunbo can see that it’s a big battle, as he tackles even larger issues of impunity, indiscriminate buildings that block water ways, and such like, and indiscriminate waste dumping everywhere.

A lot more investment is needed in new systems that will allow for waste evacuation. I urge governments at all levels to squeeze out the required money – even if they have to enter into Public-Private arrangements that allow them to spread the investment over time. The waste management business may look unappealing from a distance, but a closer look reveals a lucrative opportunity for everyone across the value chain—from collectors, recyclers and manufacturers to investors, governments and the Nigerian people. Waste is not merely a disposal problem; it is an economic resource waiting to be unlocked. It creates jobs, generates revenue, supplies raw materials, protects public health and improves the environment. In the circular economy, what one person throws away can become another person’s wealth. No investment is a waste—pardon the pun!

We need a national program though; one upon which we can anchor the emotions of our people, one around which we can rally the energy of millions of Nigerians. It is about visioning. It is about optics. We cannot keep inviting foreigners into this country while we leave our environment to chance. We already are coming from a position of disadvantage as a people. The world distrusts us. Around kitchen tables, they talk about Nigeria with suspicion, a little disdain, sometimes pity. Many are unable to express themselves openly about Nigeria because of our status. We are important. But we can do better by starting to position ourselves as a decent nation.

To this extent, as I’ve always asserted, Nigeria can employ and engage millions of her people around environmental work. We can nitpick about our environment. We can expand the circular economy and capture more of our solid waste for recycling. We can enforce more. Our people should be afraid to throw trash from their cars and buses or simply litter the streets. There should be a standing environmental taskforce. Those environmental workers of old (the wolewoles) did a great service to rewire our people’s mentality. Honestly, we need that back today. We haven’t yet graduated from that level to begin to self-regulate. We can see the reality because our now exploded population has become even more careless with the way we keep our environment. As we say in Nigeria, the ‘anyhowness’ is just galling. A renewed focus on the environment, the recruitment of millions of especially young people into sustainable careers there will achieve the following:

Reduce unemployment – especially in these times when we have to battle with the effect of AI on human employment. We have a great opportunity. Increase GDP growth by between 2 per cent to 4 per cent. Help drive new investments into Nigeria, creating new value chains and a new buzz around Nigeria. Improve our dented image by focusing the world on a new energy around Nigeria. Restore our respect in the comity of nations. Rewire the mentality of our people and infuse a new, solid pride in our young ones as they face the future. Reveal the true beauty of our nation and release a deluge of foreign capital inflow – from diaspora and foreigners alike, reversing the phenomenon whereby money only leaves Nigeria but never comes back. Takes attention away from the negative news around our country such as insecurity, corruption etc. Position Nigeria as a true leader in Africa.

I have proposed over time that Nigeria could launch a campaign titled “The Cleanest, Safest, Most-Organised Country in Africa” project. We could call it the COSMOS Project for want of something snazzy. This gives us a programme around which we can rally our efforts and set our vision in a renewable fashion. Of course, we don’t have to achieve this in a jiffy, but a lot will start changing in a short while. I dream about that day. I believe strongly that this is possible. And countries around us are getting smarter. I visited Benin Republic months back for the first time and I saw something similar on the streets of Cotonou. An American lady who came to Nigeria for holidays also visited Benin and was so incensed with Nigeria upon her return. Our population is not an excuse. Our minds, our vision, our standards are the problem. But those can be fixed. I write as an economist. I know that this is a sure bet to permanently reposition our economy for the long term. Not everything is anchored on electricity and natural resources. Sometimes the real solutions are much more subtle, and are there in the open, beckoning on us to act.

See below a chart showing the magnitude of what we can achieve:

‘Tope Fasua is the special adviser to the President on Economic Matters.

World.title: CSLS urges National Assembly to give ACJA amendment bill speedy passage
World.content:
The Centre for Socio-Legal Studies (CSLS) on Tuesday called for a speedy passage of the Administration of Criminal Justice Act Amendment Bill.

The President of CSLS, Yemi Akinseye-George, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN), made the call during the closing ceremony of the centre’s summit on improving the nation’s criminal justice administration through the National Minimum Standards (NMS) project.

Mr Akinseye-George said CSLS, which played pivotal roles in the conception and the subsequent enactment of the Act in 2015, worked with the Federal Ministry of Justice and other stakeholders to conclude the final draft of the ACJA Amendment Bill.

“It is now an Executive Bill, sponsored by the President through the Office of the Attorney-General of the Federation,” said Mr Akinseye-George, a professor of law.

Mr Akinseye-George, whose CSLS, has championed an amendment of the Act in recent years to address the gaps discovered in the law after decade of putting the law into use, urged the National Assembly to give the ACJA Amendment Bill “speedy and thorough consideration.”

He also urged “states and institutions to keep applying the National Minimum Standards,” and vowed support for “evidence-based reform in the sector.”

The ACJA 2015 governs criminal proceedings in federal courts and criminal justice administration regarding federal offences. Most states have since domesticated versions of the laws in their domains.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

However, Mr Akinseye said the Act needed amendment, which informed part of the NMS project.

The NMS project was implemented under the Rule of Law and Anti-Corruption (RoLAC) Programme, funded by the European Union and supported by International IDEA.

The project aims close the gap between what Nigeria’s criminal justice laws promise and what happens in practice.

It also sees to the efficient implementation of the provisions of the Administration of Criminal Justice Act (ACJA) in federal courts and the Administration of Criminal Justice Laws (ACJLs) of various states of the federation.

Importance of the NMS

According to Mr Akinseye-George, the NMS “gives the ACJA and related laws a clear, measurable yardstick for the police, courts, prosecutors, legal aid providers and correctional services.”

The NMS is a document compiled so that no state would fall below in the implementation of the ACJA, and for the purpose of uniformity across all states.

Some NMS project focus on pre-trial issues, dealing with interlocutory proceedings, use of remands, confessional statements, front loading, case management and plea-bargaining.

The CSLS implemented the project in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) and seven focal states – Lagos, Kano, Edo, Anambra, Abia, Plateau, and Adamawa.

Through the project, the CSLS equipped judges, magistrates, lawyers, police, and civil society.

It also trained over 700 rangers and engaged 1,700 relevant stakeholders. In April, the centre organised a capacity-building training for 100 rangers. The training equipped the rangers to champion the reform of the Nigerian criminal justice system.

Rangers are those who volunteer to support and to speak in favour of the proper implementation of the ACJA.

The centre also paid inspection visits to courts, correctional centres, ministries of justice, police commands, the Legal Aid Council and the Administration of Criminal Justice Monitoring Committees (ACJMCs). Through the visits, gaps were identified which were reflected in the Bill. Also, 1000 copies of the NMS documents were produced.

Mr Akinseye-George applauded the European Union for funding. Similarly, he commended the International IDEA, the Federal Ministry of Justice and other criminal justice institutions and the media for their partnership and support.

World.title: Mining Week: Investors demand clear rules, stronger security
World.content:
By Gabriel Ewepu

ABUJA – Investors and key players in Nigeria’s mining sector have called for clearer regulations, improved security and stronger collaboration among government agencies to attract investment and unlock the country’s vast solid mineral resources.

They made the call at the opening of the 11th Nigeria Mining Week in Abuja, identifying insecurity, regulatory conflicts, poor inter-agency coordination and inadequate infrastructure as major barriers to the growth of the sector.

President of the Miners Association of Nigeria, Oba Ayandele Ayanleke, said insecurity along mining corridors and jurisdictional disputes between federal and subnational authorities were undermining operations and eroding investors’ confidence.

Ayanleke urged the government to establish a clearer and more predictable regulatory framework, stressing that stronger partnerships between local and international stakeholders were critical to attracting capital, facilitating technology transfer, creating jobs and generating wealth.

On a recent mining incident, he disclosed that the government had constituted an investigative panel, urging stakeholders to await the outcome of its findings.

Meanwhile, the Country Manager, Segilola Resources Operating Limited, Austin Menegbo, said Nigeria must build on the achievements of its first large-scale commercial gold mine to establish a competitive and sustainable mining industry.

Menegbo disclosed that Segilola produced 91,910 ounces of gold in 2025, with Nigerians accounting for 99 per cent of its workforce.

According to him, the mine has demonstrated that responsible investment, technical expertise, effective regulation and sustained engagement with host communities can support globally competitive mining operations.

He, however, identified regulatory uncertainty, illegal mining, insecurity, poor infrastructure and limited access to finance as challenges requiring urgent government intervention.

He called for streamlined government approvals, predictable regulatory timelines and sustained engagement among operators, investors, host communities and other stakeholders to improve the sector’s investment climate.

He also advocated the formalisation of artisanal and small-scale mining through safety training, improved access to finance, technical support and cooperative structures.

He stressed that efforts to attract investment must go hand in hand with environmental protection, workers’ safety and responsible engagement with host communities.

Similarly, Head of Mission of the Swedish Embassy in Nigeria, Ambassador Anna Westerholm, called for partnerships that prioritise local value addition, workplace safety, community welfare and transparency.

Westerholm said Nigeria could leverage Sweden’s expertise in mining technology, automation, skills development and responsible mineral production to strengthen its mining industry.

She noted that the long-term success of mining projects depended largely on their impact on host communities and the environment, adding that companies must earn public trust to operate sustainably.

The Swedish envoy also underscored the importance of mineral traceability, saying the ability to verify the origin of minerals and the conditions under which they were produced would boost Nigeria’s competitiveness in international markets.

She expressed Sweden’s readiness to deepen cooperation with Nigeria through technical assistance, trade and investment partnerships.

Earlier, Partner and Mining Industry Leader at PwC Nigeria, Cyril Azobu, said the country must translate its abundant mineral resources and growing international interest into bankable projects and sustainable economic growth.

He said achieving this would require a predictable investment environment, credible projects and partnerships capable of connecting local opportunities with international capital, technology and expertise.

Azobu also called for a shift from exporting raw minerals to domestic processing and value addition, saying the move would enable Nigeria to retain more economic benefits from its mineral resources.

He reaffirmed PwC Nigeria’s commitment to supporting the sector through technical expertise, regulatory guidance and engagement with industry stakeholders.

The 11th Nigeria Mining Week is being held under the theme, ‘Unlocking Investment and Growth through Partnerships’.

World.title: Pope Leo has cancerous growth removed in lung operation
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV

Pope Leo XIV had a cancerous growth removed from his right lung in a 90-minute operation on Tuesday and “woke up normally” after the procedure, the Vatican said.

A Vatican source said further tests were being carried out to determine if the cancer had spread.

“To ensure the procedure was radical, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed,” the Vatican said in a statement.

The operation “confirmed the diagnosis of a pulmonary adenocarcinoma, as suspected from the pre-operative tests”, it said.

The pope was in the operating room for a total of three hours and the operation lasted half that time.

“The surgery was successful and there were no complications,” the Vatican said.

A Vatican source said he requested dinner after the procedure.

Leo had entered the hospital smiling and waving earlier on Tuesday hours before the surgery.

The Vatican has said it expects the pope to stay in his room on the 10th floor of Rome’s Gemelli hospital to recover for several days.

His audiences have been cancelled until October 20 and the operation raises questions about whether the pope will go on a lengthy visit to Latin America next month.

– ‘I will pray a lot’ –

The surgery marks the 71-year-old Leo’s first hospitalisation since he became head of the Catholic Church on May 8, 2025.

In a surprise announcement following Angelus prayers on Sunday, Leo told crowds in St Peter’s Square that doctors had discovered a nodule “at a very early stage” during medical checks.

“The doctors believe it would be right to intervene,” he said.

The Vatican has historically been very secretive about the health of popes, but began to be more transparent during the illness of Leo’s predecessor Francis, an Argentine who freely discussed his ailments.

Ahead of the operation, people outside the hospital expressed concern over the pope’s condition.

Giorgia Fei, a 57-year-old Italian, said she had been worried.

“However, the Holy Father is in very good hands here at the hospital because we have some outstanding doctors,” she said.

“I will pray a lot for him.”

Giuseppe Purpura, 72, said he too was concerned.

“He’s still quite young and I really wasn’t expecting this. I thought he was in better health,” he said, noting that “thankfully it was caught in time.”

The Vicar General for the Diocese of Rome, Cardinal Baldassare Reina, led a rosary prayer for the pope inside the hospital chapel which was broadcast by the Vatican. Dozens of people attended and Reina asked all the city’s parishes to join in.

The Vatican secretary of state, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, told ANSA news agency that Leo had been “very calm” about his condition when they met on Monday.

The Vatican told AFP the nodule was found during routine health checks, and there were no symptoms that led to checking the pope’s lungs.

Chicago-born Leo, the first US pope, is sporty and believed to generally be in good health.

He is scheduled to travel to South America from November 6-17 to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

It was not immediately clear what would happen if the pope was forced into a longer recovery.

Under Church law, a figure known as the Cardinal Camerlengo — or chamberlain — takes over administrative duties if the pope dies, but pontiffs do not have a deputy to replace them if they become incapacitated.
