World.title: Champions League: Lookman scores as Atletico down Carrick’s struggling Man United
World.content:
Atletico Madrid’s Nigerian forward #11 Ademola Lookman celebrates scoring his team’s second goal during the UEFA Champions League, league phase, matchday 2, football match between Club Atletico de Madrid and Manchester United at the Metropolitano stadium in Madrid on October 13, 2026. (Photo by Javier SORIANO / AFP)

Atletico Madrid eased to a 2-0 win over Manchester United in the Champions League on Tuesday to pile pressure on Red Devils coach Michael Carrick.

Pablo Barrios pounced inside the first minute for Diego Simeone’s side and after Leny Yoro’s 74th minute red card set United back further, Ademola Lookman added another for the hosts in Madrid.

Man United have made their worst domestic start in 40 years and this league phase defeat in the Spanish capital was another blow, with the team now winless in five games across all competitions.

Carrick handed Carlos Baleba his first start for the club since arriving from Brighton this summer, as well as pushing captain Bruno Fernandes out to the right side.

Atletico were without their skipper Koke, after the death of his mother, while coach Simeone selected Julian Alvarez from the off for the first time this season at the Metropolitano stadium, after he tried to force a departure this summer.

“Defend what we love,” Atletico fans ordered their supporters with a banner display before kick-off and the Rojiblancos were ahead after just 50 seconds.

Manchester United’s English head coach Michael Carrick applauds at the end of the UEFA Champions League, league phase, matchday 2, football match between Club Atletico de Madrid and Manchester United at the Metropolitano stadium in Madrid on October 13, 2026. Atletico Madrid won 2-0. (Photo by Oscar DEL POZO / AFP)

Alex Baena found a way in behind United’s defence and cut the ball across for Barrios, with Ayden Heaven unable to keep the midfielder’s shot from crossing the line.

Bryan Mbuemo might have equalised for the visitors, nudging the ball through Cristian Romero’s legs but firing just wide.

Alejandro Grimaldo came inches away from extending Atletico’s lead with a free-kick which hit the angle between post and crossbar.

The hosts thought they had a second when Johnny Cardoso finished neatly from the edge of the box before half-time but the goal was disallowed after a VAR review showed the ball had struck Marcos Llorente’s hand during the build-up.

Alvarez, yet to score this season for Atletico, hit the post early in the second half.

United rallied and Fernandes’s lob drifted narrowly wide before the Portuguese playmaker hit the crossbar from the left of the box after a corner routine.

However the three-time European champions suffered a setback when defender Yoro was harshly dismissed after a VAR review for bringing down Canada striker Jonathan David as the last man.

It opened the door for Atletico to grab their second, with David foiled by goalkeeper Senne Lammens but London-born Nigeria international Lookman on hand to tuck home the rebound after 79 minutes.

Carrick withdrew playmaker Fernandes, looking ahead to the weekend visit to face rivals Leeds in the English top flight, where improvement is badly needed.

Atletico goalkeeper Jan Oblak saved from United substitute Matheus Cunha in the final stages but there was no way back for United.

Simeone’s side were able to claim their first points after an opening defeat at Liverpool.

World.title: Court overrules El-Rufai’s objection to DSS forensic witness
World.content:
Former Kaduna State Governor, Nasir El-Rufai

A Kaduna State High Court on Tuesday has overruled an objection by former Governor Nasir El-Rufai’s defence team to the testimony of the Department of State Services (DSS) digital forensic expert.

The presiding Judge, Justice Darius Khobo ruled that the prosecution could call the witness, who was subpoenaed by the court, despite his name and evidence summary being absent from the prosecution’s witness list.

The judge held that the defence’s right to fair hearing could be protected by allowing it to cross-examine the witness.

The ruling followed objections by El-Rufai’s senior counsel, Paul Erokoro, who argued that the defence had not received the witness’s evidence summary or the subpoena.

Erokoro submitted that the omission denied the defence adequate notice to prepare for cross-examination and understand the case it was required to answer.

The ICPC prosecution counsel, Ayodele Adedipe, however, argued that failure to include a subpoenaed witness in the proof of evidence did not automatically render the testimony inadmissible.

In its ruling, the court confirmed that the witness had been subpoenaed through an order signed by the court on June 30, 2026.

Khobo said the prosecution’s position reflected the applicable law, citing previous cases in support of the ruling.

The judge held that the witness’s absence from the prosecution’s witness list and evidence summary did not prevent him from testifying because he had been subpoenaed.

He added that the defence’s fair-hearing concerns could be addressed by allowing it to cross-examine the witness.

Earlier, the DSS digital forensic examiner, Shegun Kayode, testified about a forensic examination of communication records and audio recordings allegedly linked to the defendant.

Kayode told the court that specialised software revealed two-way communications involving El-Rufai and suspected associates, including Bashir El-Rufai and another person, between October. 25 and 28, 2025.

He said the findings prompted further analysis of audio recordings received from a communication intelligence server.

The witness explained that he immediately created a forensic image of the original audio file, sealed it and secured it to preserve its technical integrity.

Kayode said subsequent software examination showed that the audio was authentic and had not been artificially generated or manipulated using artificial intelligence.

The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that El-Rufai arrived at the court amid heavy security, accompanied by his wife, Asiya El-Rufai, and Isa Ashiru Kudan, the governorship candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) in Kaduna State.

El-Rufai was brought to court for the continuation of his trial over alleged corruption in a suit filed against him by the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC).

During the proceedings, an audio recording of his interrogation by the DSS concerning the alleged importation of about 10 kilogrammes of thallium sulphate, a highly toxic and strictly regulated substance, into Nigeria was played.

The recording, which lasted about one hour and 30 minutes, contained the interrogation and other exchanges.

The case was adjourned until November. 30 and December 1 for continuation of the cross-examination of the DSS witness by the defence counsel.

Speaking with journalists after the court proceedings, Adedipe said the prosecution had opened its case by calling its first witness, a forensic expert.

He said the witness testified and tendered a forensic investigation report before cross-examination commenced.

Adedipe explained that the proceedings took considerable time because of objections and legal arguments but said the prosecution was able to conclude its presentation with the witness for the day.

He confirmed that the case had been adjourned until November 30 and December 1 for continuation of cross-examination.

Erokoro, counsel to El-Rufai, said the prosecution had opened its case and called its first witness, adding that the lengthy proceedings showed the parties’ commitment to ensuring the trial progressed.

He expressed confidence that his client would be discharged and acquitted of all the charges.

Erokoro said the defence had begun examining the witness’s testimony and would continue to scrutinise the evidence when the court reconvened.

He maintained that the next hearing would provide the defence with an opportunity to test the accuracy and credibility of the prosecution’s evidence.

World.title: ECOWAS Defence Chiefs seek sustained Nigerian support for regional security
World.content:
By Kingsley Omonobi

The outgoing and incoming Chairmen of the ECOWAS Committee of Chiefs of Defence Staff (CCDS) have called for sustained Nigerian support to strengthen regional security cooperation and address growing threats across West Africa.

The two military chiefs made the appeal on Tuesday during a courtesy visit to the Chief of Defence Staff (CDS), General Olufemi Oluyede, at the Defence Headquarters in Abuja.

The outgoing Chairman, Lieutenant General Amara Idara Bangura, who is Sierra Leone’s Chief of Defence Staff, expressed appreciation to Nigeria for its continued support for the ECOWAS defence framework and regional security initiatives throughout his tenure.

Bangura disclosed that he and his successor had spent the previous two days conducting formal handover activities ahead of the transition in the leadership of the ECOWAS defence committee.

He commended Nigeria’s longstanding contributions to peace and stability in West Africa, particularly its support for Sierra Leone during the country’s civil war and subsequent peacebuilding efforts.

He also highlighted Nigeria’s contributions to regional peacekeeping operations, counter-terrorism cooperation and logistical support, describing the country’s role as critical to the security of the sub-region.

The outgoing chairman urged Oluyede to extend the same level of cooperation and goodwill to his successor to ensure continuity in regional security efforts.

In his remarks, the incoming Chairman of the ECOWAS Committee of Chiefs of Defence Staff and Senegal’s Chief of Defence Staff, Vice Admiral Oumar Wade, thanked the Nigerian military leadership for the warm reception accorded the delegation.

Wade identified terrorism, violent extremism, transnational organised crime and maritime insecurity as some of the complex and evolving threats confronting ECOWAS member states.

He described Nigeria as a key regional power and an anchor of security in West Africa, stressing that its continued guidance, participation and support would be essential to the committee’s ability to fulfil its mandate.

Responding, Oluyede thanked the two defence chiefs for their commendation of Nigeria and its Armed Forces, describing their visit as a demonstration of solidarity and a shared commitment to regional peace and security.

The CDS called for stronger unity, cooperation and mutual understanding among ECOWAS member states, urging countries to set aside political differences, divergent interests and bilateral disputes to confront common security threats.

He emphasised that security was indivisible, noting that no country could effectively guarantee its own safety in isolation from its neighbours.

Oluyede reaffirmed Nigeria’s commitment to supporting ECOWAS security initiatives, citing the country’s determination to promote regional peace, integration and development.

He also assured Wade of Nigeria’s full support during his tenure as chairman, expressing confidence that sustained cooperation among member states would strengthen the region’s collective security architecture.

World.title: Ex-gang leader sentenced to minimum 40 years for Tupac murder
World.content:
Duane “Keffe D” Davis, the former Los Angeles gang leader who boasted for years of his involvement in the killing of rapper Tupac Shakur, only to deny it when he came to trial, was sentenced to a minimum 40 years in prison on Tuesday.

The sentence, which will likely see him die in custody, comes three decades after the gunning down of one of the most influential hip hop artists of the late 20th century, and after years of criticism over investigations that went nowhere.

Davis, 63, formerly ran a branch of the feared Crips, one of a patchwork of rival gangs that controlled parts of Los Angeles in the 1990s.

He spent years evading justice and seemingly believed he was beyond the reach of the law when he wrote in his memoir that he had ordered the killing of Shakur.

“For three years, I’ve heard you say some variation of the same thing to law enforcement… in your book, and it’s something like, ‘Yeah, I was involved in this, but I’m different. I’ve moved on. I got out of Compton. I’m a grandfather now,'” Judge Carli Kierny told Davis as she handed down the sentence in a Las Vegas courtroom.

“I’m here to tell you that’s not how this works.”

“You don’t get to take a man from his family. You don’t get to take his very life, his whole future from him, and just walk away from it. Especially when that man is Tupac Shakur,” the judge said.

Shakur was a key figure in a hip-hop rivalry pitting the US East Coast against the West Coast. He was just 25 when he was gunned down in Las Vegas.

A trial heard how Davis ordered the September 7, 1996 killing of the hip-hop artist after his own nephew had been beaten by members of Shakur’s entourage at a Las Vegas casino.

The “California Love” artist was shot about two hours after the casino confrontation by a gunman in a white Cadillac that pulled up at a red light alongside the BMW in which the rapper was riding.

Davis handed the gun to someone sitting in the back seat of the Cadillac and ordered that person to shoot Shakur, who died six days later.

The name of that person has not been definitively revealed and Davis is the only person who was in the Cadillac that evening who is still alive.

The driver of the BMW, Death Row Records co-founder Marion “Suge” Knight, was wounded.

– ‘Born an icon’ –

The killing of Shakur, also known as 2Pac, was one of America’s most famous cold cases, prompting endless debate among music fans over who did it, and why.

Known for hits including “All Eyez on Me,” Shakur — the son of a Black Panther activist — was raised in Harlem and Baltimore, but quickly became the epitome of California hip hop when he signed with Los Angeles-based Death Row Records.

His sister Sekyiwa Shakur paid emotional tribute on Tuesday to her brother, a man whom she said “was born an icon.”

She said their mother “consciously raised him to be a human rights activist, someone to stand up for those weaker and smaller than he was, and that’s who he was to me and all the family. He was the person that you go to for protection.

“He dedicated his career to the advancement of his people. He was gentle and kind to women and children. He fed anyone he knew that didn’t have. He was truly my shining star, my shining prince. He was who God trusted to take care of me.”

Davis offered no words of contrition ahead of the sentence being handed down, vowing only to appeal the guilty finding.

World.title: 2027: Hamzat unveils policy agenda, promises reforms in transport, housing, security
World.content:
The Deputy Gov. of Lagos State, Dr Obafemi Hamzat, has unveiled a policy agenda for the state, promising reforms in transportation, housing, security, technology, food distribution and justice delivery ahead of the 2027 governorship election.

Hamzat made the commitments while presenting his Promise Agenda, tagged, ‘An Afternoon to Discuss the Facts and Figures of Lagos State: The 8th Largest Economy in Africa’.

The event was organised by the Lagos Chamber of Commerce and Industry (LCCI) in collaboration with the Contact and Mobilisation Committee, Formal Sector for PBAT and KOH on Tuesday in Victoria Island, Lagos State.

.

Hamzat, the All Progressives Congress (APC) governorship candidate for the 2027 elections, described it as a social contract with Lagos residents, which he pledged to implement from May 29, 2027, if elected governor.

He said the agenda was designed to establish measurable targets for government, enabling residents to assess performance and hold the administration accountable for its promises.

Hamzat said transportation remained one of Lagos most pressing challenges, noting that traffic congestion costs the state an estimated economic losses of N1 trillion annually, with residents spending an average of four hours daily in traffic.

He said Lagos had a vehicle density of 212 vehicles per kilometre, compared with the national average of 16, making the development of alternative transportation systems imperative.

According to him, the state has identified 63 traffic junctions for improvement and addressed 33 of them, while plans are underway to expand Bus Rapid Transit services, improve terminals, develop rail infrastructure and increase water transportation.

He said his administration would prioritise waterways to reduce pressure on roads, including developing ferry terminals and improving connections between communities such as Ikorodu, Badagry and other parts of Lagos.

Hamzat also promised improved pedestrian walkways, greener public spaces and better organised bus terminals to separate commuters from vehicular traffic.

He said the state aimed to plant 10 million trees within four years.

On water supply, Hamzat said the completion of an ongoing water infrastructure project would provide additional access to water for six million people.

On Jobs, technology and business growth, the APC candidate said the Lagos State Employment Trust Fund had supported businesses and activated about 340,000 jobs since 2019.

He added that his administration if elected, would strengthen mentorship and business management support to help small enterprises survive and expand.

He said the state had proposed four industrial parks in Epe, Badagry, Ikorodu and Ojo under its 2025–2030 industrial policy.

Hamzat also pledged to harmonise government levies and regulatory processes to reduce the burden on businesses, while reviewing charges imposed on petty traders and micro-enterprises.

On technology, he described Yaba as a major technology hub, saying its technology ecosystem had developed into a 15.3-billion-dollar economy with about 2,000 start-ups.

He noted that Lagos was implementing a 1,000-kilometre fibre-optic cable network, with plans to expand it to 6,000 kilometres, while reducing broadband costs and supporting local technology companies.

The deputy governor further added that the state would adopt a local-first procurement approach by giving qualified Nigerian technology firms the first opportunity to supply products required by the government.

On food security and creative economy, Hamzat said the state was developing a 420-hectare food logistics hub and cold-chain network to reduce food wastage, improve storage and cut transportation costs between farmers and markets.

He said: “The cold-chain facilities in Mushin and Gbagada has helped market women reduce logistics costs by 40 per cent while government is expanding medium-scale markets across the state.”

“Also, the state will support farmers through a proposed N500 billion guarantee scheme, alongside arrangements in facilitating the purchase and distribution of locally produced food.”

On the creative industry, Hamzat said Lagos would strengthen training in contract negotiation and intellectual property to enable artists and other creative professionals to earn better returns from their work.

On Justice, inclusion and social welfare,

the APC governorship candidate said the state was working with the judiciary to increase the civil jurisdiction of magistrates courts from N10 million to N15 million to reduce the backlog of cases in the High Courts.

He said the government also wanted landlord-tenant disputes resolved within three months, adding that more courts would be established to improve access to justice.

He disclosed that about 198 people had been prosecuted for domestic violence, stressing the need to strengthen support for survivors and encourage more victims to seek justice.

On inclusion, Hamzat said women-led enterprises performed well among small businesses, adding that the government planned to allocate five per cent of its business support to women-led enterprises.

He also promised to certify artisans and other skilled workers in their preferred languages and establish an online platform where customers could assess their services through reviews.

He said the government would pay 40 per cent of the stipends of trainees placed in companies under its vocational and technical training programmes to encourage businesses to employ them.

Hamzat added that the state would strengthen child protection by ensuring that children below 18 years were either in school or acquiring vocational skills.

On security, he said Lagos had about 6,800 personnel in its safety agency and was recruiting an additional 2,500, adding that the personnel could form a foundation for state policing if the necessary constitutional approval was secured.

He said the state had increased insurance benefits for police officers who died in service to N4 million for junior officers and N10 million for senior officers, stressing the need to improve support for their families.

Hamzat also called for stronger climate adaptation measures, including improved drainage, community protection and early-warning systems to prepare residents for extreme rainfall and flooding.

On housing, the deputy governor said the state would collaborate with private developers to increase the supply of affordable homes, noting that the average period for an African to build a house was about 17 years.

According to him, we will explore housing and mortgage arrangements that enabled young people and low-income earners to secure decent accommodation without sacrificing other basic needs.

Hamzat said the commitments would be assessed against measurable targets to ensure accountability, adding that government, businesses and residents must work together to achieve a more inclusive and prosperous Lagos.

Earlier, the LCCI President, Mr Leye Kupoluyi, stated that the engagement provided an opportunity for the business community to assess the economic policies and development priorities of prospective political leaders.

He said: “it gives us direct impact of government policies on investment, operating costs and business growth.”

Kupoluyi identified five key priority areas for the next administration, which included reducing the cost of doing business, improving infrastructure and mobility, reforming the tax and regulatory framework, promoting economic growth and investment, and empowering small and medium-scale enterprises (SMEs).

He said addressing high energy and logistics costs, traffic congestion, freight bottlenecks and regulatory challenges would improve productivity and create a more conducive business environment.

The LCCI president also called for improved access to capital, technology and markets for SMEs, emphasising the need for stronger collaboration between government and the private sector to unlock Lagos State economic potential.

He reaffirmed the Chamber’s commitment to constructive, evidence-based engagement with political leaders and future administrations.

The LCCI Deputy President, Mr Knit Ulvmoen, emphasised the need to strengthen local manufacturing and reduce Nigeria’s dependence on imported finished goods.

He noted that the country had the people, market and raw materials required to produce more goods locally.

He cited the transformation of Nigeria’s cement industry from heavy reliance on imports to local production and exports as evidence of the benefits of adding value to domestic resources.

Ulvmoen called for greater investment in sectors such as agriculture, pharmaceuticals, textiles, petrochemicals and renewable energy, while stressing that education and skills development are essential to preparing Nigerians for industrial growth and economic self-sufficiency.

In his goodwill message, the Managing Director of Sterling Bank, Mr Abubakar Suleiman, identified Lagos State real estate sector as a major untapped source of capital.

Suleiman urged the government to make land assets more accessible to investors through funding.

He added that Lagos possessed a unique economic advantage as a financial hub, with substantial lending and investment activities already concentrated in the state.

According to him, unlocking real estate value can significantly expand development funding.

“If the government can do this, I am confident that the initiative could attract more domestic investment, boost development and strengthen Lagos ambition to become a leading global financial centre,” he said.

World.title: Appeal court panel hands off SERAP’s N101m defamation appeal
World.content:
The Court of Appeal in Abuja on Tuesday returned the case files in two appeals arising from a N101 million defamation judgment in favour of two operatives of the Department of State Services (DSS) to the Presiding Judge for reassignment.

The appeals were filed by the Incorporated Trustees of the Socio-Economic Rights and Accountability Project (SERAP) and by its Deputy Director, Kolawole Ogundare. The High Court of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) awarded the damages in May.

The panel had earlier heard the first appeal and reserved judgment. It later vacated that order, ruling that the two appeals, which emanated from one judgment, should be heard together for a composite judgment.

The development was the second setback in the matter. Last week, proceedings in Ogundare’s appeal were halted midway.

Before the panel vacated its order, a brief drama played out when SERAP’s lead counsel, Tayo Oyetibo, SAN, told the court that an application was pending for certain persons to be joined as amici curiae (friends of the court).

Prof Olarewaju Fagbohun, SAN, a former Vice-Chancellor of the University of Lagos, rose to address the panel.

He said he appeared for the Columbia Global Freedom of Expression Initiative of Columbia University and for the United Nations Special Rapporteurs on the rights to freedom of peaceful assembly and of association, and to freedom of opinion and expression.

He said the application, filed on October 12 under Order 6 Rule 1 of the Court of Appeal Rules 2021 and Section 6(6)(a) of the 1999 Constitution, sought leave to participate in the appeal.

“We’re seeking the leave of this Hon court to participate in this appeal and assist the court with independent submissions,” he said.

He added that the proposed brief would offer independent legal analysis and relevant comparative and international jurisprudence.

The panel’s lead judge, Justice Danlami Senchi, was unimpressed. “Did the court invite you? Let’s be serious. This is the kind of image we create that is not good for us. We didn’t invite you. On behalf of whom?” he asked.

He added: “I said earlier that we are not here to speak long grammar or waste the court’s time. We didn’t seek for any assistance.”

Fagbohun replied: “We are not adversarial. We’re actually trying to assist this court.”

Justice Senchi said every matter is decided on its merits and that an outsider could be heard only if its interests would be injured. “But you’re not a party in the lower court and in this court,” he said, asking the professor to withdraw the application “so that we can make progress.”

Fagbohun withdrew the application and apologised to the court. The judge commended him: “Your juniors here will be happy for that.”

Mojirayo Ogunlana, who appeared for the Southern African Litigation Centre, also withdrew her application to be admitted as amicus curiae.

The panel then turned to Ogundare’s appeal, the same one that stalled last Friday.

Midway into the hearing of an application for enlargement of time by the appellant’s counsel, Oluwatosin Adesoye, the court voiced displeasure with his presentation, saying he “should have sought the counsel of your seniors.”

“Look at the way and manner you couched your prayers. We can’t grant this. You have to withdraw and refile it,” Justice Senchi said. “This is a court of record. You’re before the Court of Appeal.”

The judge then announced: “We are sending this case file back for reassignment.”

In its appeal, SERAP argues that the judgment was legally and procedurally flawed. Its Appellant’s Brief of Argument, filed by Oyetibo, raises 24 grounds challenging the finding of liability, the damages and the consequential orders.

The group says the central question is whether the claimants proved by credible evidence that the publications referred to them.

“The publications did not name the respondents, and the descriptions relied upon were general physical descriptions which did not, without more, identify the particular individuals who brought the action,” SERAP said.

The publications followed SERAP’s call on President Bola Tinubu to investigate alleged corruption at the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPCL) and reverse fuel price increases. SERAP had alleged that DSS officers entered its Abuja office without proper notice, describing two of them as “a tall, large, dark-skinned woman” and “a slim, dark-skinned man.”

SERAP argues that neither publication identified the claimants by name, rank, designation, office or photograph. It adds that the claimants called no independent witness to show that an ordinary member of the public read the publications and understood them to refer to the two officers.

“No independent witness was called to establish the alleged identification, while the social-media reactions relied upon by the respondents were not tendered in evidence,” the group said.

SERAP also accuses the trial court of supplying the missing identification link by relying, among other things, on its own observation of the claimants’ physical appearance during proceedings.

“The issue was whether the publications identified the respondents when they were published, not whether the respondents happened to fit the descriptions when they appeared before the Court,” it said.

The group further describes the ₦100 million damages as excessive and unsupported by sufficient evidence. It says the trial court relied on claims that the publications affected the officers “mentally and psychologically” and had “gone viral,” without evidence of the extent of publication or of specific professional, financial or reputational injury.

World.title: Nigeria Mourns 140 Migrants Killed in Djibouti Boat Tragedy, Calls for Action Against Irregular Migration
World.content:
Michael Olugbode in Abuja

The Federal Government has expressed condolences to Djibouti following the death of nearly 140 migrants, including 15 children, in a boat disaster off the country’s coast, calling for urgent collective action to address the root causes of irregular migration.

Nigeria, in a statement issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Abuja, said the boat capsized between October 8 and 9, 2026, leaving scores of people missing, according to the International Organisation for Migration (IOM).

The government expressed sympathy to the bereaved families and solidarity with the government and people of Djibouti over the tragedy, describing the incident as a grim reminder of the dangers confronting migrants who undertake perilous journeys in search of economic opportunities.

The statement, signed by the ministry’s spokesperson, Oluwafemi Adeniyi, said the disaster underscored the urgent need to tackle the underlying factors driving irregular migration, strengthen the fight against migrant smuggling and human trafficking, and promote safe, orderly and regular migration.

It stressed that efforts to prevent such tragedies must align with relevant African Union frameworks and applicable international instruments.

Nigeria further emphasised that protecting migrants, particularly children and other vulnerable persons, was a shared responsibility requiring sustained cooperation among countries of origin, transit and destination, as well as regional and international organisations.

According to the government, stronger collaboration is essential to prevent further loss of life, protect migrants’ fundamental rights and dignity, and ensure that migration is managed safely and humanely.

The Federal Government reaffirmed its commitment to working with the United Nations, the African Union and other relevant stakeholders to strengthen migration management, raise awareness about the dangers of irregular migration and develop practical measures to address its root causes.

It also called for renewed international cooperation to safeguard human life along migration routes across Africa and beyond.

The tragedy adds to concerns over the risks faced by migrants travelling along dangerous routes in pursuit of better economic prospects, reinforcing calls for stronger action against criminal networks that facilitate irregular journeys and for more sustainable solutions to the factors compelling people to leave their homes.

Nigeria reiterated its deepest sympathies to all those affected by the disaster and urged collective efforts to prevent similar tragedies.

World.title: Tinubu: Corruption Can’t Be Uprooted in Nigeria Without Independent, Reform Minded Bench
World.content:
.Tasks judiciary to probe prosecution strategies, seal procedural gaps exploited by criminals

Deji Elumoye in Abuja

President Bola Tinubu has declared that the cankerworm called corruption on Nigeria can’t be uprooted without an independent and reform minded bench.

Speaking on Tuesday in Abuja during the annual EFCC/NJI Capacity Building Workshop for Judges and Justices, Tinubu maintained that there will be no meaningful progress in uprooting graft “without an independent, progressive, and reform-minded Bench.”

The President, represented at the occasion by Vice President Kashim Shettima,

while commending the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) for convening the 8th edition of the Judges and Justices Workshop said the workshop with the theme, “Investigation and Prosecution of Economic and Financial Crimes in a Digital Age,” was timely and necessary in “fostering the institutional cohesion required to confront corruption’s ever-changing architecture in Nigeria.

“My Lords, we confront a rapidly shifting criminal landscape. Technology has amplified the audacity and reach of illicit actors, ushering in sophisticated crimes driven by destructive ingenuity. The rise of blockchain technology and artificial intelligence has introduced unprecedented layers of complexity to traditional illicit activities.

“Because these modern crimes constantly mutate, law enforcement and judicial authorities must continuously build capacity to adapt and respond effectively,” he stated.

Tinubu also tasked the judiciary to dismantle the procedural loopholes and flawed prosecution tactics that allow for criminals to escape justice.

He demanded an aggressive overhaul of the justice system to ensure that no well-connected individual can manipulate technicalities to evade the full, crushing weight of the law.

The President urged the judiciary to interrogate existing statutory frameworks against the backdrop of emerging financial crimes.

“Probe prosecution strategies, dismantle outdated precedents, and seal procedural gaps that politically exposed persons and organised crime actors exploit to delay or frustrate trial,” he stated.

Tinubu warned that while financial and economic crimes pose an existential threat to Nigeria, corruption has no respect for status and spares no arm of government.

According to him, framing the anti-corruption campaign as purely an executive agenda is a fundamental error because compromised public services equally affect the executive, legislature, judiciary, and ordinary citizens.

Noting that corruption is a battle for the nation’s collective survival, the President said, “We must no longer permit legal pyrotechnics and procedural pedantry to shelter criminality. The Bench is not merely a mechanical arbiter of rules, but an active guardian of moral order and social equity.

“Law is, by design, an instrument of social engineering; it must invariably prioritise the public good over narrow, selfish interests shielded by technical manoeuvres. Our courts must embody the spirit, and not just the arid letter, of the law.”

Tinubu urged the judiciary to adapt to the shifting dynamics of financial crime, stressing that realigning the nation’s investigative and prosecutorial strategies is critical to preventing institutional obsolescence.

According to him: “We are already on the right trajectory. The EFCC’s recent momentum in tackling cryptocurrency fraud and its commendable strides in recovering virtual assets are highly reassuring. The agency has recovered billions of naira in cryptocurrency investment-related fraud cases.

“In 2025, the agency secured the forfeiture of $22,417.91 (Twenty-Two Thousand, Four Hundred and Seventeen Dollars, Ninety-One Cents) worth of Bitcoin; 1,001,301.87 USDT (One Million, One Thousand, Three Hundred and One USDT and Eighty-Seven Cents) in digital assets; and US$5.6 million linked to the CBEX scheme, while 192 foreigners arrested for cyber-terrorism and cryptocurrency fraud were successfully prosecuted and deported afterwards.”

The President observed that while EFCC’s actions shows agency that is proactive, forward-looking and resolved not to be outpaced by technological innovation, the judiciary “must complement law enforcement by rapidly upscaling its capacity.”

He acknowledged efforts by the Chief Justice of Nigeria (CJN) in reforming the judiciary, even as he pledged the full support of the executive arm of government to ensure that the Nigerian judiciary is adequately equipped to meet the demands of justice delivery in the digital age.”

Earlier, Chief Justice of Nigeria, Hon. Justice Kudirat Kekere-Ekun, said the 8th edition of the event reflects the commitment of the NJI and EFCC to sustain efforts aimed at addressing challenges confronting stakeholders in Nigeria’s justice system.

She said the trend in technology has impacted how digital evidence is obtained and recorded, noting that the effective administration of criminal justice in the digital era require firm and disciplined case management which, according to her, capacity building programmes such as the EFCC and NJI collaboration, aims to strengthen.

The CJN noted that sustained judicial education and capacity development in the justice sector was yielding positive results with the improved conduct of judicial officers especially judges in case management and the dispensation of justice in recent years.

Also speaking, Senate Committee Chairman on AntiCorruption and Financial Crimes, Senator Emmanuel Udende, said the timing of the workshop was apt given the increasing sophistication of financial crimes and corruption particularly cases involving politically exposed persons, which directly impact timely case management and the dispensation of justice.

He assured the stakeholders that the National Assembly remained committed to supporting the enhancement of the war against corruption and financial crimes in Nigeria through proactive legislation.

On his part, the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of the Federation, Prince Lateef Fagbemi, who was represented by the Director of Public Prosecution, Mr Rotimi Oyedepo, urged synergy among stakeholders in addressing emerging challenges in Nigeria’s fight against corruption, stating that one arm of government alone could not effectively address the problem.

He urged judicial officers especially judges and lawyers to leverage opportunities provided during the workshop to enhance their capacities to make investigation more thorough and prosecution more diligent.

In his welcome address, Administrator of the National Judicial Institute, Justice Babatunde Adejumo, said the collaboration between the EFCC and the NJI in enhancing the capacity of judicial officers has become an integral part of government’s efforts to frontally tackle the dynamics and scale of financial crimes in the digital age.

He said the presence of the Vice President at the event was a practical demonstration of the commitment of the Tinubu administration to boost Nigeria’s war against corruption.

Also, Executive Chairman of the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC), Mr. Ola Olukoyede, said the event was a national imperative that has become an important component of the annual programme of both the EFCC and the NJI.

He said the commission under his leadership was reform minded and has recorded unprecedented convictions as well as financial recoveries over the past three years, assuring that transparent and judicious handling of recovered money and property.

The EFCC chairman also regretted the impact of advanced technology on financial crimes as well as other forms of corruption, noting that digital innovation was fast outpacing legal instruments and provisions for prosecution.

World.title: Reps Panel Passes Vote of Confidence in Tinubu, NNPCL, PINL Over Pipeline Security Gains
World.content:
Juliet Akoje In Abuja.

The House of Representatives Committee on Host Communities has passed a vote of confidence in President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, management of NNPC Limited, Pipeline Infrastructure Nigeria Limited (PINL) and its Managing Director, Dr. Osahon Okunbor, following reported improvements in pipeline security, crude oil recovery and production.

The decision followed the adoption of a subcommittee report on a petition against PINL at a special sitting of the committee on Tuesday.

The report recommended an extension of the Federal Government’s pipeline surveillance contract with PINL and declared that the allegations levelled against the company and its managing director were not substantiated.

The petition, dated September 5, 2026, was submitted by the Niger Delta Oil-Producing Communities Reform Movement (ND-OCRIM).

The group alleged irregularities in the implementation of PINL’s contract, mismanagement of contract funds, the need for a forensic audit of the company’s finances, personal expenditure attributed to its managing director and neglect of surveillance personnel.

However, the subcommittee reported that the petitioners failed to honour three invitations issued on September 14, September 22 and October 5, 2026.

It also noted that they neither sent representatives to appear before the panel nor presented documentary evidence to substantiate their claims.

In contrast, PINL appeared before the subcommittee and submitted a written report titled The Impact of PINL Operations on Oil Production and Stability of the Niger Delta, supported by geotagged photographic evidence of its operations.

After reviewing the submissions before it, the subcommittee concluded that the allegations against PINL and Dr. Okunbor remained unsubstantiated.

It consequently recommended the dismissal of the petition, the discontinuation of further investigations into the allegations and formal recognition of the company’s contributions to pipeline protection.

The report also recommended a vote of confidence in President Tinubu, the National Security Adviser, the management of NNPC Limited and the pipeline surveillance contractors identified in the report.

Among the key achievements presented to the subcommittee was a significant increase in the volume of crude oil reaching the Bonny Terminal through the Trans Niger Pipeline (TNP).

According to PINL’s submission, the proportion of crude reaching the terminal rose from three per cent in May 2022 to 98 per cent in September 2026.

The subcommittee further noted that Oil Mining Lease (OML) 11, which had remained shut for 18 months, resumed operations within 90 days of PINL’s engagement.

The report also documented the remediation of 2,049 illegal pipeline connections and the destruction of 1,010 illegal refinery clusters.

PINL stated that its operations commenced in August 2022 and covered 215 host communities, with a workforce of more than 35,600 surveillance guards.

The operations were supported by 28 forward bases, 130 boats, 175 vehicles, 25 drones and 454 personnel from government security agencies.

On community development, the report highlighted the company’s provision of more than 5,000 scholarships, vocational and skills training for over 4,000 women and girls, and flood relief assistance to more than 10 communities in Rivers State.

The committee also commended the management of NNPC Limited for creating an enabling environment for pipeline security operations.

It urged PINL to maintain its engagement with host communities while giving sustained attention to the welfare of surveillance personnel.

The lawmakers’ resolution comes as the Federal Government continues efforts to stabilise the oil and gas sector and increase crude oil production, a critical source of government revenue and foreign exchange earnings.

Production figures attributed to the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission (NUPRC) put Nigeria’s crude oil output at approximately 1.50 million barrels per day in August 2026, while production including condensates stood at about 1.68 million barrels per day.

Average output also reportedly increased from approximately 1.388 million barrels per day in the first quarter of 2026 to 1.525 million barrels per day in the second quarter.

Despite the reported gains, crude oil production remained below the 2026 budget benchmark of 1.84 million barrels per day.

The shortfall highlights the need to sustain measures aimed at protecting oil and gas infrastructure, combating crude oil theft and bringing shut-in production back on stream.

To consolidate the reported achievements, the subcommittee recommended that the Federal Government extend PINL’s pipeline surveillance contract.

It also urged the company to sustain its operational performance and continue implementing community development initiatives.

The report will however be presented to the full House of Representatives for consideration and adoption.

World.title: Nigeria Elected into UN Human Rights Council
World.content:
Michael Olugbode in Abuja

Nigeria has been elected into the United Nations Human Rights Council by the United Nations General Assembly.

The country scored 172 votes out of 181 to get a place in the Council of 15 members expected to serve from 2027 to 2029.

Other countries elected into the Council are Brazil, Burundi, Dominican Republic, Germany, Ghana, Ireland, Japan, Jordan, Kuwait, Nepal, Republic of Moldovan, Ukraine, Uruguay and Zambia.

The roles of the United Nations Human Rights Council (UNHRC) include: Protection of human rights around the world: Promote respect for human rights by all countries; Investigate human rights violations and abuses; Recommend solutions to human rights problems; Review countries’ human rights records regularly; Protect vulnerable groups, including women, children and minorities; Promote equality and fight discrimination.

Encourage international cooperation on human rights issues; Support human rights education and awareness and; Respond to emergencies involving serious human rights violations.

The benefits of being elected into the UN Human Rights Council include international recognition; influence in decision-making; stronger diplomacy; promotion of national interests; improved human rights protection; greater global visibility; sharing experiences and increased responsibility.

Meanwhile, Nigeria Permanent Representative to the United Nations, Dr Jimoh Ibrahim, has sent a congratulatory message to President Bola Tinubu on the election of the country into the council.

World.title: Again, SERAP’s Appeal against N100m Judgment Stalls over Procedural Complications
World.content:
*Panel returns file to presiding justice

Alex Enumah in Abuja

Hearing in the appeal by the Incorporated Trustees of the Socio-economic Rights and Accountability Project (SERAP), against a N100 million judgment debt, for the second time in less than one week failed to proceed as scheduled.

Recall that SERAP and a Deputy Director, kolawole Ogundare, are in two separate appeals challenging the May 5 judgment of a High Court of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), which found them guilty of defamatory publication against the Department of State Service (DSS) and two of its officials.

However, hearing in the appeals was bungled owing to some complications surrounding some applications brought by Ogundare’s lawyer.

While the appeal filed by the Non-Governmental Organization is marked: CA/ABJ/CV/1114/2026, that of the deputy director is marked: CA/ABJ/CV/1105/2026.

Just like last week Friday, the appellate court heard the case of SERAP and reserved judgment but had to abort further proceedings following their inability to comprehend and proceed with the sister case (Ogundare’s appeal).

The development on Tuesday forced the three-member special panel led by Justice Justice Danlami Senchi to hands off from the trial and return the file to the Presiding Justice of the Abuja division of the Court of Appeal, for reassignment to another.

It would be recalled that the special panel had slated October 9 for expeditious trial in the two appeals, seeking to reverse the guilty verdict and avoid the payment of the sum of N101 million as damages for defamation against agency and its two officials.

The matter was stalled at the last hearing owing to late filing of the deputy director’s appeal against the judgment of the trial court.

The appellate court subsequently adjourned to October 13, for hearing and possible adjournment for judgment but, this could not be realized as the panel had to return the file to the Presiding Justice, to be heard on a later date.

After reserving judgment in the first appeal, the panel proceeded to hear that of the deputy director. His lawyer, Mr Oluwatosin Adesioye, sought the court’s permission to amend the reliefs in a pending application concerning additional records of appeal and an extension of time to appeal against the ruling and judgment of the lower court.

Responding, the panel expressed reservations about the application, adding that the court was “finding it difficult to grant the prayers”.

Senchi subsequently advised the counsel to refine the application owing to its complicated nature.

Taking the hint from the court, Adesioye subsequently withdrew the application and sought for a short date to enable him amend the processes.

But, the panel however noted that they don’t have the luxury of time hence, the decision to return the file to the Presiding Justice for reassignment.

“All the two files are hereby returned to the Presiding Justice, Abuja Dvision… for decision on a date for hearing of both appeals that is going to be communicated to the parties,” Justice Senchi said.

Adding that, “In the same breath, the earlier appeal numbered CA/ABJ/CV/1114/2026 and… the order reserving the appeal for judgment, is hereby vacated.”

Earlier, a mild drama ensued when SERAP’s lead counsel, Tayo Oyetibo, SAN, informed the court that an application was before it for certain persons to be joined as amici curiae (friends if the court) in the appeal.

When the court obliged the senior lawyer, Professor Olarewaju Fagbohun, SAN, a former Vice Chancellor of the University of Lagos, to address the court, Fagbohun introduced himself as representing the University of Columbus, acting through its Colombian Global Freedom of Expression Initiative United Nations Special Rapporteurs on Rights to freedom of Assembly and of association.

He also told the court that he and other lawyers were of the United Nations Special Rapporteurs on the promotion and protection of rights to freedom of opinion and expression.

However, the appellate court declined to entertain them on the grounds that the court did not invite them and that they were not parties both at the trial court and the instant court.

“Did the court invite you? Let’s be serious. This is the kind of image we create that is not good for us. We didn’t invite you. On behalf of whom? You’re supposed to be a guide to the junior lawyers in court.

“I said earlier that we are not here to speak long grammar or waste the court’s time. We didn’t seek for any assistance. We didn’t invite you,” Senchi declared.

Taking a hint from the court, Professor Fagbohun promptly withdrew the application and apologized to the court.

The withdrawal and apology promoted the judge to commend him, stressing, “your juniors here will be happy for that.”

Apparently taking a cue from the professor, Mojirayo Ogunlana, who represented Southern African Litigation Centre, also withdrew her application to be the court’s amicus curiae.

Recall that Justice Halilu Yusuf of the High Court of the FCT had on May 5, slammed a whopping N100 million as damages against SERAP and the deputy director for publishing defamatory materials against the DSS and two of its officials.

The two officials, Sarah John and Gabriel Ogundele had in the suit marked: CV/4547/2024, accused SERAP and Oluwadare of making false claims in publications on the group’s website and social media platforms that the claimants invaded their Abuja office on September 9, 2024 and subjected them to harassment.

Delivering judgment, Justice Yusuf held among others that claimants led sufficient evidence that effectively established all the ingredients of defamation.

Justice Yusuf rejected the defence of justification raised by SERAP and Oluwadare on the grounds that they failed to provide evidence that their publications were not based on falsehood.

The judge noted that the words like invasion, forceful entry and harassment were used inaccurately, the defendants having admitted at trial that the DSS officials did not forcefully enter into SERAP’s premises and did not brandish any weapon.

He held that the publications made by the defendants injured the reputation of the claimants in their professional capacity and standing in the society.

Justice Yusuf said: “Having been unable to establish invasion and harassment, the defence of justification fails. There is no doubt that the publication affected the claimants mentally and psychologically.”

The judge said, going forward, it was necessary for care and due diligence on the part of SERAP and its officials before releasing information to the public.

He added that in the exercise of their right to tweet and send information out, the defendants should be aware of the rights of others, particularly as it relates to government agencies and their officials.

The judge dismissed the objection raised by the defendants against the competence of the suit and held that the claimants possessed the requisite locus standi to file the suit over which the court has the jurisdiction to entertain.

He held that as against the defendants’ argument, the claimants must not be named in the publication complained about for defamation to be established.

Justice Yusuf noted that from when the claimants complained about the inaccuracy of the publications, the defendants failed to take any steps to pull down the injurious publication.

He proceeded to adjudge the publications as defamatory and awarded damages of N100 million against the defendants in addition to N1 million as cost of prosecuting the suit.

The judge also ordered the defendants to publish a public apology on SERAP’s website, X handle, two national daily newspapers and two television stations.

He held that the judgment sum shall attract 10 percent per annum from the date of the judgment until the sum is paid by the defendants.

World.title: Foundation Seeks FG Partnership as Screening Flags High Blood Pressure in Communities Across 20 States
World.content:
Michael Olugbode in Abuja

In Our Mind Foundation, a health and community development organisation, has called on federal and state health authorities to establish a formal partnership with its Healthy Nigeria Movement to expand community screening and improve access to medical care across the country.

The foundation, while stating that it has conducted community screening outreaches in 20 states, seeks institutional recognition and an agreed role as a community screening and referral partner working alongside established healthcare services.

It said preliminary findings from its outreach programme showed that 48.74 per cent of reported blood pressure readings fell within its high blood pressure category, while 5.74 per cent were classified as low blood pressure.

The foundation’s presentation also reported high blood glucose readings in 18.33 per cent of the screening results and low readings in 9.12 per cent.

However, the figures have yet to be validated against the underlying records and should not be interpreted as representative of the wider Nigerian population.

The foundation said the findings highlighted the need to take routine health checks closer to communities and establish dependable referral pathways through which people with concerning results can receive appropriate clinical assessment.

The call comes amid global concern over cardiovascular diseases, which the World Health Organisation identifies as the leading cause of death worldwide. An estimated 19.8 million people died from cardiovascular diseases in 2022, accounting for approximately 32 per cent of global deaths, according to the WHO. More than three-quarters of these deaths occurred in low- and middle-income countries.

The organisation’s founder, Iruoma Obiesie Onuko, popularly known as Nurse Angel, while addressing a press conference in Abuja said community-based screening could provide an opportunity to identify potential health concerns before they develop into medical emergencies.

She said the foundation was taking blood pressure and blood glucose checks to people’s doorsteps, marketplaces, streets, schools, churches and other places where communities gather.

According to her, the outreach combines screening with health education and practical support to help participants understand concerning results and seek further assessment.

The foundation noted that high blood pressure may occur without obvious symptoms, meaning people who feel well may still have elevated readings requiring medical attention.

It said its teams had encountered participants with concerning blood pressure and blood glucose readings, including people whose results required further assessment.

The organisation added that it had supported participants with severely elevated blood pressure to access urgent hospital assessment, assisted with medical costs where resources were available and provided follow-up support.

It has also engaged older people, visited hospitals and assisted individuals experiencing difficulties accessing care.

The foundation said these interventions were intended to bridge the gap between identifying a potential health problem and helping the affected person reach appropriate healthcare services.

Under its proposal, In Our Mind Foundation wants a technical partnership meeting involving federal and state health authorities, primary healthcare organisations and relevant clinical institutions.

It proposed that any agreement should clearly define community outreach responsibilities, geographic coverage, clinical oversight, screening standards, team training, equipment requirements and quality-control measures.

The proposed framework would also establish referral links with designated healthcare facilities, urgent escalation procedures, follow-up arrangements and a system for transparent reporting and joint evaluation.

The foundation said it could contribute community mobilisation, local relationships and organised teams, while healthcare institutions would provide clinical oversight, further assessment and continuing care.

It argued that a formal arrangement would help ensure that community screening did not end with the recording of a result but led to appropriate action where necessary.

The organisation is also proposing a 12-month programme to strengthen existing outreach activities and expand delivery in line with the readiness of local teams and receiving healthcare facilities.

Under the proposed arrangement, participating partners would regularly review the number of people reached, valid checks conducted, referrals made, clinical assessments completed and follow-up actions undertaken.

The foundation said it would also account for resources used and protect participants’ personal health information.

It maintained that measurable outcomes, clearly defined responsibilities and transparent reporting would be essential to building institutional confidence and ensuring that expansion was sustainable.

In Our Mind Foundation said its wider network had a presence in every state, while its community screening programme had completed outreach activities in 20 states.

Through the In Our Mind Healthy Nigeria Movement, it provides free blood pressure and blood glucose checks, health education, referral assistance and follow-up support through monthly outreach activities.

Local teams mobilise participants, provide information, conduct checks and help people understand the next steps when a concerning result is identified.

The foundation said its community relationships offered an opportunity to strengthen collaboration with established healthcare services and improve the connection between community-based interventions and formal medical care.

Onuko, a UK-based senior mental health nurse, public speaker and coach, said the foundation’s work reflected the relationship between health, opportunity and human development.

She explained that the organisation grew from a youth initiative associated with Nigeria’s centenary programme in 2014, which encouraged young people to contribute ideas and solutions. The initiative’s reflections and activities were consolidated into the book In Our Mind, followed by the establishment of the foundation and its talk show.

The organisation has since extended its activities to children, adults and older people, with community health education becoming one of the practical expressions of its broader mission.

The World Health Organisation (WHO) has emphasised the importance of early detection and management of cardiovascular risk factors, including raised blood pressure and blood glucose. These factors can be assessed in primary healthcare settings and may indicate an increased risk of heart attack, stroke and other complications.

However, screening alone does not establish a diagnosis. A concerning result must be interpreted in context and followed by appropriate clinical assessment, with treatment decisions made by qualified healthcare professionals.

The foundation acknowledged the importance of clinical oversight and quality assurance, proposing that any government-supported programme should include agreed screening standards, competent personnel, suitable equipment and clear referral arrangements.

It also proposed collaboration with universities, professional organisations, international health bodies and diaspora professionals to support training, evaluation, technical expertise and knowledge exchange.

The organisation has invited the media to publicise the initiative and encourage wider participation in efforts to make routine health checks more accessible.

It said its immediate priority was to establish a formal delivery agreement with relevant government and healthcare partners before expanding the programme further.

The foundation said its objective was to build a more dependable pathway between community screening and appropriate care, allowing people to access understandable health information, timely assessment and follow-up support.

It urged prospective partners to work with the organisation to strengthen the clinical connections behind its existing community reach, arguing that accessible screening would be more effective when people who need further care could also reach it.

World.title: Adesina: Africa’s Youth Are Assets, Not Liabilities
World.content:
*Urges leaders to invest in skills, jobs

*Former AfDB president says poor education, unemployment, lack of access to finance are wasting continent’s demographic advantage

Michael Olugbode in Abuja

Former President of the African Development Bank (AfDB), Dr. Akinwumi Adesina, has challenged African governments to stop treating their growing youth population as a potential burden and instead invest in education, healthcare, skills, technology and entrepreneurship to drive economic transformation.

Adesina warned that Africa’s demographic advantage would remain unrealised unless governments deliberately equipped young people with the capabilities, resources and opportunities to create businesses, develop technologies and generate employment.

He made the call while delivering the keynote address, titled “Africa Next: Building the Demographic Asset Class,” at the inaugural Seyi Tinubu Colloquium in Lagos on Monday.

The colloquium, which brought together political leaders, business executives, policymakers and youth advocates, provided a platform for discussions on leadership, enterprise, innovation and the role of young people in shaping Nigeria’s future.

Adesina argued that population growth alone could not guarantee prosperity, insisting that the real value of a country’s human resources depended on how effectively its people were educated, skilled, kept healthy and connected to economic opportunities.

“People are not liabilities. Young people are not liabilities. A young growing population is not a liability,” he said, according to reports of his address.

He maintained that Africa’s challenge was not simply the size of its youthful population but the failure of economic and institutional systems to develop its potential.

The former AfDB chief said governments must move beyond measuring demographic growth and ask what young people would be able to create, the businesses they could establish and the technologies they could develop to solve the continent’s problems.

He identified quality education as a critical foundation for economic development, arguing that investment in human capability was as important as spending on roads, electricity, transport networks and other physical infrastructure.

Adesina described education and the development of intellectual capacity as essential to building societies capable of innovating, competing globally and generating sustainable prosperity.

He also urged African youths to embrace artificial intelligence and digital technologies, while developing solutions tailored to the continent’s needs rather than remaining consumers of innovations produced elsewhere.

He said a skilled young person with access to technology, capital and markets could progress from being a job seeker to a business owner and, ultimately, an employer.

Adesina warned that unemployment and limited opportunities should not automatically be interpreted as evidence of a lack of ambition or ability among young people.

Instead, he said, the problem often lay in inadequate education, limited access to finance, unreliable infrastructure and institutions that failed to connect talent with productive opportunities.

The development economist called for stronger support for entrepreneurship, particularly through financing systems capable of backing promising young business owners who might lack conventional collateral.

He argued that financial institutions and governments needed to look beyond the risks associated with young entrepreneurs and recognise their potential to create businesses, jobs and wealth.

Without such support, he warned, Africa risked wasting the productive capacity of a generation that could otherwise help accelerate economic growth and improve the continent’s competitiveness.

Adesina also emphasised the importance of reliable electricity, effective institutions and an enabling business environment in allowing young people to turn ideas into viable enterprises.

His position reflects a broader development challenge facing African economies: translating a rapidly growing working-age population into productive employment requires not only education and skills but also investment, functioning infrastructure and opportunities to use those capabilities.

Adesina urged African youths to position themselves at the forefront of emerging technologies, particularly artificial intelligence, digital services and innovation-driven enterprise.

He argued that digital technology could allow African entrepreneurs to develop products and services for international markets, opening opportunities beyond their immediate geographical locations.

However, he stressed the need for Africa to develop and adapt technologies to address its own economic and social realities, including challenges in agriculture, healthcare and other essential sectors.

The former AfDB president said investment in technical education and practical skills should be accompanied by access to capital and markets, enabling young people to build sustainable businesses rather than remain dependent on limited employment opportunities.

He also called for deliberate investment in healthcare, noting that a productive population requires the health and wellbeing necessary to participate in economic activity.

Adesina highlighted youth-focused initiatives in Nigeria, including the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND), the Tertiary Education Trust Fund (TETFund) and the Investment in Digital and Creative Enterprises (i-DICE) programme.

The initiatives target different aspects of education, institutional capacity and enterprise development, but Adesina’s broader argument was that sustained investment must connect learning and skills to productive opportunities.

He said young Nigerians needed an environment in which they could acquire relevant knowledge, access affordable financing, develop innovative products and build enterprises capable of creating jobs.

For Africa’s demographic potential to translate into economic returns, he argued, governments must make human development a central component of their development strategies.

“The more important questions are: What will they be able to do? What will they create? What businesses will they build?” he asked.

He urged African leaders to make youth empowerment a core economic priority, warning that the continent’s future prosperity would depend less on the number of young people it had than on what they were enabled to accomplish.

The message adds to calls at the colloquium for greater youth participation in national development and stronger collaboration between established leaders and younger generations.

Lagos State Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu also called for greater investment in youth leadership, mentorship, education and innovation, urging established leaders to create opportunities for younger people to gain experience and contribute to nation-building.

The colloquium’s discussions underscored the importance of giving young Nigerians opportunities to participate in decision-making and develop the skills needed to assume greater responsibilities.

For Adesina, however, the central issue remains whether governments and institutions can create the conditions for young people to convert their abilities into economic value.

He maintained that Africa’s demographic advantage would only become a source of prosperity when investment in education, health, technology and skills was matched by access to finance, reliable infrastructure and opportunities to establish businesses.

The former AfDB president urged African governments to place young people at the centre of economic planning, arguing that developing their capabilities was essential to building competitive economies, generating employment and securing the continent’s long-term future.

World.title: Gbenga Adeyinka’s Laffmattazz Tour to End in Lagos

World.title: ‘Betray his whole family’: Angelique Gerber shades Jacques Potgieter?
World.content:
Did Angelique Gerber shade her ex, Jacques Potgieter? Images via IG

Angelique Gerber has shared a cryptic post alluding to her ex, Jacques Potgieter. This comes after the actress and the former Springbok fuelled rumours that they had reconciled following a four-year separation.

During that time, Jacques dated another woman, whom he split from in June.

Jacques and Angelique married in 2016 and have three children together: son Jacques Jnr and twin daughters Annabella and Olivia.



ANGELIQUE GERBER THROWS SHADE AT EX, JACQUES POTGIETER?

On her Instagram Stories, Angelique posted several cryptic quotes about “exes”.

One read: “Your ex is running someone else’s life. You are safe”.

Another stated: “If you ever feel stupid….just remember a woman saw a man betray his whole family and still thought, ‘that’s my soulmate”



Angelique Gerber’s IG Stories.

The former 7de Laan actress appeared to be shading her ex, Jacqus Potgieter, and implying that he had moved on to another relationship.

It comes as Jacques has deleted pictures of himself and Angelique, which followers believed alluded to their short-lived reconciliation.

In several since-deleted posts, the former couple are seen embracing each other. In one pic, Jacques carried Angelique in the air, whilst in a third, she sat on his lap.



“I hit the bullseye”, he captioned the post. Referring to his ex, he posted in another: “You make my heart beat fast again”.

Jacques Potgieter deleted pictures of him with his ex.

Images via IG

WHAT WENT WRONG?

Jacques Potgieter and Angelique Gerber wed a decade ago on a wine farm in the Western Cape.

The couple began dating in 2014, when Angelique played the popular character “Clara” on the now-defunct SABC soapie 7de Laan.



In mid 2022, Jacques allegedly admitted to being unfaithful to his Springbok wife, Angelique Gerber in a series of Instagram Stories.

At the same time, Angeliqe posted a cryptic post on her IG Stories that read: “The truth always comes out”.

Jacques later claimed his account was “hacked” and assured the public the accusations about his marriage and alleged affairs were false.



Angelique then posted an apology on her account, implying the same.

By Christmas, it was clear the couple had officially split after removing all romantic posts featuring each other. To further fuel the fire, Jacques began posting pictures with his new girlfriend, Lizane Wagner.

Fast forward to 2023, and Angelique put Jacques Potgieter on blast for failing to financially support their three children.



In June, the retired rugby player – now a head coach for Centurion Rugby Club – split from Lizane.

This followed a four-year relationship with the woman many have accused of being behind his marriage breakdown.

Speaking to an Afrikaans publication, Lizane confirmed their break-up, adding that she was not the “other woman” in her ex’s marriage.

World.title: Pensioner feeding several dependants on one SASSA grant shares his biggest fear
World.content:
A Mpumalanga pensioner says his biggest concern is not his own survival but his children’s future. The Older Person’s Grant recipient, who asked to remain anonymous, shared his story in The South African’s SASSA grant survey.

He has received the grant for three years. Five people depend on that single grant at home, and he says it simply does not stretch far enough.

Children’s future weighs on the pensioner

When asked about his biggest financial concern, the pensioner pointed to his children’s future.



That worry is rooted in a hard reality. Someone in his household has gone without food in the past month. He regularly struggles to make ends meet and runs out of money before the month ends.

He spends his grant on a mix of essentials, from food to everyday household costs. With several people relying on one income, every rand is already accounted for long before the next payment arrives.

Owning his home gives the family a roof over their heads, but it does not guarantee food on the table.



Still searching for work

The pensioner is unemployed and actively looking for work. He has experience in construction and general labour and says he is willing to relocate for the right opportunity.

He believes a job would give his family the security the grant alone cannot provide.

Long queues and waiting times at SASSA offices remain his biggest challenge with the grant system, although he says his payments have been straightforward. He rates SASSA’s communication with recipients as poor and has never applied for additional government support because he did not know what else was available.



His call for a bigger grant

The pensioner acknowledges that the grant helps his household.

“The grants does help a little bit,” he said.

However, he wants to see the amount rise.

“If it can be increased it will be better,” he added.



He suggested R5 000 a month would make a real difference for families like his. If he could change one thing about SASSA, he would increase the grant amount.

For now, he continues to stretch one grant across an entire household while hoping for a better future for his children.
