World.title: Africa: Rwanda Set to Welcome Formula One Back to Africa, 30 Years Later
World.content:
Frenchman Alain Prost claimed the last of his four Formula One world championships at the Kyalami Circuit near Johannesburg, South Africa, in 1993, the last time the continent hosted a Grand Prix. The event's subsequent collapse brought Formula One's presence in Africa to an abrupt end.

More than three decades later, Africa is preparing for a likely return to the sport's calendar, with Rwanda securing a 10-year partnership to host a Grand Prix, with the inaugural race projected for the early 2030s.

South Africa and Morocco have also been linked to efforts to bring Formula One back to the continent, but Rwanda's agreement marks a significant step towards making that ambition a reality.



For Rwanda, however, the proposed Grand Prix is beyond motor racing. The government sees it as an opportunity to attract investment, boost tourism, create jobs and develop technical skills, while positioning the country as a regional hub for business and international sporting events.

During an exclusive interview with The New Times, Sports Minister Nelly Mukazayire said Rwanda viewed the agreement as a responsibility to the wider continent, with the potential to open new opportunities for African talent and businesses.

"The excitement of F1 had been for so long left out of Africa, and Africans are known to be good fans," she said, describing the partnership as a long-term commitment whose benefits should be felt beyond Rwanda.

With Africa's population estimated at around 1.3 billion, much of it young, Mukazayire said bringing Formula One back would offer opportunities to expand participation in a sport that has largely been absent from the continent for decades.

The announcement follows President Paul Kagame's declaration at the FIA Awards in Kigali in 2024 that Rwanda was bidding to host a Formula One Grand Prix.

ALSO READ: Kagame says Rwanda's bid to host Formula 1 Grand Prix 'progressing well'

Why Rwanda secured the deal

According to Rwanda Development Board (RDB) Chief Executive Officer Jean-Guy Afrika, the country's experience in hosting major international sporting events was among the factors that strengthened its bid.

Rwanda has hosted several high-profile competitions and gatherings, including the Basketball Africa League (BAL), the 2025 UCI Road World Championships, the FIFA Congress and the FIA Awards.

Afrika said the country had demonstrated its ability to organise large-scale events while presenting a broader vision that links the proposed Grand Prix to tourism, infrastructure and economic development.

"I think there are several reasons why F1 ended up choosing Rwanda. It's not the first time that we organise a large-scale sporting event. We've already shown an ability to execute and deliver large-scale events here in Rwanda," he said.

"The second one was probably vision, and it was very clear when we started bidding for the event to happen here that it was bigger than just F1 itself and was part of a larger project that ties with the airport and driving tourism," he added.

The government is pursuing the project through a consortium involving public institutions, private-sector partners and technical specialists, working alongside Formula One and the Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA).

Afrika also emphasised that Rwanda's selection should not prevent other African countries from pursuing opportunities to host the sport in the future.

"We very much welcome other countries joining and placing bids and competing for Formula One," he said.

A huge boost for tourism

The planned Grand Prix will be presented by Visit Rwanda, extending the country's strategy of using international sports partnerships to raise its profile and attract visitors.

The tourism brand has partnered with prominent sporting organisations, including English football clubs Arsenal and Bayern Munich, French side Paris Saint-Germain, Spanish club Atlético de Madrid, the NBA's Los Angeles Clippers and the NFL's Los Angeles Rams. Rwanda has also been involved in the Basketball Africa League.

ALSO READ: Hamilton, Verstappen welcome Africa's potential return to F1 calendar

Afrika described Formula One as a natural extension of the strategy, offering access to a global audience while creating opportunities to attract more international and African tourists.

"It's a continuation of the strategy to use sports to increase the country's visibility and drive inbound tourism. The strategy has been very successful," he said.

According to Afrika, Rwanda recorded $685 million in tourism receipts in 2025 and is targeting $1.9 billion in 2026.

He said the Grand Prix would support efforts to grow tourism by attracting visitors beyond the race itself, with opportunities to promote Rwanda as a destination for leisure, business and other sporting activities.

More than 100 million Africans follow Formula One, according to figures cited by Afrika, with approximately 60 per cent of the audience aged below 35.

"The idea is to continue to use Visit Rwanda, which is presenting the F1 race, to drive tourism to the country and, in this particular case, not only global tourism but also African tourism," he said.

The size and age profile of the audience, he added, make the continent an important market for Formula One as it seeks to expand its reach.

Bugesera airport city at the centre of investment plans

Rwanda expects the Grand Prix to stimulate economic activity across hospitality, construction, transport, logistics, retail, financial services and real estate.

Afrika said the event should be viewed as a long-term investment rather than expenditure on a single race, with potential returns extending across the wider economy.

"It's an investment. It's not an expenditure for a single event. And it's a long-term investment with several ways in which we expect returns to come back to the economy," he said.

A key part of the plan is the development of Bugesera International Airport and an airport city around the facility. The proposed commercial hub is expected to accommodate logistics operations, hotels, apartments, restaurants and other businesses serving travellers and investors.

According to Afrika, the new airport is expected to increase passenger-handling capacity from about one million to more than five million, creating additional opportunities for businesses serving international arrivals.

He said the Grand Prix could amplify the economic potential of these developments by generating demand for accommodation, transport, food services, retail and other activities.

"Hotels, restaurants, retail outlets, but also logistics, because when tourists visit, they have to be able to move. Financial services, because there will be a lot of transactions happening," he said.

Construction is also expected to benefit as Rwanda develops the infrastructure needed for the race, including access roads and facilities for teams, officials, spectators and other visitors.

Beyond existing businesses, the government hopes the event will encourage new investors to establish operations around the airport city.

"We also expect it to drive new investments, not just for existing investments and hotels and hospitality to benefit, but for new investments to come in," Afrika said.

He added that new businesses could create jobs, expand the tax base and increase government revenue available for infrastructure and social and economic development.

However, the scale of those benefits will depend on how effectively Rwanda attracts investors and converts the expected increase in demand into sustainable business activity.

Preparing for a decade of racing

Under the agreement, Rwanda expects to host a Grand Prix annually for 10 years, with the first race projected for the early 2030s.

Mukazayire said preparations would extend well beyond the construction of a racing circuit, requiring investment in transport, accommodation, restaurants, entertainment, operational systems and the workforce needed to deliver the event.

She acknowledged that hosting Formula One would be a major undertaking but said Rwanda would draw on its experience in organising international competitions and seek expertise from across Africa and beyond.

"Our target is to make sure that we run an African Grand Prix that represents long-term value for Rwandans and for Africa," she said.

The government's ambition is to integrate the race into a wider ecosystem of infrastructure and services, ensuring that investments made ahead of the inaugural event continue to support economic activity throughout the partnership.

Afrika said the new infrastructures in Bugesera including the airport and other amenities that are part of the Airport City supporting will be important elements of that broader vision, with Formula One expected to help increase demand for the facilities and services being developed.

Close 

Creating opportunities for young Rwandans

Beyond tourism and investment, the government wants the Grand Prix to support local talent development and create career opportunities in motorsport.

Mukazayire said the initiative aligns with Rwanda's sports strategy, which prioritises talent development, increased participation and employment.

She noted that motorsport encompasses much more than professional driving, offering opportunities in engineering, mechanics, vehicle technology, technical support and event management.

ALSO READ: F1 in Rwanda: A gateway to opportunities for African youth

The government also envisages establishing a motorsport academy to help young Rwandans develop the skills needed to participate in the industry.

"We're being intentional in giving an opportunity to an African or a young Rwandan to also enter into that sport," she said.

"There is a place for a young Rwandan in this motorsport, whether it's behind the wheel, whether it's crafting the wheel or even running the event," she added.

The expected economic activity could also create employment in hospitality, construction, transport, retail and financial services, opening opportunities for people whose skills are not directly related to racing.

For Africa more broadly, the return of Formula One could provide a platform to develop technical expertise, strengthen participation in motorsport and connect local talent with the global industry.

Rwanda's challenge will be to translate the agreement into tangible benefits through infrastructure development, investment, training and job creation.

As preparations move forward, the government is betting that the Grand Prix can become more than a sporting spectacle, serving as a catalyst for tourism, business expansion and the development of motorsport in Rwanda and across Africa.

World.title: Rwanda: Kagame Announces 10-Year Formula One Grand Prix Deal
World.content:
President Paul Kagame has announced a 10-year agreement for Rwanda to host a Formula One Grand Prix, with the inaugural race expected in the early 2030s.

President Paul Kagame has announced a 10-year agreement for Rwanda to host a Formula One Grand Prix, marking a major step towards the championship's return to Africa after nearly four decades.

The inaugural race is expected to take place in the early 2030s, bringing Formula One back to the continent for the first time since the 1993 South African Grand Prix.

The agreement follows years of discussions between Rwanda, Formula One and motorsport authorities over the conditions required to bring the championship back to Africa.

ALSO READ: Hamilton, Verstappen welcome Africa's potential return to F1 calendar

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The race will be staged on a purpose-built circuit in Bugesera, about 40 kilometres south of Kigali and near the new Kigali International Airport.

The circuit will be developed to FIA Grade 1 standards as part of a wider sports, tourism and commercial development led by the Rwanda Development Board (RDB).

Designed around Bugesera's natural landscape and elevation changes, the track is expected to provide a challenging racing experience for drivers while offering strong viewing opportunities for spectators.

Beyond Formula One race weekends, the facility is expected to host other motorsport competitions, conferences, major events and entertainment activities.

Kagame said the agreement would give African motorsport fans greater access to Formula One while opening opportunities for young people to pursue careers in motorsport and related industries.

He added that the development of the circuit, alongside the new international airport, would support employment, tourism, investment and business growth in Rwanda and the wider region.

Formula One's return to Africa is also expected to open the championship to a growing audience on the continent. More than 100 million fans across Africa follow the sport, with nearly 60 per cent of fans in key Sub-Saharan African markets aged below 35.

Rwanda has in recent years expanded its profile as a host of major international sporting events.

The country has hosted the UCI Road World Championships, the Basketball Africa League, the 2023 FIFA Congress, the 2024 FIA General Assemblies and the FIA Awards Ceremony.

The Formula One Grand Prix, presented by Visit Rwanda, is expected to further support the country's efforts to attract tourists, investors and international businesses.

Beyond hosting the race, the project is expected to create jobs, develop local skills, support businesses and attract investment, with Rwanda and Formula One aiming to deliver long-term economic and social benefits.

Close 

Mohammed Ben Sulayem, president of the Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA), said Formula One's return to Africa would expand motorsport's reach and help develop talent across the continent.

He said the FIA would work with Formula One and its partners to ensure the new circuit meets the required international safety and technical standards.

ALSO READ: F1 in Rwanda: A gateway to opportunities for African youth

Stefano Domenicali, president and chief executive of Formula One, said Rwanda's addition to the calendar would bring the championship to every inhabited continent from the next decade.

He said the partnership would seek to deliver lasting benefits through tourism, investment, skills development and opportunities for local businesses.

Further details, including the inaugural race date, construction milestones and race-weekend plans, will be announced later.

World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: Ex-DR Congo President Kabila to Lead New 'Politico-Military' Alliance With M23 Rebels
World.content:
Former Congolese President Joseph Kabila signing the documents formalising the creation of the Front for the Rebuilding of the Nation (FRN), a political and military movement, on 12 October 2026 in Goma, in the east of the DRC.

Former Democratic Republic of Congo president Joseph Kabila has joined forces with the Rwanda-backed M23 armed group to lead a new political and military alliance, marking his most direct intervention yet in the conflict that has gripped the country's east.

The alliance was unveiled on Monday at a joint press conference at Kabila's residence in Goma - the main city in eastern DRC which has been under M23 control since January 2025.

The new organisation, known as the Front pour la Refondation de la Nation, or FRN, was presented as a "politico-military" movement that would bring together the resources and forces of Kabila's supporters and the rebels.

Its stated objective is to "put an end to tyranny by any means, including force".

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Kabila will head the movement, with senior rebel figures serving as his deputies.

The announcement represents a significant escalation in the former president's confrontation with the government of his successor, Félix Tshisekedi, and brings together one of the country's most prominent political figures with an armed movement that controls large areas of eastern DRC.

Kabila, 55, ruled the country from 2001 until 2019 and has largely stayed out of public view since leaving office.

He was sentenced to death in absentia in 2025 after being convicted of "complicity" with the M23.

Congolese authorities have also accused him of being one of the driving forces behind the Congo River Alliance - known by its French acronym AFC - which previously served as the political wing of the M23 before being dissolved.

Kabila has denied those allegations.

Kabila death sentence deepens political and regional divides in DR Congo

Political tensions ahead of 2028

The alliance comes as political attention increasingly turns to 2028, when Tshisekedi is due to complete his second and final five-year term under the constitution.

Figures within the presidential majority have in recent months raised the prospect of constitutional changes, prompting opposition concerns over whether the rules on presidential mandates could be revised.

Kabila first came to power in 2001 after the assassination of his father, Laurent-Désiré Kabila. He was elected president in 2006 and re-elected in 2011, before eventually stepping down following the 2018 election that brought Tshisekedi to power.

DRC opposition postpones protest after Tshisekedi announces national dialogue

Conflict and stalled peace efforts

Close 

M23, whose leadership is drawn largely from the Congolese Tutsi community, first launched an insurgency in eastern DRC in 2012 and returned to arms in late 2021.

The group has since captured extensive territory in North and South Kivu, including Goma.

The United Nations and Western governments accuse Rwanda of supporting the rebels, a charge Kigali denies.

Eastern DRC has been affected by armed conflict for more than three decades, displacing millions of people despite repeated diplomatic efforts.

A Washington-backed agreement between Kinshasa and Kigali signed in December has so far produced little change on the ground, while a separate ceasefire process agreed between the Congolese government and M23 under Qatari mediation in July 2025 has also failed to halt the fighting.

Kabila's new role now ties the eastern rebellion more directly to the political struggle over Congo's future leadership.

(with newswires)

World.title: Embattled Soros-backed DA blames ‘criminal’ police misconduct in accused Philly cop killer’s prior murder case
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Eric Lewis, the man accused of killing a Philadelphia police officer in an ambush, was acquitted of murder in 2019 in a case the district attorney says was undermined by police misconduct.

Lewis, 35, is accused of fatally shooting Philadelphia Police Officer Shane Seiber and wounding his partner. He now faces a range of charges, among them murder, homicide of a law enforcement officer, attempted murder, 10 counts of attempted homicide of a law enforcement officer, aggravated assault, terroristic threats and other related offenses. He

In a video statement Tuesday, Philadelphia District Attorney Larry Krasner said Lewis was acquitted in an earlier murder case and blamed police misconduct for the outcome.

"Why this man was out of custody? The answer is this, this man is out of custody because a balanced, good and fair judge did what he had to do because two absolutely excellent prosecutors did everything humanly possible with a case and an investigation that was so deeply flawed. It was not just full of errors and mistakes, very serious ones, But some of the conduct involving one police officer... And one detective is arguably criminal. Yes, I said criminal," Krasner said.

A Democrat running for county council in eastern Indiana was ridiculed Tuesday after critics claimed she appeared "s--- faced" and slurred her way through attacks on Republicans during a televised candidate forum.

During the forum, Fayette County Council candidate Jaime West said she would "fire all Republicans" if elected, railed against "MAGAs" she called "racist" and unintelligent, and alleged that a sheriff’s nephew had threatened to kill her. Asked for a final message to voters, West responded: "We have guns too."

"This is not a skit," said LibsOfTikTok, a popular conservative punditry account run by commentator Chaya Raichik.

"Jaime West, a Democrat running for Fayette County Council in Indiana, gave an embarrassing interview where she appears to mumble and rant the entire time. Is she intoxicated?" Raichik asked on X.

LAWMAKER’S STUNNED FACE AND OTHER VIRAL MOMENTS CAP ROUGH WEEK FOR POLITICAL CLASS

Former litigator Viva Frei tweeted that the video initially appeared to be a "skit [or] high school video project."

"I had to make sure she did not have a neurological disorder that could account for the slurred speech and insane rambling. She doesn’t. And even if she did have a diagnosed neurological disorder, ‘we have guns too’ after talking about firing all Republicans would ordinarily be disqualifying," Frei said.

When asked one decision she would make if elected that constituents would find unpopular, West told the moderator "fire all Republicans."

"I wouldn’t let them — I don’t even talk to them, I don’t like them. They voted against — their own state representative voted against her own party," West continued while also pledging not to raise taxes.

DEM SENATE HOPEFULS UNDER SCRUTINY FOR ‘CHOKE THEM OUT’ RHETORIC AFTER TRUMP ATTACK SCARE

"Y’all did this to us… you made this happen. This ICE coming into our communities, stealing people's jobs. I mean I've been threatened so many times to my face by MAGA; we’ll call them, because there's Republicans who actually get it, you know there are good Republicans out there, but then there's these MAGAs who are just racist and aren't very intelligent at all," West continued.

"They call you names. The sheriff’s nephew threatened to blow my head off. But, you know, what are you going to do?"

The moderator paused before asking West for a final message to voters:

West could not immediately be reached for comment. While it was not immediately clear which Indiana sheriff West was referring to, Zac Jones — who leads the Fayette County Sheriff's Office where she is running, was stunned by the remark:

World.title: Tim Walz warns Democrats will face reckoning if they win power and fail to deliver change
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz issued a warning to his party in an interview on Thursday, arguing that there would be backlash if Democrats win elections in November and beyond but fail to make significant structural changes.

During an interview with "The Lever" founder David Sirota, Walz was asked if the Democratic Party had an issue offering up big promises but ultimately failing to deliver.

"Yes, a hundred percent. It’s a hundred percent," Walz said. "I always use the line, as I said, we win these elections not to bank the political capital to win the next one but to improve lives. We’re too slow about it. And some of that is structural,"

WATCH: DEMOCRATS ADMIT WHEN THEY'D ELIMINATE THE FILIBUSTER AS SAVE ACT FIGHT HEATS UP

He pointed to former Sen. Joe Manchin's position that the filibuster must remain in place in the Senate.

"Look, I’m friends with Joe Manchin, but the desire to hold on to the filibuster at all costs as an institution when it had real impacts on people’s lives of real important things, and by not doing that, it played right into the hands of the Republicans. I think we’re not responsive, and then we fall into that 'But we voted for you, and you didn’t get anything done,'" Walz said.

Manchin has been consistent in his support for the filibuster. In 2022, he and then-Sen. Kyrsten Sinema voted against changing the Senate's 60-vote threshold for advancing most legislation, opposing other Democrats who sought to change the rules to pass voting legislation.

WALZ APPROVAL RATING CRATERS TO LOWEST LEVEL EVER AND TRAILS TRUMP AMID MASSIVE FRAUD SCANDAL: 'TIRED OF IT'

Walz, the 2024 Democratic vice presidential nominee, warned of a "real danger."

"Here’s where I think the real danger is. If there is not significant structural change — whether it’s inequities, you know, income inequities or opportunities — the backlash, because, I said this: I got into politics because I said we’ll never find a worse president than George Bush. And I think now, if you think that this is the pinnacle of how bad things can get, I would caution you to rethink that."

"And especially if Democrats do all of this, the public turns out, they vote for us, and kids still can’t afford a college education, can’t afford housing, that’s going to be a problem," he said.

He then predicted that Democrats would regain control of the House, Senate and eventually the presidency in 2028.

MN LAWMAKERS UNLOAD ON WALZ'S 'LEGACY' AFTER HE TOUTS FRAUD RECORD IN FINAL ANNUAL ADDRESS: 'RIDICULOUS'

Lindsey Drath, CEO of the Forward Party, told Fox News Digital, "We shouldn't advocate for abolishing the filibuster to drive home party-line votes with no effort to advance cross-partisan consensus law making. What hampers Congress' ability to deliver material solutions to the American people is a two-party system that penalizes working across the aisle."

"This circular dynamic, whereby Democrats or Republicans enter into a narrow majority, only to focus on maintaining power, accumulates a kind of figurative debt against the challenges facing the American people," she said. "This dynamic pushes our elected officials away from working on real solutions for actual problems, and toward whatever hyper polarized means by which they can to hold on to power."

"This is why a fulcrum strategy is key," Drath continued. "The Senate today passes almost nothing on a bipartisan basis, not because the problems aren't solvable, but because neither party has any incentive to negotiate. Every compromise is a political cost. If someone crosses the aisle, they are attacked by their party. It is framed as every deal made is a loss to play at home. The incentive is to obstruct, posture, and wait for the next election."

"The fulcrum strategy is that you don't need a majority to change the Senate," she added. "You need only a handful. It uses a small bloc of independents to balance power in Congress and take away full majority from either side. With an expected closely divided Congress this cycle, this is very relevant and real. It would mean both parties would have to negotiate with those few in the middle before anything passes. The party that wants their vote has to offer something real, something that actually serves the people."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Walz announced in January that he would not seek elected office again, after previously announcing he wouldn't run for a third term as governor.

He reflected on his tenure as governor in a September interview, including his handling of widespread fraud involving Minnesota social services programs.

"Fraud — should have stopped it sooner," Walz told the Minnesota Star Tribune. "We didn’t stop them. I accept that. I think there does need to be accountability with that. And part of it is that, yep, that’s with me, I’ll step aside."

The governor said the state "immediately" took action to address the fraud and then suggested that the true cost of the fraud, estimated at $9 billion by federal prosecutors, has been overstated. Walz also compared the fraud losses to the cost of President Donald Trump’s White House ballroom, which he suggested was more expensive.

"I should have been down on those agencies a little more, but I will tell you this, in the scheme of things, all the fraud that's been prosecuted, by the way, and all the fraud that's probably out there is less than the ballroom at the White House," Walz said. "So it puts it into perspective. It doesn't make it right. Doesn't make it right."

World.title: Greta Thunberg joins massive French student protests as cars burn, police fire tear gas
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Climate activist Greta Thunberg joined student protesters in France on Tuesday after weeks of violent confrontations with police, thousands of arrests and widespread school closures over demands for education reform.

The 23-year-old Swedish activist appeared outside a high school in Saint-Denis, north of Paris, where students were demanding more teachers, better facilities and shorter school days, Reuters reported.

More than 6,800 people have been detained since the protests began in September, according to French authorities. Demonstrators have set fires, erected barricades and confronted riot police in cities across France, although many protests have remained peaceful.

FRANCE EXPLODES AGAIN AS STUDENTS RIOT OVER EDUCATION

Thunberg, who rose to prominence organizing school strikes over climate change, criticized the French government's response to the demonstrations.

"We are inspired by the young people who are demanding their basic rights," Thunberg told reporters, according to Reuters. She also described the police response as "extremely violent."

About 161,500 people marched across France on Tuesday, including 41,500 in Paris, according to Interior Ministry figures. The Education Ministry said 214 schools were closed.

FRENCH SCHOOL RIOTS DEEPEN AS EXPERTS POINT TO FAR-LEFT ALLIANCE FUELING ‘BROADER CONFRONTATION’

President Donald Trump weighed in on the turmoil last week, blaming mass migration rather than complaints about education.

"What’s happening in France is nothing less than out of control mass migration. This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great Country!" Trump wrote on Truth Social on Oct. 6.

The demonstrations have become a political flashpoint ahead of France's presidential election next May, with far-left presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Mélenchon accusing the government of excessive force against young protesters.

FRANCE IS DEVOURING ITSELF AS SCHOOL RIOTS REVEAL A CRISIS FAR BIGGER THAN BROKEN CLASSROOMS

Mélenchon joined demonstrators in Paris on Tuesday, while right-wing National Rally leader Marine Le Pen has condemned violence by protesters and called for those responsible for damaging schools to pay for repairs.

The police response has drawn criticism following an incident last week in which a 15-year-old boy lost his hand and part of his lower arm after picking up a police dispersal grenade that detonated during a demonstration in Lens.

French authorities subsequently suspended the use of the type of stun grenade involved in the incident.



French President Emmanuel Macron has called for restraint and dialogue as the demonstrations continue.

Students have complained about deteriorating buildings, teacher shortages and school days that can stretch from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has asked ministers to address their demands.

World.title: JIM GRAY: Mike Ditka did it his way. Football will never see another like him
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

America knew him as a football legend. He became the NFL’s symbol of toughness and the emblem of Chicago. Mike Ditka was more than a Hall of Fame player and head coach who led the Bears to their unforgettable Super Bowl XX championship. He was a man who reached well beyond the football field. Coach Ditka was my partner on the radio for a nearly a decade.

On our show and podcast this week, "Let’s Go!," broadcast on SiriusXM NFL Radio, I paid tribute to and honored the life of Coach Ditka, along with my fellow co-hosts past and present — Tom Brady, Bill Belichick, Matthew Stafford, Drew Brees and Peter King. They joined me to speak about what Ditka meant to them and to the game of football. Here was our tribute.

It's been a very difficult few days since we've learned of the passing of Mike Ditka on Oct. 9, at age 86. Guys like Ditka are very rare. He was a once in a lifetime man. He seemed indestructible. I thought he would beat everything and everyone, and that he just might live forever because a guy like Mike Ditka isn't supposed to die.

NFL COACHES SHARE INCREDIBLE MIKE DITKA STORIES AS FOOTBALL WORLD MOURNS THE BEARS LEGEND

America's Coach, that's what I called him, and that's who he was. He was my partner on the radio for many, many years. I truly loved him. He was so much fun. He lived his life to the absolute fullest.

Tough yet tender. Generous, yet demanding. Funny as hell and a temper that was explosive. He could make you laugh, make you nervous, make you cry, and also feel like the most important person in the room, sometimes all in the same conversation.

LIONS HEAD COACH PAYS TRIBUTE TO MIKE DITKA AFTER LEARNING OF HIS DEATH FROM A PRESS CONFERENCE QUESTION

He was never polished, never predictable, never interested in being politically correct or being liked by everybody.

But perhaps there was no one in sports more beloved by his teammates, by his players, by his colleagues, by his opponents, and even by his critics.

MIKE DITKA TRIBUTES POUR IN FROM AROUND THE NFL INCLUDING FANS DRESSING LIKE HIM IN GREEN BAY

He was Iron Mike. Da Coach. A man of character, who was, a character.

The tombstone of Jackie Robinson reads, "A life is not important, except in the impact it has on other lives." Ditka's impact was enormous on Chicago, the NFL, sports, pop culture, and across the country.

I thought he would beat everything and everyone, and that he just might live forever because a guy like Mike Ditka isn't supposed to die.

He was bigger than life. Yet, he was always there and available for me personally. He traveled a great distance to introduce me and give the induction the day I was honored with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. His words were heartfelt, helpful, and instructive.

"I tell you what an honor this is when you really think about it. I don't know anybody else on this Walk of Fame, but I know you," Ditka said to me and the assembled audience. "What a great honor to be recognized by your peers for your achievements. And I know that you are a professional in everything you do, because when you do it, you do it right. Now I know that there's an art to everything in life. And if there is art to an interview, then you are Michelangelo, believe me, because you are good at that. Now, why is he good? Because he asks tough, hard, fair questions that you've got to answer. And the reason you've got to answer them is because the interview wouldn't work without your answer. And that's what makes him so good. I'm really proud to be your friend. We've been together for a long time," Ditka continued.

"Let me tell you something that I know for a fact about life. If you have no critics, you have no successes. God bless you."

That sentiment, is so enlightening and edifying to anyone in public life. He knew it, and he chose successes. Critics be damned.

Ditka truly had it all. The mustache, cigar, volatility, the winning, the loyalty. He was one of a kind.

And for the people who knew him beyond the public persona, there was another side. The one of extraordinary kindness. They saw the moments when the bluster disappeared. Mike Ditka helped, truly helped, so many people. Whether they were fellow players in need, youngsters in crisis, seniors in peril, families that were struggling, or strangers in distress. Ditka was the most generous person I've ever known. I saw his commitment to contribute, respond, and was constantly giving of his time and resources. And he wanted and expected absolutely nothing in return for his countless, truly endless acts of goodwill.

That's the part you can't put in a highlight reel, and maybe that's the part that matters most.

His life was lived to the lyrics of the song, "My Way."

"For what is a man? What has he got? If not himself, then he has not. To say the things he truly feels, and not the words of one who kneels. The record shows I took the blows and did it my way."

When somebody like that is gone, you don't just miss what he did. You miss his presence.

There will never be another Mike Ditka because as Ralph Waldo Emerson once wrote,

"When nature removes a great man, people explore the horizon for a successor; but none comes, and none will. His class is extinguished with him."

Mike Ditka, my dear friend, America's coach, an institution and national treasure, was in a class all his own.

Every time we ended a conversation, Mike would never say goodbye. His words would always be, "God bless, Jimmy."

So, I won't say goodbye to Coach Ditka. I will follow his lead. God bless, Coach.

May God rest your soul and bless your family.

***

Here is what the all-time greats had to say during the show about Coach Ditka. This week’s episode of "Let’s Go!" can be heard here.

Tom Brady, 7 time Super Bowl winning quarterback:

"There are so many things I loved about Coach Ditka from watching from afar and getting to know him over the course of my NFL career. He was as tough as the city that he coached in and he was the first tight end ever in the Hall of Fame. I heard Gronk on the pregame show say he owed a lot to Coach Ditka. Without Coach Ditka, there are no players like Rob Gronkowski who revolutionized the tight end position. And without Rob Gronkowski, I'm down a bunch of Super Bowls. So I gotta thank Coach Ditka for a lot of reasons. He won a Super Bowl as a player, he won a Super Bowl as a head coach. And as a quarterback, I always know what a great tight end means to an offense. He is my safety valve. That's your third down answer. And every one I ever threw to owes something to Mike."

Tom Brady:

"On TV, he also revolutionized the game with his media career. He never softened on a word. There was never a filter. There was no fluff. It was just all football. Rest easy, Coach Ditka."

Bill Belichick, 6 time Super Bowl winning head coach:

"As a player, Mike was extremely tough, competitive, all business, a guy you certainly didn't wanna mess with and he set the tone for the teams that he played on. It was similar as a coach. He had that same toughness that transferred to his team and, and players. And you knew anytime you went up against him, like you were going to be in an absolute brawl and fight all the way to the finish because that's the way he and his teams competed. Loved Mike. Loved Mike and what he meant to the game. And we'll miss him."

Matthew Stafford, NFL MVP Los Angeles Rams quarterback:

"I had the pleasure of being on some of the NFL shows with him. You know, his presence was really something else. All these guys, they play football, they coach football, then they move to talking about football and they become just a guy that talks about football. But Ditka was always coach, right? I mean, and I remember, getting to do those shows with him. He had the cigar unlit under the table. He was just true to himself and that was such a cool thing to be a part of."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Drew Brees, Hall of Fame, Super Bowl-winning quarterback:

"He was not only an incredible player, but an incredible coach. There's a type of leadership where you just see things happen before they happen. You just have a vision for what the way that things should be, and then your contributions to getting it to that point. It's a rare trait. I think Mike was no question, was certainly one of those guys and man, he's gonna be missed."

Peter King, Award-winning NFL sportswriter:

"Nothing ever about Mike Ditka was invented, was put on anything. He always was himself. Ditka, as a player, as a coach, as a broadcaster, was authentic and he was perfect and he was dedicated to be great at whatever he did at that moment."

Eli Manning spent 16 seasons staring down some of the NFL's most intimidating defensive players. But apparently, a largemouth bass is where he draws the line.

At least, that's what Eric Church would have you believe.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

The country music superstar recently welcomed Pro Football Hall of Famer Randy Moss to his private fishing property outside Nashville for an episode of Moss' YouTube series, "Chasing 10." And somewhere between catching bass and swapping stories, Church decided to have a little fun at the expense of another former NFL star who had visited his lake.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

"I brought Eli here about six months ago. He came fishing with me here," Church said.

When Moss asked how Manning had done on the water, Church revealed that the two-time Super Bowl champion apparently wasn't too eager to get his hands on the fish.

"I think Eli's scared to hold 'em," he said. "I had to hold the fish for him."

"Hold on, hold on. You talking about one of the Manning brothers?" Moss asked, making sure he'd heard that correctly.

Church confirmed it was Eli, prompting Moss to respond, "Eli, man. Come on, Eli."

But Church wasn't finished roasting his fishing buddy.

"I held them all for him," he continued. "It's kind of like you do with your kid. You catch them and hand them to him and say, 'Here, y'all take a picture.'"

Man, that's embarrassing. But since Eli wasn't there to defend himself, we'll take Church's accusations with a grain of salt.

Fortunately for Moss, his own fishing trip with Church went considerably better.

Eric Church owns a bass fishing paradise hidden just outside Nashville

The country singer's sprawling 1,600-acre property sits just 15 minutes outside downtown Nashville and features multiple lakes loaded with largemouth bass. Church revealed that he's caught four bass weighing at least 10 pounds in those waters, including a personal best of 11.2 pounds.

And the fish certainly weren't shy that morning. Church landed a 6.7-pound largemouth early in the outing, and the two continued catching fish throughout the day, including another hefty bass they estimated at nearly 8 pounds.

They never managed to land the double-digit monster they were hoping for, but Moss has already checked that milestone off his fishing bucket list. The former NFL receiver previously caught a 10-pound bass on "Chasing 10," a series that takes him around the country fishing with fellow athletes and celebrities.

The show also supports the Children's Cancer Research Fund, with the boat used throughout the series set to be raffled off to benefit the organization.



As for Eli Manning, perhaps Church should invite him back for another round. You know, to redeem himself.

After all, if you can survive 16 years of 250-pound linebackers trying to take your head off, surely you can muster up the courage to hold a fish.

World.title: Bank of America ordered to pay historic $1.2 billion over alleged sanctions law violations
World.content:
Bank of America was ordered Tuesday to pay $1.2 billion to the Treasury Department, which said it violated anti-money laundering and sanctions laws.

The penalty is the third largest ever issued in Treasury history, the agency said. As part of that total, the bank was ordered to pay $750 million to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the largest fine it has ever levied.

“Today’s actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement.

As the second-largest bank in the country, Bank of America has more than 70 million clients and processes about $4.5 trillion in payments for individual customers every year.

In addition, the bank handles $450 trillion in payments for corporate customers, including payrolls, corporate credit cards and supplier payments.

The Treasury Department said Bank of America “admits that it willfully violated” the Bank Secrecy Act and “failed to maintain” an anti-money laundering program that met minimum requirements under the law. The bank also admitted having failed to file mandatory Suspicious Activity Reports.

“Bank of America failed to timely report to FinCEN over $5 billion dollars in suspicious transactions, with over $1 billion of this activity implicating national security-related and other priority illicit finance risks, including suspicious transactions indicative of Chinese Money Laundering Networks, fraud, and potential trade-based money laundering with a substantial nexus to the southwest border,” the Treasury Department said in a statement.

FinCEN is the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, which combats money laundering, illicit financial activities and terrorist financing networks around the world.

“Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right,” Bank of America said in a statement to NBC News.

“We have invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to combat financial crime, and our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators.”

“We will continue to support federal and local law enforcement across thousands of investigations and report hundreds of thousands of suspicious activity reports each year.”

In addition to the FinCEN violations, the Treasury Department said Bank of America is also settling “its potential civil liability for 475 apparent violations of multiple sanctions programs” with the Office of Foreign Assets Control, which oversees sprawling U.S. sanctions.

The company “processed millions of dollars in payments in apparent violation of sanctions programs targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism,” the Treasury Department said.

Bessent said, “When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire U.S. financial system to significant illicit finance risks.”

Bank of America will report its third-quarter earnings shortly before 7 a.m. ET Wednesday.

World.title: Trump attacks Rep. Ilhan Omar and Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed at Ohio rally
World.content:
Chants of “deport” rang out Monday night as President Donald Trump criticized Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., and Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, at a rally for Republican candidates in Youngstown, Ohio.

“I don’t know what they’re doing with it, but I can tell you this: She’s a disaster,” Trump said of Omar, whose home in Washington, D.C., was searched hours earlier by federal agents, two people familiar with the investigation told NBC News.

A Justice Department spokesperson said in a statement that Homeland Security Investigations “executed a judicially authorized search warrant” as “part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation.” The statement did not specify that the investigation was related to Omar, nor did it provide more information about the search.

“She comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military, where all they do is shoot each other, and she comes into our country and she says, ‘I have a constitutional right,’” Trump said. “She’s telling us about the Constitution, and she comes from one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet.”

Trump then spoke of Somali gang activity in Minnesota and what the FBI has described as a recently thwarted shooting at the state’s Mall of America, alleged to have been plotted by an American-born U.S. citizen of Somali descent, The Associated Press reported. That’s when the first wave of “deport” chants began.

Omar, who was born in the war-torn country of Somalia, immigrated to the U.S. as a child decades ago. El-Sayed was born in Michigan to Egyptian immigrants.

“For 10 years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns,” Omar wrote earlier Monday on X. “This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.”

Speaking to reporters Monday afternoon, Trump said he had “nothing to do” with the search of Omar’s home.

At the rally, he segued from his attack on Omar and people of Somali descent in Minnesota to an attack on El-Sayed.

“These people are crazy,” Trump said. “You look at the guy running in Michigan. He’s a jihadist.”

Trump went on to praise El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, before he again referred to El-Sayed as a “jihadist” and proclaimed that “Somalia bandits, Third World gangsters, jihadist sympathizers do not belong in Ohio.”

He added: “They don’t belong in America. Better get them the hell out of here.”

More chants of “deport” then erupted from the audience at Youngstown’s Covelli Centre.

A spokesperson for El-Sayed’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday night. Last week, after Trump referred to him on social media by his middle name, Mohamed, El-Sayed condemned it as a tactic meant to raise fears about his religion.

“They point to my name and they point to my faith, trying to distract us from the challenges that we have,” El-Sayed, who is Muslim, told supporters at an event Thursday in Grand Rapids, Michigan. “My name did not raise your gas prices. My faith is not the reason you can’t afford your groceries.”

Trump’s remarks Monday continued his leading role in ratcheting up rhetoric around Muslims and immigrants. Days after El-Sayed won Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary, Trump warned that the U.S. could become a “jihadist-run country.” And Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., accused El-Sayed of sympathizing with Osama bin Laden as he was campaigning with Rogers last week in Michigan.

Trump was in Ohio’s Mahoning Valley — a once reliably Democratic region that has become increasingly Republican since his rise in politics — to campaign for Sen. Jon Husted and Vivek Ramaswamy, the state’s GOP nominee for governor.

It was his second visit to Ohio in less than 10 days. His last trip, to the Dayton area, included remarks about nearby Springfield. During a 2024 presidential debate, Trump repeated the unsubstantiated and racially charged claim that Haitian immigrants in the city were eating pets.

Trump mentioned Springfield again Monday in Youngstown, immediately after his attacks on Omar and El-Sayed.

“All of a sudden, they dropped 35,000 people in from Haiti, and it didn’t work out too well,” he said before he defiantly repeated his past falsehoods. “Remember during the debate I said some of the things they were doing? I was right.”

World.title: Cornell bans fraternity parties for the rest of the academic year amid investigation into alleged sexual assault
World.content:
Cornell University said Tuesday it is suspending all “parties and social events” at fraternity houses for the rest of the academic year amid an uproar over a former student’s allegation that she was sexually assaulted by members of the campus Chi Phi chapter nearly two years ago.

00:24 Cornell suspends fraternity events through end of year 00:00 00:00

Michael I. Kotlikoff, Cornell’s president, also announced that the Ivy League institution would bring on “experienced, trauma-informed criminal investigators” to review allegations of sexual assault on campus.

“These are first steps toward systemic change on our campus,” Kotlikoff said in a statement posted on Cornell’s website. “We will take all necessary steps to address the conditions that led to Jane Doe’s experiences, and those of other survivors.”

The former student, identified in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe, alleges she was sexually assaulted and plied with drugs Oct. 19-20, 2024. She filed a civil lawsuit last month against multiple parties, including the university, the fraternity, her sorority, Tri Delta, and seven former Chi Phi members.

Attorneys for four of the men have said their clients deny sexually assaulting Jane Doe or coercing her with drugs. The three other men have not responded to requests for comment. None of the seven has been criminally charged. The fraternity and the sorority previously declined to discuss the pending litigation.

Jane Doe’s lawsuit put renewed scrutiny on the Cornell University Police Department’s handling of the 2024 probe and the local district attorney office’s decision not to bring criminal charges. Cornell and Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten have defended their investigations, with the prosecutor saying his office was not provided with all the materials from the campus police investigation.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul has appointed state Attorney General Letitia James to oversee the case going forward. Cornell separately tasked former acting U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates with an independent review of how the school responds to sexual harassment, assault and misconduct on campus.

“I am deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024, and appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community,” Kotlikoff said in Tuesday’s announcement. “It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe. We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action.”

Tuesday’s announcement outlined other changes in response to the Jane Doe case, including additional staff members at the Cornell Office of Civil Rights.

In response to a request for comment, Jane Doe’s lawyer said his client’s “goal in filing her lawsuit was not solely for herself.”

“She wanted to achieve her aim of improving Cornell and its response to abuse claims. While the steps announced today are helpful to achieve this goal, they are too late to protect Ms. Doe,” said the lawyer, Thomas Giuffra. “However, these steps will hopefully go a long way to help ensure that there are no more Jane Does.”

World.title: Diesel futures jump, signaling higher prices to come despite Trump’s Russia deal
World.content:
Diesel futures traded sharply higher Tuesday, as doubts mounted about the likely impacts of the Trump administration’s latest efforts to push prices down.

U.S. diesel futures were up 5% by midday to their highest level in weeks.

In Europe, diesel futures rose by about 3.8%, while gas futures spiked to levels not seen all year.

A move higher in futures markets typically signals that prices will climb in the coming days.

Already, the average nationwide price of diesel is up 70% since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28. The cost of unleaded gas has risen by more than 45% over that period.

Crude oil prices, meanwhile, were mixed. Brent traded around $106 per barrel, while U.S. crude oil neared $95 per barrel. Both of those key energy benchmarks have risen around 70% since the start of the year.

Gas and diesel prices are rising especially fast in parts of the country where President Donald Trump and Republicans can least afford to anger voters ahead of November’s midterm elections.

“Absolutely stunning price spikes in wholesale diesel today,” Gulf Oil adviser Tom Kloza wrote Tuesday on X. “US retail diesel price record of $6.53/gal could be topped by the midterms.”

“Up 18cts/gal Gulf Coast and East Coast; but up 28cts/gal in Southern California and 25-30cts/gal in Great Plains and Great Lakes,” he wrote.

Patrick De Haan, the head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, wrote on X that “$6/gal diesel may be here to stay for now.”

“Truckers and farmers not going to see any relief anytime soon,” he wrote.

The broad spike higher in diesel futures came just days after Trump announced a controversial deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to increase diesel supplies in the United States by buying previously sanctioned Russian reserves.

When Trump announced the deal, he said it would result in millions of metric tons of additional diesel for the world.

While that may sound like a lot, analysts have since crunched the numbers and determined that, at best, the diesel in question would amount to less than two weeks’ worth of U.S. demand.

Tuesday’s higher diesel futures are evidence of the market “clearly not believing that Russian oil is on the way,” Kloza said.

The deal with Putin also required that the Trump administration suspend long-standing sanctions on Russian energy purchases.

The sanctions were put in place after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, and the decision to lift them until April has drawn widespread backlash both at home and abroad.

Trump has also applied pressure to European allies in an effort to get them to release more of their diesel reserves.

The president’s Oct. 2 announcement that Europe had bowed to the pressure and would release fuel temporarily cooled prices for a few days. But a lack of additional details about that release gradually erased any price relief.

A subsequent statement from the International Energy Agency confirmed what traders had suspected: Europe would not be releasing any new diesel reserves, merely continuing to fulfill a pledge it made in March as part of a multinational effort to cap rising fuel prices.

Trump also signed an executive order this month that sought to ease restrictions on an off-road formulation of diesel that is dyed red and not subject to federal gas taxes.

But industry groups quickly warned truckers to avoid using “red dye” diesel without more information about how the taxes would work.

As of Tuesday, it was unclear whether Trump’s red dye diesel order had any impact on domestic prices or supply.

World.title: What’s fueling inflation? Fuel.
World.content:
Inflation in America is being powered by diesel.

The price of the fuel, used by farmers and truckers, is up more than 75% since the start of the Iran war in late winter. Diesel costs have become a particular concern for economists, who say that higher diesel fuel costs trickle down into “just about everything.”

And the final government inflation report before November’s pivotal midterm elections will likely reflect how much of a headache it’s become for businesses and consumers.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics is set to release its September consumer price index report at 8:30 a.m. Wednesday. It’s expected to show the annual rate of inflation rose to 3.7% from 3.4%, according to a survey of economists from Dow Jones. From August to September, prices are expected to have risen by 0.6%. The monthly jump, if confirmed, would also be one of the largest in years.

Since August, oil prices have risen to more than $105 per barrel from about $80. The price of regular gas, which most consumers buy, also remains elevated by more than 45% since late February, when the Iran war was launched.

As early voting kicks off this week, a higher inflation reading would come at a precarious moment for Republicans defending majorities in the House and Senate. Polls consistently find that inflation and the high cost of living are top issues this year for voters in both parties.

Higher diesel prices this summer and fall have hit agricultural states like Kansas, Iowa and Texas especially hard. Long viewed as Republican strongholds, all three states have Democrats outperforming in Senate races with campaigns focused on the high cost of living.

In response to the outcry over the high cost of gas and diesel, President Donald Trump has pulled several policy levers in recent weeks aimed at pushing down prices. But so far, none of them has made much of a dent.

The Trump administration has pressured G7 allies to release more diesel stocks, issued an order to allow more widespread use of tax-free diesel, and announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin that Russia release some diesel supplies and drop some of its export restrictions.

The latest action has drawn global backlash after Trump also eased some sanctions on Russia in order to facilitate the Russian diesel deal.

Core concerns

Consumers’ wages are still lagging behind the rate of inflation. As of September, wage growth was 3% and has not grown faster than inflation since March.

Still, despite the pressure on prices and wages, consumers continue to spend. The CEOs of the nation’s largest banks on Tuesday reported that consumers remain spending at a steady pace.

“While various headwinds, most recently higher energy prices, and tighter monetary policies have been challenging, the global economy has held up remarkably well in the U.S.,” said Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser. “While much has been made of the AI boom, the consumer is still driving much” of the economy’s momentum, she added.

“Our data shows that our consumer and business customers are doing well,” said Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said the economy “continued to be fueled by strong business investment and ongoing consumer spending” over the last three months.

Core inflation, which is more closely watched by the Federal Reserve and which strips out food and energy prices, is expected to rise as well, to 2.5%. If confirmed, that would be its highest level since June.

One key sector fueling higher core inflation is airfare. “Airfares remain the core category most directly affected by higher oil prices,” said economists at Morgan Stanley. “Airfare CPI is already up 23% y/y, which raises the question of how much further prices can increase.”

They noted that jet fuel prices have risen 90% since this time last year, “and typically account for roughly 20-30% of airline operating costs.” As a result, “Airlines may already be approaching full pass-through of the increase in fuel costs to consumers.”

iPhones and interest rates

Another major consumer item that could impact September’s inflation rate: pricier iPhones.

Apple’s latest iPhone began selling on Sept. 12, and Morgan Stanley’s economists said “price increases were generally in the 10%-14% range across models.”

“Given Apple’s roughly 50% share of the U.S. smartphone market,” this could translate into what they said could be a small upside impact on overall inflation.

But while these higher iPhone prices are likely contributing to September’s inflation, they are also the product of inflation earlier his year — inflation that traces back to the ever-expanding buildout of AI data centers.

The race to build data centers and chips for AI has triggered a scramble for memory, in particular. Given that the supply of memory chips is limited, prices have soared at an unprecedented pace.

In June, Apple told NBC News that it has “never seen a component price increase this much, this quickly.”

Economists at Goldman Sachs also expect to see a jump in September in other key consumer categories.

“We expect a pickup in autos inflation, reflecting a 0.5% increase in used car prices, a 0.2% increase in new car prices, and a 0.2% increase in the car insurance category,” they wrote in a note.

Wednesday’s data could also “determine whether the Fed’s next hike is imminent, or simply still ahead,” said economists at UBS. Already, the central bank has interest raised rates once this year to try to slow inflation. A number of top Fed officials have also spoken about the need to raise rates even higher.

“If the economic data continue to come in as expected, I anticipate additional hikes to support a timelier return of inflation to our two percent goal,” said Federal Reserve governor Christoper Waller on Thursday. “But there is some flexibility about when those hikes will occur.”

The Fed is expected to raise rates one more time this year, most likely in December. But an inflation reading on Wednesday that comes in hotter than expected could increase that urgency and lead to a pre-Election Day rate hike at the central bank’s Oc. 27-28 meeting.

World.title: OpenAI employee accused of planting recording device in office
World.content:
An OpenAI employee suspected of secretly planting a recording device in one of the company's conference rooms has been arrested on criminal charges, the Justice Department said Tuesday.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national, was arrested Friday and made his initial appearance in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California on Tuesday. Alfozan was charged with trying to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.

Prosecutors said that Alfozan had worked at OpenAI as an engineer since July 2025.

On Sept. 30, the company's employees discovered the audio recording device inserted into a USB port on the back of a television inside an executive conference room. The company later determined that the recording device had been concealed in toilet paper and installed about two days before it was discovered.

Undated photo of secret recording device found in OpenAI conference room Government photo

The meeting room where it was hidden was often used by OpenAI's employees to discuss highly confidential and proprietary matters, including research, product plans and business development, the Justice Department said.

In a statement, OpenAI said that after discovering the device, it contacted the FBI and has terminated the employee accused of planting it.

"The FBI's investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work. At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," the company said.

"We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance. Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states, and this case is an example of how AI can help address these sophisticated security threats."

FBI Director Kash Patel said in a post on X that the FBI and its partners had carried out the arrest and that the investigation is ongoing.

The criminal complaint, made public on Tuesday, alleged that Alfozan used a productivity tool to make inquiries about OpenAI's building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars, and locations of "leadership and exec" and external partner meetings.

Other evidence gathered in the investigation, meanwhile, showed that a chatbot account associated with Alfozan's spouse had also submitted prompts between Sept. 24 and Sept. 30, related to building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating and remote accessing a continuous audio recording device.

A photograph included in the complaint also shows that Alfozan entered the conference room where the device was hidden on Oct. 5 and looked behind the television.

That same day, the complaint says Alfozan left his bag unattended in another room, and the company's security personnel opened it and found his ID, wallet and another recording device similar to the one planted in the conference room.

Alfozan is due to appear in federal court again on Oct. 19 for a detention hearing.

CBS News has asked Alfozan's lawyer for comment.

World.title: Pope Leo diagnosed with lung cancer after undergoing surgery
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV's surgery confirmed that he has lung cancer, and he had the lower lobe of his right lung removed, the Vatican said Tuesday.

The tests confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin after the surgery. It said the diagnosis had been suspected by preoperative tests and was confirmed during surgery.

The 71-year-old pontiff was in the operating room for about 3 hours, the statement said. The surgery itself lasted approximately 90 minutes. "The surgery was successful, and there were no complications," the statement said.

"To ensure a radical resection, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique," the Vatican said in a statement. "Intraoperative histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of pulmonary adenocarcinoma, as suspected from pre-operative tests."

According to the Vatican, the pope "regained consciousness normally" following the procedure and was then taken back to his room on the 10th floor of Rome's Gemelli Hospital.

In its statement, the Vatican did not disclose what stage the cancer was in or whether the cancer may have spread. It also did not detail what further procedures the pope may have to undergo.

Pope Leo XIV waves as he leaves the Vatican before being admitted to Rome's Gemelli University Hospital for an operation to remove a lump from his lung on Oct. 13, 2026. Tiziana FABI /AFP via Getty Images

"The Vatican tends to keep these things under wraps, so there'll be a lot of reading between the lines to try and detect what is the state of the pope's health," Candida Moss, the Edward Cadbury professor of theology at the University of Birmingham in England, told CBS News.

Leo is known for living an active and healthy lifestyle, including swimming and playing tennis, all factors that likely worked in his favor going into the surgery.

Leo had walked into Gemelli Hospital through the main entrance earlier in the day and waved to dozens of well-wishers who had gathered to greet him. The Vatican said the surgery was performed by a team led by Gemelli's chief thoracic surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora.

The Vatican on Monday canceled all Leo's audiences through Oct. 20. There was no word on whether Leo would be able to keep his planned trip to South America next month.

The typical recommendation for a procedure of this kind is to avoid air travel for about three weeks, which would put the pope right up against the start of that trip, which is scheduled for Nov. 6.



Moss told CBS News that Vatican protocol calls for the pope's cardinals and aides to step in and take up many of his duties as needed.

"We should also expect that, inasmuch as is possible, Pope Leo is going to continue to work," Moss said. "We have a long tradition of popes — not just Pope Francis, but also Pope John Paul II, who had Parkinson's for 10 years — who continued to remain as active as they could, and as active in Catholic liturgies as they could, right up until the end of their tenures."

While Gemelli has a specific papal apartment that past popes have used, complete with a private chapel on the 10th floor, Leo will actually be staying in a nearby room since the papal apartment is undergoing renovations, according to the Vatican press office.

The Vatican had announced on Sunday that Leo would undergo surgery after a nodular lesion was found in his lung. A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 1.2 inches that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen. A nodule can be benign or malignant.

"The doctors believe it's best to take action, so, following their advice, I've decided to have surgery to remove it," Leo said in remarks during his Sunday noon blessing. "Thank you for your spiritual support, and I entrust myself to your prayers."

Lung adenocarcinoma is the most common type of lung cancer in the United States, according to the Lung Cancer Foundation of America, and makes up about 40% of all diagnosed lung cancers.

It forms in glandular cells on the outer parts of the lung and is likely to be diagnosed earlier than other lung cancers because it spreads more slowly, the LCFA said. Symptoms can include fatigue, shortness of breath and upper back and chest pain. Treatments can include surgery, chemotherapy, immunotherapy and radiation.

World.title: Selma Blair arrested after allegedly biting flight attendant
World.content:
Actress Selma Blair was arrested after allegedly biting a flight attendant on board a Delta Air Lines flight from Los Angeles to New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport on Sunday night. Following her arrest, she allegedly kicked a police officer and a nurse and is facing two assault charges.

Two flight attendants reported injuries during the flight, and one was taken to the hospital after the incident, according to the Port Authority Police Department. One of the flight attendants was bitten and the other sustained a laceration, according to a law enforcement source.

Her attorney said Blair experienced a "medical emergency" on the plane, but did not get into specifics. Blair has been outspoken about her struggle with multiple sclerosis.

The incident happened at 11 p.m. on Delta Air Lines Flight 938. The flight crew needed to restrain Blair, a law enforcement source said.

On air traffic control audio, the pilot could be heard calling for medical personnel to come to the plane.

"Ah, a bloody nose as well as some bite marks as well, so I don't think we need an ambulance or anything like that but if we could get some medical personnel at the gate, to look at their injuries," the pilot said in audio captured on ATC.com. "It sounds like the disruptive passenger also bashed her head on the bulkhead or something like that, so we'll obviously have to get her potentially checked out as well as well as law enforcement."

Law enforcement sources said Blair tried to open one of the cabin doors and had to be restrained for the rest of the flight.

Port Authority Police were called to the plane, along with the FBI. Blair was transported to Jamaica Hospital for evaluation after the incident. While in the ambulance, she allegedly kicked a PAPD officer, and once at the hospital, she allegedly assaulted a nurse, prosecutors said.

Blair was later released from the hospital and taken to Queens Central Booking. She was then arraigned on two counts of second-degree assault at a court in Queens, where she pleaded not guilty. A judge set her bail at $20,000 cash or $60,000 bond and set the next hearing for Jan. 19.

The assault charges are state charges related to the alleged incidents in the ambulance and hospital.

This isn't the first time Blair has been removed from a flight. Back in 2016, she was removed by stretcher after an episode on another Delta flight. As for what allegedly happened on Sunday night, the FBI gave her a summons for assaults within special maritime and territorial jurisdiction of the United States, a federal law enforcement source said.

No date has been set for the federal case against her.

"Delta has zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behavior, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first," the airline said in a statement.

Blair was traveling with her service dog, which is now in the custody of her attorney.

Blair has been outspoken about her struggle with multiple sclerosis. In 2025, she gave an interview to People magazine and Travel & Leisure talking about the difficulties she had traveling. In her 2022 memoir, she also has a chapter called "Bite Me," where she wrote about past instances where she bit other celebrities while drinking.

Blair has appeared in such films as "Cruel Intentions," "Legally Blonde," and "Hellboy," among others. In 2022, she was a contestant on "Dancing with the Stars."

World.title: Duane "Keffe D" Davis sentenced to 40 years to life for Tupac's murder
World.content:
A judge in Las Vegas, Nevada, sentenced Duane "Keffe D" Davis to 40 years to life in prison on Tuesday for the 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur. Judge Carli Kierny said he would receive credit for time already served.

Davis, 63, was convicted in August of murder with a deadly weapon with the intent to promote, further or assist a criminal gang for his role in the killing, although prosecutors said at the time that the state would dismiss the gang-related portion of his charge. He had pleaded not guilty.

At his sentencing hearing, Davis spoke briefly in court, telling the judge that he wanted some of the belongings police took from his house, like his pictures, to be returned to him. He said there was nothing more he wanted to say.

"Today, justice has been served for Tupac Shakur and his loved ones," Clark County District Attorney Steve Wolfson said in a statement. "While no amount of time in prison can bring Tupac back, we hope this sentencing brings some measure of closure and peace to his family after nearly 30 years. This case is a reminder that no matter how much time passes, our commitment to seeking justice never wavers."

Shakur is widely considered a hip-hop music legend, and his death is among the most notorious celebrity deaths in modern history. He died six days after being shot while stopped at a red light in Las Vegas on Sept. 7, 1996. The mystery of who may have fired the shots persisted for years, until Davis started to speak publicly about his own presence inside the white Cadillac that investigators had known pulled up beside Shakur's vehicle at that stop light on the night of the shooting.

The prosecution in Davis' case argued that he had gone "hunting" for Shakur as an act of retaliation against the rapper and Marion "Suge" Knight, the co-founder of his record company, Death Row Records. Referencing what was Davis' own account for a time, Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal said Davis shot Shakur after he and Knight had beaten up Davis' nephew.

Palal recognized during Davis' trial that the defendant had changed his accounts somewhat since he initially began to speak openly about the fatal shooting. But he told the jury that fundamental details of his story remained consistent, including the fact that Davis described himself as being inside a white Cadillac, from which the gunshots that killed Shakur emanated.

But Michael Sanft, an attorney for Davis, argued that no evidence beyond his client's statements had placed him in Las Vegas on the night that Shakur was shot. Surveillance footage, phone logs or other tangible records weren't available, he told the jury.

Prosecutors said four men were inside the white Cadillac, and Davis was the only one of them still alive by the time of his 2023 arrest and eventual conviction. Another man, who prosecutors said initially gave the gun that Davis used to shoot Shakur, was also dead.

Davis detailed his involvement in the shooting that led to Shakur's death and also wounded Knight, who was in the targeted vehicle, too, in his 2019 memoir, "Compton Street Legend." His attorneys fought to exclude the memoir as evidence in his trial, but the prosecution refused that request.
