World.title: Bipartisan group of senators call on Trump to rescind Russian diesel deal
World.content:
Bipartisan group of senators call on Trump to rescind Russian diesel deal

toggle caption i Win McNamee/Getty Images

A bipartisan group of senators is calling on President Trump to rescind his recent diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, calling it a "betrayal of the people of Ukraine."

Last week, Trump announced via social media he had struck a deal with Putin, whereby Russia will supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and one million tons "immediately thereafter."

"Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel," Trump wrote.

Sponsor Message

His announcement stunned lawmakers, who passed legislation this summer directing the president to impose significant tariffs on the top importers of Russian oil.

Those sanctions are aimed at targeting Russian officials, companies and financial institutions helping fuel Russia's war in Ukraine. The legislation was named in memory of the late GOP Sen. Lindsey Graham, who helped negotiate Trump's support for the package.

"This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our allies; it should be rescinded," wrote six Republican and six Democratic senators in a letter Tuesday to the president.

"The deal you struck with President Vladimir Putin on October 9th will not achieve just ends, nor will it benefit Americans," it read.

Senators said they recognized the need to lower energy costs for Americans — but maintained that allowing Russian diesel into global markets will offer "limited to no relief to Americans."

They added the deal "only provides Putin with more fuel to finance his war machine and enables Russia to continue its brutal attacks on Ukrainian civilians."

When asked about the letter, the White House referred back to comments President Trump made to reporters on Tuesday about concerns that Russia will use proceeds from the diesel agreement to purchase weapons.

Sponsor Message

"Nobody's telling me anything," Trump said. "That's a diesel deal. Not for us. That's being released into the world. That's not being released to us. That's a diesel deal that's going to be released into the world for the world market, because the world market suffered with high prices."

The letter was signed by Democrats Richard Blumenthal, Chris Coons, Dick Durbin, Jack Reed, Jeanne Shaheen and Sheldon Whitehouse. They were joined by Republicans Alan Armstrong, Susan Collins, John Cornyn, Mitch McConnell, Lisa Murkowski and Thom Tillis.

World.title: A judge blocks the government's tree-clearing spree at a municipal D.C. golf course
World.content:
A judge blocks the government's tree-clearing spree at a municipal D.C. golf course

toggle caption i Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR

A federal judge has temporarily barred the Trump administration from cutting down additional trees at a D.C. municipal golf course, the latest example of a court intervening in the government's efforts to reshape pieces of the nation's capital.

The long-simmering fight over East Potomac Golf Links — which President Trump wants to redevelop into a championship-level course — erupted over the weekend, after the administration cut down hundreds of trees with little notice.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes had ordered the administration in May to get court approval before cutting down more than 10 trees at the golf course. Officials notified the court just before 5 p.m. on Friday of their plan to remove "up to 529 trees" in phases starting on Saturday — and had razed at least 430 by the end of the day, prompting Reyes to call an emergency hearing on Monday.

Sponsor Message

"What has happened has cost the government all of its credibility with me in this case," Reyes said during the nearly four-hour hearing, held via videoconference.

Reyes ordered a short-term stop to the tree-clearings, which she extended on Tuesday through Oct. 26. She warned Monday that "if that order is violated by two seconds, there are going to be contempt proceedings."

Reyes also ordered top officials from the Department of Interior and the National Park Service to testify at a hearing next Monday, to shed more light on the government's motivations and the future of the historic course.

"The questions go to whether or not I've been lied to," Reyes said. "Whether I've been lied to in declarations about the plans, whether or not I've been lied to about the timing of things, and whether I've been lied to about what kind of notice the court was going to receive."

East Potomac has emerged as another flashpoint in Trump's unilateral quest to remake D.C., and it's the subject of a lawsuit by critics who fear it could go the way of the now-lost White House East Wing unless a court intervenes. The D.C. Preservation League, along with two concerned residents, sued the government in February over what it calls an unlawful takeover.

Sponsor Message

"This is a tactic we're seen before from the Trump-Vance administration – act quickly to irrevocably alter a cherished national landmark, just to advance another one of President Trump's pet vanity projects," Skye Perryman, president and CEO of Democracy Forward — one of the firms involved in the lawsuit — said in a statement this weekend.

Perryman told NPR on Tuesday that the golf course is the latest in a pattern of the Trump administration "undermining the entire checks and balances process in this country, which includes undermining court proceedings."

Trump has long floated the idea of redeveloping East Potomac into a championship-caliber course and announced plans to do so earlier this year, though his target Sept. 1 start date has come and gone without a formal proposal.

The prospect — and the lack of clarity since — has raised alarm among locals concerned about losing access to the historically affordable course and to the surrounding recreational area, which is popular with cyclists, runners, fishers and picnickers.

Loading...

"This is a broader story than just about golf, especially when there's been this little transparency, … to say, 'Here's what the future of this little man-made peninsula is actually going to look like,'" Alex Rosen, a D.C.-based consultant who started the nonprofit Save East Po, told NPR in July.

A National Park Service official said in a Friday court filing that plans for renovations "remain in the conceptual stage." And the Interior Department told NPR in a statement on Tuesday that it is "committed to continuing the relationships we have built with the local golf communities to ensure these courses are safe, beautiful, open, affordable, enjoyable, accessible, and world-class."

But critics are growing increasingly concerned about the process itself. They worry the Trump administration is using so-called routine maintenance as a pretext to begin redevelopment without the proper authorization.

"You can't continuously say, 'There's no plan' … while you're clearly taking steps to effect a plan," Rosen, who is not involved in the lawsuit, told NPR after watching the hearing. "It's just frankly lying."

Sponsor Message

Why the rush? The court hopes for answers next week

At Monday's hearing, Reyes expressed regret that she hadn't issued a formal restraining order earlier, which she said was because "I have done everything humanly possible to give the government the benefit of the doubt in this case."

For example, after the administration quietly removed what it has since said were roughly 150 dying and invasive trees in late August, Reyes acknowledged that people were upset but declined to intervene: "I am not the Lorax," she said at an early September hearing.

By Monday, that benefit of the doubt was gone. When a government lawyer said they had done their best to notify the court, Reyes offered a sharp rebuke.

"You did not do your best," she said, voice raised. "You did your absolute worst."

Perryman, of Democracy Forward, said, "What was really remarkable about the hearing yesterday is that the government did not appear to have a defense for its failure to notify the court."

In Friday's court filing, National Mall and Memorial Parks Superintendent Kevin Griess described the tree-clearing as part of an effort "to address deferred maintenance needs and implement treatment recommendations to restore the cultural landscape."

Griess specifically cited a 2019 National Park Service report about D.C. municipal golf courses, which says several waves of tree planting at East Potomac over the last century have obscured views and changed the feel of the course from its original 1920s "links-style" design.

Griess said in his filing that NPS was able to act on the report because it had received a temporary surge of "approximately 20 to 50 trained personnel capable of performing labor-intensive grounds maintenance activities." Under questioning in court, he confirmed that surge was connected to the administration's 250th anniversary events, including the IndyCar race on the National Mall in August.

Sponsor Message

But critics are skeptical, given the president's public statements. Alex Dickson, one of the plaintiffs, said in a statement that "the administration is using a preservation report as cover to begin tearing out the course it was written to save."

Griess said he had gotten the green light last week from Frank Lands, the park service's deputy director of operations. At the judge's request, Lands then joined the hearing from his car in a parking lot. He said he had gotten the directive from Greg Wischer, deputy chief of staff to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum.

Wischer was not reachable to join the hearing, despite Reyes' request that he do so. She has ordered Wischer and Jessica Bowron, the acting director of the National Park Service, to testify at another hearing next Monday.

The Interior Department didn't answer NPR's questions about the timeline and resources for the tree-clearing, but said in a statement that "President Donald J. Trump is fulfilling his commitment to make D.C. Safe and Beautiful as shown by the working fountains, clean parks and safe streets across the district for the first time in decades."

In granting the plaintiffs' request for an extended restraining order on Tuesday, Reyes wrote that they had "proven they will likely suffer irreparable harm absent injunctive relief." She also said the government must provide "three business days' written advance notice prior to making any irreparable modification" to the golf course.

World.title: Cornell University bans frat parties, vows to address 'disturbing' campus culture
World.content:
Cornell University bans frat parties, vows to address 'disturbing' campus culture

toggle caption i Jeongyoon Han for NPR

Cornell University has banned parties and social events at fraternities for the rest of the school year and will bring sexual assault investigators into its police unit, in response to a former student's allegation of gang rape in 2024.

The changes came on Tuesday as the university said it is committed to addressing a "deeply disturbing" culture of drug and alcohol abuse, and a rise in sexual violence on campus following a civil lawsuit filed by a former student, Jane Doe, which set off national outrage and a crisis at Cornell.

Sponsor Message

"I am deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024, and appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community," Michael I. Kotlikoff, who is Cornell's president, wrote in a letter addressed to the campus on Tuesday. "It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe. We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action."

The lawsuit, which Doe filed nearly one month ago, alleges that Doe was plied with ketamine and was sexually assaulted by members of the Chi Phi fraternity during a party in October of 2024. The details of the allegations, which disclosed how fraternity members used a Snapchat group chat to discuss the woman and events at the party with openly crude language, sparked fury across the nation.

Doe's lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, told news outlets that Doe has been sent death threats and police swarmed her family's home since she filed the lawsuit.

The administration's changes come after student groups organized protests last week on campus.

"The administration is clearly feeling the heat and needed to make a move," says John Hartnett, a sophomore at Cornell who has helped organize protests. He called the changes a "half measure," and said that banning frats was not a long term solution to systematic issues at the university.

Sponsor Message

The faculty senate is considering a vote of no confidence in the university administration at a meeting scheduled for Wednesday. It's a rare move that demonstrates the deep seated frustration and distrust stemming from the 2024 case.

"Trust is still eroded on campus — that hasn't changed," says Julia Chang, an associate professor of Hispanic studies in the Department of Romance Studies. "The fact that these changes are coming about now — two years later — is a testament to the power of the student movement and the global conversation it has sparked; not the integrity of the administration."

The moratorium on events at fraternities is expected to have a reverberating effect on campus, where about one-third of all students participate in fraternities and sororities. The university's ties to Greek life, Kotlikoff said, has in part created a toxic culture on campus that requires serious course correction.

"While this is not a problem unique to Cornell, we are committed to setting a higher standard for education, oversight, and enforcement of safe social behavior and citizenship," Kotlikoff wrote.

Ray Epstein, who works with a consent education company, and is one of the organizers of a rally planned just steps away from Cornell's campus on Tuesday, said that while the measures from Cornell are "overall a win," they also serve as an "effort to save face."

"What I think they should be doing, is operating first instead of as a business, the way that they are now, as institutions that are meant to educate and keep their students safe," Epstein said.

Kotlikoff said that in addition to enhancing bystander training programming, the university will also improve its services to survivors of sexual assault by increasing staffing in its civil rights office, which would help individuals navigate the reporting process for incidents.

Additionally, the university will work with the New York State Police's criminal investigators on campus sexual assault investigations. The move allows the investigators, who are independent from the university, to take on cases in which survivors pursue criminal charges.

Sponsor Message

The university plans to bring in faculty who are experts in sexual assault and rape culture to help reform the Presidential Task Force on Sexual Assault through listening events with the Cornell community.

Kotlikoff's letter did not explain why these events are only being issued now — two years after administrators at Cornell learned about the allegations in 2024.

Although the district attorney did not prosecute the case in 2024, Cornell's Title IX office conducted an investigation in 2025. In March 2025, a panel of staff and faculty at Cornell moved to expel or suspend some of the men. The panel required the remaining men to write "essays" in addition to other sanctions.

Cornell also barred the Chi Phi fraternity chapter, which was closed in 2024.

World.title: The Trump administration warns Ukraine it could cut off intel, Zelenskyy tells NPR
World.content:
The Trump administration warns Ukraine it could cut off intel, Zelenskyy tells NPR

toggle caption i Svet Jacqueline for NPR

KYIV, Ukraine — The Trump administration warned it could cut off intelligence-sharing with Ukraine unless Ukrainian forces stop long-range drone strikes on oil refineries inside Russia, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told NPR.

In an interview with NPR on Tuesday, Zelenskyy said the Trump administration's decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel will not bring down fuel prices. He also refuted President Trump's assertion this weekend that Ukraine was to blame for the rise in diesel fuel prices. Zelenskyy pointed out it is because of the Iran war.

"Mostly people in the world know why their prices on any kind of energy, including diesel, raised up, why they increased. Because of Hormuz. Yes. Because of blocking the Strait of Hormuz," Zelenskyy said, referring to the vital shipping chokepoint between the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman.

Sponsor Message

President Zelenskyy's sit-down with NPR comes as Russia's full-scale invasion nears the five-year mark, at a time when the White House has renewed efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war. Tensions between Zelenskyy and President Trump have also flared up again after the U.S. made a key concession to Moscow.

On Friday, Trump moved to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports. Zelenskyy said in a statement it was a "a weak decision by strong partners."

Trump lashed back hard at Zelenskyy, saying, "I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president," a leader who can reach a peace deal with Putin.

Then on Sunday, Trump announced on social media Russia and Ukraine had allegedly agreed to a partial ceasefire to halt attacks on each other's energy infrastructure — catching Kyiv by surprise — even as Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure continued.

Zelenskyy told NPR he found out about Trump's assertion of an energy ceasefire agreement "through social like you" — meaning, from Trump's post on his Truth Social account.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was asked Sunday about the announced energy truce and told reporters that contacts were ongoing.

Zelenskyy told NPR his country is striking Russian energy and logistics sites to weaken the Kremlin's ability to wage war. Ukraine wants the war to end, he said, but will not stop these strikes unless Russia stops attacking Ukrainian energy sites.

Sponsor Message

Putin doesn't respond to diplomacy, the Ukrainian leader said, "he understands force."

However, asked on Tuesday whether the U.S. stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine, Trump told reporters: "We are helping them and we are sharing intel, we want the war to end."

Meanwhile, high fuel prices have been a major concern in the U.S. as the midterm elections approach next month. In the U.S., diesel fuel costs an average of $6.27 per gallon — more than 70% above what it was a year ago when it was a little over $3.65 a gallon, according to AAA.

Zelenskyy said said Trump's decisions to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel would not influence "the price in the United States. I'm sure … because the volume is not enough."

What it would do, he said, is provide the Kremlin with more money to spend on its war.

World.title: Writer Yiyun Li lost both of her sons. When words fell short, she turned to music
World.content:
Writer Yiyun Li lost both of her sons. When words fell short, she turned to music

toggle caption i Hannah Yoon/Macmillan

If you or someone you know may be considering suicide or is in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.

Writer Yiyun Li does not talk about "grief" or the "grieving process." To her, those words make it sound that at some point you emerge from grief. Instead, Li prefers to use the word "abyss," which, she says, is where she expects to be for the remainder of her life.

Li's teenage sons both died by suicide six years apart, Vincent in 2017 at age 16, and James in 2024 at age 19. Her Pulitzer Prize-winning 2025 memoir, Things in Nature Merely Grow, chronicled the loss of her sons and her effort to go on.

Sponsor Message

"James' death taught me to suffer better," she says. "To say, 'I can do it, and I can live with my pain and sorrow without ever wanting to stop feeling.'"

Li's new novel, Music Against the Night, is set in the late 1700s and early 1800s and centers on two prodigies who are brought together by music, and drawn apart because of their aspirations. The novel focuses on music, which sits outside of words.

"I think I've had the feeling both times after my children's death that words often fall short, and falling short doesn't mean not succeeding, falling short doesn't mean failing," she says. "But when I start a new project, I would like a subject [where] words naturally fall short. So music is that choice."

Li grew up in China and served a year in the Chinese military before coming to the U.S. to study immunology. She eventually left her Ph.D. program to become a writer. Li is now a professor in the creative writing program at Princeton University.

Macmillan

Interview highlights

On the decision to set Music Against the Night in a different time period

I was in the middle of the novel when James died. This is a novel far from my usual interests or concerns, and the reason I think I went back to history is I would like to live again through history, through historical figures, through my characters living in the late 18th and early 19th century. ... I'm making the past into a new now for myself and possibly for my readers.

Sponsor Message

On how playing piano connects to her grief

I began my piano lessons at the end of 2023, purely to get to know how to play the piano. And James died in February 2024, so two months into my piano lessons he died, and it occurred to me that piano or music is a good way for me to count time — because music is about time. It's about counting the measure, counting the rhythm. And also music is about ... be[ing] engaged with something else. You can sit in your sadness all day long, do nothing, or crying. Or, like me, I could just sit there and just play the same drill again, and again, as a way to know I was, in a way, staying in touch with the world. ...

I'm not a concert pianist, but somehow I find it liberating and healthy to do something that you absolutely love but cannot do well. Every time I go to my piano lesson, I'm so intimidated. I'm sweating because I just can't do it. I can hear other people do it, I cannot do it myself. But I think that's, again, acknowledging the limit of my capacity.

On raising two gifted children

Both my children could be called prodigies, but James, my younger son, especially was extraordinarily odd and brilliant. ... We were greatly baffled. I remember he was 5 or 6, he said, "Mommy, you will never see the world. I see it full of dots and squiggly lines." And that again was a strange perception of the world [that] we adults did not have access to. …

What is the responsibility or the difficulty of bringing up a child [who is] very brilliant? … Some people would say, well, you really have to train him to be the next Einstein, but we did not want him to be the next Einstein, we want him to be a normal, happy boy living in an ordinary life.

Sponsor Message

On her son Vincent

He was a brilliant painter and we still have all his paintings around the house. He was an oboist and when he wanted to learn the oboe, the oboe teacher said he was a bit young, because he was 8 when he want to learn oboe, but he was certain. ... [He had] started on the piano and he could articulate that piano was not his instrument. He wanted to play the oboe. But mostly, he wrote beautiful poetry. He was a great poet. And he was a greater reader. I wouldn't call him an outlier, as James was, but he was brilliant and fun and interesting.

On struggling with suicidal ideation

Sometimes I think people have all sort of thoughts about or against people who have chosen suicide, and people who've chosen or attempted suicide are often called selfish. But my experience is oftentimes people [are] in great pain, whether it's great mental pain or great physical pain. And sometimes people in deep depression cannot tell the difference between mental pain and physical pain, because everything together is a great kind of suffering. I think it's not that people who experience that kind of suicidal urge, it's not that they want to die or they want [to] use this to hurt other people.

On becoming a writer

I was born with innate curiosity and also sensitivity to things that did not quite make sense. So I grew up in China. And for instance, when I was little, all the adults would say, since you're a child, you have no right to decide who you want to be or what you want to do. And my mother even had a saying, something along the [lines] that an adult decides and the child follows. I was quite young, you know, 4 or 5. I just couldn't make sense of all of these teachings because I thought I was as capable of thinking as the adults, and why did I have to follow them? So I think that sort of sensitivity to things that are very, very nonsensical, I think maybe that's one thing that made me into a writer.

Sponsor Message

Anna Bauman and Nico Gonzalez Wisler produced and edited this interview for broadcast. Bridget Bentz, Molly Seavy-Nesper and Beth Novey adapted it for the web.

World.title: Government spent millions on Trump ads. And, federal agents raid Ilhan Omar's home
World.content:
Government spent millions on Trump ads. And, federal agents raid Ilhan Omar's home

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

The U.S. government continues to pay for ads promoting President Trump, even after he announced that his MAGA Inc. super PAC would take over funding. A federal judge ordered the ads to be taken down, yet they remained on air. An NPR analysis of data from AdImpact finds that nearly $22 million in taxpayer funds have been spent since the campaign began in late September. Almost $10 million of that was spent after Trump pledged on an Oct. 5 Truth Social post to fund the campaign privately. The White House has called the ads public service announcements, but a lawsuit by Common Cause and others argued they were funded without congressional approval, violating restrictions on taxpayer-funded publicity and propaganda.

toggle caption i Alex Wong/Getty Images

Trump has ramped up his campaign travel ahead of the midterm elections. He rallied supporters in Youngstown, Ohio, last night and is heading to Alaska today. More events are planned for later this week. He has been trying to encourage his supporters to vote by telling them to pretend he is on the ballot.



Sponsor Message

🎧 Trump's events resemble his presidential campaign rallies: He emphasizes his accomplishments while calling out superfans and insulting Democrats, NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben tells Up First. Kurtzleben adds that Trump's campaign trail emphasizes that the GOP is still his party, despite his declining approval. Candidates like Ohio GOP gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and GOP Sen. Jon Husted saw large, appreciative, but Kurtzleben says the benefits of appearing alongside Trump remain unclear.

He emphasizes his accomplishments while calling out superfans and insulting Democrats, NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben tells Up First. Kurtzleben adds that Trump's campaign trail emphasizes that the GOP is still his party, despite his declining approval. Candidates like Ohio GOP gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and GOP Sen. Jon Husted saw large, appreciative, but Kurtzleben says the benefits of appearing alongside Trump remain unclear. ➡️ With just weeks until Election Day , polls may start to flood the landscape. While they serve as a helpful tool, remember they can't predict the future. Keep these tips in mind as polls pour in.

, polls may start to flood the landscape. While they serve as a helpful tool, remember they can't predict the future. Keep these tips in mind as polls pour in. ➡️ The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country, to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.

Federal agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar's home in Washington, D.C., yesterday morning. Omar, D-Minn., says the search was politically motivated by the Trump administration. The Department of Justice told NPR in a statement that Homeland Security Investigations agents "executed a judicially authorized search warrant," approved by the DOJ, as part of an ongoing federal investigation. Current and former federal officials with knowledge of the search who were not authorized to speak publicly confirmed the details, revealing that this multi-year probe includes whistleblower complaints and focuses on allegations of immigration fraud.



Sponsor Message

🎧 One of Omar's neighbors, 79-year-old Sharon Jackson, tells NPR's Luke Garrett she was awoken yesterday at around 4:30 a.m. by loud knocking and that vans and agents wearing gloves were walking to and from the congresswoman's house. Vice President JD Vance previously accused Omar of immigration fraud, which she denies. Omar is an American citizen who left Somalia as a refugee. She stated on social media that the president has spent a decade targeting her with smear campaigns and vowed not to be silenced. Trump says that he is not involved in the investigation into Omar.

Living better

toggle caption i Malte Mueller/Getty Images

Living Better is a special series about what it takes to stay healthy in America.

The U.S. is experiencing its worst measles resurgence in decades. More than 3,600 confirmed cases and two deaths have been reported as of late September. Outbreaks in several states and exposures in public places like bars, sports stadiums and public transit have raised concerns about travel safety. Almost all U.S. measles cases involve unvaccinated individuals, and as the outbreaks grow in some states, the risk of exposure is getting higher. Here's what to know before traveling by plane or train.



✈️ People who've had two doses of the MMR vaccine are considered protected against measles.

✈️ The disease is highly contagious. It spreads through the air when an infected person coughs, breathes or sneezes. That airspace can remain contaminated for up to two hours.

✈️ Check with your healthcare provider about your vaccination status. They may recommend a booster based on your medical history and health.

✈️ Immunocompromised individuals may be unable to receive vaccination and often rely on herd immunity for protection. For measles, the vaccination threshold for herd immunity is 95%.

✈️ Measles can be hard to track because symptoms — such as fever, cough, and rash — typically appear seven to 14 days after exposure and can sometimes take long as 21 days to surface.

Sponsor Message

Picture show

toggle caption i Ernst Haas/Getty Images

The Metropolitan Museum of Art's new blockbuster exhibition showcases the works of two 20th-century artists. Jackson Pollock is well-known for his drip paintings. His wife, Lee Krasner, has often been overshadowed by her husband. This show finally gives Krasner the recognition she deserves. With more than 120 pieces on display — 74 from Krasner and 48 from Pollock — the show highlights Krasner as a titan of Abstract Expressionism, too. Check out some of the photos from the exhibit.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP via Getty Images

Americans Robert Hall from Stanford University and Michael Woodford from Columbia University have won the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for their work on managing boom-and-bust cycles to reduce inflation and unemployment. Trump's new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, will hold her first press briefing today. She has raised her profile by appearing on conservative outlets and promoting right-wing conspiracy theories. Hectic early-morning traffic can make breakfast a luxury in Lagos, Nigeria. Akara is a roadside staple. For NPR's Breakfast Around the World series, Emmanuel Akinwotu explores the savory snack's deep roots in Nigeria and West Africa, and its spread around the world during the trans-Atlantic slave trade.

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

World.title: 12 U.S. senators, including 6 Republicans, tell Trump to drop diesel deal with Russia
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A dozen U.S. senators, including six of U.S. President ‌Donald Trump's fellow Republicans, called on the president on Tuesday to rescind his diesel oil deal with Russia, days before his administration must decide whether to formally impose new sanctions on Moscow over its war in Ukraine.

The lawmakers' letter to Trump said the agreement provides Russian President Vladimir Putin's government with more fuel to finance its war, and will not benefit Americans, adding to a torrent ​of congressional criticism since Trump announced the deal on Friday.

The resistance marks a shift from what had been ​Republicans' near-unanimous support for Trump's foreign policy decisions, weeks before ⁠Nov. 3 midterm elections ⁠that will determine whether the party ‌retains control of Congress.

Trump said Friday he was lifting sanctions ​on Russian diesel exports, and that Moscow would immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons (2.25 million barrels) of diesel ⁠to U.S. and global markets.

Although Trump ⁠said he wanted to reduce prices, the amount he referenced is less ‌than a day's supply for the U.S. transport sector alone, according to U.S. Energy Information Administration data, which shows daily use of around 2.94 million barrels per day.

'Betrayal' of allies

"Granting Moscow the ability to sell Russian diesel freely in global markets damages American security interests and is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine, who continue to defend themselves from Putin's murderous, illegal war," the senators said in their letter.

"This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of ‌our Allies; it should be rescinded."

The letter was signed by Republicans Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, Thom Tillis of North Carolina, Susan Collins of Maine, Alan Armstrong of Oklahoma, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska ​and John Cornyn of Texas, as well as six Democrats.

WATCH | Trump announces diesel deal with Russia: Trump reverses course on Russian oil sanctions | Duration closed caption 2:08 U.S. President Donald Trump has announced a deal to import Russian diesel as fuel prices soar, reversing course on sanctions against Moscow. Ukraine is condemning the move, warning it will directly benefit Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Under a law Trump signed last month, he faces an Oct. 18 deadline to impose sweeping new sanctions and tariffs on Russian energy over the Ukraine war, or waive them because he has determined that doing so is in the national interest.

The letter ​urged Trump to execute the sanctions authorities included in the new law, called the "Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026," in honour of the late senator — a Russia hawk ⁠and close Trump ally who died in July.

The administration has not yet told lawmakers whether it would impose the sanctions or issue ⁠a waiver.

Urged to 'reverse course'

Collins, Murkowski and Tillis had joined ⁠Democrats in a joint statement on Sunday calling on Trump to "reverse course" on the ⁠deal, saying it runs counter to U.S. law barring imports of energy ⁠until ⁠Russia ends its aggression ​against Ukraine.

A man stands near a building in Kharkiv, Ukraine, on Monday, which was struck by a Russian jet-powered drone. (Sofiia Gatilova/Reuters)

Earlier on Tuesday, Trump was asked whether anyone had told him Russia could use proceeds ​of the diesel deal to purchase more ⁠bombs. "No, nobody told me anything," he responded, adding the deal benefited not just the U.S. but the world.

Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on Monday that Russia will be able to return diesel exports to levels above those Trump had outlined under the deal.

The Democratic senators who signed the letter were Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, Richard Durbin of Illinois, Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, Jack Reed of Rhode Island and Chris Coons of Connecticut.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The two countries have been in a state of all-out war ever since.

World.title: Alleged Tumbler Ridge co-conspirator James Cody Bryant denied bail
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A district court judge in Seattle has refused bail for alleged Tumbler Ridge co-conspirator James Cody Bryant.

Bryant, a 30-year-old resident of Bellingham, Wash. — whose lawyers say uses she/her pronouns and goes by the name Melody — was arrested Oct. 6 and charged with one count of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country.

Prosecutors say that conspiracy involved encouraging and supporting Tumbler Ridge Secondary School shooter Jesse Van Rootselaar in the lead-up to the Feb. 10 attack, in which she killed five students and one staff member at the campus after shooting and killing her mother and stepbrother at their home.

Police allege that in online interactions on the social media platform Discord, Bryant agreed to livestream the attack, gave Van Rootselaar money, and provided months of logistical support.

In making her ruling, Magistrate Judge Mary Alice Theiler described Bryant as a "tragically vulnerable, unstable individual" with serious mental health concerns and substance abuse problems.

She added that release would require constant supervision to prevent Bryant from accessing the internet, something she did not believe authorities could achieve.

Bryant — dressed in prison greens — wept throughout the proceedings.

Assistant United States attorney Todd Greenberg, who is prosecuting the case against Bryant, had argued that Bryant posed a flight risk and a danger to the public.

The home of alleged Tumbler Ridge shooting co-conspirator James Cody Bryant in Bellingham, Wash. (Caroline Barghout/CBC)

"It does not get much more serious or dangerous for the community," he said in a memorandum filed Tuesday in support of a detention order.

"Bryant’s participation in the charged murder conspiracy took place primarily through online communications … There are simply no conditions of release that can be fully and effectively enforced to ensure that Bryant does not pose a continuing threat to the community through online behavior."

Efforts to assist in shooting

Tuesday's memorandum drew on conversations alleged to have taken place between Bryant and Van Rootselaar as the attack was planned.

On Feb. 9, the day before the shooting, Van Rootselaar reportedly told Bryant she didn't want to carry out the shooting if she didn't "know for certain" someone would livestream it, the court documents outline.

"I literally fixed my sleep schedule to help me stay up to be there after work," Bryant replied.

According to the memorandum, a livestream was initiated in the moments before the attack but failed after about 20 seconds due to technical issues.

"The livestream’s failure was despite Bryant’s best efforts to make it happen," Greenberg said.

Greenberg also pointed to a payment of $14.33 Bryant sent to Van Rootselaar's PayPal ID to enable her to purchase a lighter to ignite an explosive device constructed for use in the attack. The payment was reversed because the account had been deactivated.

The District of Tumbler Ridge town hall as pictured on Aug. 21, 2026. (Tom Summer/CBC)

"Van Rootselaar ultimately deployed this explosive device," Greenberg said.

"Although $14.33 may not be a lot of money, it speaks volumes about the seriousness of the offense and the defendant’s character that Bryant was willing to help purchase the ignition source for an explosive device that was to be used to attack schoolchildren."

He also argued substance abuse and mental health concerns should be factored in, including evidence of suicidal ideations that were shared with Van Rootselaar but not disclosed to the Probation Office.

"Bryant repeatedly acknowledged being in a unique position to stop Van Rootselaar," he said.

"Anyone whose character allows them to help plan a mass shooting and then sits back and (literally) tries to watch as schoolchildren are murdered … is a danger to the community and should be detained pending trial."

Defense argues for conditional release

In their application opposing a motion for detention, assistant federal public defenders Gregory Murphy and Dennis Carroll argued Bryant had co-operated with investigators in the days following the attack.



"She expressed horror at Van Rootselaar’s crimes," they said.

The defence argued that law enforcement had acknowledged Bryant repeatedly tried to dissuade Van Rootselaar from carrying out the attack, and pointed to their client's clean criminal record.

"There is no evidence that she has ever personally committed an act of violence. There is no evidence that she is in contact with anyone else planning an act of violence," Murphy and Carroll said.

Defense counsel underscored Bryant's stable residence, close ties to the community, and long-term employment at a local McDonald's restaurant.

In his submission, Greenberg said Bryant had admitted to being "on thin ice" at work due to repeatedly calling in sick.

"It’s not clear whether that job remains available due to the arrest in this case," he said.

Murphy and Carroll also disputed Greenberg's mental health concerns, arguing that although Bryant had "briefly" seen a psychologist during high school and had taken medication for panic attacks, there was no evidence to support claims of suicidality.

"There is no evidence she has expressed a thought of harming herself in the last fourteen months. There is no evidence she ever has made plans to hurt herself," the application read..

World.title: ‘Catastrophic’ brake failure, neglected repairs contributed to deadly 2020 icefield bus rollover, judge finds
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A complete failure of the braking system triggered by neglected mechanical repairs contributed to a deadly tour bus rollover in the Columbia Icefield, a fatality inquiry has concluded.

In a report made public late last week, Judge Vaughn Myers of the Alberta Court of Justice details a string of catastrophic oversights that preceded the rollover that killed three passengers and severely injured 14.

It was the afternoon of July 18, 2020, when a heavy-duty vehicle known as an Ice Explorer — carrying 24 tourists across the scenic expanse of the Athabasca Glacier in Jasper National Park — tumbled down a steep embankment, landing on its roof.

Dionne Durocher, 24, of North Battleford, Sask., Kamleshbhai Patel, 58, and Griva Patel, 28, of Edmonton, were ejected from the vehicle and died of their injuries within minutes.

In his findings, Myers calls on the tour company Pursuit — also known as Brewster — to make a series of safety improvements, concluding that warnings about the faltering safety of the vehicle went unheeded in the days and weeks before the crash.

The investigation determined the Ice Explorer had dangerously worn components, inadequate brake power and lacked routine maintenance.

Rapid speed, no braking force

Myers said the fatality inquiry, held in October 2025, sought to examine not only policy measures that could prevent similar tragedies but also “questions that were not clearly answered” by the RCMP and Occupational Health and Safety investigators, most critically any lapses in the maintenance of the vehicle.

Ice Explorers are large, wide-bodied, three-axle, off-road buses, also known as snow coaches, that have been used in the Columbia Icefield since the 1980s.

They’re purpose-built for icy terrain, with specialized brake systems that include a transmission lock-up to assist when the machine is on a descent — but only if the vehicle is in gear.

Court heard that, in the moments before the crash, the Ice Explorer was descending a steep slope known as the Lateral Moraine Road.

The vehicle was in neutral and, lacking engine-retarding force, accelerated to a speed between 41 to 49 km/h, far beyond its maximum powered speed of 14 km/h.

The driver applied the manual brakes, but due to severe mechanical defects, they failed.

The driver lost control and the bus rolled one and a half times down the slope, with passengers ejected into the rocky terrain below.

“There are two primary contributing factors,” Myers wrote. “The first is the driver, for reasons unknown, negotiating the lateral moraine in neutral and without the six-wheel drive engaged,” Myers wrote.

“This configuration, on such a grade, would create a situation in which vehicle speed accumulates rapidly. Unable to use engine power to slow the bus, the driver would have to rely on conventional braking.”

Pursuit’s policy at the time was for drivers to put the Ice Explorers in neutral at the top of the hill and then, at the start of the steepest descent, put them in gear.

In this case, the bus was never put into gear or it popped out of gear almost immediately, the judge found.

“This leads to the second primary contributing factor: effective braking force. During the mechanical inspection, it was determined that this vehicle did not have sufficient braking power to stop the vehicle, even in ideal situations.”

'Worn, improperly inspected'

An inspection after the crash showed that only one of the six wheels had the power to safely brake as required.

Court heard that five days before the crash, a driver formally reported a major braking issue on a daily inspection report. He noted that full pedal depression was required to stop the rig and requested an inspection of the brake slack adjusters.

But the defect wasn’t inspected or repaired, nor was it carried forward on subsequent daily reports as the company required, the judge found.

Furthermore, on-site mechanics were new and inexperienced with Ice Explorers and also lacked proper training, the inquiry found.

“In short, the brakes suffered a catastrophic failure because they were worn, improperly inspected and concerns with respect to the brakes functioning were not attended to,” Myers wrote.

'Inconceivable to the court'

Court also heard the Ice Explorer bus had been serviced two months earlier by Wajax, a company that offers repairs and maintenance for heavy-duty vehicles.

It was sent to Wajax for a scheduled 1,000-hour inspection, returning to service just 12 days before the fatal crash.

However, the judge noted serious issues with the Wajax inspection report, which was undated and did not reference a specific vehicle.

“The inspection report tendered indicated the brakes were satisfactory and passed inspection,” Myers wrote.

“It is inconceivable to the court that the tires were removed to properly inspect the faulty braking. Secondly, the court has serious concerns whether this inspection report actually applied to this vehicle.”

Myers said the lack of seatbelts and the route itself were contributing factors. Parts of Lateral Moraine Road reach an incline of 40 per cent, exceeding the maximum limit of 36 per cent specified by the Ice Explorer manufacturer.

The court determined that though medical response was prompt, no intervention could have saved the victims.�

Myers called on Pursuit to improve its inspection protocols.

The company must ensure that external maintenance and inspection reports are dated and detail exactly what work is performed on which vehicle, and that a copy is kept inside for driver review.

The company should also work alongside OHS and the provincial government to immediately implement a training program for all mechanics working on its Ice Explorer fleet, Myers wrote.

The judge encouraged OHS and Alberta Transportation to establish a rigorous, standardized three-year service and inspection procedure for off-road tour vehicles and a new policy for defect reports.

RCMP didn't lay criminal charges in the crash, but Pursuit pleaded guilty in 2023 to two charges under the Alberta Occupational Health and Safety Act and was fined $475,000.

In a statement to CBC News, officials with Pursuit said the operator has since made significant safety changes including enhanced driver training, seatbelts in all Ice Explorers, and updated processes for vehicle inspection, maintenance and defect reports.

“[We] will continue working with the appropriate authorities to ensure our practices meet the standard expected of us.

“Our thoughts remain with the families of Dionne Durocher, Griva Patel and Kamleshbhai Patel and with everyone affected by the July 2020 tragedy at the Columbia Icefield.”

World.title: B.C. NDP Leader David Eby defends family's enrolment in $10-a-day child-care
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

B.C. NDP Leader David Eby is defending his family's enrolment in the provincial $10-a-day child-care program.

Eby is under attack from Conservatives who say his "wealthy family" should not benefit from the program that they say is inaccessible to many low-income families.

In a post on X Monday, Eby said one of his children was already attending a child-care centre when it was designated as a $10-a-day site.

"When that occurred, we chose as a family to make a donation to that excellent facility," Eby said.

"We felt that we did not need that discount and we wanted to make sure that the child-care centre could provide other supports for families in the community."

Eby said his family will make a similar donation to the child-care centre for their youngest child who attends the same facility.

At a news conference on Tuesday, Eby would not specify the donation amount or if it was used as a tax write off.

"We certainly didn't need that discount," Eby said.

"We paid the difference between what it was before and what it was after the $10-a-day daycare," he added.

Now, Eby is taking heat from the B.C. Conservatives during the snap provincial election campaign.

"It's shocking to learn that while hundreds of thousands of British Columbians are struggling with the most expensive child care in the country, David Eby's family landed a plum $10-a-day child care spot," said Margareta Dovgal, the B.C. Conservative candidate for Vancouver-Yaletown, in a news release Monday.

The Conservatives called attention to Eby's compensation from 2025 to 2026 as premier, which totalled more than $226,000, and criticized his "wealthy family" for benefiting from the subsidized child-care program.

After Eby's Tuesday news conference, Dovgal said Eby was dodging the tough questions.

"David Eby should look a working single mother paying thousands in childcare costs in the eye explaining why his wealthy, powerful family deserves $10/day childcare first," Dovgal said in a second news release.

"David Eby is trying to defend the indefensible, as British Columbians are seeing Eby for the opportunistic hypocrite he is."

The Conservatives are demanding Eby answer a number of questions, including around the value and proof of his first donation, whether it was a tax write-off, and more information on the value of the second planned donation.

What is the $10-a-day child-care program?

The $10-a-day program is operated by independent businesses who have chosen to participate; access to one of the facilities is based on each location's licensed capacity and waitlist, according to the provincial government.

When a child-care centre is approved to be a part of the $10-a-day program, the child's space is automatically converted into the $10-a-day program, according to a provincial Q&A webpage.

The B.C. NDP say their Conservative opponents "have been silent" around whether their party would reverse child care fee caps.

Eby said Tuesday the Conservatives are proposing to cut certain child-care programs. However, the Conservatives have not laid out their plan yet.

CBC News has reached out to the B.C. Conservatives for their child-care proposals.

Experts weigh in

Sharon Gregson, provincial spokesperson for the $10-a-day child-care campaign with the Coalition of Child Care Advocates of B.C., said Eby's situation is less newsworthy than the structural system.

"What's newsworthy is that expansion of the system has stalled," Gregson said on CBC's BC Today.

"I don't think any reasonable person would begrudge a family have access to quality affordable child care," she said.

"But the point is, as a decision-maker and as the leader of the province, he should have been — and whoever is elected next — should make sure that the $10-a-day system is expanded."

Gregson said thousands of families have benefited from the program.

B.C. has about 18,000 $10-a-day child-care spaces, or about 10 per cent of the province's licensed child-care spots, according to Gregson.

She said there shouldn't be income-testing for the program.

"The point [is] that all programs should have the opportunity to be $10-a-day, not just 10 per cent of spaces."

Hamish Telford, associate professor of political science at the University of the Fraser Valley, said the Eby issue may concern some residents.

"A lot of people will have raised eyebrows from this story," Telford said.

But Telford added, based on the premier's messaging, it sounds like he did the right thing by paying the difference and that as long as he didn't get special access because of his role as premier, there's nothing necessarily nefarious unless other information emerges.

But it's still poor optics, according to Telford.

"It looks like the privileged are getting a privilege — and that never, never looks well on a politician."

World.title: Surgery confirms Pope has lung cancer, Vatican says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Pope Leo's surgery confirmed that he has lung cancer, and he had the lower lobe of his right lung removed, the Vatican said Tuesday.

The tests confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin after the surgery. It said the diagnosis had been suspected by preoperative tests and was confirmed during surgery.

The statement made no mention of treatment going forward, and the Vatican said doctors were not currently speaking of chemotherapy or other therapies. The Vatican press office noted the medical statement spoke of the "radical" removal of the lobe as an indication that doctors removed all suspect tissue in hopes of removing any lingering traces of the cancer.

Human lungs have five lobes — three in the right lung and two in the left.

A medical expert said that ​to assess the pope's case, more information would be needed about the size of the tumour and whether the cancer had ⁠spread to his lymph nodes. The Vatican ⁠did not immediately provide those details.

"While we have the diagnosis, we do not yet have ‌the stage. This is critical to prognosis and treatment," said Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown University in Washington and division chief of hematology-oncology at MedStar Georgetown University Hospital.

"If this is a small lung cancer with no lymph nodes involved, surgery itself is likely to be curative," he told Reuters. "But if final analysis reveals a greater extent of cancer involvement, this indicates a poorer prognosis."

LISTEN | Learn more about lung cancer: The Dose 24:16 What should people who’ve never smoked know about lung cancer?

The 71-year-old was in the operating room for about three hours, the statement said. The surgery itself lasted approximately 90 minutes. The pope regained ⁠consciousness normally after the operation and later returned to his hospital room, where he was resting, the bulletin said.

Leo had walked into the hospital through the main entrance earlier in the day and waved to dozens of well-wishers who had gathered to greet him. The Vatican said the surgery would be performed by a team led by Gemelli's chief thoracic surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora.

Oncologists said prior to the operation that even if the nodule turned out to be cancerous, Leo's prognosis is "excellent" since it will have been removed at an early stage.

People wait for Pope Leo to arrive at the Agostino Gemelli Polyclinic in Rome ahead of his operation. (Alessandra Tarantino/The Associated Press)

Prayers for the Pope

The operation got under way as medical staff recited the Rosary prayer in the hospital chapel Tuesday evening.

"Let us join together in prayer, asking the Lord to sustain our bishop, Pope Leo, and to comfort all those who are hospitalized here," said the Vicar of Rome, Cardinal Baldassare Reina, at the start of the prayer.

The American pontiff has offered a rare level of transparency about the first publicly disclosed major health problem of his 17-month papacy. He revealed the discovery of the small, localized nodule during his Sunday noon prayer and announced that he would have it removed.

The surgery will require a weeklong hospital stay, and the Vatican on Monday cancelled all Leo's audiences through Oct. 20.

The pontiff is expected to spend a week in hospital after the operation. (Gregorio Borgia/The Associated Press)

A churchman who saw Leo on Monday, Tokyo Cardinal Kikuchi Tsutomu, said Leo told him he felt fine and decided to have the surgery immediately so that he wouldn't have to alter his upcoming travel plans to Latin America.

But the decision clearly came as a surprise: While Gemelli has a specific papal apartment that past popes have used, complete with a private chapel on the 10th floor, Leo will actually be staying in a nearby room since the papal apartment is currently undergoing renovations, according to the Vatican press office.

Leo, elected ‌by the world's cardinals in May 2025, is relatively young for a church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to be a smoker or to have had health issues previously.

November trip to South America

EIO advises patients not to fly for three weeks after surgery, which would give the pope just the interval needed to make his planned Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, depending on his recovery.

The current itinerary for the trip is ambitious and the longest of his papacy to date, calling for Leo to clock just over 31,000 kilometres on a dozen flights and two helicopter rides, and a significant altitude change in Peru.

"I think the Holy Father is in excellent hands at Gemelli," Spaggiari said. "They have everything needed to keep the Holy Father alive for a long time."

WATCH | Pope Leo urges compassion for migrants: Pope Leo urges compassion for migrants during Spain trip | Duration closed caption 2:11 During a visit to Spain’s Canary Islands, Pope Leo urged compassion for migrants and asylum seekers. His comments align with the Spanish government’s plan to grant legal residency to half a million undocumented migrants — making it an outlier in Europe.

Kikuchi, the Tokyo archbishop who is also head of the Vatican's charitable federation Caritas Internationalis, said Leo told him he felt no different than usual and was looking ahead to the trip.

"He has decided to undergo surgery soon in order to not change his plans for future overseas trips, so there is no need to worry, as it is not an emergency," Kikuchi wrote on the Facebook page of the Tokyo archdiocese.

World.title: Roller coaster fatality in Georgia leads to temporary closure of 3 rides at Canadian parks
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A 42-year-old man killed while riding a roller-coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia was thrown from his seat and struck other patrons before landing below the ride, police said Tuesday.

Visitors to the Atlanta-area park watched in horror as he fell out of the coaster Monday, prompting Six Flags to temporarily close nine similar roller-coasters countrywide.

Investigators and park officials have not said how he ended up coming out of his seat.

"It was horrific to watch," said Summer Bates, who was at the park with her husband and three children. "One thing I think that will stick with us is the sound of his body coming down."

Bates said she and her family rode the Goliath roller-coaster earlier in the day. The park's tallest coaster, which towers over its entrance at 61 metres, has lap bar restraints that pull down over the riders' legs and waist. There are no seat belts.

"My older two children rode on the cart ahead of us," she said. "I noticed they kept trying to push theirs down tighter. I assured them that they were OK. But once my husband, youngest child and I loaded our cart and headed up the incline, I quickly understood why my older two were messing with theirs. It just didn't feel secure and tight."

The man who died was 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, according to Cobb County police. Officials have not released any other information about those who were injured when they were struck by the man.

Kariem worked as the information technology manager at a public charter school in Atlanta and before that was the school's technology teacher, according to an online resume.

Witness describes seeing man come out of his seat

Logan Conner said he was on the Goliath with his fiancée when he saw the man come out of his seat.

"The man started levitating in the air sideways," he told NBC. "We made direct eye contact with him."

WATCH | 1 dead, several injured in U.S. roller-coaster incident: One dead, several injured after incident on a Six Flags roller-coaster in Georgia | Hanomansing Live | Duration closed caption 3:04 One person has died and several others were injured in an incident involving a Six Flags roller-coaster Monday afternoon in Georgia, according to police.

Britny Landry had been on the ride earlier Monday and was waiting in line to go again. She could see part of the Goliath track.

"We just look, and I just see somebody fly out," she told KTVU-TV. She said she wasn't sure if that's what she saw at first. "Maybe somebody had a bag or something."

Investigators say they spoke with park visitors and employees who saw what happened in the incident Monday at Six Flags Over Georgia in Mableton, about 24 kilometres northwest of Atlanta.

Coasters closed in Canada and U.S.

Nine roller-coasters at six North American parks that are similar to the coaster in Georgia were closed "out of an abundance of caution," according to a Six Flags Entertainment Corporation spokesperson, who said staff members and local authorities responded immediately and the park is co-operating with the investigation.

"We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today," the spokesperson said, adding that the company is providing support to guests and staff who were impacted.

CBC News has confirmed that the list of nine rides includes the Behemoth and Leviathan at Canada's Wonderland, north of Toronto. A park spokesperson said it did not have a timeline for when the rides might be available again.

Canada's Wonderland is open to the public for 12 more Halloween-themed evenings and weekends until it closes for the winter.

Montreal's La Ronde amusement park said it was temporarily shutting down its Goliath roller-coaster until an update is received from the manufacturer of the ride. La Ronde was a Six Flags property until this spring, when the park's purchase by EPR Properties was finalized.

Authorities and Six Flags did not identify the roller-coaster at the Georgia location. However, local TV stations showed video of passengers being evacuated from the Goliath coaster.

The roller-coaster, which was opened in 2006, reaches top speeds of about 113 km/h and heights of 61 metres, the park's website reports. During about 3½ minutes, riders "navigate through razor-sharp turns and soar over colossal hills," according to the website.

"I cannot imagine the horror the patrons and employees witnessed today, and my heart aches for the family who lost a loved one," Lisa Cupid, chair of the Cobb County Board of Commissioners, said in a statement. She added that next of kin have been notified.

The amusement park is a major part of the county's tourism and brings in visitors from across the southeast, Cupid said.

"We are all grappling with how something so devastating could happen at a place that has given generations of families such happy memories," she said.

The X2 roller-coaster, seen at Six Flags Magic Mountain in Valencia, Calif., has been closed following lawsuits alleging riders suffered brain injuries. (Jae C. Hong/The Associated Press)

Georgia's Office of Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner, which oversees ride inspections, is "conducting an in‑depth and comprehensive review," said Garrison Bennett, a spokesperson. The park was already scheduled to be closed Tuesday.

This death would be at least the seventh at the Georgia park, including one in 2006 in which a man had a likely heart attack on the Goliath coaster, according to the Doan Law Firm, which focuses on amusement park accidents.

It also comes less than two weeks after Six Flags Magic Mountain, in Southern California, announced that it is retiring its famous X2 roller-coaster amid lawsuits alleging serious brain injury caused by the ride. The park had settled one wrongful-death lawsuit from the family of a 22-year-old man who died after riding the coaster in 2022.

Last year, a 32-year-old man died after riding a high-speed roller-coaster at the Universal Epic Universe theme park in Florida. He died from blunt impact injuries, and his death was ruled accidental.

World.title: Quebec author accused of using AI admits past plagiarism but maintains novel is his own work
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

After spending the last few weeks quietly watching his reputation be torn apart, Quebec-based author Thélyson Orélien is speaking out and addressing the allegations that he used artificial intelligence to write his debut novel.

"It is slander and heresy," he wrote in a statement distributed Tuesday by his Quebec publishing house, Éditions du Boréal.

C'était ça ou mourir, which translates to "It was either that or die," tells the story of a Haitian migrant who leaves his home for Canada, much like Orélien did following the 2010 earthquake.

The novel was lauded by many in the French-language literary world until an anonymous X account ran excerpts through an AI detection tool and publicly shared those screengrabs on Sept. 21 — the same day the novel won the Prix du roman Fnac.

According to the tool Pangram, the novel was "100 per cent" the work of generative AI.

In Tuesday's statement, Orélien says he used AI tools "here and there" for research, particularly when it comes to foreign idioms, but he says the text, structure and plot all come "straight from my gut."

He says for the past few weeks, he's been subject to a "lynching" through the media and racist harassment, which he says has been unbearable.

"The experience I am going through is cruel," he wrote in French.

"By attributing to a machine a text that is mine, that belongs to all my people, they have challenged not only my status as a writer but my humanity."

WATCH | A look back on the scandal that broke in September: Award-winning Quebec author accused of using AI for bestselling book | Duration closed caption 2:25 In recent months, Thélyson Orélien became a sensation for his debut novel C'était ça ou mourir, which follows a teacher escaping gang violence in Haiti’s Port-au-Prince. After the book won a prestigious award on Monday, an anonymous X account accused Orélien of using AI to write it, which he vehemently denies. Since then, other allegations of plagiarism have surfaced against the author.

In his statement, he also seemingly discredits the experts who have largely praised Pangram for its reliability and accuracy in detecting AI.

As the debate around the tool and Orélien's writing swirled, the author was accused of plagiarism for various columns dating back to 2012 for newspapers like La Presse. Those accusations became the clincher for different literary festivals and prizes, like the Prix Goncourt, which then distanced themselves from Orélien.

French columnist Samuel Fitoussi has since come out as one of five people behind the X account that made the initial allegation.

Author calls his plagiarism a 'youthful indiscretion'

Where the allegations of plagiarism are concerned, Orélien admitted to it in some of his earlier work, saying on Tuesday they were "unacceptable" mistakes from his youth.

An avid reader, he says he was in a "hurry" to write after leaving Haiti. There were authors whose style captivated him, he says.

"I admired rhythms, ways of phrasing sentences that would stay in my head for days," he said. "But admiration did not give me the right to take — to claim as my own — texts that were not mine."

Thélyson Orélien's debut novel, C'était ça ou mourir, tells the story of a man who undertakes a journey across the Americas to escape gang violence in Haiti. (AFP via Getty Images)

Orélien says he's now asking that C'était ça ou mourir be judged for what it is, saying it was inspired by his own lived experience and conversations he's had with migrants over the years.

"A youthful indiscretion cannot serve as evidence against a novel begun in 2017 that was finally published in 2026," he said.

"I didn't write this book to win awards or to become famous. I have nothing to prove to the people who accuse me."

Orélien was in the midst of a press tour in France when the scandal broke, and media outlets are reporting he has since returned to Quebec.

Éditions du Boréal says the author won't comment further on the matter and will not be doing any interviews, for now.

C'était ça ou mourir is still in the running for the Prix Renaudot, considered the second most prestigious French literary award after the Prix Goncourt, as well as the Prix littéraire de la Porte Dorée and the Prix Médicis.

World.title: Five forgotten Canadian children’s shows that are worth another look
World.content:
Article content

Essentially a Second City for teenagers, this low-budget variety series was a blend of sketch comedy, music videos and call-in contests where transistor radios and record albums were up for grabs. Initially produced by and aired on Ottawa’s CTV station, it managed to grasp the attention of a wider North American audience, finding a second home on U.S. cable network Nickelodeon — and going on to become the its highest rated show. What made it so popular? The slime, of course. Any time a contestant on the show would say, “I don’t know,” a goopy helping of green slop would fall on them (apparently the mixture was concocted with green gelatin powder and flour, then oatmeal and eventually cottage cheese and food colouring).

World.title: Colombia’s national strike organizers “are instigators of evil,” claims De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called labor unions and social organizations who organized anti-government protests for Wednesday “instigators of evil” who “seek to once again cause chaos.”

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella stressed that the security forces were instructed to allow peaceful protests, but warned the protesters that “if they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is lawfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians.”

Wednesday’s protests are a preparation for a national strike that is set to take place in November and is supported by the country’s political opposition to the far-right government.

According to the president, “those who are promoting the strike and seeking to use it to once again cause chaos and destabilize the government are the very same people who left the country bankrupt, on the brink of a blackout, with the healthcare system in intensive care, energy sovereignty compromised, and public resources plundered and looted.”

“They are instigators of evil, not fighter for freedom,” said De la Espriella.

If they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is rightfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president stressed that he would be signing a decree that regulates public protests in an attempt to avoid the chaos that erupted during massive strikes in 2019 and 2021 an killed 80 people.

De la Espriella additionally is expected to present an “anti-terrorism stature” to Congress, which could see the prosecution of protest organizers on terrorism charges, according to opposition leaders and security experts.

World.title: Colombia declares official start of El Niño, warns of strong impacts
World.content:
Colombia’s meteorological institute IDEAM officially declared the arrival of El Niño, and warned that the climate phenomenon could trigger water shortages and forest fires.

In a press statement, the IDEAM said that its “confirmation reflects the sustained warm conditions in the Pacific Ocean, which, according to the latest measurement, broke records, reaching a sea surface temperature anomaly of +3.49°C.”

The meteorological institute said it expected that this year’s “Godzilla El Niño” could continue to disrupt local climate patterns until March next year.

Initially, the weather phenomenon is expected to reduce rainfall between October and December, which is normally the rainy season in large parts of the country.

“Given this situation, and in light of the alerts issued since the beginning of the year, the national government launched an interagency response,.. with specific instructions for the responsible agencies to have their contingency plans formulated and activated by November 30 at the latest,” said the President’s Office in a statement.

The National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD) coordinates response capabilities across the country and enhances the monitoring of wildfires using satellite technology. For its part, the Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development is taking steps to protect strategic ecosystems, water sources, and the most vulnerable areas. President’s Office

The Mining Ministry “is implementing an emergency plan aimed at ensuring the country’s energy security by strengthening thermal power generation, securing fuel supplies, and implementing efficiency and conservation measures,” according to the President’s Office.

EPM, the local utilities firm in Medellin, has been testing the effectiveness of water rations as they fear the lack of rain could affect the hydro-electric power plants that provide the northwest of Colombia much of its energy.

Before leaving office on August 7, former President Gustavo Petro ordered the mass purchase of solar panels to reduce the pressure on the electric grid.

World.title: Colombia’s draft counterterrorist statute “creates foundations of dictatorial and inquisitorial regime:” opposition
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella’s antiterrorist statute would criminalize political opposition, social movements, and social protest, and essentially form a dictatorial regime, said opposition leader Ivan Cepeda on Wednesday.

In a video, Cepeda said that the true purpose of the bill that was leaked earlier seeks “to advance in the formation of essentially a dictatorial regime,.. which, moreover, has such a regime prostrate to drug trafficking.”

“The true objectives of this statute are to wage a crusade against the political opposition, social movements, and social protest, which is a legitimate right of citizens,” said the Senator of the Historic Pact party.

“Most of the articles in this draft are devoted to provisions that seriously undermine civil liberties, human rights, and the right to protest—not to illegal armed groups,’ according to Cepeda.

The broad legal definition of the word terrorism would allow the government to prosecute protest organizers on terrorism charges if any clashes occur between protesters and police.

This law could serve to intensify the persecution already underway in Colombia against journalists, judges, students, teachers, union members, peasants, indigenous people, people of African descent, LGBTIQ+ individuals—in short, any person or group that criticizes the citizen Abelardo de la Espriella, his government, law enforcement, or any state institution. Such a person could be taken to prison—without even prior warning—and subjected to abuse and torture. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Furthermore, the creation of a National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors would allow the government to criminalize citizens based on an administrative rather than a legal basis, and “grants extraordinary powers to the president to regulate a statutory judicial procedure, specifically the expedited preventive detention proceeding,” said the opposition leader.

The aim is to criminalize social protest; the alleged crime of “manipulating the civilian population” punishes anyone who promotes, finances, organizes, or leads crowds—this is the language of the draft statute—and this is nothing less than the institutionalization of political persecution and the criminalization of free speech. Senator Ivan Cepeda

The antiterrorism statute will be facing opposition when the government tries to push the legislation through Congress, Cepeda said.

“The Historic Pact rejects this and will do whatever is necessary to ensure that the opposition’s rights and guarantees are respected,” said the opposition leader.

World.title: De la Espriella announces first $309M in aid for earthquake reconstruction
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella announced that his Miracle Fund received COP1 trillion ($309 million) for the reconstruction of western Colombia, which was hit by a 7.4M earthquake on August 10.

The announcement followed announcements by the press, which reported that the Finance Ministry allocated ($192 million) COP625 billion to the fund almost two months after the disaster.

Thank you for your patience, but please understand that the government’s bureaucratic inertia and the situation we’ve inherited are extremely complex. However, we’re working to resolve the issue, and the Milagro Fund is now up and running, thanks to God and the efforts of all the officials in this administration. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“In November, the government will move forward with contracting another COP2.7 trillion ($835 million),” Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo told Caracol Radio.
