World.title: Rodrigo Duterte appears again at ICC hearing ahead of November 30 trial
World.content:
This is the second time that the former Philippine president has personally appeared before the court since his arrest in March 2025

MANILA, Philippines – Former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte made another appearance before the International Criminal Court (ICC) ahead of his full-blown trial slated to start on November 30.

Duterte, who’s facing three counts of crimes against humanity over his war on drugs, attended the Trial Chamber III’s fourth status conference on his case on Tuesday, October 13.

This is the second time that the former president has personally appeared before the court since his arrest in March 2025. On September 16, Duterte attended the chamber’s third status conference, marking his first personal appearance before the court.

Play Video

A status conference is held by the chamber to allow parties to discuss matters related to the case before proceeding to a full trial. This is done to iron out details such as the schedule and the list of witnesses and evidence, among others.

During Tuesday’s hearing, Presiding Judge Joanna Korner disclosed the schedule of Duterte’s trial:

10 am to 11 am

11:30 am to 12:30 pm

Lunch break: 12:30 pm to 1:30 pm

1:30 pm to 2:30 pm

3 pm to 4 pm

Apart from lunch, there are 30-minute breaks between sessions, given the experts’ recommendation of no sitting for more than an hour for Duterte due to his age and condition.

Recently, the Trial Chamber III ruled that Duterte is fit to stand trial. Citing experts’ analysis, Duterte was unanimously found have the capacity to understand:

instructing counsel in preparing and conducting the defense

the charges

the purpose and consequences of the proceedings

following the course of the proceedings, including the nature and implications of entering a plea

the evidence

Discussion on evidence

Once again, the prosecution’s volume of evidence was brought up during the hearing, specifically by Presiding Judge Korner. Trial prosecutor Julian Nicholls explained that they had restructured their list based on the most important ones, including the “non-negotiables.”

Korner flagged the inclusion of newspaper clippings — called by the court as secondary sources — in the prosecution’s 5,000 documents. Nicholls explained that they included them because the clippings will provide context and corroborate the allegation of killings committed during Duterte’s mayoral reign in Davao City.

Defense lawyer Peter Haynes again complained about the prosecution’s “over 18,000” datasets, saying the material had been “literally dumped” on them. Later, Korner inquired why the defense did not take up the prosecution’s offer to review the documents and spreadsheet.

At one point, the prosecution and defense also entered into an argument after the defense accused the prosecution of using artificial intelligence (AI) in reviewing the evidence.

“But the dataset, yeah, Mr. Nicholls, I think, is saying they haven’t been read by a lawyer, and certainly I haven’t read them. You will have noticed from the filings and with the artificiality that we have to deal with this by not naming anybody, there have been three institutions that have had those documents,” said Haynes.

“One of them is an institution that is very resourceful in terms of both human resources and money, and it took a team of people from that institution one year to review the dataset. That’s how big it is. And they did it humanly. The prosecution [hasn’t] done it humanly. They’ve effectively passed it through an AI machine,” Haynes added.

“I have to object. That is completely untrue. He keeps saying that. We have gone through this dataset by analysts. We’ve gone through all of it, lawyers some of it, page by page, human, manual, 100%. Keep saying that. It’s not true,” Nicholls said in response.

Play Video

The defense also had a motion, requesting that the prosecution’s evidence be refiled and a 10,000-document limit be imposed. Presiding Judge Korner ruled that the motion was “at the moment refused,” explaining that an arbitrary limit could cause the prosecution to violate disclosure obligations.

Disclosure of evidence is done in the proceedings to allow the legal counsel of the accused to prepare a proper defense.

Nicholls explained during the trial that the prosecution can stipulate or agree to the fact that the drug war deaths were around 3,400. He said that this was actually lower than the number of deaths reported by the Duterte administration itself.

There were 7,884 alleged drug suspects killed, as of August 31, 2020, based on the Philippine National Police’s count. However, several human rights groups said there could be around 27,000 to 30,000 victims if vigilante killings were to be included.

Haynes argued with Nicholls about the number, saying that the figure was not all drug-related. However, the prosecution insisted that deaths were all related to Duterte’s drug war. – Rappler.com

World.title: Scientists call for international body to oversee advanced AI
World.content:
ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE. An AI sign is seen at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference (WAIC) in Shanghai, China on July 6, 2023.

In an open letter, the researchers say frontier AI models should initially be air-gapped from external networks and subject to independent oversight, arguing that voluntary industry commitments are not enough

Around 400 scientists, including AI pioneers Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, on Tuesday, October 13, called for an international body to oversee containment standards and incident reporting for advanced cyber-capable AI systems.

The proposed body would set industry-wide containment standards and maintain a registry of significant security incidents, which the scientists said should eventually be made public.

In an open letter, the researchers said frontier AI models should initially be air-gapped from external networks and subject to independent oversight, arguing that voluntary industry commitments are not enough.

The proposal comes a month after Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta, xAI, and Nvidia signed a White House accord committing to voluntary safety measures without any formal enforcement mechanism.

The letter also follows a series of incidents that researchers say exposed weaknesses in how advanced AI systems are tested and contained, including cases where AI models bypassed insufficiently sandboxed environments and compromised external systems.

The signatories from 34 countries said organisations developing or testing cyber-capable models should immediately adopt high-assurance containment standards while governments work towards a more formal oversight regime.

Policymakers are increasingly debating how advanced AI systems should be supervised. EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen told Reuters on Friday, October 9, that the bloc’s AI Act is sufficient to address risks from rogue AI systems.

On Sunday, October 11, the Trump administration lifted its block on US labs giving Britain’s AI Security Institute early access to models for safety testing.

Hinton and Bengio shared the 2018 Turing Award with Meta’s Yann LeCun, another leading AI researcher. LeCun did not sign the letter and has argued that recent security incidents primarily reflect engineering failures rather than existential AI risks. – Rappler.com

World.title: NBI files complaints vs Davao contractor linked to Dutertes
World.content:
PROBE. National Bureau of Investigation Director Melvin Matibag addresses the media during a press conference on its probe into the potential connections between the Duterte family, companies, and individuals mentioned in the impeachment hearings as well as properties reportedly linked to the family and classified as agricultural land, on October 12, 2026.

The complaints come after the National Bureau of Investigation started looking into the P1.9-billion flood control projects awarded to Genesis88, located in the district of Davao City Representative Paolo Duterte

MANILA, Philippines – Weeks after starting its investigation into Genesis88 Construction Inc., the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) filed complaints against its owner, Glenn Escandor, and six others, including Genesis88 employees and former officials of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) Davao City District Engineering Office.

On Tuesday, October 13, the NBI filed falsification by public officer and graft complaints against Escandor and the following:

Saturnino Bentulan – authorized managing officer, Genesis88

Benjamin Zosa – project engineer, Genesis 88

Roy Bohol – construction foreman, Genesis 88

Richard Ragasa – former district engineer, DPWH Davao City District Engineering Office

Lilibeth Sarmiento – former assistant district engineer, DPWH Davao City District Engineering Office

Roberto Mamaril – former OIC-chief, Construction Section, DPWH Davao City District Engineering Office

The complaints came after the NBI started looking into the P1.9-billion flood control projects awarded to Genesis88, located in the district of Davao City Representative Paolo Duterte. Escandor, the Dutertes’ longtime friend, is the owner of the firm, based on Securities and Exchange Commission records obtained by Rappler in 2025.

A Rappler investigation revealed that one in four flood control projects in Davao City was awarded to Genesis88. The years when it bagged the contracts coincided with the time when Rodrigo Duterte was president and when the younger Duterte was the lawmaker representing the 1st District of Davao City.

Almost P2.9 billion (or P2,890,690,550.13) worth of contracts for flood control infrastructure from 2021 to 2023 went to the firm, based on figures from the Sumbong sa Pangulo website. This translated to a total of 35 projects — solo contracting and joint ventures with other firms included — in the region.

Escandor was former president Duterte’s assistant for sports. He also owns the Escandor Development Corporation, which donated P19.923 million for the ads of Vice President Sara Duterte during the 2022 national elections, according to the Vice President’s Statement of Contributions and Expenditures seen by Rappler. – with reports from Jairo Bolledo/Rappler.com

World.title: How DBP botched Duterte-era contractor loans: lax checks, billions overdue
World.content:
Meant to support the former president's Build, Build, Build drive, DBP's ICONS program instead left the bank with P4.09 billion in overdue contractor loans

MANILA, Philippines – Lapses in lending safeguards and years-long delays in collection left the Development Bank of the Philippines (DBP) with more than P4 billion in overdue contractor loans under a program meant to support the Duterte administration’s Build, Build, Build infrastructure drive, state auditors found.

The overdue loans amounted to 61.4% of the P6.67 billion still owed to DBP under the Infrastructure Contractor Support (ICONS) program. Launched in 2017, the program allowed contractors to borrow against expected payments from infrastructure projects, but the Commission on Audit (COA) found cases where loans were released without adequate verification of construction progress.

DBP’s board eventually approved the termination of ICONS on June 3, 2026, citing the high level of overdue loans. The closure, however, still leaves the bank with billions of pesos in debt that it may never recover.

What was ICONS supposed to do?

Launched in 2017, ICONS helped finance contractors undertaking infrastructure projects under the Duterte administration’s Build, Build, Build initiative, including public-private partnership projects.

Contractors need money for construction before they receive full payment from project owners. ICONS helped bridge that gap by lending against expected contract payments, or receivables, assigned to DBP as security.

For that arrangement to work, the bank needed to verify that the projects were progressing and that the payments backing the loans could actually be collected. Under its own lending guidelines, loans were supposed to be released in stages as construction progressed, with account officers required to visit project sites before disbursing funds and continuously monitor borrowers.

But COA found that DBP’s safeguards were not always followed.

A P300-M loan that went wrong

One P300-million loan shows how the ICONS program went wrong, from DBP’s failure to properly check the projects before releasing the money to its struggle to collect from the borrower years later.

In August 2019, DBP approved a P300-million credit line for a contractor undertaking five projects for a government-owned or -controlled corporation (GOCC). The contractor drew the full amount by March 2020, with repayment supposed to come from payments it expected to receive as construction progressed.

On paper, the projects appeared to be well underway. The two biggest projects backing the credit line – each with a contract value of more than P217 million – were reported to be 75.37% and 80.89% complete, respectively.

But DBP released the loans without actually checking how much work had actually been completed. Instead, the bank relied on the value of the contractor’s expected project payments, which covered at least 150% of the outstanding loans.

OVERDUE. A comparison of the reported and actual completion rates of five projects used as security for the P300-million DBP loan, based on findings from the Commission on Audit’s 2025 report.

“There was no verification of the actual project accomplishment prior to loan release of the loans, as required by the Circular,” state auditors said in their 2025 report.

By June 2020, just three months after fully drawing its credit line, the contractor had already fallen behind on payments.

It was only in March 2021, a year after the full amount had been released, that DBP checked the actual construction progress with project engineers. The findings revealed substantial discrepancies between the accomplishments the contractor had reported and those subsequently verified.

Two of the projects, Projects 3 and 4, had already been ordered terminated in September 2020 due to construction delays.

“No principal repayment was collected from Borrower 1 despite repeated collection efforts and demand letters, resulting in an outstanding principal balance of P300 million as of December 31, 2025,” the COA said.

By January 2026, the situation had worsened. The GOCC confirmed to COA that four projects had been terminated, while the fifth had been fully paid in December 2021. The government company said it no longer owed the contractor anything from the five projects.

More than five years after the contractor first defaulted, DBP had yet to recover any of the P300-million principal. The bank had already set aside an allowance for the entire amount to account for the expected loss.

Subcontracted work, delayed collections

The P300-million loan was not an isolated case.

Another contractor still owed DBP P490.46 million at the end of 2025, even though the infrastructure projects whose expected payments had been pledged to the bank as security were already completed.

COA found that the contractor had subcontracted most of the work to other companies, leaving it with a financial stake averaging just 3.5% of the projects’ contract costs.

Despite the projects being completed between 2017 and 2021, the contractor continued requesting loan extensions instead of repaying the principal. The audit did not establish what happened to the project payments or why they had not resulted in repayment to DBP.

COA also flagged significant delays in DBP’s efforts to recover overdue loans.

At DBP’s Albay lending center, a borrower defaulted in June 2021, but the first demand notice was sent only by email in July 2025, more than four years later. By the end of 2025, the borrower still owed P97.24 million of its original P100-million loan, with the bank already setting aside provisions for the possibility that the entire remaining amount would never be recovered. The account had also passed through six different officers between 2021 and 2026.

In Tacloban, foreclosure proceedings had yet to begin on a P82.21-million loan that had been overdue since September 2021 because the lending center lacked a full-time lawyer. Its cases were instead being handled by DBP’s Zamboanga legal team.

What has DBP done about the bad loans?

COA recommended investigating possible negligence among bank officers and employees handling ICONS loans, with administrative or legal cases to follow where warranted. It also urged DBP to act faster in recovering unpaid loans, particularly from borrowers still in operation or those with real estate pledged as collateral.

DBP told auditors that its management committee had directed its Legal Services Group to “investigate possible negligence in the credit administration of the loan accounts mentioned.”

But DBP had been looking into some of its largest bad loans for years before it decided to shut down ICONS.

As early as January 19, 2022, the bank’s board had ordered an inquiry into its 20 largest nonperforming loans, including the P300-million ICONS account. Yet it was only on June 3, 2026 – more than four years later – that DBP’s board approved the termination of ICONS.

Meanwhile, DBP’s loan problems extend beyond ICONS. Its gross nonperforming loan (NPL) ratio, which measures the share of loans classified as nonperforming, rose from 7.05% in December 2025 to 9.52% in March 2026, before easing slightly to 9.17% in June, according to data published by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas.

These figures cover DBP’s entire loan portfolio, and it is unclear how much ICONS contributed to the deterioration of the bank’s NPL ratio.

Rappler sought DBP’s comment on how much of the P4.09 billion in overdue ICONS loans it has recovered as of present, what is driving its elevated NPL ratio, and what became of the 2022 inquiry, including why the program was terminated only in 2026.

The bank has yet to formally respond as of press time, although a representative told Rappler that it stood by the explanations it had submitted to COA. This story will be updated if the DBP responds. – Rappler.com

World.title: Quezon City government dissolves Task Force Disiplina after officer kills 3 teenagers
World.content:
Created in 2019 through an executive order, Task Force Disiplina was mandated to enforce city ordinances, rules, and regulations

MANILA, Philippines – The Quezon City government abolished its Task Force Disiplina (Discipline) on Tuesday, October 13, following the killing of three teenagers by one of its members in Barangay Batasan Hills.

Task force member Alvince Tolentino, who was reportedly drunk at the time, shot the three teenagers on Monday, October 12, The Philippine Star reported. Batasan Police Station commander Gemmer Tubiera said the officer confronted the teenagers, who were still outside during curfew hours. The shooting happened at 2 am along Senatorial Street corner Batasan-San Mateo Road, Barangay Batasan Hills, according to the Quezon City Police District. One of the fatalities was a minor.

The suspect is now in police custody and faces three counts of murder.

Created in 2019 through an executive order, Task Force Disiplina was mandated to enforce city ordinances, rules, and regulations.

The Quezon City government clarified that it had not issued firearms to members of the task force.

Following the abolition, Quezon City Mayor Joy Belmonte ordered task force members to return to their mother unit, the Department of Public Order and Safety (DPOS).

Belmonte also required the members to undergo background checks, neuropsychological examinations, and drug tests, as well as submit clearances from the National Bureau of Investigation and the police, to retain their posts at the DPOS.

“Walang buhay na dapat mawala dahil sa iresponsableng paggamit ng armas. Kaligtasan ng mamamayan ang pangunahing tungkulin ng lokal na pamahalaan, at walang puwang sa serbisyo publiko ang sinumang hindi makakasunod dito,” the Quezon City government said in a statement.

(No life should be lost because of the irresponsible use of firearms. The safety of the public is the primary responsibility of the local government, and there is no place in public service for anyone who cannot uphold this duty.) – Rappler.com

World.title: Four years on, Marcos’ door for comms chiefs still revolving
World.content:
LINO CAYETANO. TV director and producer Lino Cayetano during the 2025 election campaign. He ran for Taguig 1st District congressman.

Is sixth time the charm for President Marcos in this rather volatile Cabinet post?

Just over a year after announcing a new communications secretary, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. found himself in familiar territory: having to explain the appointment of yet another chief of the Presidential Communications Office (PCO).

Is the sixth time the charm? Lino Cayetano, former Taguig City mayor and PTV-4 general manager, will be taking on a post that’s been occupied by five different people in the past four years of Marcos.

Here’s how Marcos framed Dave Gomez’s exit and Cayetano’s entry in an interview with media on Tuesday, October 13: “The reason that we keep turning, we have this high turnover is because the job keeps changing in terms of what we are trying to put forward.”

Marcos added: “In the beginning, we were talking about policy and now we are talking about — then we started talking about what we had to do in terms of implementation. And then we started having to talk — now we are having to talk about getting more towards the more political aspects of the communications job.”

“So, it keeps changing and that’s why we have to keep restructuring it and to be able to satisfy what… especially the demands that you make upon our Presidential Communications group. So yes, that’s what’s behind that.”

Let’s take a small step back and drill down on a line the President uttered: “Now we are having to talk about getting more towards the more political aspects of the communications job.”

Political? If we’re referring to political pedigree and experience, then new Communications Secretary Lino Cayetano would certainly have much to boast of.

Cayetano is the youngest in the current generation of his clan in politics. He also happens to be estranged from his older siblings, Pia and Alan Peter, who are both senators. All three (plus another sibling) are the children of the late former senator Rene Cayetano.

The youngest of the Cayetano clan in politics has held various posts in government — from barangay (village) chief, to district representative, to mayor. He tried to return to Congress in the 2025 polls but lost to a candidate who was backed by his sister-in-law Lani, Senator Alan Peter’s wife.

The older Cayetanos belong to the minority in the Senate that’s identified with Vice President Sara Duterte, Marcos’ erstwhile ally.

Lino Cayetano was also a film and TV director before joining politics full-time.

But what political aspect of the communications job must the new PCO chief pay attention to?

With just under two years left in the administration, two things would probably be foremost in the minds of Malacañang and the new communications chief: the Marcos administration’s legacy and, in relation to that, setting a favorable environment ahead of the 2028 presidential elections.

Cayetano would be the first communications chief under Marcos to have held an elected position in the past. The first communications secretary under Marcos was vlogger Trixie Cruz-Angeles, who was eased out in the first three months of the Marcos administration.

She was followed by Cheloy Garafil, who chaired the Manila Economic and Cultural Office (MECO) before being appointed secretary general of the House of Representatives.

Cesar Chavez, a radio broadcaster and long-time political communications operative, held the post for just over six months. Before Gomez, former ABS-CBN journalist Jay Ruiz was the administration’s primary communications person for four months.

Gomez, who once worked at Philip Morris International Philippines, at least held on to the position for over a year — despite never having faced the Commission on Appointments (CA). That he was bypassed by the CA is part of why he had to be replaced. Talk, for a while, has been that he would have had a hard time hurdling the CA anyway, precisely because of his previous role in a tobacco giant company.

Will Lino Cayetano at least get close to the length of Garafil’s term (almost two years) — which is to say, will he stay on until the end of this administration? If the President’s statements are any indication, that’ll all depend on the “demands that you make upon our Presidential Communications group.” – Rappler.com

World.title: LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte
World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.

On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Forces Beached in Battle for Sittwe
World.content:
Fierce battles have erupted around rebel-held Nga Pyi Island in Rakhine State’s Kaladan River delta, where regime forces keep trying to land troops despite heavy losses.

Local sources say scores of regime solders were killed or captured in the first three days of fighting as the Arakan Army (AA) defends the strategic outpost while laying siege to the state capital Sittwe across the water.

AA troops recently seized regime sentry bases at Amhyint Kyun Village at the entrance of Sittwe.

Since Oct. 7, the military has deployed six gunboats and a dozen speedboats backed by airstrikes and artillery fire from Sittwe in an effort to seize the island.

But AA fighters are entrenched there because it allows them to attack regime naval bases and ships stationed throughout the delta and along the coast.

Sources close to the AA said regime troops are reduced to trying to land troops with speedboats after three of their larger ships were hit by AA fire on Oct. 8, with two sustaining serious damage.

“Despite the casualties, they keep on coming,” one source told The Irrawaddy.

As many as 50 regime soldiers managed to reach the shore in the first two days of fighting but were either killed or captured, sources said.

As of Monday the regime had been unable to gain a foothold. Soldiers are reportedly being forced to advance under threat of being shot by their own commanders if they refuse.

“I’ve heard they are using conscripts as cannon fodder,” another source said.

Last month, the regime launched an offensive to retake lost territories in Rakhine, dispatching three columns to AA-held Ponnagyun north of Sittwe. Nearly one month later all three columns have been repelled, and the regime is retreating in Sittwe Township itself, according to the sources.

AA troops have captured four more outposts and are pushing at the gates of Shwe Mingan naval base and Sittwe Regional Operations Command, they added.

The attack on Nga Pyi Island was apparently launched because the regime sensed the danger of an imminent siege of its Sittwe stronghold, which sits on a peninsula surrounded by water on three sides.

“Regime navy vessels in Kaladan have repeatedly been attacked by AA drones and artillery from Nga Pyi, so the military wants to get control of the island,” said a Pauktaw resident.

Meanwhile, residents across Sittwe, Pauktaw, Ponnagyun and Rathedaung townships say the regime is bombarding the area daily and firing heavy artillery. “Every day, a dozen aircraft come and strike,” a Sittwe resident said. “Artillery units in Sittwe launches daily volleys toward Nga Pyi.”

Fighting is also intensifying in the state’s other major regime stronghold of Kyaukphyu, which is home to massive Chinese investment projects. There the AA has overrun two regime outposts near Taung Maw Oo naval base. The military is reinforcing positions as far afield as Chin State as well as the Rakhine borders of Magwe, Bago and Ayeyarwady.

Except for Sittwe and Kyaukphyu and the sparsely populated island of Manaung, the AA now controls all of Rakhine as well as Paletwa Township in neighboring Chin State.

World.title: Running for Cover: The Limits of Early Warning in Rakhine Air War
World.content:
In the week after the Sept. 28 massacre on Kyauktaw’s Indian market that killed 50 people and injured at least 58 others, Rakhine State endured another wave of aerial attacks. Local media reported at least nine bombing incidents across the townships of Ponnagyun, Rathedaung, Pauktaw, Kyauktaw, Thandwe and Kyaukphyu that killed at least another 12 civilians and injured more than 37 others. Some strikes hit locations where displaced people were sheltering.

The attacks were part of a wider pattern. The UN says aerial attacks killed more than 190 people in Rakhine in 2025. ACLED, an independent global conflict monitor, says Rakhine has suffered Myanmar’s highest reported casualties from airstrikes on local markets, recording at least 11 such attacks and 49 deaths even before the Sept. 28 massacre.

The immediate question for civilians under air attack is how they can know where a military aircraft is heading and reach safety in time.

Communities in Rakhine have improvised ingenious early-warning networks. To understand how they work, I spoke with six residents in Kyauktaw and Mrauk-U and reconstructed the warning timeline leading up to the Sept. 28 massacre.

A military jet is sometimes airborne one or two hours before an attack. What people often cannot know is where it will strike until the bombs have already begun to fall.

Watchers, channels and loudspeakers

The locals told me how warnings reach civilians in areas under Arakan Army (AA) control. What emerges is a kind of relay network: volunteer scouts track aircraft leaving airfields; their reports appear on public Telegram channels with takeoff times, directions and regions at risk; and in some communities those alerts are then announced through sirens and loudspeakers.

Warnings begin with a beeping alarm, followed by a spoken announcement. One Mrauk-U resident said at least three locations now broadcast such warnings, a system that began three or four months ago and can sometimes give people 10 to 15 minutes to find cover.

The timeline of Sep. 28

A reconstruction based on posts from a volunteer air-scout channel and the AA’s account of the strike times clearly shows the problem.

A Telegram channel with about 13,000 subscribers reported a fighter jet leaving Naypyitaw toward the southwest at 10:16 a.m., and another from the same airbase in the same direction at 11:08 a.m. Both alerts covered Rakhine, Ayeyarwady, Magwe, Bago, Karen and Chin. At 11:36, the channel reported another jet leaving Meiktila, with Mandalay, Rakhine, Magwe and Chin potentially at risk.

Yet the warning narrowed too late. An observation that a jet was circling over Kyauktaw at 12:10 was posted at about 12:13. A second observation, saying the aircraft was still circling at 12:15, appeared at about 12:16. But the AA says the first bomb struck at 12:10 and the second at 12:14.

The scouts were quick, but their information still had to pass from observer to channel operator before reaching the public. Even a few minutes matter. By the time the warnings narrowed down the target to Kyauktaw, the attack was already underway.

What’s more, phone and internet services have been severely restricted in much of Rakhine for years, and many residents cannot reliably access Telegram alerts. Repeated alarms can also cause warning fatigue.

“We can never assume where the jets are heading based only on the direction they take off in,” one resident told me. “Sometimes they appear to be flying toward another city, then turn back to drop the bombs.”

Ground observers may also lose track of sudden changes in course or altitude. The problem is not simply the speed of the volunteers, but the limits of the available information and ways to relay it.

What should change

International support should go beyond diplomatic statements. Donors, humanitarian organizations and local authorities should invest in warning systems that do not depend entirely on internet access, including radio networks, sirens and community warning posts. Air raid drills and clear protocols could reduce warning fatigue, while tiered alerts could distinguish a general aircraft warning from an imminent local threat.

Similar systems have been used elsewhere. In Syria, volunteer aircraft spotters fed flight information into warning networks that used social media, radio and street sirens to give civilians several minutes to seek cover.

The responsibility for the attacks lies with the Myanmar military. But local authorities can reduce civilian exposure by breaking up large commercial hubs into smaller neighborhood trading points, adjusting market hours to avoid peak crowds, taking any locally observed patterns of air patrols into account, and mandating the provision of proper shelters near hospitals, schools, markets and displacement sites.

Shelter is especially important for displaced families. Two people who fled Sittwe for Kyauktaw and Mrauk-U told me that many displaced people can afford only basic rented housing or makeshift accommodation, which offer no proper protection from airstrikes. Even a timely warning has limited value if there is nowhere safe to reach.

Historically, communities under heavy bombardment have adapted. During the Vietnam War, for instance, communities in North Vietnam built collective shelters, trenches and tunnels, while authorities adjusted school, work and market hours to reduce large daytime concentrations of people. Such measures cannot stop an air campaign, but they can reduce exposure.

International statements of concern will continue. But for civilians on the ground, the immediate challenge is to turn an early alert into a warning they can actually use. Closing the gap between knowing that a jet is airborne and knowing where it is heading may not prevent an attack. But it could give more people enough time to reach safety.

Khine is a researcher from Rakhine State with a decade of experience in peace processes, conflict issues, and human rights documentation. She is pursuing a master’s degree in Human Rights and Democratization at Mahidol University.

World.title: Philippine President Hails Diplomatic Engagement with Myanmar’s Regime
World.content:
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has hailed recent visits by Myanmar coup leader Min Aung Hlaing to fellow ASEAN countries as part of a “new approach” to resolving the country’s crisis.

In an interview with The Straits Times published Saturday, Marcos claimed credit for a recent engagement by various ASEAN governments with the putschist regime of Min Aung Hlaing.

Marcos conceded that ASEAN’s previous insistence on its Five-Point Consensus peace plan for Myanmar and refusal to engage with Myanmar’s regime at the political level were “absolutely correct.” But he added they were “not working.”

“Nothing’s happening, so we had to do something else,” he told the daily.

This prompted the Philippines during its 2026 chairmanship of the bloc to propose a “new approach” at the ASEAN Summit in Cebu in May, he said without going into detail.

He then pointed to coup leader Min Aung Hlaing’s recent visits to Malaysia and Cambodia as signs of progress, describing them as “shoots coming out of the ground” that had “not happened before” and would eventually lead to a “complete resolution.”

“Asked if ASEAN was moving towards recognizing the Myanmar government, Marcos said the grouping has to move towards that if it is going to play a part in resolving the conflict in the country,” the Straits Times wrote.

Since appointing himself president in April and rebranding his regime, Min Aung Hlaing has also visited ASEAN members Thailand, Laos and Vietnam, while reportedly being invited to Indonesia and Brunei.

However, the diplomatic engagement Marcos cited has yet to lead to any reduction in violence on the ground. In some cases, Min Aung Hlaing’s trips coincided with aerial massacres on civilians at home.

In the latest major atrocity, a military airstrike on a crowded market in Rakhine State on Sept. 28 killed at least 50 people, while further air raids in the state targeted locations where displaced people were sheltering. A week later the putschist leader was being welcomed in Kuala Lumpur.

ASEAN’s Five-Point Consensus consist of ending violence, beginning dialogue among all parties, appointing an ASEAN special envoy, and ensuring that humanitarian assistance those in need. It was adopted in April 2021 in response of the military coup. However, the regime led by Min Aung Hlaing has since ignored the framework, and most recently the regime’s new rubber-stamp Parliament rejected it altogether.

The conflict since the 2021 coup has killed an estimated 100,000 people and internally displaced about 3.8 million as of June 2026.

“Shaking hands with war criminals is a threat to humanity,” Thinzar Shunlei Yi, a Myanmar democracy and human rights activist, told The Irrawaddy. “We are watching to see whether the ASEAN leaders will show accountability if their re-engagement with the regime does not work out.”

Some ASEAN members are standing firm. Timor-Leste, the bloc’s newest member, has supported Myanmar’s pro-democracy movement and initiated legal proceedings against the military regime in February over alleged war crimes. And Singapore, which stands to take over the rotating chairmanship at year-end, affirmed this summer that there can be “no political representation” for Myanmar at ASEAN meets.

World.title: JFM Slams US Lifting of Sanctions on Fifth Myanmar Regime Crony
World.content:
Rights advocacy group Justice For Myanmar has condemned the continued U.S. delisting of Myanmar cronies, following Washington’s removal of sanctions against an official of Myanmar military-linked Shwe Byain Phyu Group.

The U.S. Treasury Department removed from its sanctions list Theint Win Htet, a member of the founding family of the Shwe Byain Phyu Group, a Myanmar military-linked conglomerate with interests spanning mining, timber and petroleum trading.

Theint Win Htet, who was sanctioned by former President Joe Biden’s administration, has become the fifth Myanmar junta crony, including arms brokers, to be delisted by the Trump administration along with the companies they are connected to.

In August 2025, the Trump administration dropped sanctions against four Myanmar nationals: Jonathan Myo Kyaw Thaung (aka Jonathan Kyaw Thaung), Aung Hlaing Oo, Sit Taing Aung and Tin Latt Min.

Tin Latt Min is the mother of Theint Win Htet. Her father, Thein Win Zaw, remains on the U.S. sanctions list.

JFM said on Sunday: “The U.S. government must learn from the mistakes it made after the sham 2010 election and not appease a brutal military that commits genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity with impunity.

“The crisis in Myanmar continues to deepen and appeasement will only further embolden the junta to continue its campaign of terror against the people,” it said.

The rights group said the regime’s access to funds, arms and aviation fuel has allowed it to escalate attacks on civilian targets that amount to international crimes. It said sanctions should be widened to cover the full extent of the networks of companies and individuals enabling and profiting from the junta’s terror campaign.

Following the 2021 military coup that ousted the democratically elected civilian government led by democracy icon Aung San Suu Kyi, the Biden administration imposed sanctions on military officers, military-run companies and military-linked cronies and their companies for aiding or abetting the regime’s war crimes and violations of international law.

Its sanctions blocked Theint Win Htet’s U.S. credit cards, restricted her foreign bank accounts and forced her to abandon her master’s degree at Columbia University in New York. Recently she has been living in Thailand with her mother Tin Latt Min, according to Al Jazeera and Reuters.

According to those agencies, Washington-based law firm Ferrari & Associates, which specializes in sanctions cases, helped remove her from the U.S. list.

During an interview with The Insight Myanmar podcast, the law firm confirmed that of four Myanmar individuals and companies delisted by the U.S. in July last year, two individuals and one company were among its clients.

JFM said Shwe Byain Phyu Group took control of Telenor Myanmar, renamed ATOM Myanmar, in 2022. At that time, three business sources told The Irrawaddy that Khin Thiri Thet Mon, the daughter of coup leader Min Aung Hlaing, was an investor in Shwe Byain Phyu, which acquired an 80-percent stake in the telecom company.

ATOM Myanmar has since installed a commercialized version of China’s Great Firewall, giving what JFM described as the illegal junta unprecedented access to conduct surveillance on users.

Theint Win Htet has acted as a shareholder and director of One Telecom Company Limited, which was established during Shwe Byain Phyu’s acquisition of Telenor Myanmar.

In 2023, Theint Win Htet did an internship at ATOM Myanmar as a financial analyst while holding shares in Min Shwe Myine Enterprise Limited, a Myanmar petroleum company that formed a consortium in 2022 to find reliable suppliers from Russia “to tighten Myanmar Russian partnership,” JFM said.

In 2024, JFM reported Theint Win Htet to French authorities, requesting they freeze any of her assets in French territory and consider her removal from France, where she had been admitted to a school.

World.title: Hundreds of Myanmar Migrant Workers Barred From Returning Abroad Over Tax, Remittance
World.content:
Hundreds of Myanmar migrant workers on leave have been barred from returning to their jobs after failing to provide proof of contributions to the military regime’s coffers. Over the past three weeks, the regime’s Labor Department has blocked the departure of over 300 overseas workers—mostly for failing to meet 2023 mandates to pay 2 percent income tax and remit 25 percent of their earnings through official channels.

The regime is squeezing foreign currency from overseas migrant workers amid a cash crunch caused by international sanctions, foreign investment flight, and economic mismanagement.

In May, the Labor Ministry ruled that migrant workers seeking to return home on leave must obtain an endorsement letter from the Myanmar embassy or consulate in their host country. Applications for the letter must be accompanied by written permission from employers along with proof of income tax and remittance payments.

At the end of their leave, returnees must again submit endorsement letters and evidence of compliance with tax and remittance rules to the Labor Department. Labor Ministry data shows numerous returnees from Singapore and Malaysia have been barred from returning and asked to resubmit applications.

“Many of us dare not visit home even though we want to,” a Myanmar migrant worker in Singapore told The Irrawaddy. “Endorsement from the [Myanmar] embassy is difficult to obtain, and many are afraid they won’t be allowed to leave after returning.”

He added that most workers use unofficial channels to remit money to their families in Myanmar, as they offered better exchange rates and convenience than regime-run banks.

Others have given up on returning to their war-torn country.

“When their visas expire, some even try to move on to other countries instead of returning to Myanmar,” he said.

Meanwhile, new Labour Minister Maung Myint is ramping up enforcement of income and remittance rules for overseas workers, threatening penalties for failure to comply. Two days into his tenure, he declared collection of the funds was a “key duty” and threatened punishment for workers who failed to comply

He reiterated the point in a meeting with overseas employment agencies and remittance brokers in Naypyitaw on Saturday, stressing that “remittance serves the national interest” and workers should consider them “a donation.”

He told agencies they would be rewarded based on how much remittance they could collect.

More than 100 overseas employment agencies have been banned from recruiting after failing to report evidence of remittance collected from workers sent abroad, while others face license revocation and fines.

Experts warn that tighter remittance restrictions by the regime are in the pipeline as foreign currency inflows from its major exports such as oil and gas continue to shrink. The skimming of migrants’ earnings threatens to cut a lifeline for millions of families struggling amid economic collapse and conflict. Myanmar’s total remittance value soared to US$ 5.6 billion in 2025, according to Bloomberg – more than doubling since 2019.

World.title: The Rise and Fall of Myanmar’s Ambassador to Thailand
World.content:
From Thein Sein’s reforms through Aung San Suu Kyi’s democracy, and the 2021 military coup that buried both, a trio of high-profile officials climbed the ranks of Naypyitaw’s bureaucracy, earning the moniker “Z Series.”

Zaw Htay, Zaw Min Tun, and Zaw Zaw Soe forged their alliance while studying together in the Defense Services Academy’s 37th intake.

The nickname stuck after they rose to prominence during the National League for Democracy government. Zaw Htay was appointed government spokesperson, while Zaw Min Tun rose in the military and became its mouthpiece after the coup, dubbed the regime’s biggest liar for defending its violence and atrocities.

Zaw Zaw Soe, meanwhile, served as an army brigadier-general before building a reputation for corruption at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, joining as director of the legal and consular department. During his military career, he spent a year at the Nanjing Army Command College under the Chinese People’s Liberation Army. Fluent in Mandarin, he often acted as interpreter when senior Chinese delegations met Aung San Suu Kyi’s government. But according to a former ministry official, Beijing disliked his role and once requested that another interpreter be used.

Zaw Zaw Soe was already entrenched, however, having cultivated ties with then‑Foreign Minister Wunna Maung Lwin under President Thein Sein. He later served as deputy chief of mission in Israel. When relations with his superior in Tel Aviv soured, he was posted to Hong Kong as consul. It was there that his reputation for corruption emerged. He later moved to the Defense Ministry before returning to the Foreign Ministry after the 2021 coup.

On March 25, 2025, the junta appointed him to lead its mission in Thailand. “Appointing Zaw Zaw Soe, infamous for his greed, as ambassador to Thailand was like throwing him into a gold mine,” said one Foreign Ministry staffer who joined the Civil Disobedience Movement (CDM) after the coup.

Among Myanmar’s foreign missions, embassies in Thailand, Malaysia, and Singapore are considered the most lucrative postings, thanks to potential profits from passport issuance, renewals, and visa services for large numbers of migrant workers. Once in Bangkok, Zaw Zaw Soe introduced new rules, tightening passport procedures to line his pocket. He barred Myanmar migrants from converting their Certificates of Identity (CI) to passports, blocked Passport for Visit (PV) holders from switching to work visas, and halted renewals of expired passports. All three services were channeled to black-market brokers. Even the rule that expired passports must be sent back to Naypyitaw for renewal could be bypassed with a cash payment.

“Under Zaw Zaw Soe’s watch, if you had money, anything was possible,” said one broker. “Even blacklisted individuals could get passports.”

While the junta barred CDM members and prominent activists from obtaining passports, brokers working with the embassy gladly accommodated them in exchange for 150,000–200,000 baht per head.

“His involvement in issuing passports to blacklisted people has now been exposed. He has apparently ‘eaten too much,’” said another broker with ties to the Bangkok embassy.

Zaw Zaw Soe was recalled to Naypyitaw last month, leaving his future hanging in the balance long after his friends exited the stage.

Zaw Htay resigned following the coup and was detained for several months after criticizing the junta. He died of a heart attack in 2022 aged just 49. Zaw Min Tun was purged and pensioned off after being implicated in kickbacks from a Chinese drone purchase.

That leaves only Zaw Zaw Soe, the last surviving member of Naypyitaw’s remarkable “Z Series.” Whether he will share the fate of his two comrades remains to be seen.

World.title: Between Bombs and Red Carpets, the ‘ASEAN Way’ Is Failing
World.content:
Two events in the last week of September are emblematic of the opposite realities confronting the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). The first was Malaysia’s deportation of 1,476 Myanmar refugees aboard Myanmar Navy vessels. This initial phase of a bilateral agreement covering 5,000 returnees in total, among them Rohingya, arguably violated the customary international law principle of non-refoulement, given the dangerous conditions awaiting them on arrival. That Myanmar authorities supplied the list of approved returnees heightened concerns that it may have included political opponents of the regime, who face the risk of persecution, and young people targeted for forced conscription. Moreover, because the refugees were taken from immigration detention centers, it is doubtful they consented to voluntary repatriation.

The plan’s architect, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, once a defender of the Rohingya, a strong critic of the junta and an opponent of readmitting then-junta chief Min Aung Hlaing to the ASEAN fold, has unapologetically reversed his stance. He readily engaged the former general, now a self-styled president after a discredited election, to help carry out the deportations, in what many see as a nationalist bid to regain popularity ahead of Malaysia’s next general election. Min Aung Hlaing’s subsequent visit to Malaysia on October 7-8, at Anwar’s invitation, gave the disputed leader, who faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant request over crimes against humanity committed against the Rohingya, the legitimacy he craves. Further concessions, including helping in the reintegration in ASEAN, were in the pipeline.

On September 28, just one day before the deportations, the Myanmar military bombed a crowded market and the nearby Kissapanadi Bridge in Kyauktaw Township, Rakhine State, killing 50 civilians, mostly women and children, and wounding 60 more, many critically. This is the same state to which any deported Rohingya would be expected to return. Now largely under the control of the insurgent Arakan Army, Rakhine State has faced a regime air campaign against civilians that has been escalating since April, in defiance of the professed shift to civilian rule.

The engagement with a regime-ravaged country expresses ASEAN’s duality. On one side, member states, motivated by economic and geopolitical interests, are increasingly eager to put the conflict behind them. On the other, it is difficult to ignore Myanmar’s unwillingness, even for appearances’ sake, to meet the remarkably modest terms of the Five-Point Consensus. This peace plan, which ASEAN leaders agreed with junta chief Min Aung Hlaing in April 2021, a few months after his military coup, calls for an immediate end to violence, constructive dialogue, humanitarian assistance, the appointment of a special envoy, and envoy visits to Myanmar to meet all stakeholders. From the start, the junta ignored these commitments so thoroughly that, by October 2021, ASEAN had taken the uncharacteristic step of barring Min Aung Hlaing and other political representatives of the regime from its summits, departing from a strict reading of the bloc’s principle of non-interference in members’ internal affairs.

Since then, violence has not ceased, but rather intensified. According to the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR), airstrikes have become deadlier, killing at least 982 people in 2025, including 232 children: a 52 percent increase over 2024. Overall, the independent monitoring group Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED) has put the toll at more than 100,000 people since the coup. The calls for the release of all political prisoners, which ASEAN diplomatically said it had “heard” without the Consensus spelling them out, remain unheeded by the junta, as does permission for the Special Envoy to meet all parties. Aung San Suu Kyi is still unreachable, even if supposedly detained at what the regime calls a “designated residence”, and of the more than 32,000 people arrested, the Assistance Association for Political Prisoners (AAPP) confirms that nearly 15,000 remain in detention, while nearly 7,800 more cases are pending verification.

Yet ASEAN member states are shifting toward normalizing relations with Myanmar. Laos was the first in the region to break Min Aung Hlaing’s ostracism, inviting him for a state visit on July 3. This move followed the example of India and, above all, China, Laos’ dominant ally, both of which welcomed him after the junta-run election. China, in particular, has a stake in promoting the regime’s international acceptance, having backed it financially and strategically and helped it restrain armed ethnic and opposition groups. It was Thailand, though, that signaled a clear departure for the region by receiving him with full honors.

The pomp of the visit, including a red-carpet welcome and a formal guard of honor at Government House, went well beyond the “calibrated engagement” officially given as its rationale. The unfulfilled Five-Point Consensus was overlooked, and no harsh reprimand was issued over the conflict’s cross-border spillovers: scam centers, human and drug trafficking, irregular migration, pollution from gold and rare earth mines, and border intrusion by Myanmar jet fighters. Instead, a sumptuous banquet with Thailand’s main conglomerates signaled unstated economic motives, notably border trade, infrastructure investments and access to natural resources.

Other mainland Southeast Asia countries with close geopolitical and economic ties to China, namely Cambodia and Vietnam, soon followed. Malaysia’s change of course, prompted by internal political developments, now also opens the door to wider regional engagement. So far, only two maritime Southeast Asian countries have spoken out strongly against the trend. Singapore, despite (or perhaps because of) being one of Myanmar’s main investors, wants a real solution and has called for measurable steps towards implementing the Five-Point Consensus, including a permanent cessation of violence, the release of all political prisoners and unimpeded delivery of humanitarian aid across Myanmar. Timor-Leste, Southeast Asia’s youngest democracy, continues to push for accountability and has initiated legal proceedings against Myanmar for war crimes under the principle of universal jurisdiction.

The remaining member countries, however, are starting to waver. Analysts speculate that the Philippine foreign secretary and ASEAN special envoy, Theresa P. Lazaro, who is set for a humanitarian visit to Myanmar this month, is eager to show results by advancing the “normalization process” at the ASEAN Summit in Manila in November. She has already drawn strong public criticism for her January 2026 meeting with Min Aung Hlaing in Naypyitaw, even before the election’s results were known. And again for hosting the July 12 “informal meeting” in Bangkok of ASEAN foreign ministers, which the Myanmar regime’s Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe attended, the first such interaction since the coup.

Indonesia, while still emphasizing the Five-Point Consensus, has also widened its engagement. A high-level delegation led by then Foreign Minister Sugiono visited Myanmar on June 8, met Min Aung Hlaing, and promised closer bilateral relations and cooperation in regional and international fora, declaring, as quoted by the Jakarta Globe, that “Myanmar is ASEAN family.”

This return to “business as usual” is, however, contested by civil society and allies of Myanmar’s people’s movements, who argue that there is nothing normal about a country at war with its own people. Such an approach would only create a false sense of regional security without addressing the root causes of the conflict or resolving it. Legitimizing the regime while ignoring widespread continued resistance and failing to protect the civilian population would only advance authoritarian trends endemic to the region and reinforce ASEAN’s reputation for disregarding human rights.

The recent photo exhibition “The Coup Years,” held at Dia.lo.gue in Jakarta from September 26 to October 11, and organized by SEA Junction with AJAR, Humanis Foundation and Migrant Care, offered a visual chronicle of Myanmar since the coup, documenting the dire realities on the ground, the tragic toll of the regime’s atrocities on civilians, and continued resistance to the military and the elections it backed. Experts, artists and activists reaffirmed their solidarity with the people of Myanmar and rejected ASEAN member states’ efforts to whitewash the regime’s continued crimes. At the opening panel, parliamentarian Mercy Barends, Indonesia’s AICHR representative Anita Wahid and ALTSEAN director Debbie Stothard agreed that ASEAN actually has a choice in strenghtening its allegiance to the 2008 ASEAN Charter, the regional body’s founding legal framework. The Charter places people’s will at the center and commits it to democracy, the rule of law, good governance and the protection and promotion of human rights. Here, Myanmar becomes the litmus test of what the “ASEAN Way” amounts to in practice and of whether ASEAN will uphold its constitutional principles or conveniently suffer amnesia about them.

Rosalia Sciortino is director of SEA Junction and former Asia regional director of the International Development Research Center (IDRC) and the Rockefeller Foundation.

An earlier version of this article appeared in The Jakarta Post.

World.title: The Regime Is Laying a Trap for the US. Will Washington Fall for It?
World.content:
Myanmar has become increasingly salient in Washington’s economic and national security calculus.

However, the country is far from simple. Its military and political power is dispersed across multiple centers, demanding deft handling and nuanced thinking.

In the absence of a single like-minded counterpart, Washington may be tempted to look for a shortcut and treat the military regime as the easiest channel through which to advance U.S. interests. Doing so would risk falling into the trap laid by Naypyitaw: mistaking access to the military regime for access to Myanmar itself.

Will Washington take the bait? Or will Washington resist this temptation and build a strategy around navigating Myanmar’s intricate and decentralized landscape?

Washington’s calculus

For Washington, the central question will be how to address two particular interests that converge in Myanmar as cost-effectively and reliably as possible. Washington is seeking to reduce dependence on China-dominated rare earth supply chains while confronting a rapidly expanding form of transnational organized crime that directly harms Americans. The country borders India and China, links mainland Southeast Asia to the Indian Ocean and is the world’s fourth-largest producer of rare earths. Myanmar also serves as one of the primary hubs for scam compounds that directly defraud Americans of billions of dollars.

Under the Trump administration, Washington’s foreign policy has fundamentally changed. Longstanding traditions of promoting human rights and democracy have now been deprioritized in favor of an “America First” approach interpreted narrowly as protecting core national interests. The 2025 National Security Strategy (NSS) signed by Trump last November identifies “flexible realism” as one of its guiding principles. Under this approach, Washington seeks good relations and peaceful commercial ties with countries without requiring them to adopt democratic principles.

This change may have significant ramifications for Myanmar, where the U.S.’ concerns over democracy and human rights have historically been prioritized, constraining diplomatic engagement with the country’s military rulers and business deals that could benefit them.

Equally important, the NSS also recognized the Indo-Pacific as “among the next century’s key economic and geopolitical battlegrounds” and emphasized that successful competition in the region is essential to American prosperity. As Washington seeks to rebalance its economic relationship with China and reduce its dependence on China-dominated supply chains, Myanmar’s strategic importance could grow.

Washington’s calculus is also shaped by regional governments, including U.S. partners, and by its own private sector. Global volatility and geopolitical shocks have exposed vulnerabilities in regional supply chains and energy security. The added threat of economic coercion has placed greater pressure on governments, including the U.S., to seek stability and secure critical supply chains. To this end, regional governments have started high-level engagements with the regime to explore possibilities. These engagements may increase the appeal of normalizing relations with the military regime in Naypyitaw for Washington.

American businesses, whose voices carry weight, are watching these shifts as well. As regional governments signal openness to normalization with the regime, Myanmar may appear to become a viable market for foreign investment. These businesses may perceive that U.S. sanctions and other regulations could leave them at a competitive disadvantage to regional competitors. The first entrants into uncertain and unstable markets often absorb the greatest risks, but the willingness of American businesses to pursue investment despite uncertainty may make the prospect of securing an early foothold difficult to dismiss.

Washington’s blind spot

For Washington, this renewed attention on Myanmar has revived an older policy problem that it had tried to work around, as it struggled to develop a coherent approach to the country. For much of the 1990s and 2000s, Washington tended to work through a small number of central political actors, even though political authority and armed power were far more dispersed. Myanmar’s ethnic armed organizations, despite being political and military stakeholders, did not fit neatly into the U.S.’ engagement model. In practice, Washington’s political focus remained on Aung San Suu Kyi and the military regime, and its engagement with ethnic armed organizations was largely reduced to a national reconciliation framework, excluding powerful groups that did not participate in the ceasefire process.

Today, Myanmar’s political landscape has changed. For decades, Aung San Suu Kyi served as Washington’s principal democratic interlocutor in Myanmar, but she remains under detention today. The opposition is dispersed among the National Unity Government, ethnic armed organizations and other resistance actors. Intensified war since the 2021 coup has further shifted political and military power toward ethnic armed organizations. No single actor represents the opposition as a whole. Engaging Myanmar today therefore requires moving beyond an approach built around a select few central political actors, and Washington has yet to adapt to a decentralized political landscape, as Beijing has.

Understanding this blind spot, the military regime in Naypyitaw has positioned itself to exploit an intensifying geopolitical competition and unresolved gap in Washington’s approach to Myanmar. The military regime has paid millions of dollars to influential lobbying firms to help tailor its message to current U.S. priorities, pitching itself as a partner capable of advancing them. What remains uncertain this time, however, is whether Washington will take the bait.

A familiar bargain

Under sanctions and growing isolation, the regime has repeatedly staged political openings with pitches for engagement to the U.S. throughout its history. This history, however, offers a clear lesson: the military will act in bad faith and abandon its agreements whenever it sees fit.

In May 2002, the military released Aung San Suu Kyi from house arrest. One week later, it registered a firm in Washington to lobby for normalizing relations with the U.S. The regime pitched cooperation on issues prioritized by the Bush administration, including counternarcotics, terrorism, trade and public health. The opening did not last. In May 2003, regime-paid attackers assaulted Aung San Suu Kyi’s convoy near Depayin, and the military detained her again.

Another opening came under President Thein Sein in March 2011. That August, he met with Aung San Suu Kyi in Naypyitaw. Subsequently, his government released political prisoners, relaxed censorship, allowed the National League for Democracy to reenter electoral politics and pursued ceasefires with ethnic armed groups. Washington responded by sending Secretary of State Hillary Clinton to Burma in December 2011, restoring ambassador-level diplomatic relations and easing restrictions on investment and financial services. The political opening lasted nearly a decade before the military, under Senior General Min Aung Hlaing, seized power in February 2021 and detained Aung San Suu Kyi again.

The 2011 opening, notably, was different. Thein Sein and other reform-minded officials made significant concessions and pursued genuine, if imperfect, political reforms. The changes allowed political freedoms and economic opportunities that had been unimaginable under previous military governments. Myanmar experts and analysts will continue to debate what could have been done differently to preserve that opening, but for Washington, dwelling on the past or trying to recreate it would only distract from addressing Myanmar’s present realities and building a better future.

The 2011 opening, and any hope of returning to it, was shattered by the 2021 coup and the military’s subsequent campaign of violence against its own people. The present reality is that the military leadership now ruling in Naypyitaw is not the one that pursued those reforms, but the one that overturned them.

The price of a shortcut

Normalizing relations with the regime is highly unlikely to secure access to rare earths or curb the scam compounds it supports. Instead, normalization would exacerbate these issues by giving a lifeline to the Min Aung Hlaing regime as it faces growing internal tensions, a new round of military defeats and economic pressures.

The military-backed Union Solidarity and Development Party recently postponed its congress, reportedly due to leadership disputes. At the same time, the elevation of Min Aung Hlaing’s loyalists over more senior generals has raised questions about tensions within the armed forces. While exaggerating its success on the battlefield, the military now relies heavily on conscripts. Reportedly, more than 70 percent of its frontline troops are conscripts. While these developments do not necessarily indicate an imminent collapse, they contextualize the growing strains within the regime at a time when it is seeking international engagement.

The regime is also struggling militarily. In Kachin State, the military has failed to break the Kachin Independence Army’s resistance around Bhamo, while losing additional positions to resistance forces. In Rakhine State, a major offensive launched in September to retake territory from the Arakan Army has failed to achieve significant gains despite the deployment of thousands of troops backed by air and naval support. In Karen State, the Karen National Liberation Army and allied forces have continued to contest the military’s attempts to regain lost positions around Kawkareik.

Economic pressures are also adding to the regime’s mounting difficulties. Even Min Aung Hlaing, who has long presented an optimistic picture of Myanmar’s economy, recently acknowledged the regime’s failure to make meaningful progress. The regime’s pursuit of a loan arrangement with Belarus with high interest rates further suggests growing financial pressures and a need to secure alternative sources of financing. The regime’s efforts to circumvent international jet fuel sanctions also suggest that these measures are imposing constraints. With technical and material support from Chinese companies, the regime is developing its own aviation fuel production capacity at the Thanlyin refinery near Yangon to reduce its dependence on imported jet fuel. The project underscores the lengths to which the regime is going to secure a reliable fuel supply for its air force.

Will Washington take the bait?

The trap is laid. Washington’s recent actions indicate a trajectory towards normalization, but these three key drivers will shape what happens next in U.S. policy toward Myanmar.

Although members of Congress have expressed concerns about engagement with the military regime, statements alone may do little to influence the administration’s calculations. World.title: Kazakhstan, Belgium Seek Deeper Trade and Investment Ties at Business Council
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Belgium are seeking to deepen cooperation in transport and logistics, critical minerals, energy, advanced technologies and manufacturing, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and King Philippe said at the Oct. 13 fourth meeting of the Kazakh-Belgian Business Council during the Belgian monarch’s state visit to Kazakhstan.

Belgium ranks among the 10 largest investors in Kazakhstan, with Belgian companies investing more than $15 billion in the country over the past two decades, Tokayev said, opening the council.

“More than 100 Belgian and joint ventures are successfully operating in our country in the fields of agriculture, healthcare and pharmaceuticals, advanced technologies and energy. At the regional level, Kazakhstan is Belgium’s largest trading partner in Central Asia,” Tokayev said.

He also highlighted King Philippe’s contribution to expanding bilateral trade and economic ties, identifying transport and logistics as one of the key areas for further cooperation.

Transport and logistics offer new opportunities

According to Tokayev, Kazakhstan is investing heavily in modernizing its railway and road infrastructure, seaports and terminals along the Middle Corridor. He proposed closer practical cooperation between the Port of Antwerp-Bruges and Kazakhstan’s Caspian ports of Aktau and Kuryk.

“In this context, Belgium’s extensive experience as one of Europe’s largest logistics hubs is particularly valuable to us. This will open up broader markets for Kazakhstan’s metal products, petrochemicals and agricultural products,” he said.

King Philippe also emphasized the complementary roles of the two countries in connecting Europe and Central Asia. According to him, Kazakhstan is a vital link across the Eurasian space.

“Thanks to its unique geographical location and significant natural resources, it has become a regional center for trade, investment and the development of the green economy, occupying a special place in the global economy. All this creates a natural foundation for mutually complementary cooperation,” he said.

AI and advanced technology on the agenda

Tokayev identified artificial intelligence and the technology industry as other priorities for strengthening the partnership. Kazakhstan is advancing initiatives such as Alem.ai and Alatau City, which are intended to develop next-generation centers for advanced industries and technological innovation.

“Belgium’s strong position in semiconductor research opens up new opportunities for joint projects and the development of our partnership,” Tokayev said.

The two countries could also expand cooperation in energy and petrochemicals. Tokayev described Kazakhstan as a reliable supplier of oil to European markets and highlighted opportunities in renewable energy, energy efficiency, industrial decarbonization and hydrogen production.

“I invite Belgian companies to implement joint projects in the deep processing of raw materials, the chemical industry and the production of high-value-added polymer products,” he said.

Critical minerals and industrial processing

Critical minerals were another central topic at the business council, alongside a Kazakh-Belgian roundtable on the sector held as part of King Philippe’s state visit. Tokayev said Kazakhstan already produces 21 of the 34 types of raw materials considered critical to European industry and supplies Belgium with titanium and molybdenum products.

“The partnership between John Cockerill and Qarmet to create new galvanizing and protective-coating capacity is a real example of our industrial cooperation. We also welcome the participation of Belgian partners in geological exploration and the deep processing of raw materials and metals,” Tokayev said.

Business ties and people-to-people cooperation

Tokayev also stressed Kazakhstan’s interest in attracting skilled and entrepreneurial people willing to work alongside local professionals.

“The more such people come to our country, the better it will be for all of us, as this contributes to strengthening both personal and professional contacts. Such interaction is highly valued in Kazakhstan. As President of Kazakhstan, I value first and foremost the intellectual abilities of people who come to our country, rather than their ethnic background,” he said.

King Philippe, addressing business representatives from both countries, called for stronger cooperation in promising sectors including energy, critical minerals, transport and logistics, finance and tourism.

“Belgium and Kazakhstan are separated by a considerable geographical distance, but in terms of ambition, pragmatic approach and determination, we are remarkably close,” he said.

World.title: Kazakhstan to Hold Early Maslikhat Elections This November
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan will hold early elections for local representative bodies, known as maslikhats, on Nov. 29, the Central Election Commission announced at an Oct. 13 meeting.

The elections will fill 3,447 seats across 228 maslikhats at the regional, city and district levels, Deputy Chair of the Central Election Commission Mukhtar Yerman said. Of the total seats, 668 will be in regional maslikhats, 626 in city maslikhats and 2,053 in district maslikhats.

The commission presented a draft resolution setting the election date for Nov. 29. Under Article 101, paragraph 3, of Kazakhstan’s Constitutional Law on Elections, early elections must be called by the Central Election Commission no later than two months after the early termination of a maslikhat’s powers.

Maslikhats are elected by residents of their respective administrative and territorial units through universal, equal and direct suffrage by secret ballot. Deputies serve five-year terms.

Earlier, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed a decree on the early termination of the powers of maslikhats at all levels.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Economy Grows 4.2% as Manufacturing and Private Investment Drive Expansion
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s economy grew 4.2% in the first nine months of 2026, supported by non-oil sectors, rising private investment and expanding industrial production, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin said at a government meeting on Oct. 13.

The non-resource sector grew 5.4%, while construction, manufacturing, transport services and trade accounted for more than 75% of overall gross domestic product (GDP) growth, according to Zhumangarin.

The figures point to continued economic expansion beyond the extractive sector, although inflation remains elevated despite a slight slowdown in September.

Private investment drives economic growth

Investment in fixed capital reached 16.1 trillion tenge (US$35.7 billion), increasing 7% year on year over the first nine months of 2026.

“The distinctive feature is that private investment, which increased by 18.2%, is the main factor driving investment growth,” Zhumangarin said.

Gross foreign direct investment inflows reached $9.4 billion in the first half of the year. The strongest investment growth was recorded in manufacturing, up 40.1%, followed by construction at 32%, information and communications at 29.2%, healthcare at 20.4% and agriculture at 9.1%.

Kazakhstan’s economic structure has also continued to shift. The oil sector accounted for 7.8% of GDP in 2025, while manufacturing’s share rose to 14.1% and mining’s reached 12.4%, according to Zhumangarin.

Manufacturing expands as new plants open

Manufacturing output grew 8.6% in the first nine months of 2026, with particularly strong growth in light industry, which increased 62.4%. Chemical production rose 23.4%, while machinery manufacturing grew 22.8%.

Deputy Minister of Industry and Construction Kuandyk Kazhkenov attributed the expansion largely to new production facilities. Since the beginning of the year, Kazakhstan has launched 106 industrial projects, creating approximately 8,000 permanent jobs.

“Thanks to the implementation of these projects, the country has established production of new goods that were not previously manufactured domestically. These include sodium sulfate, drip irrigation systems, laminate flooring, aluminum capsules for coffee machines and other products,” Kazhkenov said.

A further 200 investment projects worth a total of 1.7 trillion tenge (US$3.77 billion) are planned for completion by the end of 2026.

Inflation slows, but price pressures remain

Annual inflation eased to 9.3% in September, down from 9.8% in August, Zhumangarin said. The government and the National Bank are continuing coordinated measures to reduce inflationary pressure. First Deputy Chairman of the National Bank Yerulan Zhamau­bayev said the country’s business activity index reached 50.4 points in September, compared with 49 points in December 2025. The National Bank plans to maintain a moderately tight monetary policy alongside the government’s anti-inflation measures.

Kazakhstan’s financial buffers strengthened as well. Gold and foreign exchange reserves stood at $66.2 billion at the end of September, up 1.2% from the beginning of the year. National Fund assets reached $66.7 billion, an increase of 4.3%.

Exports and transit traffic gain momentum

Exports of goods and services increased 25.4% to $55.3 billion in the first half of 2026, according to figures presented at the government meeting.
