World.title: Georgia to raise pensions for under-70s by 45 lari instead of 20
World.content:
Pension increase in Georgia

From 1 January 2027, the Georgian government will increase pensions for people under 70 by 45 lari instead of the planned 20 lari. Their monthly pension will therefore rise to 415 lari (around $160). Meanwhile, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze argues that setting a minister’s salary below 12,000 lari encourages officials to engage in corruption.

As of August 2026, 905,000 people in Georgia received an old-age pension. Of these, 420,000 were under 70, while 485,000 were aged 70 or older. The initial draft budget for 2027 allocated up to 5.6bn lari (around $2.16bn) for pensions. The announced change will increase this amount by 128m lari (around $49.4m), bringing the total to 5.7bn lari. Under the law, an ordinary member of parliament’s salary, before tax, should rise by 1,080 lari, from 12,800 to 13,880 lari (around $5,359). The Georgian Dream party may decide not to implement this increase.

Kobakhidze said the indexation mechanism under current legislation would have increased pensions by just 20 lari. However, the government decided to raise payments further. The change does not apply to pensioners living in mountainous settlements, where different rules govern pension supplements.

Implementing the decision announced today will require an additional 128m lari in state budget spending.

What did Irakli Kobakhidze say?

According to the prime minister, social spending accounts for more than 33% of the state budget. Available figures show that the government allocated more than 5bn lari for old-age pensions in 2026, while 540m lari went towards co-financing the funded pension system. For comparison, Kobakhidze noted that pension spending totalled 1.065bn lari in 2012.

Kobakhidze said further increases in social spending carry fiscal and macroeconomic risks. He stressed that social spending had already reached the upper limit recommended by international financial institutions. Exceeding that threshold, he warned, could slow economic growth, fuel inflation and undermine Georgia’s access to international financing.

Nevertheless, he promised that the Georgian Dream government would continue looking for ways to increase pensions for people under 70 beyond the statutory indexation rate in the coming years. He added, however, that any increase must remain within acceptable budgetary limits.

Alongside the pension announcement, Kobakhidze addressed public sector pay, linking low ministerial salaries to potential corruption risks.

“Paying a minister less than 12,000 lari means pushing them towards corruption,” he said, explaining that new figures put a minister’s take-home salary at around 12,000 lari.

Kobakhidze argued that a private sector role with comparable responsibilities and workload could pay between 50,000 and 100,000 lari a month. He rejected the suggestion that 12,000 lari was a high salary for a minister.

“Given the work a minister does and the responsibilities they bear, they would earn at least 50,000–100,000 lari in a comparable private sector role. Yet we are expected to accept that 12,000 lari is a high salary for a minister. Is that reasonable? Is it really that high?” Kobakhidze said.

He noted that ensuring public officials receive decent salaries forms part of the government’s anti-corruption policy. In this context, he recalled the previous government’s time in office, saying that Bidzina Ivanishvili, the founder of Georgian Dream, had used his own money to pay salary supplements to public servants. Kobakhidze presented this practice as a measure to combat corruption.

How much will the pension increase cost Georgia’s budget?

Paata Kvizhinadze, chairman of the parliamentary Finance and Budget Committee, said that raising an MP’s salary by 1,080 lari would cost the state budget 1–1.3 million lari. By contrast, increasing the old-age pension by just 1 lari would require 11 million lari.

“MPs’ salaries are not set to increase under the initial draft budget. Even if the increase had been included, it would have added only slightly more than a million lari to budget expenditure — around 1.3 million lari. Meanwhile, raising pensions by 10 lari requires 111 million lari, while an increase of just 1 lari costs 11 million lari. Therefore, we should not link MPs’ salary increases to pension increases,” Kvizhinadze said.

Pension increase in Georgia

World.title: From Uzbekistan to EU: Where Armenian goods are exported after Russia imposes restrictions
World.content:
Changes in the geography of Armenian exports

On 10 October, a preferential trade regime for Armenian goods exported to the European Union came into force. Under the EU decision to apply autonomous trade measures, the bloc will liberalise around 80% of imports from Armenia by removing import duties. The measures will cover a wide range of goods, including agricultural products.

The European Union has decided to support Armenia in response to restrictions that Russia has imposed on Armenian goods. Since May, Russia has banned imports of Armenian fruit, vegetables, fish products, alcohol and many other goods. Russian agencies responsible for enforcing the restrictions cited alleged failures to meet quality standards. However, it later became clear that Armenia’s closer integration with Europe had prompted the measures.

Exports of Armenian-origin goods to EU countries have grown for several months. In effect, this trend began before the preferential trade regime came into force. From January to June 2026, Armenia exported more than $516m worth of goods to the EU. This marked an increase of more than 80% compared with the same period last year.

Exports to EU countries are now expected to grow further. At the same time, Armenia is seeking other markets.

The local outlet Factor TV analysed the results of these efforts. Drawing on data from the Ministry of Economy and the Food Safety Inspection Body, it compiled a list of countries that received significant volumes of Armenian goods. The findings show that products traditionally exported to Russia now go to Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Georgia, Ukraine and Iraq.

More than 94% of exports went to three countries

According to data from the Food Safety Inspection Body, Uzbekistan, Georgia and Ukraine accounted for more than 94% of Armenia’s fruit exports in June 2026:

48% of fruit exports went to Uzbekistan,

around 34% went to Georgia,

approximately 12% went to Ukraine.

Georgia took the lead in July, accounting for around 35.3% of exports. Uzbekistan followed with 21%, Kazakhstan with 13%, Ukraine with 10.5% and Iraq with around 8.2%.

By comparison, in June 2025, Russia alone accounted for 86.7% of Armenian fruit exports. The figure rose to 87.2% in July.

State budget compensation for exporters

In response to the restrictions Russia imposed, the Armenian government launched support programmes for local exporters. These include subsidies and cash compensation, including payments to cover export duties in other markets.

In June and July, the government paid around 3.96bn drams ($10.3m) in compensation to exporters of strawberries, apricots, sweet cherries, plums, nectarines and peaches.

Over these two months, the state covered costs associated with around 90% of the export volume:

“The total volume of strawberry, apricot, sweet cherry, plum, nectarine and peach exports reached around 16,752 tonnes. The state budget provided compensation for 15,083 tonnes.”

Support programmes also continued in August. The government allocated around 4.52bn drams ($11.8m) that month to support exports and purchases of agricultural produce. This sum also covered costs for exporters of vegetables and flowers.

How the compensation was distributed

The figures for June and July show that apricots and sweet cherries accounted for 81% of the 3.9bn drams ($10.3m) allocated to fruit exports:

The government allocated around 1.86bn drams ($4.8m) for apricots.

Sweet cherries received around 1.33bn drams ($3.5m).

The government also paid compensation for strawberry, peach, nectarine and plum exports, but the amounts were smaller.

Exporters do not receive compensation automatically for every kilogram of produce they ship abroad. They must apply to the Ministry of Economy and submit customs or transit declarations, along with invoices confirming the exports. The ministry reviews each application and pays the compensation if it finds no discrepancies in the documents.

Under the government’s decision, compensation rates per kilogram stood at 770 drams ($2) for strawberries, 200 drams ($0.5) for apricots, 250 drams ($0.6) for nectarines and 400 drams ($1) for sweet cherries. For some fruits, the compensation came close to the average market price. In June, for example, strawberries sold for an average of 933 drams ($2.4) per kilogram.

Changes in the geography of Armenian exports

World.title: Non-medical support during childbirth in Armenia: who are doulas and what do they do?
World.content:
Doulas in Armenia: non-medical support for pregnant women

The first certified doulas appeared in Armenia six years ago. Yet few women know that they can turn to doulas for support during pregnancy, childbirth and even after giving birth.

Doulas are not medical professionals. They help women manage labour pain through massage and breathing techniques, while also providing emotional support. Women now have a choice about who accompanies them during these hours. Some still prefer to have their husbands, mothers or sisters by their side. Others choose to give birth with a doula.

A doula with a woman in labour in the antenatal ward. Photo: Yvetta Kosyan-Suvorova

Most doulas enter the profession after a negative personal experience

Yvetta Kosyan-Suvorova says women decide to become doulas after giving birth themselves. Sometimes they want to share a positive experience. More often, however, they turn to the profession because of a negative experience.

“I took a long journey to get to this point. I gave birth twice. My second birth was therapeutic and healing. I realised that a woman’s preparation, knowledge and expectations largely determine how childbirth unfolds. The problem is that women often have expectations that do not match reality. This can lead to traumatic consequences,” she says.

Иветта с мужем и сыновьями

Yvetta says her husband stayed by her side during both births. The first was a terrifying experience for both of them. The second went differently because they had both prepared for it. This time, they could talk to each other, joke and even dance during labour. She remembers the birth as “a wonderful process”.

She recalls that seven days before her second child was born, she listened to a lecture by an American doula. She remembers everything that might prove important during childbirth:

“Before that lecture, I was determined not to let anything that happened during my first birth happen again. For eight months, I told my doctor that I refused to give birth naturally. I insisted on a caesarean section. But that one-hour lecture changed everything for me. I realised I could understand my hormones and my surroundings, and that I could control many things. Ultimately, I could simply give it a try.

“My second birth went smoothly, without anxiety, and so quickly that after I was discharged, I kept telling my husband I wanted to offer to help pregnant women during labour and reassure them. Of course, those plans never came to fruition because they were unrealistic expectations.”

Yet the idea stayed with Yvetta for the next ten years. Eventually, she began working with pregnant women and women in labour, but as a photographer. Her family was living abroad at the time, where maternity photography was very popular. When she moved to Armenia, she expected to find plenty of clients for similar photo shoots. However, she says, almost all women in labour there turned down her offers.

“Either they invited me into the maternity ward not to take photographs that would capture this important moment in their lives, but simply because they did not want to be alone. But a photographer cannot intervene; they are like a shadow. Their presence should be as discreet as possible. I realised that, ultimately, I could not help women.”

Immediately after childbirth. Photo: Yvetta Kosyan-Suvorova

Yvetta’s dream of becoming a doula came true during the coronavirus pandemic, when many training centres moved their courses online. Yvetta completed a course, passed her exams and received an international doula certification. She became the first doula in Armenia.

Who are doulas?

Doulas are trained professionals who support pregnant women, women in labour and those who need help during the postnatal period. They prepare women for childbirth and stay by their side throughout labour in the delivery room. Doulas provide informational, emotional and physical support.

During labour, doulas help women through massage, pressure techniques and touch. Sometimes they simply offer encouragement; at other times, they explain what is happening in a woman’s body at that moment. They suggest different positions and help women feel comfortable and safe throughout the process. This can increase the likelihood of a positive birth outcome.

Yvetta helps a woman in labour manage the pain.

According to Yvetta, in countries where many women use doula services, they start looking for a doula in the early stages of pregnancy, sometimes even when planning to conceive:

“Since doulas can take on only a small number of pregnant women each month, women book their services well in advance. They try to avoid complications this way, as there may be no available doulas when they go into labour. The situation in Armenia is different. Women who have given birth before usually contact us earlier in their pregnancy. First-time mothers tend to get in touch later, around weeks 28–30, when they start preparing for childbirth.”

Yvetta believes women should not leave the search for a doula until the final weeks of pregnancy. Sometimes doulas have to turn women away because the medical facility where they plan to give birth does not allow them into the maternity ward.

Armenia’s Ministry of Health has yet to recognise how much the work of a trained doula differs from the support a husband, mother, friend or anyone else can provide. Armenian law also contains no regulations governing their work.

There are only five or six doulas in Armenia

Most trained and received certification through Doula Link, a platform run by Russia’s Institute for Perinatal Support. They thereby became members of the European Doula Network. This allows them to provide doula services in Russia, Germany, Switzerland, Serbia, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Spain, Italy, Israel and Panama.

In Armenia, people regard doulas as unqualified assistants.

A 2020 order issued by the health minister gives all women in labour the right to have a companion present during childbirth. However, some medical facilities still refuse to let doulas into the delivery room.

Moreover, some maternity hospitals charge a fee for allowing a companion to attend the birth. The Ministry of Health does not regulate this practice.

Why do women turn to doulas?

Yvetta says women in Armenia mainly choose to give birth with a doula because they want someone they trust by their side. They need someone who understands what is happening and what to do, can keep track of the situation and looks after them. They also hope to avoid traumatic experiences, including obstetric violence.

“Of course, having a support person present cannot guarantee that a woman will never experience abuse. But a doula is someone who will listen to her and understand her. I am convinced that in 99% of cases involving abuse, doctors do not intend to cause harm.

“They often intervene to reduce certain risks. Yet they do not answer the woman’s questions or explain why they have decided to intervene, even when the intervention involves surgery. A doula will at least ask why the intervention is necessary and why it needs to happen at that particular moment. Women feel safer when a doula is by their side,” Yvetta says.

A mother with her baby after childbirth. Photo: Yvetta Kosyan-Suvorova

In 2024–2025, the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) conducted a study of women’s experiences during pregnancy and childbirth in 16 countries across Eastern Europe and Central Asia, including Armenia.

The study found that 67% of the women surveyed had experienced at least one form of obstetric violence.

In Armenia, around 55% of respondents said medical staff had performed obstetric interventions without their consent or any explanation. Meanwhile, 32% reported mistreatment by medical staff, highlighting a lack of information or pressure to make them agree to certain interventions.

Another 27% reported poor-quality care, such as inadequate staff qualifications. Around 15% of women experienced verbal aggression, while 5% reported physical violence. Eleven per cent of respondents reported various forms of sexual violence, including excessive or inappropriate touching.

Why don’t women turn to doulas?

Yvetta admits that 80% of the pregnant women who contact her are foreigners who, for various reasons, give birth in Armenia. Local women tend to be more cautious. The main problem, in the doula’s view, is a lack of information. Stereotypical attitudes also play an important role. Many people see childbirth as something women must go through on their own, without any need for additional support.

Waiting for childbirth. Photo: Yvetta Kosyan-Suvorova

“But this is the wrong approach, because every woman in labour is vulnerable. It is very important that, by the end, she feels like a winner because she has brought a new person into the world, rather than feeling broken and miserable after enduring unbearable suffering. Unfortunately, most women still prefer to overcome their fears of childbirth and pain not with a doula’s help, but by paying for a caesarean section. They believe this will solve the problem,” she says.

Sometimes women do not turn to doulas because they assume their services will be expensive. Yvetta does not specify how much she charges. However, she says she sometimes helps pregnant women entirely free of charge because she sees this work as her mission.

“Being a doula is a calling. This work is first and foremost about your inner world and your heart, and only then about your skills.”

She recalls that when she first started working as a doula, she sometimes returned home exhausted and upset. She even considered giving it up. Poor working conditions and hostility from doctors and hospital administrators were the main sources of stress. She also felt distressed when her presence created additional difficulties for the woman in labour.

Now she knows which maternity hospitals allow her to do her job most effectively. Some doctors there see doulas not as competitors but as professionals who support their work. Every birth has therefore become a wonderful experience for her.

“Now I come home happy because I no longer suffer alongside a woman during labour; instead, I help her avoid suffering. I can see that my work makes a difference. I see a woman who was screaming in pain and fear stop screaming, get up and start dancing,” Yvetta says.

Yvetta with the parents of a baby born with her support

Doulas in Armenia: non-medical support for pregnant women

World.title: Azerbaijan's insurance sector capital exceeds prudential requirements
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 13. Azerbaijan's insurance sector had total capital of 312 million manat ($183.5 million) in the first half of 2026, compared with required capital of 205 million manats, indicating that the sector's capital position remained above prudential requirements.

According to the Financial Stability Report published by the Central Bank of Azerbaijan (CBA), 15 insurance companies and one reinsurance company were operating in the country during the reporting period. Of the insurance companies, five provided life insurance services and 10 specialized in non-life insurance. The sector also included 23 insurance brokers and 459 insurance agents.

Total insurance premiums rose by 6.2%, or 51 million manat ($29.9 million), year-on-year in the first six months of 2026 to 867 million manats. Life insurance accounted for 60% of premiums, while non-life insurance made up the remaining 40%.

Life insurance premiums increased by 8.8%, or 42 million manat ($24.7 million), to 516 million manat ($303.5 million), while non-life insurance premiums rose by 2.6%, or 9 million manat ($5.2 million), to 351 million manat ($206.4 million). Voluntary insurance products were the main drivers of growth in both segments.

Compulsory insurance premiums fell by 23%, or 45 million manat ($26.4 million), to 150 million manat ($88.2 million). In contrast, premiums from voluntary life insurance rose by 14%, or 61 million manat ($35.8 million), to 483 million manat ($284.1 million), while voluntary non-life insurance premiums increased by 17%, or 35 million manat ($20.5 million), to 235 million manat ($138.2 million).

Concentration in the insurance market remained high. At the end of the reporting period, the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) for life insurance fell by 119 points to 6,822, while the index for non-life insurance rose by 593 points to 3,813.

Premiums ceded to reinsurers also increased, rising by 23%, or 14 million manat ($8.2 million), year-on-year to 74 million manat ($43.5 million). They accounted for 8.6% of total premiums. Of the premiums ceded, 4.9%, or 3.6 million manat ($2.1 million), came from life insurance, while 95.1%, or 70.7 million manat ($41.5 million), came from non-life insurance.

Insurance claims also increased significantly during the reporting period. Payouts rose by 27.3%, or 118 million manat ($69.4 million), compared with the same period last year, reaching 550 million manat ($323.5 million). Of this amount, 402 million manat ($236.4 million) related to life insurance and 148 million manat ($87.05 million) to non-life insurance. Life insurance payouts increased by 32.5%, while non-life insurance payouts rose by 14.5%.

The insurance sector's assets increased by 5.8%, or 123 million manat ($72.3 million), in the first half of the year to 2.26 billion manat ($1.3 billion). Bank funds accounted for 37% of assets, government securities for 31%, non-government securities for 7%, accounts receivable for 10%, and other assets for 14%.

The sector's liabilities rose by 10%, or 151 million manat ($88.8 million), to 1.65 billion manat ($970.5 million). Insurance premium reserves accounted for 68% of liabilities, reserves for insurance claims for 23%, and other liabilities for 9%.

Insurance companies' investment portfolios expanded by 9.7%, or 140 million manat ($82.3 million), from the end of last year to 1.6 billion manat ($941.1 million). Investments consisted mainly of government and corporate securities, as well as bank deposits. Investment portfolios accounted for 76% of the assets of life insurance companies and 64% of the assets of non-life insurance companies.

The report also outlined the sector's liquidity indicators. At the end of the first half of 2026, the sector held 1.2 billion manat ($705.8 million) in high-quality liquid assets, against expected cash outflows of 793 million manat ($466.4 million) and expected cash inflows of 301 million manat ($177.05 million).

The sector's liquidity ratio (ILR) stood at 237%. The ratio was 206% for life insurance and 315% for non-life insurance.

Accounts receivable for insurance premiums increased by 9%, or 11.6 million manat ($6.8 million), from the beginning of the year to 140 million manat ($82.3 million). Receivables in life insurance fell by 6.1% to 48.5 million manat ($28.5 million), while those in non-life insurance rose by 19.2% to 91.6 million manat ($53.8 million). Receivables accounted for 6.9% of the sector's total assets.

The insurance sector's net profit rose by 11.9%, or 10 million manat ($5.8 million), year-on-year in the first half of 2026 to 90 million manat ($52.9 million). Life and non-life insurance companies each recorded profits of 45 million manat ($26.4 million).

At the same time, the sector's loss ratio increased by 4 percentage points to 89%. The loss ratio for compulsory motor third-party liability insurance rose by 6 percentage points to 115%, while the ratio for motor vehicle insurance increased by 2 percentage points to 87%.

The report noted that the sector's total capital fell by 69 million manat ($40.5 million) from the end of last year to 312 million manat ($183.5 million), taking dividend payments into account. Required capital increased by 1 million manat ($588,235.29) to 205 million manat ($120.5 million). Despite these changes, the sector's total capital remained above the required level.

World.title: Prime Minister of Cambodia visits enterprises of the Ministry of Defence Industry (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 13. As part of the official visit to Azerbaijan, Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Cambodia Hun Manet visited the enterprises operating under the Ministry of Defence Industry on Tuesday.

Accompanied by Deputy Ministers of Defence Industry Mehman Bakhishov and Hidayat Azimov, Hun Manet was briefed on the operating principles, production capabilities, and technological potential of the enterprises.

During the visit, the Prime Minister was provided with detailed information on the systematic efforts undertaken to develop Azerbaijan’s defence industry under the leadership of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, Ilham Aliyev, the achievements attained in recent years, and the modern technological solutions being implemented. It was noted that expanding domestic production capabilities, adopting innovative technologies, strengthening research and development activities, and building a highly qualified workforce are among the key priorities for the development of the defence industry.

Information was also provided on the ongoing modernisation work at the enterprises, the improvement of production processes in line with modern standards, the introduction of new technological equipment, and the renewal of existing infrastructure.

During the visit, the sides discussed prospects for the development of the defence industry and opportunities for international cooperation in this field. They highlighted the importance of such visits for expanding relations between the two countries and exploring new opportunities for partnership.

World.title: Azerbaijan's Sabah FC secures their first victory in Champions League main stage
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 13. The second-round match of the UEFA Champions League main phase between Azerbaijan’s Sabah and Czech side Slavia Prague has come to an end.

The match, held at the Baku Olympic Stadium, ended in a 2-0 victory for the Azerbaijani champions.

Kahim Parris opened the scoring in the 49th minute, while Joy-Lance Mickels added the second goal in the 88th minute.

Thus, the “Owls” secured the first victory in their history in the Champions League main phase.

In their opening match, the team lost 4-0 to England’s Manchester United.

World.title: 'Beautiful weed' steadily choking landscapes across southern WA
World.content:
The sea of white lilies carpeting the forest floor south of Margaret River is a picturesque view, but an ugly sight for conservationists.

The arum lily, considered one of the most damaging weeds in the country, was banned from sale in WA more than 20 years ago, but the rogue garden plant's infestation of forests across WA's South West shows no sign of slowing.

Arum lilies in Boranup Forest, south of Margaret River. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

More than 3,000 private landowners have requested help to eradicate the weed on their properties.

But there are questions over the WA government's willingness to do the same in the state's national parks.

Forests under threat

In Boranup Forest, 300km south of Perth, Obelia Walker has mapped an enormous arum infestation through her work for Nature Conservation Margaret River.

Arum lilies are a major issue in sections of the Boranup forest. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

The organisation is co-ordinating a three-year blitz helping private landholders control the spread of lilies on their properties, funded by the WA government.

Those efforts have been successful, but she is worried about the infestation on public land.

Obelia Walker says arum lilies are causing problems in native forest, but key areas are being protected. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

"If you think about where the majority of diversity happens in the forest, it's in the understorey," she said.

" The way the arum lily behaves when it gets out of control like this is it's just smothering the understorey, out-competing native plants and destroying habitat for wildlife as well. "

The arum lily is worsening in the Tuart Forest National Park, near Busselton, conservationists say. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

Further north, in the Ludlow Tuart Forest near Busselton, local volunteer Des Donnelly has petitioned the Cook government to do more about the national park infestation.

"It's probably worse than it ever was," he said.

" If we don't manage them, we can probably kiss [the forest] goodbye in the next 50 years. "

Mr Donnelly was behind a petition presented to state parliament earlier this year, calling for government agencies to do more to fight the flower in the forest

Arum lilies on the roadside in Tuart National Park near Busselton. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

"It's a token effort if you like; Main Roads do a little bit, DBCA do what they can do with their small budget," he said.

" Generally, we're only just fiddling around the edges. "

Glen Taylor's beef farm sits opposite the Boranup National Park, where there is a large infestation.

Glen Taylor says arum lilies are infesting the forest neighbouring his property. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

He has managed to all but eradicate the lily from his own land, but it still encroaches at the borders.

"That is where it's a struggle," he said.

" It's a difficult thing to educate people how much damage they are doing to the natural environment. "

March of the arum continues

The state government's focus is on controlling arum lily in priority areas, rather than trying to eradicate the plant, prompting criticism from conservationists.

But a state government spokesperson said eradication was not realistic, with more than $2.6 million granted to arum lily control programs across the South West over the past nine years.

Arum lilies can be seen throughout the Ludlow Tuart National Park. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

"While arum lily can be managed, it is not currently considered feasible to completely eradicate the species from the landscape due to its extensive distribution and ability to regenerate and spread," the spokesperson said.

The spokesperson said it had undertaken control across areas in the Tuart Forest National Park, Leeuwin-Naturaliste National Park, Wooditjup National Park, Yelverton National Park, and selected state forest and nature reserve sites.

Creative solutions required

Conservationists agreed that the National Biosecurity Committee's inclusion of the arum lily on its list of Nationally Established Weed Priorities could lead to more innovative methods of control.

Nature Conservation's Obelia Walker hoped it would unlock funding for research into more cutting-edge methods to tackle the weed.

"We can't spray out way out of this problem," she said.

"It might be something quite novel; it might be a fungus or a disease, but it's an exciting space."

Arum lilies are infesting the Boranup forest. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

Invasive Species Council policy director Carol Booth said the war on the lily was ultimately reliant on political will.

"I mean, the arum lily is one of the classic examples in Australia of a garden plant that's just gone rogue," she said.

"Which of these weeds are our state and federal governments prepared to put funding into to generate a much more collaborative and concerted approach to managing their risks?"

World.title: De Minaur sets up Shanghai quarterfinal with Zverev
World.content:
Alex de Minaur has taken a giant stride towards clinching another ATP Finals berth after roaring into the last eight of the Shanghai Masters.

Continuing to defy the hip flexor injury that threatened to end his season less than a week ago, de Minaur downed dual grand slam semifinalist Karen Khachanov 6-3, 6-4 to jump to seventh place in the Race to Turin's live standings.

Crucially, Australia's baseline warrior has leapfrogged Novak Djokovic and Frances Tiafoe, who have already been eliminated in China, as he chases more valuable rankings points in the quarter-finals — and potentially beyond.

De Minaur retires injured, handing China Open title to Djokovic Alex de Minaur says he did not want his Beijing campaign to end in the way it did, with injury forcing the Australian to retire early in the second set.

But Alexander Zvererv, who will be the year-end world number one, stands in his way after the German beat Alexander Bublik 7-6(6), 4-6, 7-6(1).

In his fifth encounter against Khachanov, de Minaur knew efficiency was key.

"It was really important for me to serve well and I think I definitely did that, especially down the stretch," he said.

"I got into a little bit of trouble, a couple of love-30 games, and I was able to find some good serves when I needed it."

De Minaur, who reached the semi-finals at the prestigious season-ending tournament last year, cut a forlorn figure after being forced to retire early in the second set of last week's China Open final against Djokovic, when a set down.

His comeback has been nothing short of remarkable.

"Ultimately I've been getting better and better every day," the 27-year-old said.

"Today was by far my best match and I think that I'm only going to get better.

"I know that once I'm fit physically and mentally, I'm the player that I [want to be] and I'm excited to be competing and going to the tail end of these tournaments and feeling great about myself."

Despite a 4-8 record against Zverev, de Minaur prevailed in their past two meetings, both at Laver Cup, including two weeks ago. Zverev has fitness problems of his own.

"My ankle was acting up, unfortunately," Zverev said, who saved three set points against Bublik in the first-set tiebreak.

"It was understandable because I have been playing a lot of tennis, which is kind of a good sign because I have been playing well. I am starting to feel my body more and more but I am happy to get through."

AAP

World.title: 'Sluggish' Australia joins criticism of Trump administration's ICC attack
World.content:
The federal government has belatedly joined international criticism of the Trump administration's latest assault on the International Criminal Court (ICC), prompting questions about Australia's "sluggish" response to sweeping US sanctions designed to cripple it.

Japan, Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom issued a statement late on Friday reaffirming their "continued and unwavering support for the independence, impartiality, and integrity of the ICC".

It came just hours after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio unveiled new sanctions freezing the court's US assets and cutting it off from American companies.

"As committed supporters of the ICC we regret and strongly disagree with the announcement of sanctions to be imposed upon the Court by the United States," they said.

"If put into effect, these sanctions will have a significant impact on the Court's work, its dedicated staff and their families. They work every day to bring those accused of the most serious international crimes to justice and to support their victims."

Australia was not listed on the statement when it was first issued on Saturday morning, local time, and the government's initial silence drew fierce criticism from legal experts, who accused it of cowardice.

Marco Rubio has led the Trump administration's policy on the ICC. (Reuters: Eric Lee, file)

But late on Monday Australia's name was added to the list of countries on the joint statement, which was then uploaded to the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) website.

A federal government spokesperson told the ABC that Australia was invited to join the statement only after it was first published, and that Australia signalled to the Netherlands on Sunday that it would be willing to put its name on it.

US threats against ICC The Trump administration has vowed to dismantle the International Criminal Court "brick by brick", drawing fierce criticism from around the world.

An official from a European country backed that account and defended Australia's approach, saying it took time to coordinate a position across continents over the weekend.

A second official from another Western country also said they did not believe that Australia had "hesitated" to join the statement and the process simply "took time".

But they said the Australian government was still taking a much more "careful" and "low profile" approach to defending the ICC when compared with other US allies.

They drew a contrast between Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi — who on Friday night issued a statement in English and Japanese sharply criticising the sanctions — and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Foreign Minister Penny Wong, who have not made any personal statements on the issue.

"There was nothing stopping Australia from doing the same," they said.

Canberra's cautious approach

Last month the foreign minister declined to directly criticise the Trump administration over the sanctions during an interview with SBS, saying that she "spoke for Australia" not the US.

Professor Catherine Renshaw said it was disappointing Australia did not sign onto the original statement. (ABC News: Lydia Feng)

Officials told the ABC earlier this year that while there was deep unease in Canberra about the sanctions, Australia was wary of a fight with the Trump administration over it, particularly as the campaign against the court has been championed by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Australia dismayed over US move to 'dismantle' ICC There are real concerns within the Australian government about what US President Donald Trump is doing in regards to sanctioning the International Criminal Court, government sources tell the ABC.

The Dean of Law at the University of Western Sydney, Professor Catherine Renshaw, said the government's initial response was "sluggish" but that she was still pleased to see Australia eventually join the statement.

"It was disappointing to see Australia not sign onto the original statement — it was particularly disappointing given Australia's long history of building international law and support of institutions like the ICC," she said.

"But it's a welcome development that Australia has now joined friends and allies in supporting international law."

" The foundational principle here is the defence of the rule of law and that is most important when the actions of powerful states threaten those fundamental principles. "

The government has also been working with Australians employed by the ICC to help them "work through" the implications of the sanctions, although the Trump administration has offered a 180-day grace period before they are fully implemented.

One official from a third country said it was "surreal" to watch Western diplomats working out how they could best shield their nationals from US sanctions.

Professor Renshaw said the US sanctions would create a "very difficult problem" because US companies and financial institutions played a "central" role providing the court with legal, travel and banking services.

"Australians who work for the court will need to know that the Australian government will support them carrying out their work when it's made far more difficult, complex and perilous by the actions of the US," she said.

World.title: Police say person stabbed during 'concerning' roadside incident in Belconnen
World.content:
The ACT chief police officer says a young person was stabbed in a "concerning" incident in Belconnen this morning.

Police allege four people were throwing objects at passing vehicles on Coulter Drive.

ACT Policing Deputy Commissioner Scott Lee told ABC Radio Canberra that one person got out of his vehicle after something was thrown at his car and was stabbed multiple times.

"An object was thrown at a motor vehicle and the driver's got out of the motor vehicle and he's ... suffered multiple stab wounds," he said.

"And then that individual, that young person, after that incident has taken himself home and then his parents have got him to hospital."

He said that while that person's condition had been stabilised, "our thoughts and prayers do go to him and his family".

'Multiple calls made to police'

The four people allegedly involved in the incident are still at large, Deputy Commissioner Lee said.

"Those people remain outstanding, so what I would ask is for anyone that has information in relation to these people we would ask you to come forward and talk to police as a matter of priority this morning," he said.

"Either do that directly to the ACT Police and Communications Centre or via Crime Stoppers.

" It is an active investigation this morning and we've got our crime team investigating this incident along with our general duties teams as well. "

Deputy Commissioner Lee said there were "multiple calls" made to police this morning about objects being thrown at a number of vehicles.

A crime scene has been established and traffic is being disrupted.

World.title: Regulator says he would quit over political influence in Man City scandal
World.content:
The chair of English football's regulatory body says he would resign if any political interference affected potential sanctions against Manchester City.

City has been found guilty of widespread breaches of the Premier League's financial rules, which could result in punishments including a massive fine, points deductions or even expulsion from England's top flight.

Separately, the Independent Football Regulator can force club owners to sell and can withhold a license to operate if it deems them unfit.

An independent panel found the United Arab Emirates-backed City had artificially inflated its revenue by more than $1 billion over nearly a decade, circumventing fair-play rules.

Loading...

Football regulator chair David Kogan said it was still awaiting the outcome of City's appeal against the verdict.

The UAE is a big investor in the UK. Asked about the regulator's ability to remain independent given wider relations between the governments, Kogan said: "Any form of political interference in the way we operate is going to result in my resigning from this role, and I stand by that completely.

"We've come under absolutely no political pressure whatsoever on this or any other topic. And I don't expect to in the future," he said.

Kogan's comments came after UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he would be "really concerned" to lose City's current ownership. Mr Burnham also said he would not get "directly involved in the process."

City is accused of providing misleading information about its finances over a nine-year period from 2009-18. During that time, it won three titles and signed some of the world's best players. It went on to enjoy a period of unprecedented dominance of English soccer.

The guilty verdict marks the biggest scandal in Premier League history and raises questions about the club's future, owned by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, deputy prime minister of the United Arab Emirates and a member of Abu Dhabi's royal family.

Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan owns Manchester City. (Reuters: Ameer Al-Mohammedawi/Pool)

The British government established the Independent Football Regulatory Commission last year to set governance standards in English soccer.

Part of that includes the issuing of licenses for clubs to be able to operate, which will begin in November.

Kogan suggested the guilty verdict would not affect issuing a license to City because its appeal is ongoing.

"A verdict once it's gone through an appeal process will certainly be something that we would clearly be taking into account when looking at awarding a license or looking at the owners, directors and senior executives," he said.

Majority of English clubs are loss-making

Kogan was speaking in Manchester about the regulator's "State of the Game" report on English soccer.

The report states that despite the success of English soccer — including the Premier League, the world's richest and most popular league — 94 per cent of clubs across the pyramid are loss-making, and more than a quarter would be unable to survive more than 30 days if owners pulled funding.

It says a major problem is teams spending too much to keep up with rivals.

"At the heart of English football's success is a massive contradiction. While some of our clubs are among the richest and most competitive in the world, others are standing on the edge of financial disaster," Kogan said.

"This lack of resilience can no longer be ignored."

Seventeen clubs "would be loss-making even if their players played for free," the regulator's CEO Richard Monks said.

"Owners in many football clubs will inject the money two or three days before payday and not keep any cash in the club. This is not how most businesses are run, and it's a major issue which we will require football to address."

The regulator has been involved in negotiations between the Premier League and the English Football League regarding what are known as solidarity payments to help develop England's lower leagues. That includes parachute payments to teams relegated from the top flight.

The regulator is proposing to spread those payments more evenly among teams. It is part of a suite of proposals, including measures to help clubs improve financial risk management.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: They're vital community hubs, but regional post offices face uncertain futures
World.content:
Advocates say small-town post offices need to be kept alive as aging licensees and changing community needs threaten their future.

A Senate inquiry is underway into Australia Post's retail network that will look into, among other factors, the role licensed post offices (LPOs) play "in delivering community services".

An inquiry into Australia Post's retail network will report back this month. (ABC News)

But in Tarpeena, in South Australia's south-east, locals already know what losing the local post office can mean.

In 2022, the LPO running out of the local pub, the Pines Hotel, was closed, leaving the closest post office 20 kilometres away.

Long-time postie Shirley Little's mother owned and managed the LPO for more than four decades, back when it operated alongside the local general store.

Shirley Little at Tarpeena's post office in 2015. (Danielle Grindlay)

"I think when the post office did eventually close down, the older people missed it because it was somewhere they could go every day and someone would say hello to them," she said.

" From a mental health point of view, it wasn't good for a lot of older people in the community. "

An asset for communities

About two-thirds of the Australia Post network is made up of LPOs, with about 2,900 operating across the country.

Unlike general post offices, which are run by Australia Post, LPOs are run by licensees either as a standalone post office or alongside another business.

The peak body representing LPO licensees, LPO Group, said other post office services, such as banking, were being "run down" as focus shifted towards parcel services.

LPOs make up two-thirds of Australia Post's retail network. (ABC Pilbara: Louise Miolin)

"When you're in the rural and regional parts of Australia, that's one of the most important businesses in your town," LPO Group CEO Scott Etherington said.

" If that's taken away and replaced by just a point of presence … I would suggest that community has lost an awful lot. "

Pines Hotel licensee Lynton Cram said after the post office moved into the hotel, it failed to attract business.

Pines Hotel licensee Lynton Cram ran Tarpeena's post office for a few years. (ABC South East SA: Josh Brine)

"During the week I had very little business, apart from delivering the mail and sorting it," he said.

"As far as doing any other transactions like parcels or cash transactions, it was very minimal."

Changing nature of the post

In its submission to the inquiry, Australia Post said it faced growing challenges in the regions, including declining foot traffic, increasing costs and a lack of workers.

It said 38 per cent of LPO owners were aged 60 or older, and 39 per cent in non-major cities intended to exit the network within three years.

The post office in Tarpeena closed in 2022. (ABC South East SA: Josh Brine)

An Australia Post spokesperson said it had been engaging with the inquiry, and would review and consider the committee's report.

"Supporting communities is at the heart of what we do and Australia Post rejects claims it is abandoning communities," the spokesperson said.

"We have expanded how and where customers can access our services.

"We've done this by adding self-service options like parcel lockers, which are in addition to our reported retail outlets. These services complement post offices, not replace them."

Australia Post says it's committed to continuing to serve regional communities. (ABC Radio Brisbane: Anna Levy)

The spokesperson said Australia Post had paid $635 million in commissions to licensees in the previous financial year, and that those payments had increased each year for the past 15 years.

"For the past two years, we have been engaging with licensees and their representative associations to update the current LPO model, which is more than 30 years old," they said.

"This consultation is ongoing."

More than 140 submissions have been made to the inquiry, with the committee's report due on October 22.

World.title: Live: Bank of America fined $US1.2 billion for anti-money laundering failures
World.content:
The Treasury has released a detailed statement of what it alleges against America's second-largest bank.

It says the bank was given a cease-and-desist order requiring it to repair its anti-money laundering program as far back as December 2024 but not enough was done.

According to the regulator, more than a year later the bank was still failing to escalate potentially suspicious activity to investigators and it had a persistent systemic gap in its monitoring.

The OCC said the bank's monitoring system failed to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions, and that the bank knew for years it was not escalating suspicious activity. It also alleged that key personnel were not adequately trained.

FinCEN said compliance staff escalated concerns about potential ties to narcotics proceeds, but the bank did not respond in a timely or meaningful way.

There were 475 apparent violations involving Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics and global terrorism.

In terms of what happens now, BoA must work with a third party to look back over past transactions and report suspicious activity that went undetected. Documents will also be submitted that will test the program against three priority risks: the southwest border, cartels and potential drug trafficking; Iran; and Russia.

Treasury used the announcement to send a message to the rest of the industry. It said institutions cannot rely on law enforcement inquiries or referrals from other banks as a substitute for their own controls. They're also looking for whistleblower tips and offering awards.

World.title: What's happening with the AFL's new Illicit Drugs Policy?
World.content:
The issue of Illicit Drugs Policy (IDP) reform in the AFL remains in limbo after seven months of waiting and increasing scrutiny of the parties involved, and no clear indication of when it might be resolved.

An in-principle agreement for a new policy was announced in March by the AFL in conjunction with the AFL Players Association but is yet to be implemented.

The AFL and AFLPA said it would be the "toughest in Australian sport" and become operational in 2026 once outstanding matters had been resolved.

The policy is in the news now because of allegations of drug use by the so-called "Pullman Five"; five Sydney Swans players involved in the Pullman Hotel scandal in August.

Last weekend, Advanced Life Support paramedics attended a house owned by a Carlton player.

There is no suggestion any of the Carlton players were using illicit drugs.

So what is the current state of play, and what is the plan for the future?

What is the current AFL Illicit Drugs Policy?

The IDP was first established in 2005 and was, according to the AFL, "unashamedly a harm minimisation policy".

Players caught breaching the IDP are subject to a three-strike system.

If a player is caught with drugs in their system for the first time, they are given a suspended $5,000 fine and receive targeted testing and counselling. The club doctor is the only staff member informed of the player's drug use.

A second strike means the player will be named and suspended for four games.

A third strike results in a 12-match suspension. Travis Tuck in 2010 is the only player to have ever recorded three strikes.

Most players who are caught using drugs in public or through social media, such as Bailey Smith (when he was at the Bulldogs), are generally suspended under the AFL's "conduct unbecoming" rules.

Bailey Smith was given a two-match suspension for illicit drug use when he was with the Bulldogs in 2022. (AAP: Hamish Blair)

The policy has come under enormous criticism in the two decades it has been in place, most notably from independent senator Andrew Wilkie, who denounced the policy in a speech to federal parliament in 2024.

What is the proposed new policy?

When the AFL and Players' Association announced the new policy in March, they said it would strengthen "the game's response to illicit drug use across both the AFL and AFLW competitions".

AFL reveals new illicit drug policy The AFL says its new illicit drugs policy, which includes biannual hair-testing of all players, is the most stringent in Australian sport.

The organisations maintained the policy was based on medical advice for players' health and wellbeing.

When in place, the new policy will see all AFL and AFLW players undergo annual education programs and have a hair sample tested twice a year for evidence of drug use.

Hair samples retain evidence of drug use for up to three months, whereas urine samples, which are currently used, may only show evidence of drug use for a handful of days.

It's expected the players will be tested during the pre-season in order to cover the period when they're on leave and then again following their mid-season bye.

If a player tests positive, they will enter a behavioural change program overseen by their club doctor.

If a player records a second positive test, they'll be put on an individual management plan, which will be overseen by an AFL IDP manager.

A third positive test will see the player referred to a Fitness to Play assessment by an independent panel, and at that point, the club president, chief executive and general manager of football would be informed.

Players who use illicit drugs publicly will be suspended for two to four weeks.

So, what's happened?

Seven months after the AFL and Players' Association announced an in-principle agreement on the policy, it still hasn't been put into place.

ABC Sport understands there are still points of disagreement between the two bodies.

The outstanding matters include designing the education program and the behavioural change program for players who are found with drugs in their system, and appointing members to a joint committee to oversee the program.

Until the new program is in place, the old system will continue to operate.

ABC Sport has asked the AFL and the AFLPA why the current policy was not in place, when it's expected to begin and who, if anyone, has been employed to run the program?

The AFL didn't respond to those questions, and the Players' Association declined to comment.

World.title: AFL trade deadline day LIVE: Bombers push to land premiership Lion
World.content:

London: Pope Leo XIV has emerged from surgery after doctors found he had lung cancer, leading them to remove the lower lobe of his right lung. The Vatican said the surgeons found the pontiff had a lung adenocarcinoma, as they suspected after examinations and preoperative tests before he had the operation on Tuesday in Rome. Pope Leo XIV arriving at the Agostino Gemelli Polyclinic in Rome on Tuesday AP Photo/Alessandra Tarantino Leo, 71, was in the operating room for about three hours and underwent surgery for about 90 minutes, the Vatican said in a statement on Tuesday night (about 7am on Wednesday, AEST). “The surgery was successful, and there were no complications,” the statement said.



“Following the operation, the Pope awoke normally and, after a brief period of observation, returned to his room on the 10th floor.” Leo had walked into the Gemelli hospital in Rome through the main entrance earlier in the day and waved to dozens of well-wishers who had gathered to greet him. The Vatican said the surgery would be performed by a team led by Gemelli’s chief thoracic surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora. The Gemelli Hospital in Rome. Getty Images The doctors said their examination confirmed the diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma. “To ensure a radical resection, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique,” the Vatican said.



News service AFP reported that a Vatican source said further tests were being carried out to determine if the cancer had spread. The Lung Cancer Foundation of America describes lung adenocarcinoma as one of the most common forms of lung cancer, accounting for about 40 per cent of all lung cancers in the US. Loading “Whatever the stage and whatever the treatment, more people are living with this disease than ever before,” it says. Treatments include surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation, it says. Oncologists said before the operation that even if the nodule turned out to be cancerous, Leo’s prognosis was “excellent” because it would have been removed at an early stage, the Associated Press reported.



The Vatican on Monday cancelled all Leo’s audiences until at least October 20. He held a general audience in St Peter’s Square last Wednesday when he thanked pilgrims including visitors from Australia. Related Article Analysis

Catholic church From AI to war, Pope wields the Vatican’s soft power amid growing distrust of political leaders Leo revealed the concerns about his medical condition in a statement on social media shortly before he was due to go to hospital. “Dear friends, during some recent medical examinations, the doctors found a small, localised nodule in my lung,” he posted on X on Sunday in Rome (midnight that night, AEST). “It was detected at a very early stage and is well-localised. The doctors believe that it is best to intervene, so, following their advice, I have decided to undergo surgery to remove it. The operation is already scheduled to take place in the coming days.



“I thank you for your spiritual closeness and entrust myself to your prayers.” Related Article Updated

Catholic church Albanese invites Pope Leo XIV to visit Australia in private meeting at the Vatican The Gemelli hospital has a papal apartment that past popes have used, complete with a private chapel on the 10th floor, but Leo is staying in a nearby room since the papal apartment is currently undergoing renovations, according to the Vatican press office. Vatican News said that following the operation on Tuesday, Leo was served dinner in his room and spent the evening in the company of his secretaries and other Vatican staff. The Pope is due to travel to Latin America in early November for a major visit to several countries including Peru, where he spent a decade working with local communities during his time in the Augustine order.



The Vatican estimated that about 800,000 people attended a mass with Leo in Paris in late September during his visit to France, drawing bigger crowds than some expected. The Catholic Church in Australia is working on plans for Leo to visit Australia in 2028, and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese formally invited the Pope to visit when they spoke in Rome in May last year. The Vatican is yet to announce a visit. Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican’s Secretary of State, described Leo as showing “great composure” on Monday evening ahead of the operation the next day. “We are confident, but, of course, we accompany him with our prayers,” Parolin told reporters on Monday, the ANSA news service reported. “Am I worried? Yes, because I certainly didn’t expect something like this.”



Parolin said he was thankful the lung nodule was detected straight away. With AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slide, Wall Street mixed Stan Choe Updated October 14, 2026 — 8:26am ,first published 5:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The first big batch of summertime profit reports from US companies made waves on Wall Street after topping analysts’ expectations, but many cancelled each other out. That left US stock indexes little changed near their records on Tuesday. The S&P 500 edged down by less than 0.1 per cent and pulled a bit further from its all-time high set last week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 180 points, or 0.3 per cent, while the Nasdaq composite dipped 0.2 per cent. Wall Street’s modest moves masked some big swings happening underneath the market’s surface. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to retreat, with futures pointing to a fall of 30 points, or 0.3 per cent, at the open. The Australian dollar was trading at US69.85¢. The modest Wall Street moves masked some big swings happening underneath the market’s surface.



Goldman Sachs, for example, jumped more than 4 per cent at the start of trading after the bank delivered a profit for July through September that blew past analysts’ expectations. But its stock quickly erased all of it and then flipped between gains and losses before finishing with a dip of 0.2 per cent. Related Article Opinion

Inflation Don’t blame Ukraine: Prices go up and up, thanks to Trump’s wars Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The firm benefited in the summer from strong growth for its business that offers loans to clients for trading stocks, among other things, even as chief executive David Solomon said it’s dealing with a “complicated operating environment” created by lots of uncertainty. Expectations are high for profits across all kinds of US companies. Analysts are forecasting overall growth of nearly 30 per cent for companies in the S&P 500 during the summer from a year earlier, according to FactSet. If they’re correct, it would be the third straight quarter of growth better than 25 per cent. And companies need to hit those high numbers to justify the record-setting runs for their stock prices despite the many worries on Wall Street about high inflation, increased pressure from the bond market and the war with Iran.



UnitedHealth Group’s stock swung sharply even though it reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. The healthcare company also raised its forecast for profit over the full year of 2026. After rallying as much as 5.6 per cent shortly after trading began, it erased all of it and finished with a dip of 0.2 per cent. More firmly in the losing column was Wells Fargo, whose stock dropped 3.1 per cent after the bank reported weaker revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, even though its profit topped Wall Street’s estimates. CEO Charlie Scharf cited weaker revenue from its venture capital investments, among other things. But Scharf also gave a potentially encouraging signal about the broader economy and future profits for companies across industries. He said that “our data shows that our consumer and business customers are doing well.” That’s despite uncertainty about the economy and recent surveys showing Americans have become more discouraged about their finances. At the country’s biggest bank, JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon highlighted “elevated asset prices” as one of the potential risks for the economy. He also mentioned high inflation, rising interest rates and “geopolitical conditions.”



“These forces may be manageable, but we remain prepared for a wide range of outcomes,” he said. JPMorgan Chase’s stock flipped between gains and losses through the day before finishing with a drop of 0.9 per cent. It reported a weaker profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected, but it also gave a forecast for net interest income in the current quarter that topped Wall Street’s estimate. Outside of earnings reports, some of the sharpest action was for stocks in the computer chip industry. Worries have been high for a while about whether chip stock prices have shot too high in the frenzy around artificial-intelligence technology, and concerns climbed further following reports that China’s memory chipmaker CXMT is making advances that could challenge industry heavyweights. That includes companies like Micron Technology of Boise, Idaho, and Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix of South Korea. Micron fell 3.6 per cent and was the single heaviest weight on the S&P 500. South Korea’s Kospi stock index tumbled 5.5 per cent for its worst day in nearly two months.



Bumble, meanwhile, leaped 56.6 per cent after the app company that helps people make relationships said it agreed to a $US1.3 billion ($1.9 billion), all-cash buyout by Ithaca Holdings. Related Article Intellectual property Can Adidas really own stripes – and did White Fox copy them? All told, the S&P 500 edged down by 1.79 points to 7,805.45. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 180.45 to 51,670.10, and the Nasdaq composite fell 41.52 to 27,204.38. In the bond market, Treasury yields eased after oil prices fell. The yield on the 10-year Treasury slipped to 5.21 per cent from 5.24 per cent late Friday. Trading in the US bond market was closed Monday for a holiday. Yields sank following a 0.9 per cent dip for the price of a barrel of Brent crude oil to $US105.69. Oil prices have been yo-yoing because of uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global energy industry to return to normal.

Actor Selma Blair has been reportedly released on bail after pleading not guilty to two assaults following an alleged violent incident aboard a flight to New York while she was in “a state of severe confusion and disorientation” after missing “powerful” medication. The Cruel Intentions star, 54, had allegedly become physically abusive and injured two Delta flight attendants on Sunday (Monday AEDT). During the flight from Los Angeles to New York, Blair was restrained after allegedly punched one flight attendant midair, biting another and attempting to open the aircraft door during the flight, according to the Hollywood Reporter. Selma Blair has been released on bail. Pictured leaving court on Monday after her arraignment on charges of injuring two flight attendants during a cross-country flight. AP Photo/Ryan Murphy After landing, the Legally Blonde actor allegedly kicked a police officer taking her to hospital for an evaluation and later allegedly kicked a nurse once she got there. On Monday (Tuesday AEDT), Blair pleaded not guilty in a New York court to two assault charges relating to the officer and the nurse, according to the Associated Press. She also faces separate federal charges from the FBI, which investigates alleged assaults aboard aircraft.



Loading Charging documents state while a police officer was securing Blair to a stretcher en route to the hospital, the actor pulled a leg from the straps and allegedly kicked her repeatedly around the face, neck and chest, causing serious pain and substantial swelling. A nurse moving Blair also alleged she was kicked in the chest, causing substantial pain. Blair was arraigned on two counts of second-degree assault and her lawyer entered a not guilty plea on her behalf. According to the Associated Press, the actor appeared to cry as she stood in court in handcuffs, wearing jeans and a white hooded sweatshirt. Lawyer Shawn Barnes told the court that “this was not an intentional assault,” according to the New York Post. He said the actor, who has multiple sclerosis, “missed several doses of … a powerful medication that controls severe neurological symptoms”.



Actress Selma Blair, pictured last month, has been charged following an in-flight incident in which two flight attendants were injured. AP “Blair boarded this flight after being on set and working extensive hours and exhaustive hours in the days leading up to this flight,” Barnes said. “Additionally, at one point, during the flight, there was an incident where Miss Blair actually fell and hit her head. “These factors, coupled with the altitude, resulted in a state of severe confusion and disorientation.” The judge set her bail at $US20,000 cash ($28,600) or $US60,000 bond and set the next hearing for January. In audio recorded by a witness and obtained by TMZ, Blair can allegedly be heard screaming as she exited the plane in New York. In a separate dispatch audio also obtained by TMZ, officials can be heard requesting medical personnel at the gate after reports of minor injuries, including a bloody nose and bite marks.



Delta told the Hollywood Reporter it had “zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behaviour, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first”. With AP

World.content:
Updated NationalNSWCrime Sydney man charged with murder of 12-year-old boy fatally shot in face Daniel Lo Surdo Updated October 14, 2026 — 7:56am ,first published 6:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. A 19-year-old man has been charged with the murder of a 12-year-old boy who was shot in the face inside an apartment in Sydney’s north-west last month. Isaac Bechara was 18 when he allegedly killed the boy in the Moda apartment complex in Norwest on September 21, in what detectives believe was an accidental gunshot delivering fatal wounds to the 12-year-old’s face and neck. Tactical and general duties officers rushed to the Norwest apartment complex on September 21. Wolter Peeters Bechara was charged with murder at Silverwater Prison on Tuesday, having been in custody since being charged with concealing a serious indictable offence in the aftermath of the shooting. Police believe 10 people were in the apartment at the time of the shooting, including the boy’s mother and several 18-year-old men, some of whom fled after the boy was shot. The murder weapon was removed from the scene before responders arrived, and still hasn’t been found.



Detectives laid the murder charge after working through several accounts of events from the boy’s family and responders to the scene. Two other 18-year-olds present at the apartment were arrested with Bechara following the shooting, where they faced police questioning before being released without charge. Investigators believe the boy, who cannot be legally identified, may have been one of several people handling an illegal gun when it discharged inside an apartment in the Moda complex in Norwest. The boy died three days after he was rushed to The Children’s Hospital at Westmead suffering wounds to his face and neck. The boy’s father, who is a convicted cocaine dealer, was among the family members who paid tribute to the boy after his life support was switched off. “RIP my baby,” he wrote alongside a photo of the pair. Other members of the boy’s extended family are linked to organised crime and known to police. The boy’s father paid tribute to his son on social media. Instagram



The boy’s family has co-operated with police. However, none of the other occupants inside the apartment have co-operated with investigators, who as a result have been unable to establish how the boy was shot. Related Article Crime Alleged Coconut Cartel gang member arrested after boy, 11, fatally shot in face Bechara will appear in bail court on Wednesday following his latest charge. Police haven’t ruled out further arrests as they continue to investigate the circumstances leading to the boy’s death. The murder charge comes one week after Reece Fakr, an alleged key player for the high-profile Coconut Cartel, was arrested at Sydney International Airport as he attempted to leave the country. Fakr, 18, allegedly left a phone at the Norwest apartment, on which detectives found evidence of alleged criminal offences. He has been charged with 10 offences, including conspiracy to murder, kidnapping, arson and directing a criminal group.



Fakr isn’t related to the child. He remains behind bars ahead of his next court appearance on December 8. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Tupac Shakur’s killer has been sentenced and is ‘guaranteed to die behind bars’
World.content:
CultureMusicPop music Tupac Shakur’s killer has been sentenced and is ‘guaranteed to die behind bars’ Jessica Hill October 14, 2026 — 7:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Las Vegas: Duane “Keffe D” Davis was sentenced Tuesday to 40 years to life in prison for orchestrating the murder of rap icon Tupac Shakur, who was gunned down off the Las Vegas Strip over 30 years ago. Davis, 63, was convicted in August of first-degree murder with the use of a deadly weapon. He is the only person ever charged in the death of Shakur, whose popularity was peaking at age 25. More than 30 years after his death the man accused of orchestrating the killing of Tupac Shakur has been sentenced. nna\sswain Prosecutor Marc DiGiacomo said Tuesday that whatever sentence the court imposes, Davis is “guaranteed to die” behind bars. “It’s not just about losing a family member,” DiGiacomo said as Shakur’s sister Sekyiwa “Set” Shakur nodded her head in the audience.



The killing went unsolved for years until Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips, gave interviews and published his role in the shooting in his 2019 tell-all memoir. DiGiacomo said Davis was trying to profit off a killing that he committed and for that, he did not deserve the minimum sentence. Duane Davis, centre, is escorted by police from a sentencing hearing after his murder conviction in the death of rapper Tupac Shakur. John Locher/Pool AP via AP “In my mind, he deserves the maximum possible sentence,” DiGiacomo said. Davis spoke briefly in court, telling Judge Carli Kierny he wanted items back that police took from his house, including his pictures. Asked if there was anything else he wanted to say, Davis said: “No I’m good.”



Davis’ lawyer, Michael Sanft said he planned to appeal the verdict. Sanft said prosecutors waited too long to bring the case. How the shooting occurred On the night of September 7, 1996, Shakur was in the passenger seat of a black BMW with music mogul Marion “Suge” Knight when a white Cadillac pulled up at a red light, and shots erupted. Shakur was shot multiple times and died six days later, while Knight survived. Tupac in 1994. Shakur is considered one of the most influential and versatile rappers of all time and had a burgeoning film career as an actor at the time of his death. His legend has only grown since. His songs still resonate among fans with themes of hardship, love and Black struggles.



In his memoir, Davis explained how Shakur and his entourage beat up Davis’ nephew hours before the shooting in Las Vegas. He said he sought retaliation, and that he was in the passenger seat of the Cadillac and passed the gun to the backseat, where shots were fired. Davis had spoken to detectives years before but avoided prosecution because of an agreement he made with law enforcement. During the weeks-long trial, prosecutors relied on Davis’ own statements to law enforcement and documentarians. They argued that Davis orchestrated the shooting and provided the gun used in Shakur’s death, which was the result of a rivalry between the South Side Compton Crips and Mob Piru. Duane Davis, right, with his attorney Michael Sanft during the sentencing hearing. John Locher/Pool AP via AP Davis’ defence attorney pointed to a lack of physical evidence that connected his client to the 30-year-old crime, and he portrayed Davis as a liar who was trying to make money. After nine days of hearing testimony in August, the jury deliberated for three hours before returning a guilty verdict.



Related Article Courts After 30 years, the man accused of orchestrating Tupac’s murder is on trial. Here’s what to know Shakur was an icon, a brother Shakur’s family spoke at the sentencing, including his siblings Maurice “Mopreme” Shakur and Sekyiwa “Set” Shakur. Following the verdict, prosecutor Binu Palal said that to many people, Shakur was an icon or an idea, “but to the family, Tupac Shakur was a brother, a son, a cousin, a loved person ripped from them 30 years ago.” Palal said the family had to sit through years of Davis “bragging about killing someone they loved”.



“They loved that man. And the arrogance that Mr Davis had in expressing his joy in killing that man ultimately was his undoing,” Palal said. Prosecutors said they had insufficient evidence to charge anyone else. Tupac’s sibling Sekyiwa “Set” Shakur, centre, the sentencing hearing. John Locher/Pool AP via AP Davis was the only person to be charged and convicted in the killing of Shakur. The three other people who allegedly were in the Cadillac — including Davis’ nephew Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson, who Davis said was the one who pulled the trigger — have died. Clark County District Attorney Steve Wolfson has said his office didn’t believe it had sufficient evidence to charge anyone else.



“But like any other case, if we come into more information, more evidence, we can always consider filing additional charges,” he said following the guilty verdict. “But today, we don’t believe that’s the appropriate move to make.” AP Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.
