World.title: Gas exporters to be forced to prevent Australian shortfalls under new laws
World.content:
BusinessConsumer affairsEnergy Gas exporters to be forced to prevent Australian shortfalls under new laws Nick Toscano October 14, 2026 — 7:08am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Large Australian gas producers will be forced to hold back up to 20 per cent of their export volumes for local customers for the first time, as the Albanese government presses ahead with a policy aimed at easing domestic energy prices despite industry warnings it could stunt investment. Federal Resources Minister Madeleine King is expected to bring Labor’s long-awaited domestic gas-reservation bill to parliament on Wednesday after months of talks with major gas corporations, customers in the energy-intensive manufacturing sector, and some of the nation’s biggest liquefied natural gas (LNG) buyers in Asia. Most of Australia’s LNG is produced in Queensland or Western Australia, and is sold on long-term contracts to Asia. Under the proposed scheme, starting from January 2028, companies wanting to continue shipping LNG from Australia’s eastern seaboard will be forced to set aside up to 20 per cent of their annual export volumes for local use only. The policy is designed to deliberately flood the domestic market with about 10 per cent more gas than it needs each year, with the aim of easing supply pressures and putting downward pressure on the cost of the fuel, which remains widely used in heating, cooking, electricity generation and manufacturing. King is expected to outline the government’s final changes to the policy in a speech to the National Press Club on Wednesday. The changes are intended to close potential “loopholes … making it harder to game the scheme”, she said.



The new rules seek to address a long-standing grievance: that Australia, despite its vast gas resources, has allowed an LNG export boom to leave households and businesses more exposed to tightening gas supplies and soaring prices at home. Related Article Energy The Iran war is making Australia’s gas industry richer “This is a landmark moment for our country – one of the Albanese government’s most significant structural economic reforms,” King will say on Wednesday, according to a draft copy of her speech. “It is Australia’s first national gas-reservation scheme, securing the Australian gas Australian homes and Australian businesses need at fair prices.” Western Australia has long required its LNG exporters to keep 15 per cent of their production at home. Queensland’s export industry, by contrast, was established a decade ago without such rules. The new national scheme will have the biggest impact on the joint ventures that run the three giant LNG export terminals on Queensland’s Curtis Island, operated by Shell, Origin Energy and Santos.



For gas-connected homes and businesses across the southern states, the stakes of the policy are particularly high. Energy authorities warn that unless new gas supplies are made available, Victoria and NSW could face gas supplies running dangerously low by the end of the decade as production from ageing oil and gas fields in the Bass Strait rapidly declines. The looming shortfall threat highlights a deepening challenge for Australian governments, which are having to balance goals to reduce emissions released from burning fossil fuels with the need to shore up supplies for those who still depend on them. Federal Resources Minister Madeleine King. Alex Ellinghausen Households are increasingly switching from gas appliances to electric alternatives, which is having a positive impact improving gas availability: residential gas demand has fallen 16 per cent in Australia since 2020, according to figures from the Grattan Institute. But the Australian Energy Market Operator warns that shift is not happening fast enough to remove the urgent need to boost gas supplies as output from the Bass Strait dwindles.



For gas-intensive manufacturing businesses, the reservation marks a long-awaited intervention. Industry leaders have rallied behind the policy, arguing the domestic gas market is “broken” following a three-fold surge in gas prices over the past decade. Unless cheaper fuel is made available on longer-term contracts, they say, more Australian factories that depend on gas to fire their kilns and furnaces or as a raw material in their manufacturing processes would be forced to close. Representatives for plastics and chemicals manufacturers said the legislation would “inject confidence and certainty” into a sector that has watched jobs move offshore for years. “A functioning domestic gas reservation scheme can underpin our sector which produces many of the industrial products other manufacturers, businesses and consumers rely on,” said Matthew Flugge, chief executive of industry body Chemicals Australia. “It’s only 20 per cent of Australia’s east coast gas production, but it will make a massive positive impact for the Australian economy - and there is still 80 per cent of gas production available for export.” Australian steel giant BlueScope, which uses gas in its steel mills, has also supported key elements of the plan. When the government released a draft of the legislation last month, BlueScope chief Tania Archibald said it retained many of the design features manufacturers had been fighting for. “It keeps the gas companies honest,” she said.



The government has sought to balance domestic gas supply pressures with the interests of Australia’s multibillion-dollar gas industry and the nation’s major overseas trading partners, including Japan, South Korea, Malaysia and China, which are major consumers of locally produced LNG. Following consultations in Australia and overseas, the government has agreed to certain concessions to keep the domestic surplus “modest” while reassuring Asian customers that their long-term contracts will be honoured. Related Article Exclusive

Energy Labor sends emergency delegation to defuse Asian gas alarm Among the recently announced changes is the possibility of lowering the reservation level when forecast domestic demand is weak, while also giving ministers the discretion to reduce how much gas each producer must supply the local market when they are constrained by pre-existing contracts and pipeline capacity. The national energy regulator would set the overall reservation volume annually, based on a rolling five-year demand forecast, plus an extra 10 per cent buffer. Still, the Australian oil and gas sector remains deeply concerned about the policy’s design and its potential consequences. Australian Energy Producers, an industry group, warns the proposed 110 per cent oversupply of the east-coast gas market would threaten to “destroy investment signals and crowd out smaller, domestic-focused producers”.



Cecile Wake, chair of Shell Australia, operator one of Queensland’s three LNG terminals, told an Australian Financial Review energy conference on Tuesday that the government’s proposed policy was a “blunt instrument” that could force prices “below the long-run marginal cost of bringing on new production”. Pope Leo XIV arriving at the Agostino Gemelli Polyclinic in Rome on Tuesday AP Photo/Alessandra Tarantino Leo, 71, was in the operating room for about three hours and underwent surgery for about 90 minutes, the Vatican said in a statement on Tuesday night (about 7am on Wednesday, AEST). “The surgery was successful, and there were no complications,” the statement said.



“Following the operation, the Pope awoke normally and, after a brief period of observation, returned to his room on the 10th floor.” Leo had walked into the Gemelli hospital in Rome through the main entrance earlier in the day and waved to dozens of well-wishers who had gathered to greet him. The Vatican said the surgery would be performed by a team led by Gemelli’s chief thoracic surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora. The Gemelli Hospital in Rome. Getty Images The doctors said their examination confirmed the diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma. “To ensure a radical resection, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique,” the Vatican said.



News service AFP reported that a Vatican source said further tests were being carried out to determine if the cancer had spread. The Lung Cancer Foundation of America describes lung adenocarcinoma as one of the most common forms of lung cancer, accounting for about 40 per cent of all lung cancers in the US. Loading “Whatever the stage and whatever the treatment, more people are living with this disease than ever before,” it says. Treatments include surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation, it says. Oncologists said before the operation that even if the nodule turned out to be cancerous, Leo’s prognosis was “excellent” because it would have been removed at an early stage, the Associated Press reported.



The Vatican on Monday cancelled all Leo’s audiences until at least October 20. He held a general audience in St Peter’s Square last Wednesday when he thanked pilgrims including visitors from Australia. Related Article Analysis

Catholic church From AI to war, Pope wields the Vatican’s soft power amid growing distrust of political leaders Leo revealed the concerns about his medical condition in a statement on social media shortly before he was due to go to hospital. “Dear friends, during some recent medical examinations, the doctors found a small, localised nodule in my lung,” he posted on X on Sunday in Rome (midnight that night, AEST). “It was detected at a very early stage and is well-localised. The doctors believe that it is best to intervene, so, following their advice, I have decided to undergo surgery to remove it. The operation is already scheduled to take place in the coming days.



“I thank you for your spiritual closeness and entrust myself to your prayers.” Related Article Updated

Catholic church Albanese invites Pope Leo XIV to visit Australia in private meeting at the Vatican The Gemelli hospital has a papal apartment that past popes have used, complete with a private chapel on the 10th floor, but Leo is staying in a nearby room since the papal apartment is currently undergoing renovations, according to the Vatican press office. Vatican News said that following the operation on Tuesday, Leo was served dinner in his room and spent the evening in the company of his secretaries and other Vatican staff. The Pope is due to travel to Latin America in early November for a major visit to several countries including Peru, where he spent a decade working with local communities during his time in the Augustine order.



The Vatican estimated that about 800,000 people attended a mass with Leo in Paris in late September during his visit to France, drawing bigger crowds than some expected. The Catholic Church in Australia is working on plans for Leo to visit Australia in 2028, and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese formally invited the Pope to visit when they spoke in Rome in May last year. The Vatican is yet to announce a visit. Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican’s Secretary of State, described Leo as showing “great composure” on Monday evening ahead of the operation the next day. “We are confident, but, of course, we accompany him with our prayers,” Parolin told reporters on Monday, the ANSA news service reported. “Am I worried? Yes, because I certainly didn’t expect something like this.”



Parolin said he was thankful the lung nodule was detected straight away. With AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slide, Wall Street mixed Stan Choe Updated October 14, 2026 — 8:26am ,first published 5:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The first big batch of summertime profit reports from US companies made waves on Wall Street after topping analysts’ expectations, but many cancelled each other out. That left US stock indexes little changed near their records on Tuesday. The S&P 500 edged down by less than 0.1 per cent and pulled a bit further from its all-time high set last week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 180 points, or 0.3 per cent, while the Nasdaq composite dipped 0.2 per cent. Wall Street’s modest moves masked some big swings happening underneath the market’s surface. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to retreat, with futures pointing to a fall of 30 points, or 0.3 per cent, at the open. The Australian dollar was trading at US69.85¢. The modest Wall Street moves masked some big swings happening underneath the market’s surface.



Goldman Sachs, for example, jumped more than 4 per cent at the start of trading after the bank delivered a profit for July through September that blew past analysts’ expectations. But its stock quickly erased all of it and then flipped between gains and losses before finishing with a dip of 0.2 per cent. Related Article Opinion

Inflation Don’t blame Ukraine: Prices go up and up, thanks to Trump’s wars Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The firm benefited in the summer from strong growth for its business that offers loans to clients for trading stocks, among other things, even as chief executive David Solomon said it’s dealing with a “complicated operating environment” created by lots of uncertainty. Expectations are high for profits across all kinds of US companies. Analysts are forecasting overall growth of nearly 30 per cent for companies in the S&P 500 during the summer from a year earlier, according to FactSet. If they’re correct, it would be the third straight quarter of growth better than 25 per cent. And companies need to hit those high numbers to justify the record-setting runs for their stock prices despite the many worries on Wall Street about high inflation, increased pressure from the bond market and the war with Iran.



UnitedHealth Group’s stock swung sharply even though it reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. The healthcare company also raised its forecast for profit over the full year of 2026. After rallying as much as 5.6 per cent shortly after trading began, it erased all of it and finished with a dip of 0.2 per cent. More firmly in the losing column was Wells Fargo, whose stock dropped 3.1 per cent after the bank reported weaker revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, even though its profit topped Wall Street’s estimates. CEO Charlie Scharf cited weaker revenue from its venture capital investments, among other things. But Scharf also gave a potentially encouraging signal about the broader economy and future profits for companies across industries. He said that “our data shows that our consumer and business customers are doing well.” That’s despite uncertainty about the economy and recent surveys showing Americans have become more discouraged about their finances. At the country’s biggest bank, JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon highlighted “elevated asset prices” as one of the potential risks for the economy. He also mentioned high inflation, rising interest rates and “geopolitical conditions.”



“These forces may be manageable, but we remain prepared for a wide range of outcomes,” he said. JPMorgan Chase’s stock flipped between gains and losses through the day before finishing with a drop of 0.9 per cent. It reported a weaker profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected, but it also gave a forecast for net interest income in the current quarter that topped Wall Street’s estimate. Outside of earnings reports, some of the sharpest action was for stocks in the computer chip industry. Worries have been high for a while about whether chip stock prices have shot too high in the frenzy around artificial-intelligence technology, and concerns climbed further following reports that China’s memory chipmaker CXMT is making advances that could challenge industry heavyweights. That includes companies like Micron Technology of Boise, Idaho, and Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix of South Korea. Micron fell 3.6 per cent and was the single heaviest weight on the S&P 500. South Korea’s Kospi stock index tumbled 5.5 per cent for its worst day in nearly two months.



Bumble, meanwhile, leaped 56.6 per cent after the app company that helps people make relationships said it agreed to a $US1.3 billion ($1.9 billion), all-cash buyout by Ithaca Holdings. Related Article Intellectual property Can Adidas really own stripes – and did White Fox copy them? All told, the S&P 500 edged down by 1.79 points to 7,805.45. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 180.45 to 51,670.10, and the Nasdaq composite fell 41.52 to 27,204.38. In the bond market, Treasury yields eased after oil prices fell. The yield on the 10-year Treasury slipped to 5.21 per cent from 5.24 per cent late Friday. Trading in the US bond market was closed Monday for a holiday. Yields sank following a 0.9 per cent dip for the price of a barrel of Brent crude oil to $US105.69. Oil prices have been yo-yoing because of uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global energy industry to return to normal.

Actor Selma Blair has been reportedly released on bail after pleading not guilty to two assaults following an alleged violent incident aboard a flight to New York while she was in “a state of severe confusion and disorientation” after missing “powerful” medication. The Cruel Intentions star, 54, had allegedly become physically abusive and injured two Delta flight attendants on Sunday (Monday AEDT). During the flight from Los Angeles to New York, Blair was restrained after allegedly punched one flight attendant midair, biting another and attempting to open the aircraft door during the flight, according to the Hollywood Reporter. Selma Blair has been released on bail. Pictured leaving court on Monday after her arraignment on charges of injuring two flight attendants during a cross-country flight. AP Photo/Ryan Murphy After landing, the Legally Blonde actor allegedly kicked a police officer taking her to hospital for an evaluation and later allegedly kicked a nurse once she got there. On Monday (Tuesday AEDT), Blair pleaded not guilty in a New York court to two assault charges relating to the officer and the nurse, according to the Associated Press. She also faces separate federal charges from the FBI, which investigates alleged assaults aboard aircraft.



Loading Charging documents state while a police officer was securing Blair to a stretcher en route to the hospital, the actor pulled a leg from the straps and allegedly kicked her repeatedly around the face, neck and chest, causing serious pain and substantial swelling. A nurse moving Blair also alleged she was kicked in the chest, causing substantial pain. Blair was arraigned on two counts of second-degree assault and her lawyer entered a not guilty plea on her behalf. According to the Associated Press, the actor appeared to cry as she stood in court in handcuffs, wearing jeans and a white hooded sweatshirt. Lawyer Shawn Barnes told the court that “this was not an intentional assault,” according to the New York Post. He said the actor, who has multiple sclerosis, “missed several doses of … a powerful medication that controls severe neurological symptoms”.



Actress Selma Blair, pictured last month, has been charged following an in-flight incident in which two flight attendants were injured. AP “Blair boarded this flight after being on set and working extensive hours and exhaustive hours in the days leading up to this flight,” Barnes said. “Additionally, at one point, during the flight, there was an incident where Miss Blair actually fell and hit her head. “These factors, coupled with the altitude, resulted in a state of severe confusion and disorientation.” The judge set her bail at $US20,000 cash ($28,600) or $US60,000 bond and set the next hearing for January. In audio recorded by a witness and obtained by TMZ, Blair can allegedly be heard screaming as she exited the plane in New York. In a separate dispatch audio also obtained by TMZ, officials can be heard requesting medical personnel at the gate after reports of minor injuries, including a bloody nose and bite marks.



Delta told the Hollywood Reporter it had “zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behaviour, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first”. With AP

World.content:

A 19-year-old man has been charged with the murder of a 12-year-old boy who was shot in the face inside an apartment in Sydney’s north-west last month. Isaac Bechara was 18 when he allegedly killed the boy in the Moda apartment complex in Norwest on September 21, in what detectives believe was an accidental gunshot delivering fatal wounds to the 12-year-old’s face and neck. Tactical and general duties officers rushed to the Norwest apartment complex on September 21. Wolter Peeters Bechara was charged with murder at Silverwater Prison on Tuesday, having been in custody since being charged with concealing a serious indictable offence in the aftermath of the shooting. Police believe 10 people were in the apartment at the time of the shooting, including the boy’s mother and several 18-year-old men, some of whom fled after the boy was shot. The murder weapon was removed from the scene before responders arrived, and still hasn’t been found.



Detectives laid the murder charge after working through several accounts of events from the boy’s family and responders to the scene. Two other 18-year-olds present at the apartment were arrested with Bechara following the shooting, where they faced police questioning before being released without charge. Investigators believe the boy, who cannot be legally identified, may have been one of several people handling an illegal gun when it discharged inside an apartment in the Moda complex in Norwest. The boy died three days after he was rushed to The Children’s Hospital at Westmead suffering wounds to his face and neck. The boy’s father, who is a convicted cocaine dealer, was among the family members who paid tribute to the boy after his life support was switched off. “RIP my baby,” he wrote alongside a photo of the pair. Other members of the boy’s extended family are linked to organised crime and known to police. The boy’s father paid tribute to his son on social media. Instagram



The boy’s family has co-operated with police. However, none of the other occupants inside the apartment have co-operated with investigators, who as a result have been unable to establish how the boy was shot. Related Article Crime Alleged Coconut Cartel gang member arrested after boy, 11, fatally shot in face Bechara will appear in bail court on Wednesday following his latest charge. Police haven’t ruled out further arrests as they continue to investigate the circumstances leading to the boy’s death. The murder charge comes one week after Reece Fakr, an alleged key player for the high-profile Coconut Cartel, was arrested at Sydney International Airport as he attempted to leave the country. Fakr, 18, allegedly left a phone at the Norwest apartment, on which detectives found evidence of alleged criminal offences. He has been charged with 10 offences, including conspiracy to murder, kidnapping, arson and directing a criminal group.



Fakr isn’t related to the child. He remains behind bars ahead of his next court appearance on December 8. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Tupac Shakur’s killer has been sentenced and is ‘guaranteed to die behind bars’
World.content:
CultureMusicPop music Tupac Shakur’s killer has been sentenced and is ‘guaranteed to die behind bars’ Jessica Hill October 14, 2026 — 7:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Las Vegas: Duane “Keffe D” Davis was sentenced Tuesday to 40 years to life in prison for orchestrating the murder of rap icon Tupac Shakur, who was gunned down off the Las Vegas Strip over 30 years ago. Davis, 63, was convicted in August of first-degree murder with the use of a deadly weapon. He is the only person ever charged in the death of Shakur, whose popularity was peaking at age 25. More than 30 years after his death the man accused of orchestrating the killing of Tupac Shakur has been sentenced. nna\sswain Prosecutor Marc DiGiacomo said Tuesday that whatever sentence the court imposes, Davis is “guaranteed to die” behind bars. “It’s not just about losing a family member,” DiGiacomo said as Shakur’s sister Sekyiwa “Set” Shakur nodded her head in the audience.



The killing went unsolved for years until Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips, gave interviews and published his role in the shooting in his 2019 tell-all memoir. DiGiacomo said Davis was trying to profit off a killing that he committed and for that, he did not deserve the minimum sentence. Duane Davis, centre, is escorted by police from a sentencing hearing after his murder conviction in the death of rapper Tupac Shakur. John Locher/Pool AP via AP “In my mind, he deserves the maximum possible sentence,” DiGiacomo said. Davis spoke briefly in court, telling Judge Carli Kierny he wanted items back that police took from his house, including his pictures. Asked if there was anything else he wanted to say, Davis said: “No I’m good.”



Davis’ lawyer, Michael Sanft said he planned to appeal the verdict. Sanft said prosecutors waited too long to bring the case. How the shooting occurred On the night of September 7, 1996, Shakur was in the passenger seat of a black BMW with music mogul Marion “Suge” Knight when a white Cadillac pulled up at a red light, and shots erupted. Shakur was shot multiple times and died six days later, while Knight survived. Tupac in 1994. Shakur is considered one of the most influential and versatile rappers of all time and had a burgeoning film career as an actor at the time of his death. His legend has only grown since. His songs still resonate among fans with themes of hardship, love and Black struggles.



In his memoir, Davis explained how Shakur and his entourage beat up Davis’ nephew hours before the shooting in Las Vegas. He said he sought retaliation, and that he was in the passenger seat of the Cadillac and passed the gun to the backseat, where shots were fired. Davis had spoken to detectives years before but avoided prosecution because of an agreement he made with law enforcement. During the weeks-long trial, prosecutors relied on Davis’ own statements to law enforcement and documentarians. They argued that Davis orchestrated the shooting and provided the gun used in Shakur’s death, which was the result of a rivalry between the South Side Compton Crips and Mob Piru. Duane Davis, right, with his attorney Michael Sanft during the sentencing hearing. John Locher/Pool AP via AP Davis’ defence attorney pointed to a lack of physical evidence that connected his client to the 30-year-old crime, and he portrayed Davis as a liar who was trying to make money. After nine days of hearing testimony in August, the jury deliberated for three hours before returning a guilty verdict.



Related Article Courts After 30 years, the man accused of orchestrating Tupac’s murder is on trial. Here’s what to know Shakur was an icon, a brother Shakur’s family spoke at the sentencing, including his siblings Maurice “Mopreme” Shakur and Sekyiwa “Set” Shakur. Following the verdict, prosecutor Binu Palal said that to many people, Shakur was an icon or an idea, “but to the family, Tupac Shakur was a brother, a son, a cousin, a loved person ripped from them 30 years ago.” Palal said the family had to sit through years of Davis “bragging about killing someone they loved”.



“They loved that man. And the arrogance that Mr Davis had in expressing his joy in killing that man ultimately was his undoing,” Palal said. Prosecutors said they had insufficient evidence to charge anyone else. Tupac’s sibling Sekyiwa “Set” Shakur, centre, the sentencing hearing. John Locher/Pool AP via AP Davis was the only person to be charged and convicted in the killing of Shakur. The three other people who allegedly were in the Cadillac — including Davis’ nephew Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson, who Davis said was the one who pulled the trigger — have died. Clark County District Attorney Steve Wolfson has said his office didn’t believe it had sufficient evidence to charge anyone else.



“But like any other case, if we come into more information, more evidence, we can always consider filing additional charges,” he said following the guilty verdict. “But today, we don’t believe that’s the appropriate move to make.” AP Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Gas exporters to be forced to prevent Australian shortfalls under new laws
World.content:
BusinessConsumer affairsEnergy Gas exporters to be forced to prevent Australian shortfalls under new laws Nick Toscano October 14, 2026 — 7:08am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Large Australian gas producers will be forced to hold back up to 20 per cent of their export volumes for local customers for the first time, as the Albanese government presses ahead with a policy aimed at easing domestic energy prices despite industry warnings it could stunt investment. Federal Resources Minister Madeleine King is expected to bring Labor’s long-awaited domestic gas-reservation bill to parliament on Wednesday after months of talks with major gas corporations, customers in the energy-intensive manufacturing sector, and some of the nation’s biggest liquefied natural gas (LNG) buyers in Asia. Most of Australia’s LNG is produced in Queensland or Western Australia, and is sold on long-term contracts to Asia. Under the proposed scheme, starting from January 2028, companies wanting to continue shipping LNG from Australia’s eastern seaboard will be forced to set aside up to 20 per cent of their annual export volumes for local use only. The policy is designed to deliberately flood the domestic market with about 10 per cent more gas than it needs each year, with the aim of easing supply pressures and putting downward pressure on the cost of the fuel, which remains widely used in heating, cooking, electricity generation and manufacturing. King is expected to outline the government’s final changes to the policy in a speech to the National Press Club on Wednesday. The changes are intended to close potential “loopholes … making it harder to game the scheme”, she said.



The new rules seek to address a long-standing grievance: that Australia, despite its vast gas resources, has allowed an LNG export boom to leave households and businesses more exposed to tightening gas supplies and soaring prices at home. Related Article Energy The Iran war is making Australia’s gas industry richer “This is a landmark moment for our country – one of the Albanese government’s most significant structural economic reforms,” King will say on Wednesday, according to a draft copy of her speech. “It is Australia’s first national gas-reservation scheme, securing the Australian gas Australian homes and Australian businesses need at fair prices.” Western Australia has long required its LNG exporters to keep 15 per cent of their production at home. Queensland’s export industry, by contrast, was established a decade ago without such rules. The new national scheme will have the biggest impact on the joint ventures that run the three giant LNG export terminals on Queensland’s Curtis Island, operated by Shell, Origin Energy and Santos.



For gas-connected homes and businesses across the southern states, the stakes of the policy are particularly high. Energy authorities warn that unless new gas supplies are made available, Victoria and NSW could face gas supplies running dangerously low by the end of the decade as production from ageing oil and gas fields in the Bass Strait rapidly declines. The looming shortfall threat highlights a deepening challenge for Australian governments, which are having to balance goals to reduce emissions released from burning fossil fuels with the need to shore up supplies for those who still depend on them. Federal Resources Minister Madeleine King. Alex Ellinghausen Households are increasingly switching from gas appliances to electric alternatives, which is having a positive impact improving gas availability: residential gas demand has fallen 16 per cent in Australia since 2020, according to figures from the Grattan Institute. But the Australian Energy Market Operator warns that shift is not happening fast enough to remove the urgent need to boost gas supplies as output from the Bass Strait dwindles.



For gas-intensive manufacturing businesses, the reservation marks a long-awaited intervention. Industry leaders have rallied behind the policy, arguing the domestic gas market is “broken” following a three-fold surge in gas prices over the past decade. Unless cheaper fuel is made available on longer-term contracts, they say, more Australian factories that depend on gas to fire their kilns and furnaces or as a raw material in their manufacturing processes would be forced to close. Representatives for plastics and chemicals manufacturers said the legislation would “inject confidence and certainty” into a sector that has watched jobs move offshore for years. “A functioning domestic gas reservation scheme can underpin our sector which produces many of the industrial products other manufacturers, businesses and consumers rely on,” said Matthew Flugge, chief executive of industry body Chemicals Australia. “It’s only 20 per cent of Australia’s east coast gas production, but it will make a massive positive impact for the Australian economy - and there is still 80 per cent of gas production available for export.” Australian steel giant BlueScope, which uses gas in its steel mills, has also supported key elements of the plan. When the government released a draft of the legislation last month, BlueScope chief Tania Archibald said it retained many of the design features manufacturers had been fighting for. “It keeps the gas companies honest,” she said.



The government has sought to balance domestic gas supply pressures with the interests of Australia’s multibillion-dollar gas industry and the nation’s major overseas trading partners, including Japan, South Korea, Malaysia and China, which are major consumers of locally produced LNG. Following consultations in Australia and overseas, the government has agreed to certain concessions to keep the domestic surplus “modest” while reassuring Asian customers that their long-term contracts will be honoured. Related Article Exclusive

Energy Labor sends emergency delegation to defuse Asian gas alarm Among the recently announced changes is the possibility of lowering the reservation level when forecast domestic demand is weak, while also giving ministers the discretion to reduce how much gas each producer must supply the local market when they are constrained by pre-existing contracts and pipeline capacity. The national energy regulator would set the overall reservation volume annually, based on a rolling five-year demand forecast, plus an extra 10 per cent buffer. Still, the Australian oil and gas sector remains deeply concerned about the policy’s design and its potential consequences. Australian Energy Producers, an industry group, warns the proposed 110 per cent oversupply of the east-coast gas market would threaten to “destroy investment signals and crowd out smaller, domestic-focused producers”.



Cecile Wake, chair of Shell Australia, operator one of Queensland’s three LNG terminals, told an Australian Financial Review energy conference on Tuesday that the government’s proposed policy was a “blunt instrument” that could force prices “below the long-run marginal cost of bringing on new production”. World.title: US learned 'absolutely nothing' from post-9/11 wars - Peter Bergen
World.content:
America has learned "absolutely nothing" from its wars with Afghanistan and Iraq, and now, its war with Iran could drag on for another two years, CNN security analyst Peter Bergen says.

"We're in this stalemate, with no resolution in sight," Bergen told Midday Report's Guyon Espiner.

He said he did not expect any change to the state of the war until after the US midterm elections on 3 November.

"Then who the hell knows, because Trump changes his mind on a dime very quickly. One day he's saying, 'we've got a great deal with the Iranians'. The next day 'we're going to bomb them back into the Stone Age'.

"It's very hard to negotiate with somebody like that," Bergen said.

He described the conflict as a "mutually hurting stalemate", but said the two sides were not taking the steps needed to reach a peace agreement.

"This could go on for another two years, I think. While Trump is in office, he doesn't seem to be in the mood for compromise. The Iranians also, right now they're very far apart."

Peter Bergen and New Zealand journalist Peter Arnett conducted the first-ever televised interview with Osama bin Laden for CNN in 1997.

Smoke rises following missile strikes in Tehran on 1 March 2026. AFP / Atta Kenare

Bergen's new book, All the Presidents' Wars, assesses the key decisions made by four presidents - George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Joe Biden and Donald Trump - in the US response to the September 11 attacks.

US response to 9/11 'got a lot of things wrong'

He said the US military response to 9/11 in Afghanistan and Iraq did achieve its goal of preventing a major foreign terrorist attack on the United States, but it came at a cost.

"There were 200,000 Iraqi civilians killed, 45,000 Afghan civilians killed, 66,000 Afghan police and military killed, $6 trillion of American taxpayer dollars, 7,000 American service members, and then, of course, our allies as well.

"And we got a lot of things wrong. The Iraq war, of course, being the principal exhibit.

"But also the botched Afghan withdrawal in 2021, and now the stalemated war in Iran.

"So we see that the post-9/11 conflicts have a very long tail."

Bergen told Midday Report the September 11 attacks by Al-Qaeda were not a result of an intelligence failure in the US, but a policy failure.

He said the Bush administration had plenty of strategic warning from the CIA that something big was coming from Al-Qaeda, but didn't absorb the advice.

A man walks through the rubble after the collapse of the first World Trade Center tower, 11 September 2001, New York. AFP / Doug Kanter

"They were veterans of the Cold War and they couldn't conceive of a non-state actor like Al-Qaeda and Bin Laden being a significant threat, even though they'd already blown up two US embassies in Africa in 1998 and almost sunk a US destroyer in 2000 in Yemen. They just didn't register this as a problem."

Bergen said the failure to capture Osama bin Laden at the Battle of Tora Bora in Afghanistan in 2001 was a monumental blunder.

"The CIA had plenty of information that bin Laden was at the Battle of Tora Bora. They requested additional American boots on the ground.

"By my calculation, there were more international journalists at the Battle of Tora Bora than American soldiers, which kind of speaks for itself."

He said a CIA request for a battalion of about 800 US Army Rangers was turned down, allowing bin Laden and other senior Al-Qaeda figures to escape.

"I think we wouldn't be having this conversation in the same way if bin Laden and many of his top leaders had been captured," Bergen told Midday Report.

World.title: NZ First wants to change fast-track regime, to save Kiwis 'suffering' through developments
World.content:
New Zealand First wants to make changes to future fast-track residential approvals, saying there needs to be the necessary roads, pipes, water, wastewater, and other essential service approvals first.

The party is campaigning on making changes to the fast-track regime, saying when it "brought the blueprint" for the regime to the government three years ago it did not envisage New Zealanders would be picking up the tab or "suffering" through developments being approved without the adequate infrastructure in place.

"The cart is being put before the horse, and we will ensure that ends," it said in a statement on Wednesday.

It said fast-track housing developers would be required to detail what infrastructure they need, and demonstrate whether it exists, is funded, and can be delivered when needed.

Dedicated expert panels for housing would also be created, given the power to decline projects if they were not satisfied the required infrastructure would be in place. The housing minister would be given responsibility for project referral decisions.

"People don't live in a world where critical infrastructure is an afterthought. They live in communities that rely on reliable roads, water, wastewater systems and transport links," New Zealand First said.

"We want a system that is faster, smarter and more practical. If we are serious about housing for New Zealanders, then we must be equally serious about the pipes, roads and services that make those developments viable."

National leader Christopher Luxon said New Zealand First's policy was "quite bizarre", as what it was announcing was already law.

"They were in the room where it happened, as Hamilton would say, and I'm not quite sure what they're banging on about today, because that is not quite right."

Luxon said fast-track panels were already applying "quite serious" conditions on infrastructure development, including building other enabling infrastructure.

"They've caught up, that's good."

Chris Bishop had recently changed the law so councils could charge development contributions.

"They've literally released a press release that says they will change the law to do things that are already in the law," Bishop said.

World.title: 'No sense': Outrage over government order to limit nurse enrolments
World.content:
Nurse educators say a government directive to limit nurse enrolments makes "no sense" as pressure builds on the workforce.

The Tertiary Education Commission wrote to educators in early October asking them to limit enrolments to 2025 levels because there was not enough room for extra student nurses to complete clinical placement.

It comes as concerns about hospital staffing grow louder and election-year battles rage on between Labour and National over how many nurses have been hired.

"Growth in nursing enrolments over the last few years has put pressure on clinical placement capacity across all Health NZ districts," TEC delivery deputy chief executive Gillian Dudgeon said.

"TEC has asked tertiary providers to manage enrolments within 2025 numbers, to ensure quality clinical placements that are safe and so learners have the best chance of completing their qualification."

Dudgeon said TEC was working with Health NZ on opportunities to increase capacity, where possible.

"Tertiary education providers may increase enrolments if they can demonstrate available clinical capacity in their district," she said.

Massey University associate professor Andrea Donaldson raised the problem with Labour leader Chris Hipkins during his visit to the Manawatū campus this week.

She said the directive to restrict enrolments made no sense given current workforce pressures and an ageing population.

"Who's going to care for them?" she said.

"Earlier in the year, the Tertiary Education Commission came in and were like, 'grow your programmes, grow your programmes, grow your programmes', and now suddenly last week [they said] 'no, no, nursing needs to cap their numbers at 2025 levels', and we're like, what? Why?"

Demand for nursing courses was high and they would now be forced to enrol considerably fewer nurses than planned, Donaldson said.

Her colleague, senior lecturer Maree Sheard, said the demand for nurses would only increase.

"So we just really need to make sure that New Zealand's ready for that, and I don't feel that some of these fiscal decisions are thinking long term," she said.

"We need to be forecasting and being really careful about gradually growing the workforce for increasing population demand. So irrespective of what we're facing now, in the immediate 2030 year, we need to be thinking about 2040 and 2050, and having a sustainable nursing pipeline."

Sheard said nurses could get placements outside Health NZ and hospitals - with Plunket, or within primary healthcare, for example - so she did not buy the argument that a squeeze on Health NZ placements should result in capped enrolments.

Tertiary Education Minister Penny Simmonds said nursing enrolments had increased significantly in recent years, reaching 11,270 enrolments in 2025.

She repeated the TEC's explanation for the limit and said it was not new for all providers: "with some providers having been asked to manage availability of clinical placements for the second consecutive year."

World.title: Cash, drugs, rifle and Taser seized in Taranaki raids, six arrested
World.content:
Police say six people have been arrested after cannabis, methamphetamine, a rifle, and a taser were found at New Plymouth properties.

The arrests were part of a three-month intensive operation into drugs and crime in Taranaki.

Acting Senior Sergeant Ben Patterson said two New Plymouth properties were searched last week.

As a result, $15,000 was seized, along with several stolen items identified from historic burglaries. Cannabis, methamphetamine, a 308 rifle, shotgun ammunition, and a homemade taser were also discovered.

The six arrested will appear in the New Plymouth District Court separately throughout October.

A 43-year-old man faces charges relating to the possession drugs, possession offensive weapons, and receiving stolen property. He will appear in New Plymouth District Court on 15 October.

A 30-year-old New Plymouth based gang member will appear in New Plymouth District Court on 20 and 22 October facing charges including unlawful possession of a weapon and ammunition, drugs charges, and receiving stolen goods.

A 27-year-old New Plymouth woman is in custody, and faces cannabis possession and supply charges as well as possession of methamphetamine and utensils. She will reappear on 29 October in New Plymouth District Court.

A further two 31-year-old men will appear in New Plymouth District Court on 14 and 15 October on unlawfully possessing offensive weapons, pistols and other firearms, as well as supplying cannabis.
