World.title: Test results show maths, reading improving
World.content:
Audio player for " Checking in on how our children are going at school " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/education/1886412%2Ftest-results-show-maths-reading-improving

Checking in on how our children are going at school Morning Report Download MP3 5m

Analysis of more than 3 million maths and reading tests shows sharp improvement in primary school children's maths and vocabulary skills, but their understanding of what they read is in a serious dip.

The New Zealand Council for Educational Research study of results from 15 years of its widely-used Progressive Achievement Tests (PATs) shows children in Years 4-8 are now better at reading words than any point in that period.

Meanwhile, children's maths improved markedly in the past two years and their reading comprehension improved this year.

Education Minister Erica Stanford told RNZ the figures were proof the government's reforms were working.

However, the report by researcher David Coblentz said the improvements in maths and reading vocabulary began before the government's changes started.

The study found average maths scores began to drop in 2019, reaching a low in 2022 before starting to improve.

A graph showing the PAT mathematics overall national trend with refreshed segment visually aligned. Supplied / New Zealand Council for Educational Research

The tests changed in 2024 so could not be directly compared to earlier years but results continued to improve to the point where in term 1 this year they were a third-of-a-year's learning better than at the start of 2024.

Reading vocabulary scores hovered around a baseline set in 2012 before starting to increase in 2021.

That improvement acclerated in the past year reaching a high at the start of this year equivalent to one-fifth of a year's learning better than the baseline set in 2012.

Reading comprehension scores began dropping in 2015, reaching a low point in 2024 that was about a quarter of a year's learning below the 2012 baseline.

The comprehension tests were changed in 2025 and this year's result was better than last year's.

A graph showing the PAT reading comprehension overall national trend with refreshed segment visually aligned. Supplied / New Zealand Council for Educational Research

The report said the figures covered more than half the children who had attended primary schools since 2012 and did not show achievement moving uniformly towards decline or recovery.

"Reading Comprehension declined substantially... and remains a concern despite the positive first refreshed movement. Mathematics has rebounded broadly, but that improvement has not yet proved durable. Reading Vocabulary has risen, though not equally for all learners," it said.

"The next few years will show whether the most recent gains foreshadow lasting increases in assessment scores."

The report said the results did not show why students' scores had changed, but it advanced some possible influences.

They included an increase in online testing affecting reading comprehension scores, Covid affecting maths and reading comprehension, and improved attendance helping maths scores.

"A broad change in engagement, attendance, access to learning, assessment behaviour, digital activity, or experiences in and outside school could have affected all three assessments while interacting with subject-specific teaching and learning in different ways," the report said.

David Coblentz told RNZ his personal view was that digital devices might be behind the changes in reading scores.

"There's a spike in reading vocabulary gains right around the time kids get cell phones. So, part of the story could be a technology story," he said.

"It could be that in recent years, the way kids consume media has not been great for their ability to derive information from longer texts. But nonetheless, it's been just fine or even a little better at some ages for the acquisition, the overall acquisition of vocabulary."

A graph showing the PAT reading vocabulary overall national trend. Supplied / New Zealand Council for Educational Research

Coblentz said the maths improvements were driven more by better scores among Year 4 students rather than by improvements in older students' scores.

"Kids that are just coming into the testing window now are kids that have gone through their early years of school in an environment in which attendance has been more regular and in an environment that has been not disrupted Covid, which has not been the case for other cohorts of kids in recent years," he said.

"It's also possible, and I'm speculating here, that the hour a day of mathematics in particular might have disproportionately affected kids who were very young."

Coblentz said the study revealed unexpected changes in gender differences.

New Zealand Council for Educational Research researcher David Coblentz. Supplied / New Zealand Council for Educational Research

"In mathematics, the long story since as long as we've been testing is that male students tend to do a little bit better in mathematics in primary school. That's become more true, the recent improvements have helped everybody but they've disproportionately helped boys a bit more than girls," he said.

"In reading comprehension, the story has been one of decline, but girls have declined more than boys. Girls started ahead of boys and are still ahead of boys. Those two lines have gotten closer due to greater attrition over time among girls.

"And in reading vocabulary, the recent gains have primarily been gains among boys, whereas the girls' scores have basically been static."

Minister claims gains

Education Minister Erica Stanford told RNZ the government's reforms and teachers' implementation of those reforms were behind the improvements.

"The uptick you see just prior to our government was just children coming back to school ... You can see how it just pops back up to where we were pre-Covid," she said.

"The acceleration off the baseline has been the thing that our government has done."

She said that was down to the work of teachers.

"Teachers should feel incredibly proud and principals that this is because of them. They are the ones who picked up the curriculum, they implemented it in their classrooms, they did the PLD, they used the resources and these are the outcomes," she said.

"I can make all of the policy decisions I like and resource everything I like, but unless teachers and principals are implementing with fidelity on the ground, nothing will change."

Stanford said the improved reading comprehension scores this year were a direct result of structured literacy and the mandated approach to teaching children to read and write.

"Children can now lift words off the page. It is very hard to comprehend a word you cannot read," she said.

"Structured literacy is ensuring that children can decode words with confidence and lift the word off the page before they can start to comprehend it."

Education Minister Erica Stanford. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Asked if schools could sustain the improvements at the same time as introducing new curriculums, Stanford said the government would continue to support better teaching of maths and reading.

"It is a long-term implementation and we will continue to put in resource into literacy and numeracy," she said.

"This is years and years and years of supports and resources to the front line to make sure that we are locking in these gains."

The Education Ministry said the results reflected work happening across the education system to lift achievement.

"The report highlights a range of possible factors, including improved attendance, schools' ongoing efforts to support learning following Covid-19 disruption, and targeted support for students who need extra help," it said.

Teacher union the Educational Institute Te Riu Roa said it was too soon to claim improvements.

"True progress requires longitudinal data tracking the same cohort over time," it said.

"We will celebrate when we see sustained, long-term improvements in reading comprehension and writing across all ages."

The institute said the results showed persistent gaps between ethnic groups and the government should not have cut programmes such as the Pasifika Early Literacy Project and literacy resource teachers.

The Principals' Federation said the report did not show the government's reforms had worked, but it also did not show that they had failed.

"The mathematics rebound began in 2023, before the daily hour requirement was introduced in 2024 and before the revised mathematics curriculum became compulsory in 2025," it said.

World.title: Heritage Lifecare buys NZACS to become second-largest aged-care provider
World.content:
Retirement village operator Heritage Lifecare has bought New Zealand Aged Care Services (NZACS), for an undisclosed price.

NZACS's 15 care homes, eight villages, residents, families and employees made Heritage the second-largest aged-care provider with a combined 55 care homes and 28 retirement villages across New Zealand.

"This is an important and positive step for Heritage, bringing together two organisations with complementary strengths and a shared commitment to delivering high-quality care for older New Zealanders," Heritage Lifecare CEO Brent Pattison said.

He said the expansion built on Heritage's existing strengths, bringing greater scale, capability and opportunity.

"Our experienced people, established systems and support platform mean we understand what it takes to bring new homes, villages and teams into Heritage while supporting people throughout the transition.

"Care and services will continue, and we will work closely with residents, families and employees to keep them informed and supported as we bring our communities together," he said.

NZACS managing director Peter Leathem said the businesses were a good fit.

World.title: Selection critics silenced as Australia's old guard wins first Test
World.content:
That Australia wrapped up the Durban Test in such a resounding fashion on day five was, on the one hand, a quite spectacular validation of the selection strategy that plunged an entire cricket nation into conspiracy theories and conniptions last week.

Viewed another way, it simply added weight to the confidence bordering on arrogance that Pat Cummins's world-beating bowling attack maintains that it can win any game, against any opposition, from any position, on every corner of the globe.

Though South Africa pushed the contest well into the second session, and ever-so-briefly prompted speculation of a draw, Josh Hazlewood performed a quite ruthless clean-up job with 6-49 from 16.5 overs — his 15th five-wicket haul in Tests and his career-best figures. It hastened a 214-run victory for the tourists in a game they began entirely on the back foot.

Hazlewood's bundle included an assortment of his specialities: he broke the crucial partnership of the day by removing Wiaan Mulder after 25 overs of patient accumulation in the morning session; his delivery to clean bowl Marco Jansen was almost unplayable; the snorter that soon after sent Simon Harmer packing had reared up nightmarishly from a decent length.

The savage beauty of Harmer's dismissal brought to mind a piece of sponsor content featuring Hazlewood that was floating around earlier in the week — one of those cutesy interviews where the star athlete is interviewed by a bright-eyed little kid. The interlocutor asked the burly quick for his favourite thing about being a paceman.

"Intimidating batsmen", Hazlewood replied without hesitation. Welcome into the mind of an Australian fast bowler, kid.

As far as Australia goes, quite against most predictions, almost everything went right. But it is strange to consider the way a team that continues to set the world standard was, in this instance, composed from so many moveable and removable parts: opening batsmen variously underprepared and out of position, a number three on a very unpopular final chance, a four on borrowed time, a five who normally opens, a six who should be at seven and a seven who had recently been, well, at sixes and sevens.

Matt Renshaw (left) was player of the match for his 272 runs and two wickets. (AP Photo: Themba Hadebe)

Outside the Durban formation, Cameron Green, Josh Inglis, Scott Boland, Cooper Connolly and Michael Neser would not feel presumptuous mentally slotting themselves into a plausible XI.

Nathan Lyon, meanwhile, was less threatening in the second innings than spin dabblers Matt Renshaw, Beau Webster and Nic Maddinson, although it was not in the end a memorable game for the slow bowlers.

These are good problems for Australia to have, of course, and to get through a heavy schedule of Tests in the next 12 months, it will need to draw upon its reserves and pay particular attention to the workloads of its quicks.

In the immediate term, at the very least Australia will probably look to tinker with its batting order and switch Travis Head and Matt Renshaw, the latter of whom was the most popular man of the match in recent memory after adding a two-wicket cameo of off-spin to his batting masterclass.

How does South Africa regroup from such a comprehensive loss?

Perversely, compared to Australia, a larger percentage of its line-up is set in stone: opener Aiden Markram and number three David Bedingham were the shining lights in both innings, while skipper Temba Bavuma and gun all-rounders Wiaan Mulder and Marco Jansen are undroppable.

Anrich Nortje, the man most would have earmarked to be replaced by Kagiso Rabada for the second Test, was far and away the Proteas best bowler.

Markram was the batting standard-bearer for the Proteas on day five with another innings of tremendous substance — a lone hand of 75, which made him the only half-centurion of the game other than Renshaw.

Statistically speaking, when playing Australia Markram is twice the batsman who otherwise averages 35 in Tests. He just needs a few more mates.

The most straightforward change for the Gqeberha (formerly Port Elizabeth) Test starting on Sunday would be the demotion of wicketkeeper-batsman Kyle Verreynne, a walking wicket at present.

Given the premium on players who can shift the momentum of a game in a single session, South Africa could only gain by replacing him with 20-year-old Lhuan-dre Pretorius, a rising star of the T20 world whose five centuries in 15 first-class games include a century on Test debut last year. Stylistically, think Rishabh Pant. Physically, also think Rishabh Pant.

Most enticingly, there is also the fearsome spectre of Rabada, the only undisputed great South Africa currently possesses and a past tormentor of the Australians.

The sight of him limbering up in the nets throughout this game has been tantalising. South Africa would do well to take his lead and be more attacking with the ball from here onward.

Another unknown is whether South African fans will rally around the Proteas and make life less comfortable for the Aussies.

Australia was not met with any sort of hostile crowd in Durban. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

In Durban, spectators were a non-factor. By Cape Town, they will surely be out in greater numbers and taking up Proteas coach Conrad Shukri's pre-tour advice to "give [Australia's players] some stick, but respectfully so".

A few decades ago a South African newspaper offered a slightly less generous assessment of this dynamic, lamenting the experience of the touring Australian cricketer: "They must wonder if our game parks are fenced."

World.title: Tassie team, Chinese and WNBA imports to boost new WNBL season
World.content:
Thursday night will mark the start of the second season of the Women's National Basketball League (WNBL) under new, private ownership, with the league hoping to build on some of the gains made.

Last season, crowd figures were up 43 per cent, and broadcast reach 130 per cent, but that did not stop the league making its CEO Jennie Sager redundant, in a restructure it said would bring the men's and women's codes under one umbrella.

Sager later called the decision "genuinely disappointing", arguing that "women's sport leagues are strongest when they have dedicated leadership and a staff that wakes up every day solely focused on driving them forward".

Under the 2026/27 leadership model, retired Opals star Lauren Jackson has a key role as Chief Strategy and Basketball Partnerships Officer, and said she was buoyed by the change the consortium of owners had brought.

"Being privatised has been super important for the league in the way we are growing and going through a new phase," Jackson told ABC Sport.

"It has been a long time coming, but it's very exciting.

"I take a lot of pride in the league and feel very honoured that I get to work in it."

Lauren Jackson is a legend of Australian basketball, and is now helping oversee the WNBL. (Getty Images)

Now in its 47th edition, the WNBL is the oldest women's professional league in Australia, with Jackson saying she was passionate about giving back to domestic basketball.

"The sport has given me so much," she said.

"My legacy off the court is about getting back and building [the WNBL] to a point in Australia where it is sustainable, where it's providing young women with the opportunities that we really had to work and work hard for."

Jackson referenced the league's most recent collective bargaining agreement (CBA) as evidence of that progress, which awarded players a 104 per cent increase in minimum wages.

"The visibility piece is happening globally [and] the sport is taking off," she said.

Chinese and WNBA imports a drawcard

Aiding in its aspirations for new audiences, the first game of the WNBL season will feature new franchise the Tasmania Jewels, following the success of 2024 NBL champions the JackJumpers.

Darcee Garbin (left) will captain the Tasmania Jewels in their inaugural WNBL season. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

The Jewels will host the Geelong Venom in Hobart, led by Opal Steph Reid.

The league has also been buoyed by the signing of Chinese national team players including Shuyu Yang (Canberra Capitals) and Siyu 'Rainy' Yang (Southside Flyers), while 211-cm Han Xu will return for Geelong, having played for Perth Lynx last season.

"We want to be leaders in the Asia Pacific in particular, so being able to have Chinese representation here, and to be able to have some of the best players in the world who are competing in the WNBA, has been really, really good," Jackson said.

Former rookie of the year Jaz Shelley said she was embracing the prospect of further international competition.

"It's really exciting, it has become a global game; we have some unreal American imports and then we have the Chinese coming in, it's just so cool to have players from all different areas, and for the game to be developing," she told ABC Sport.

This season, Shelley has made the move to join coach Renee Garlepp at the Sydney Flames, whose season will launch against the Flyers.

Manuela Puoch has joined the Canberra Capitals, where she will play alongside her older sister, Nyadiew Puoch.

"She said it'll be intense, it'll be fun, she's next door to me," Manuela Puoch said.

And after after having been drafted by the New York Liberty with the 41st pick in the 2026 WNBA draft, her sights are set on the world's top league.

"[My long-term aspirations] are definitely to go to New York, and just keep developing as a player and a person," she said.

World.title: Matildas fire in second half to secure dominant 7–1 win over Haiti
World.content:
Midfielder Leticia McKenna bagged a first-half brace to bolster her case for a first 2027 Women's World Cup call-up as the Matildas overcame Haiti 7–1.

Fresh off a humbling 4–2 defeat to powerhouses Germany, and without Arsenal star Steph Catley (managed), Australia got their World Cup preparations back on track in Chambly, France.

McKenna was the spark, as she produced two classy strikes before an own goal by Haiti defender Kethna Louis on the even of the break.

Then goals from Caitlin Foord, Daniela Galić, Clare Wheeler and Holly McNamara completed the victory.

Coach Joe Montemurro flagged in his pre-match press conference that he planned to switch things up as he looked to get a clearer picture of his side before next year's global showpiece event in Brazil.

Questions loomed over captain and star striker Sam Kerr's fitness after she complained of ankle soreness following the German clash, but she was also influential, playing a big role in two of the goals.

The rousing victory helped the Matildas firmly keep their number 15 world ranking, which currently puts them in pot two out of four for the World Cup draw, meaning a mathematically better chance for a more favourable draw.

It wasn't all smooth sailing for Montemurro's players, though, as their first-half defence looked timid when their Caribbean opponents employed their counterattack.

But they utterly dominated the second half as Haiti's wheels fell off, and gave Matildas fans plenty to cheer for, including a Kerr-Foord combination goal and Wheeler and McNamara each with their fourth international goals.

Catch up on all the action through the live blog below.

World.title: Quick hits: Carey's classic starts the rot and Hoff finishes it off
World.content:
Alex Carey breaks the game open with a spectacular take, Pat Cummins confuses Beau Webster for Muttiah Muralitharan, and Josh Hazlewood's career-best wins it for Australia.

Here are the quick hits from the final day of the first Test between Australia and South Africa.

1. Smith returns to the field

The Australians were worried they might have to push to victory without the fielding brilliance of Smith. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

After not taking to the field after Pat Cummins's tea time declaration on day four, there were serious concerns that Australia would have to push for victory without the fielding brilliance of Steve Smith.

The Australia vice-captain was hit in the helmet by an Anrich Nortje bouncer while batting and was held back over fears of a delayed concussion.

But Australian fans would have been delighted to have seen Smith out on the field and warming up ahead of the final day's play, with the slipper supreme right to re-assume his role in the cordon.

Speaking on Fox Cricket, Mitch Starc said Smith appeared to have "the light back in him" and he certainly seemed to as he snared a sharp chance at first slip, his fifth of the match, to get rid Kyle Verreynne in the 67th over.

2. Carey's screamer starts the rot

Alex Carey's brilliant catch ended a troublesome Wiaan Mulder-Aiden Markram partnership. (Supplied: Fox Cricket)

Australia tried a lot of tricks to break the Aiden Markram-Wiaan Mulder partnership on the final morning of the Test at Kingsmead.

For 154 balls, near misses elicited plenty of "Ooh"s and maybe even the occasional "Aah", but little more despite some sensational bowling.

Then, in the space of four balls, everything changed.

Josh Hazlewood swung one towards the pads of Mulder, facing his 110th delivery, and it kept going down the leg side.

Mulder tried to help it on its way to fine leg as he'd done many times before, but only managed to get a faint tickle on it and that wasn't enough to evade Alex Carey.

Australia's phenomenal wicketkeeper shuffled and leapt to his left, sticking his gloved hand out and plucking the ball out of the air just centimetres off the grass.

The partnership broken, wicket-taking suddenly looked straightforward as Matt Renshaw nicked off Kyle Verreynne just three balls later to allow the Aussies to breathe a little easier.

3. Australia's shocking review

Webster would have needed to produce some serious turn for it to be a successful review. (Fox Cricket)

With six overs still remaining between lunch and the new ball, Cummins had time to kill.

The Australia captain decided that cycling through his part-time spinners would be the most efficient way to get the 80th over.

But with the pitch offering some substantial turn and the South African tail exposed, the Australian fielders were an in excitable mood.

And in the first over after the break, that excitement was channelled into one of the most questionable reviews of Cummins's captaincy career.

Beau Webster, who has never been a big spinner of the ball to start with, pitched his off break far enough from the stumps that Jansen felt comfortable kicking it away.

Webster would have had to have transformed into a prime Muttiah Muralitharan to have gotten that one back towards the pegs — and he hadn't. The DRS projected the ball to be missing by a considerable distance.

4. Hazlewood's career-best figures

Hazlewood ripped through the South African lower order. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

Jansen and Markram made it to the new ball, but things went downhill pretty quickly after Starc and Hazlewood got their hands on the fresh cherry.

Hazlewood, who had started things off with the first two wickets of the innings on day four, produced a sensational 85th over double strike to all but end the South African resistance.

First, he found some movement off the pitch to castle Jansen, then, he procured some extra bounce to have Simon Harmer caught for a three-ball duck.

Mitch Starc then got in on the act to have the brilliant Aiden Markram caught behind on review, before Hazlewood fittingly ended the Test with the dismissal of Anrich Nortje.

The Proteas had lost their final four wickets for five runs and Hazlewood had career-best figures, with his 6-49 eclipsing the 6-67 from Bengaluru in 2017.

5. Markram in his element

Aiden Markram has a habit of doing this to Australia. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

Every time Aiden Markram bats in Tests against Australia, many of us find ourselves perplexed by his Test average in the mid-30s.

But all the ingredients were there to turn him into a modern Graeme Pollock.

Markram averages over 60 against Australia, comfortably highest among any of his Test opponents. His fourth-innings average is in the mid-40s — for reference, Steve Smith's run-chase average is 31.65. And, among grounds he's played more than two Tests on, Kingsmead is his best.

Australians may remember him for his fourth-innings 143 in Durban back in 2018, but more recently for a match-winning 136 in the World Test Championship final run chase last year.

And Markram was almost chanceless as he held South Africa's innings together with a marathon 237-ball 75, before his late dismissal spelled the end for the Proteas.

World.title: Australia defeats South Africa by 214 runs on day five in Durban
World.content:
Australia has taken a 1-0 lead in the three-Test series against South Africa after a dominant 214-run victory on day five at Kingsmead.

The Proteas lost their last four wickets for just five runs to be bowled out for 206, with Josh Hazlewood finishing with career-best figures of 6-49.

Matt Renshaw was named player-of-the-match for his knocks of 190 and 82, as well as his two second-innings wickets.

His spot in the team is now assured for the foreseeable future, but with Cameron Green still to return from injury, questions will be asked about where Renshaw is best suited in the line-up and he said after the match it was "pretty nice" to settle in the middle order.

"It's a bit different to opening the batting, but happy to do whatever the team needs me to do," he said during the post-match presentation.

Renshaw's batting set up the victory but his part-time off-spin became key to winning the game in the fourth innings after a dogged 69-run partnership between Aiden Markram (75 off 237) and Wiaan Mulder (29 off 110).

It finally came to an end after 34 overs when Mulder got a feather on a Hazlewood delivery down the leg side, where wicketkeeper Alex Carey completed a phenomenal one-handed grab.

Loading Instagram content

Four balls later, Renshaw nicked off Kyle Verreynne for a duck to give Australia momentum heading into lunch.

Markram, the hero of South Africa's run chase in last year's World Test Championship final victory over Australia, continued his resistance alongside Marco Jansen (35) before Hazlewood clean bowled him with the second new ball.

Simon Harmer (0) gloved one through to Alex Carey later in the over and Markram's vigil finally ended when Australia successfully reviewed an appeal for caught behind, with DRS showing a faint inside edge.

When Anrich Nortje (4) lobbed Hazlewood to the leg side, South Africa had lost 4-5 in three overs and the match was over.

Look back on all the day five action in our live blog below, and check out all the stats in our ScoreCentre.

World.title: How NRL's Super League bid could revive a fallen giant
World.content:
As talks over the NRL's proposed investment in Super League near the pointy end of negotiations, Trent Robinson says a partnership between the two competitions could help reinvigorate the sport in France.

After guiding the Sydney Roosters to the fourth NRL premiership victory of his tenure earlier this month, Robinson would have every right to be sat somewhere in the south of France with his feet up sipping a glass of red.

But instead he finds himself offering his services to the French national team, where he supports head coach Laurent Frayssinous as director of rugby, in preparation for Friday's World Cup opener against Samoa.

On the other side of the world, club owners in England and the Super League's two French sides — Catalans Dragons and Toulouse Olympique — are weighing up an offer that would lead to the NRL providing an investment into the code's only other professional competition.

NRL's Super League investment offer Britain's Super League has revealed it has received an investment offer from the NRL, taking Australian involvement in British rugby league's premier tournament a significant step closer.

Some British clubs are reluctant to cede power to the NRL but Robinson is a firm believer in how Australia can help revive France as an international force.

"I think the NRL will have a world vision of rugby league, and I know they see the value of French rugby league and the importance of it," the Roosters coach told AAP.

"I think it would continue the progression of having a place at the table."

France was one of the sport's leading powers in the 1950s and 1960s but their stock has fallen considerably.

The presence of two French clubs in Super League, from which the majority of the national team is drawn, has so far failed to translate into international success.

France was supposed to host this year's World Cup until the government pulled the pin, citing the expense of hosting rugby union's World Cup in 2023 and the Paris 2024 Olympic and Paralympic Games.

Ranked 11th in the world, France are seen as $21 outsiders by bookmakers for their meeting with a Samoan team laden with NRL talent at Western Sydney Stadium.

Mitchell Pearce, who has retired in France after playing for Catalans, said: "There's some great French talent and they'll be enjoying the opportunity (to play in the World Cup).

Samoa plans World Cup tilt With the men's and women's Rugby League World Cup officially launched, Samoa are looking to repeat their fairytale run to the 2022 final.

"I think it'd be great for the NRL to expand and open up French rugby league and help the development pathways."

France's struggles to field a strong international side, they were hammered 62-4 by Samoa four years ago, can surely be attributed to the fact their clubs are operating in the most cash-rich market in any rugby code.

France's top rugby union competition, the Top14, has a salary cap of roughly $18 million, the NRL's is around $12 million, while the Super League's is approaching $4 million.

"There's a respect that is growing in France for rugby league from when I first went 24 years ago," Robinson said.

"It's because we've got a great sport and because of the Catalans and Toulouse.

"It's a fair mountain to climb, the Top 14, and trying to catch up with that.

"But it (league) does have respect and the NRL would add to that because there's an enormous amount of respect for it in rugby union circles."

AAP

World.title: Michael Jordan Last Dance jersey sells for record $20m
World.content:
The jersey Michael Jordan wore during Game 2 of the 1998 NBA Finals, featured in the Last Dance documentary, has sold for a record $US14 million ($20 million).

Hunt Auctions announced yesterday that the game-worn, autographed Chicago Bulls jersey was purchased by Miami real estate investor Ron Firman in a private sale.

It is the highest price ever paid for a piece of basketball memorabilia, and according to the auction house, the newly sold Jordan jersey ranks as the second-largest sale in history among game-worn sports jerseys.

The New York Yankees jersey worn by Babe Ruth in Game 3 of the 1932 World Series — during which Ruth called his shot ahead of a home run — went for $US24.12 million in 2024.

Jordan and the Bulls defeated the Utah Jazz in six games to win the 1998 championship, the sixth and final title of his career in Chicago.

Game 2, played on June 5, 1998, in Salt Lake City, saw Chicago even the series 1-1 in large part due to a dominant performance from its superstar guard.

Jordan put up 37 points, five rebounds, and three assists in a 93-88 victory. He would go on to collect his sixth and final Finals MVP award, two more than anyone else in NBA history, nine days later.

The wildly popular Last Dance documentary, released in 2020, was centred around that 1997-98 Bulls season.

"The record-setting price achieved for the related Michael Jordan jersey is yet another corroborative result as to the significance of Jordan within the industry and popular culture. This remarkable garment bore witness to one of Jordan's most hallowed NBA Finals appearances as part of his 'Last Dance' season to complete his illustrious career," David Hunt, president of Hunt Auctions, said in a statement.

"While Michael Jordan's importance within the sports memorabilia marketplace has long been established, it has now escalated to an elite asset class more typically reserved for iconic works of art."

The previous record for a basketball memorabilia item was $US12.26 million for the home jersey worn by Jordan in Game 3 of the 1998 Finals, which was sold via auction in September.

Reuters

World.title: European Tour gives LIV golfers ultimatum and shuts door on playing both
World.content:
The European Tour has delivered an ultimatum to players contemplating the new version of LIV Golf, saying anyone who joins will not be allowed to remain a tour member.

"Players need to make a choice," Guy Kinnings, chief executive of the European Tour, said in a statement yesterday first reported by the BBC.

The tour previously let LIV players keep their European membership as long as they paid fines for playing LIV events that conflicted with the tour.

LIV Golf files for bankruptcy LIV Golf files for bankruptcy, flagging a restructure with a massive loan from the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia.

Australian golfers Cameron Smith, Lucas Herbert, Elvius Smylie and Marc Leishman all played in the LIV league in 2026.

It extended an olive branch earlier this year to nine players, allowing them to play LIV events without sanctions provided they settled all previous fines and agreed to add European Tour events to their 2026 schedules.

Kinnings delivered a much stronger message — us or them — as LIV tries to emerge from bankruptcy after Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund cut off financial support.

LIV has up to $300 million from BC Partners as it leans into a 10-tournament season focusing on team competition and players owning equity in LIV 2.0. Players have until October 25 to decide whether to stick with LIV, which could determine whether the beleaguered circuit can move forward out of bankruptcy.

The European Tour, however, is requiring anyone seeking to join to disclose where they intend to play in 2027. The tour said it would terminate membership if the disclosures prove false.

"As we have said for many years, we have rules and regulations which are there to protect our tour and which our members must all abide by," Kinnings said. "Players who are not willing to comply with our rules and regulations should not be seeking to join our tour."

Players must be European Tour members to compete in the Ryder Cup next September, adding pressure to the likes of Tyrrell Hatton of England, Tom McKibbin of Northern Ireland, Adrian Meronk of Poland and Thomas Detry of Belgium.

A lawyer for Jon Rahm said last week in a bankruptcy hearing for LIV that the former number one wanted to terminate his LIV contract. The question for Rahm, a two-time major champion, is how he works his way back to the PGA Tour.

Sergio Garcia also asked to end his LIV contract, and David Puig of Spain has indicated he is ready to take on a European Tour schedule.

The European Tour is negotiating a renewed alliance with the PGA Tour, which involves commercial opportunities and a path for the 10 leading players on the Race to Dubai to get PGA Tour cards.

Patrick Reed and Eugenio Chacarra, who both previously played for LIV Golf, are a lock to earn PGA Tour cards this year off the European Tour points list. Bernd Wiesberger of Austria, another player who signed early with LIV, also has a chance at a tour card.

The plan of LIV 2.0 is to have such a streamlined schedule to allow players to compete elsewhere. But the PGA Tour bans LIV players for at least one year dating to their last LIV appearance, and now the European tour is demanding them to pick a tour.

AP

Tech.content:
We discovered a sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices. We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier. We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI’s investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work.

Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states, and this case is an example of how AI can help address these sophisticated security threats.

Tech.title: Shopify opens its catalog up to more AI agents
Tech.content:
is features writer with five years of experience covering the companies that shape technology and the people who use their tools.

More AI agents will soon be able to browse and purchase from Shopify listings, marking an expansion of the company’s agentic commerce ambitions.

Shopify announced Tuesday it will let shoppers configure their AI agents to purchase products on their behalf, giving more agents access to over a billion listings in Shopify’s catalog. (The catalog consists of both items on and off Shopify storefronts.) In September, Shopify announced it was partnering with Meta to allow its Muse agent to browse and purchase items on a human’s behalf; now, shoppers can use any agent without a partnership integration.

To set up the feature, customers connect an agent with their account on Shop, a Shopify-owned platform that consolidates orders, tracks packages, and recommends products. Like the Muse partnership, customers use the one-click Shop Pay feature to check out within the conversation with the agent. Orders placed through the agent are funneled back to the Shop app. Shopify is marketing the feature as a “personal shopper” that humans can give rules to, like setting budget guardrails or only displaying products with fast shipping. Buyers must approve each purchase.

E-commerce has become one of the battlegrounds in the era of AI — it’s no coincidence that many demos of agentic tools end with a transaction, whether it’s buying clothing, booking a flight, or ordering takeout on a human’s behalf. The tech industry, including big commerce players like Google and Amazon, are investing in AI-driven shopping tools where the end goal is an “agent” purchasing things for a human user. It’s also the basis of an ongoing fight between Amazon and AI companies like Perplexity — and more recently, Meta’s Muse — over whether agents should be able to shop on a customer’s behalf.

Tech.title: Xbox is officially embracing the chaos of AI-powered game ports
Tech.content:
Team,

The first video games emerged some 75 years ago. In the time since, there have been booms and busts, but every year there are more great games to play, more devices to play them, and best of all, more people than ever playing. That growth helped make XBOX what it is today, and we’ve helped shape the industry in return, from bringing hard drives to consoles and online gaming through Xbox Live to Game Pass and cloud gaming, alongside franchises that have brought millions of people together.

In recent weeks, we’ve seen games rapidly decompiled and rebuilt to run on hardware they were never originally designed to support. Windows PC builds have been translated to run on Apple Silicon or ported to run inside a browser through WebAssembly and WebGPU, the latter now approaching 90% global browser support. Perhaps more surprisingly, we’ve seen many of the biggest games in the world have been remixed into the source code of another.

These experiments challenge long-held assumptions about our industry: the tether between software and hardware, the boundary between creation and play, and how people discover and experience games. While it is hard to predict the future of gaming, it is easy to see the possibilities in making great games easier to access, giving old games new life and allowing more players to become creators and co-creators. These are unmistakably good outcomes for players, even when (and sometimes because) they challenge our existing business models. To explore these possibilities, I’ve asked Scott to stand-up XBOX LABS, a small group of game makers, engineers and scientists whose job is to turn emerging ideas into things our players and developers can experience. We’ll build in the open, learn from what people do, and measure success by whether more people are playing and creating.

I think XBOX has an important role to play here. Coding became the first major workload for agents because they can write, run, and test software. Games share many of those same properties, and people spend more than 72 billion hours a year playing XBOX games, roughly five times the estimated time spent writing code worldwide. We’ve spent 25 years learning how to make great games, and I want our game makers to help shape what these new technologies make possible. As we learn, we’ll share the tools we build with developers across the industry, just as we always have.

Our priorities aren’t changing. We remain committed to the 4Cs, to making great games, to our hardware and to being responsible stewards of IP and the communities built around it. LABS gives us a way to explore new technology without abandoning the work already underway.

Asha
